## XIII. Of the Parting of the Rites

Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich, chosen Keeper, found in the Hall's roll that more than half the Keepers of the age had come from his own house, and had that fact struck from the preface. An unstruck copy survives. He also had the Hall list every rite that burned the handful or claimed the vein, so the council would know what it was keeping. The list named the Hall's own rite, the old ancestor-keeping, the dawn-hawk, the wood-watchers, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath and both schools of the stag.

The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell sent back the Hall's cutter unheard, saying the measure was the hawk's and the hawk was not the Keeper's: the first rite to refuse the Hall's check outright. The wolf-sworn built a hall round their stone at Caol leathan and swore oaths there that were no longer guards' oaths. One god, they said, watches the whole island as the guard watches the road. At the western Seann Skell the sting-oath became a creed: one power stings the liar wherever he is, and the scorpion is only its sign. It was the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one. Seann Vell, below Cuan shean, carved a yellow stone scorpion for worship. The wood-watchers stopped bringing disputes to the Hall and judged them under the trees. They held that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same two.

By 11 an Gearran 144 BDE the common ancestor of the nine faiths had visibly split: one folk practice had become the threads later ages would name, and Rodian belief was no longer one thing. The council, which had sat by hearth and house, began to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complained that he kept the flame for eight peoples, each of which thought itself the only keeper.

Two customs stayed outside the companies. Pilgrims of every rite still walked to Allt an Àigh at the right quarter of the moon, the one custom the Hall's list set under no company, and in one season pilgrims of four rites repaved the path from Caol shean together. And the keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh ruled that the sick of every rite should be bathed without being asked which. It was the last ruling of the age that every company accepted, and it came from the one office the Hall had made that had nothing to do with the ore.

## XIV. Of the Last Quiet Years and the Close of the Age

The last generations of the age live in the provincial rolls, which care about what was made and what was owed. The eastern Cnoc dhìreach wove the carriers' heavy cloth and Muileann bhàn dyed it a pale hill-blue; the Keepers wore theirs undyed, and said so. A flood at Àth chiar took six townsfolk, but the granary on its rise fed the town through the winter. The south-eastern Seann Vell grew into a city on fish and silver and built the island's first stone quay. The beacon at Tobar dhearg was raised on a stone tower. At Muileann naomh a mill and a shrine shared a roof, and the Keeper's cutter found the measure kept and the flour good. Dùn thais built the stag's first temple of stone. Baile Mòr mhòr sent a member to the council, and the Four Houses seated him at the foot of the hall.

When drought burned the pastures of Achadh shean, grain came from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the rolls at Baile chaol record it repaid measure by measure, the first such debt repaid in full. At Baile ruadh a timber watch-tower was manned against island raiders, the only tower of war the age built. At Inis chrom the families of the drowned set an empty place for each of the lost at a yearly feast on the shore, and the custom spread north to Seann Warr. At Cnoc naomh the ancestors were still kept in the old way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag, and the Hall's list counted the old reverence as one company among the others.

Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, received the stone cup from the Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich at Dùn ìseal, as Gilleasbuig Mòr had. Hers is the last name in the king-list of the Holy Age. At the close of the age the Keepers' roll held one hundred and forty names from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list more than ninety from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law had not changed by a word since Fionnlagh Dall's cup, and the cup still stood on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach.

Later chroniclers look back on these years with some unease. The years about 1 an Cèitean 50 BDE belong to the last age of even population, the final stretch of Rodian history in which no family held meaningfully more years of life than any other. Keepers aged at the same pace as carriers, and every ruler died in their time. No one then thought of this as something that could be lost, so no one recorded it as a blessing. It is recorded here only because the record knows what came after.

The next age began at sea, which this one had never wished to cross. Crews from the western harbours brought word of a land across open water, empty of anyone like the Ròdaich, and none of them claimed to have been first. The report would be heard in the red hall at Cathair dhearg, and it would put to the Ròdaich a question the Keepers had never had to answer: who would choose to go. The Holy Age had counted every hand that held the right to the flame. The next would count those willing to leave it. That is the Age of Sundering, An Aois Scaraidh, and it is told in the book that follows.


# The Third Book: An Aois Scaraidh, the Age of Sundering

> *Roghnaich iadsan, agus dh'fhuirich sinne.*
> They chose, and we stayed.
>
> — written in the margin of the custody-book at Muileann dhearg, in a hand the keepers have never identified

## I. Of the Land Across the Water

The Third Age begins with a rumour, and the chroniclers of Rodos have never been able to do better than that. On 6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE word came back to the island of a land across open water, a coast unpeopled by anyone who resembled the Ròdaich. Who brought that word first, in what boat, after how many days at sea, no record says. The kings kept their hall at Cathair dhearg, the custodians kept the vein under the mountain, and the Small-Burning Law measured out the black ore hearth by hearth as it had since the early centuries of the Holy Age. Into that order came a story about a shore.

By the winter the story had reached the capital. In the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg three crews from the western harbours told it, one after another, and none of them claimed to have been first. The queen's scribe took down all three accounts and noted at the foot of them that they agreed on the coast and on nothing else. It is a fair summary of most of what Rodos has ever known about the land beyond.

What followed is called the Choosing, and the later chronicles call it a vote. Whether it was one, or a word laid over something older and looser, no one who wrote it down was there to see. All the accounts agree on one thing. Those who went, went because they wished to. No lots were drawn, and no conscription is recorded. The Choosing is remembered on 8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE, though it was a season of choosing more than a day, and the next thing the record shows is how unsettled it was.

At Seann Skell, the western port that would give the age its harbour, the scribes opened a roll for those who meant to go. They entered it by household and not by name, as though going were something a family did together or not at all. The roll was kept on boards in the harbour-house, and a later hand notes that entries were struck out as often as they were added.

The crown decided for no one. In the autumn of 38 BDE Queen Beathag declared that she would neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back. The custody-book gives her words only in substance; the harbour songs of Seann Skell, younger and less careful, give them like this:

> *Cha chuir mi duine thairis, agus cha chùm mi duine air ais.*
> I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back.

Within that same season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, entered her own household on the roll at Seann Skell. The record makes no comment. Later chroniclers have made a great many, none of them evidence.

Up at the vein-house above Muileann dhearg, heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal, the custodians counted what the Choosing would cost them. They reckoned which of the households holding the customary right to burn the ore had entered the roll, and put it at nearly one household in five. The custody-book adds that the reckoning was made twice, because the first figure was not believed. The people going were fishers and farmers and the queen's own sister, and many of them were also people whose hands the vein had answered.

## II. Of the Building of the Ships

The island had no ships fit for the crossing. The craft of Rodos until then were sewn-plank coasters that never slept out of sight of land. A fleet had to be made for the first time in Rodian memory, and the making took the better part of a generation.

At the centre of it was the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor. In 35 BDE, on the strand below Seann Skell, he laid down the first deep-keeled hull ever built on Rodos.

The keels came from the oak grove that had given Doire fhionn its name. It was felled and carried down to the coast by ox-sled, and it never regrew, and the village kept a name it no longer had a reason for.

Alasdair Saor bound the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into a single fellowship, each apprentice bound for seven years in the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights. The fleet cost lives before it sailed. In 34 BDE the first finished hull was taken out past Inis àrsaidh to be tried in open water, and it foundered in a following sea, and eleven were drowned. Alasdair changed the setting of the keel, and every later hull was built to the changed pattern. What the change was, the record does not say. Some three centuries later nobody on the island could remember it.

The rest of Rodos went to work with him. Cuan shean laid out long rope-walks along its harbour front and turned its hemp fields over wholly to cordage. Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh was asked for a length of close-woven sail-cloth, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat; the tallies survive, and how many households paid does not. On the eastern coast the old steersmen of Cuan ruadh, the only sailors on the island who had ever kept a course by night, taught the fleet's pilots to hold a heading by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.

In 22 BDE the households on the roll met at Seann Skell and chose their own leaders: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein. The custody-book records the choice and nothing of how it was made. Seven years later the vein-house ruled on whether departing custodians might carry the ore. Each ship might take one sealed measure, no more than a single household might burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only text in the custody-book addressed to people who were leaving, and it gives no blessing. A later custodian wrote a couplet beside it, which is still said at the measured burning in some of the old houses:

> *Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir,*
> *is an seann teallach fhathast blàth.*
> A handful for the new hearth,
> and the old hearth still warm.

Masons came from the capital to lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls could lie alongside at low water. No one then knew that the later rite would be held on those stones.

In 2 BDE, with the Diosal little more than a year off, the whole enterprise nearly came apart over grain: how much of the island's stored harvest might the departing ships take? The chronicle says the dispute was resolved within a season, and that how it was resolved is unrecorded. One piece of it survives. At Àth shean, while the quarrel was still open, the reeve of the granaries, Tormod mac Coinnich, barred the store-houses and set a watch on them until the matter was settled. Tormod is not recorded as holding office afterward. When it was settled, a tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counted forty-one grain barges passing down Abhainn dhomhain for the fleet.

By the spring of that year the fleet lay complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives it as nineteen hulls. A later hand in the margin corrects this to twenty-one, and no one since has been able to settle which is right.

## III. Of the Sunwise Turn

On the last night before the sailing every house along the Seann Skell waterfront set a lamp on its sill and kept it burning until morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering recorded as a custom.

On 19 an Giblean 1 DE the volunteers departed.

The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbour. There is no account of the crowd, or the weather, or who wept. The harbour scribe gives one thing only. Before making for open water the fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, *diosal*, for luck, and the watchers on the quay counted the hulls as they passed. The record ends at the harbour mouth.

The years of Rodos are counted from that turn, though not at once. In 5 DE Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, began to number the years from the sunwise turn and called them the years of the Diosal. The crown's scribes took up his count only a generation later. So an island that had counted by kings and harvests began, in one clerk's hand, to count by an absence.

In the same year a report of the fleet reached Seann Skell. The custody-book does not say how or by whom it came, only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water and missing its end.

What that report, or whatever fragments followed it, describes is two landfalls: two separate coasts reached, and not one. The chroniclers have read this as the seed of two later peoples rather than one, and the keepers set it down the same way, as a reading. Which hulls went to which coast, and whether the fleet parted by storm or quarrel or plan, is not known. When Beathag nic Thòmais of Muileann chaol found three copies of the landfall report sixteen centuries later, they differed in the order of the coasts and in the number of hulls. She wrote all three out side by side and did not choose between them, and the library has followed her ever since.

In 7 DE Queen Beathag removed her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Rodos. The act is entered without comment, between a grain ruling and the repair of a bridge. It is the last time the crown of Rodos wrote Mòrag's name, and it wrote it in the ordinary way.

What happened across the water after that, the island learned in pieces if it learned it at all. The chronicle calls it the thinning. Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing had required faded across the departed's own children, and by the third generation abroad nothing remained that Rodos would recognize. How the island came to know even this much the library cannot say.

Then comes the second silence. Some twelve years after the thinning is first entered, there was a rumour of a second and smaller crossing: fewer ships, and no surviving record of where they meant to go. Nothing that survives confirms it or denies it, and the keepers enter it and let it stand.

## IV. Of the White Sorrow and the Empty Harbour

In 14 DE the vein-house counted again the households that held the right to the ore, and set the loss down as one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid wrote that the vein itself answered no differently for those who stayed. It has been argued over ever since. Donnchadh did not say whether he meant it as comfort or complaint.

The next year Rodos made a rite for the departed, which the chronicle calls the Mourning Custom. It was not quite grief and not quite celebration. Queen Beathag kept it first for her sister, in undyed wool, with one place set empty at a meal that was neither feast nor fast. The court called it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and by the next generation it was kept in every harbour town on the island. It would be taken up again, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age, and that belongs to its own book.

The year after, the island reshaped itself around what was left. With part of the ore-bonded people gone, the custodian class became smaller and more concentrated, and that is the shape every later aristocracy of Rodos inherits. In 16 DE the remaining custodian households were regrouped into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. The keepers ask the reader to mark that list. It is the first division in the record to treat the right to the ore as something inherited by house rather than earned by apprenticeship.

Queen Beathag died at Cathair dhearg in the summer of that year, the last ruler of Rodos to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim was crowned in the same hall.

Then came the long work of getting used to it. At Seann Skell a ceremony grew up around the dock the ships had left from, the empty-harbour rite, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can now date precisely. By 25 DE the harbour-master recorded his berths at half their former use, because the fishing households that had crewed the fleet were gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean laid off hands for the first time. On the north-west coast the fishers of Ceann mhòr kept a watch from the headland for returning sails, by household in turn. It lapsed within a generation, and no sail is recorded.

By 28 DE Seann Skell had found a way to go on trading. The dock the ships had left from was given a new name so that ordinary trade could keep using the old one without the association. The chronicle calls it an act of managed forgetting. In the harbour rolls the departure berth became Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn, and the name Cidhe an Iar passed to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, where within a few years the fishers used it without a thought.

The language kept what the harbour put away. From 28 DE the custody-book uses the verb *roghnaich*, to choose, with no object at all, meaning to have chosen the crossing, and the next century's scribes use it so without explaining it. By that same year a generation had grown up that had never seen the harbour with those ships in it. For them the departure was no longer an event but a fact of history. A saying of the western shore claims to come from about this time:

> *Is fhada an cuan, is goirid a' chuimhne.*
> Long is the sea, and short is memory.

Alasdair Saor died at Seann Skell at the end of that summer. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh. Seventeen years later his fellowship quietly dissolved, since no one wanted ocean-going hulls any more, and its techniques were half forgotten by the time anyone thought to need them again. Its patterns and keel-moulds were broken up and burned as firewood in a hard season. The harbour-master noted the loss of the shed and said nothing of what had been in it.

In 70 DE the seven houses drew lots at the vein-house for the galleries each would keep, and the lot-stones were shown to visitors at Muileann dhearg for centuries after. Doire fhionn, its oaks gone to the fleet, began to coppice its woods, and the law spread to every shire with a *doire* in its name.

At Seann Skell the waterfront kept the night of lamps every year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite. Children were told the lamps were for ships coming home, and the priests did not correct them. The children's verse is still known on the west coast:

> *Solas air an uinneig,*
> *solas gus an tig iad dhachaigh.*
> A light on the window,
> a light till they come home.

Donnchadh mac Thormoid died at Muileann dhearg in 70 DE. His last entry is a list of the ore burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first. Sixteen years later, in 86 DE, King Raghnall died after a long and uneventful reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill was crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line. After the shaking of its first years the age seems to have wanted no more than that.

## V. Of Hawks and Wolves, and the Firlot of Cathair dhearg

The chroniclers call the centuries that followed the quiet ones, and they were quiet the way a well-kept house is quiet: much was going on, and most of it was small. The silver of Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, was worked into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses, and the smiths' fellowship of the seam closed its methods within four families. Inis mhòr built coasting barges for the grain, sewn-plank boats of the old kind that never slept out of sight of land. The road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burned to its footings and was rebuilt in stone by its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, and the account of her rebuilding mentions the jugged buffalo it was already known for.

Beathag's line ended in 141 DE, when King Ìomhar died with no living child. The heads of the seven houses were summoned to the capital, and in 143 DE they chose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair. He was the first king in the record crowned by decision of the custodian houses and not by descent. His son Fearchar Donn followed him without dispute.

The faiths began to divide. In 190 DE at Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age was still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair taught that the vein was Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, who must be fed the measured handful and no more: a hawk overfed will not hunt, and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gathered the old rite into the first house of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig, and her pupils founded a second at Ros gheal. After her death her sayings were written down as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth, and there are more of these than of the rest. The first in the book is one he heard:

> *Beathaich an seabhag, ach na sàsaich e.*
> Feed the hawk, but do not glut him.

In 222 DE Clann Ìomhair walled Dùn dhearg in stone, the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house and not the crown. That year too Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father, fixed a single measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket, and sent firlots of oak bound with iron to every shire seat. Later she set a tally-house in every royal granary, where each exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour was cut on paired sticks. It was the first island-wide account of trade, and it ran entirely without coin. She reigned more than half a century, and her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill followed her in 285 DE.

It was a good time to be a carter. The herders near Imrich nam Pantar began clearing the panther roads on the days the great cats crossed, which was the first thing the southern shires agreed on in writing. An Leòmhann Buidhe on the northern mining road served fried olives and fire water to the ore-carters, and its keeper was fined for watering the fire water. Ros fhionn laid out salt pans on its flats, and its salt, carried inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn, became the common measure of value in the north-east.

Not everything was quiet. In 275 DE Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a teacher of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, founded a house of disputation at Dùn thais, where the school's old question, why the vein answers some hands and not others, was argued by rule. Ten years later Coinneach asked in open disputation whether the hands that went with the fleet had been the ones the vein answered best, and whether it now answered fewer. The seven houses forbade the question at their tables. The record notes that it was the first time they forbade a question rather than an act.

The skills of the fleet were already going. In 305 DE a merchant of Inis àrsaidh paid for a deep-keeled hull, but the wrights could not remember how Alasdair Saor's keels were scarfed, and it listed so badly at launch that it was broken up for timber.

Aonghas mac Uisdein, crowned in 355 DE, was the first king to learn his letters as a child, and in his reign two more faiths came. In 370 DE Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone stood, gave the one god of the wolf-sworn a name, Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, who keeps the island as a wolf keeps its range. When the Hawk and the Wolf both claimed the harbour shrine at Caol leathan, the king's reeve divided its days between them as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the arrangement held. In 402 DE Aonghas himself took up the wood-watchers' teaching of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn, that light and dark are two powers in balance and the vein belongs to both. The court followed him, and Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh became the faith of Cathair dhearg.

In 445 DE Eilidh nic Iain of Doire chiar, called Eilidh Dhubh, revived the Holy Age's rival teaching that the vein answers effort and not birth, and her tracts were read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east. The vein-house ordered every copy brought to Muileann dhearg and burned, and some hundred were surrendered. Eilidh was not punished, and she died at Doire chiar still teaching.

Aonghas died that winter and was the first king buried by the rite of the Unicorn. His son Iain reigned briefly, and Iain's son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, was sworn to without dispute. The ox-teams of the mountain now waited out the snow at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, whose keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, built them a second byre and kept a book of the teams that lodged.

## VI. Of the War of the Three Claimants

In 495 DE both sons of King Tormod Bàn were drowned when a ferry overturned crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king had no other child. He died at Cathair dhearg thirteen years later without naming an heir, and three claims were laid before the houses at once. Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais was the late king's niece. Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain was his half-brother. Raghnall Ruadh was head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among them, and in 513 DE the War of the Three Claimants began.

The keepers have wondered how so ordinary a cause led to so long a war. Perhaps, having held the ore by inheritance for five hundred years, each house had come to think of the crown as something that could be inherited too.

Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, shut its gates to all three and declared for none. It was besieged twice and taken by neither. At the ford of Àth shean, the northern town of that name and not the granary town, Dùghall Garbh's host broke Raghnall Ruadh's, and the custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford. Raghnall's men burned Doire mhin and its granary as they retreated, and the villagers wintered at Cathair mhòr on the charity of the Unicorn's priests. Catrìona besieged Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and took it after forty days, when its wells were poisoned by the dead of the siege lines, and she let the garrison go free on their oath.

On 24 am Faoilleach 519 DE Raghnall Ruadh did what Rodos remembers him for. Holding the vein-house, he refused the measured handful to every hearth and temple in the shires that stood against him. Hearths lit with the ore for generations went cold. For as long as the Small-Burning Law had existed it had measured the ore out, and this was the first time it was used to hold the ore back. The chronicle says the act turned more people against him than any battle. A verse from the cold shires survives, unsigned:

> *Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine.*
> We did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire.

Catrìona and Dùghall joined their hosts and met Raghnall below Muileann chrom on 14 am Faoilleach 521 DE. Raghnall was killed on the field, and the next day his own custodians opened the vein-house. Dùghall died of his wounds at Baile Mòr dhomhain in 522 DE, and his followers went over to Catrìona without another fight. She was crowned at Cathair dhearg in 523 DE, Catrìona Bhuadhach, and the war was over after about ten years.

Three years later she did what she is remembered for. With the vein-house she fixed it in law that no claimant, house or king might withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. This was the ruling of the hearth, the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves. She granted Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and tolls in memory of its standing aside, and had the grant cut over the landward gate. When she died in 565 DE the houses swore to her son Lachlann mac Iain in a single day, and the record remarks on it.

In 585 DE Seònaid nic Coinnich, a clerk of the late queen's household, wrote the war's history from the custody-book and from the testimony of those who had fought. It is the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as a single narrative rather than as entries, and every later history of the island descends from it, this one included. That same year a spotted fever killed some three hundred at Inis chrom. The Wolf's preachers nursed the sick, and many of them died of it, and the town was the Wolf's for good after that.

## VII. Of the Scorpion, and the Crown Joined to the Vein

The record calls Lachlann's reign quiet, and means it as praise. His daughter Anna followed him in 615 DE.

In 615 DE, at Seann Skell of all places, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age had first called itself the only true one, a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaimed its one power as Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion. He taught that Cnut had closed the western sea behind the fleet and that it must not be tried again. His hearers were the first congregation of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe, and the teaching went down the west coast with the fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers, whose walks had been laid out for the fleet, were among the first converts. In 655 DE the Scorpion's priests at Ros bheag ruled that no boat of the faithful might go beyond sight of the headlands. The rule was kept on the west coast for centuries, and the steering of boats by the stars, already half lost, was lost there entirely. Of all the faiths of Rodos, the keepers have been least easy with the Scorpion. It is the only one whose teaching rests on the Sundering, and what it teaches is that the island must never again do what the fleet did.

In 700 DE the vein-house and the crown's scribes found that their counts of years since the Setting-Out disagreed. They settled the difference by agreement, and fixed by the same agreement the day of the empty-harbour rite, which each count had placed differently. Later scribes stopped pretending it had been fixed by evidence. Every year in this book rests on that compromise between two offices, and the keepers think the reader should know it.

Eilidh Bhàn, fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, was crowned in 730 DE, and the record of her long reign is almost all harvests. The north-west did not share in them. From 745 DE boats working out of the small islands off that coast took fish and grain from the coasting traders. The sea-thieves were Ròdaich of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names. Baile chrom reported half its houses empty, and the crown remitted its grain dues. In 762 DE a force sent by Eilidh Bhàn landed on Eilean dhubh and burned the thieves' boats on the strand, and their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, was hanged at Cathair dhearg. It did not save the coast. In 780 DE a run of failed harvests brought a dearth to the north-west shore that the shared-meal custom could not carry. Families left for the interior and the east, and the north-west stayed thinly held until the age ended.

In 790 DE the queen's scribes recopied the king-list from its oldest surviving roll and added the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet, and this book keeps that order. Eilidh Bhàn died childless twelve years later, and the seven houses met to choose, this time at the vein-house and not at the capital. They named Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom, and he kept the mastery of the vein-house together with the crown. In 820 DE his reeves wrote into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. From then on the heads of the seven houses sat as the king's council, and the custodian class and the court were one body. What Raghnall Ruadh had seized in war, his descendant now held by law. The ruling of the hearth still bound the custodians, but the custodians were now the crown. Dòmhnall Ruadh was buried at Muileann dhearg and not at the capital.

The Hawk split in 850 DE over whether Mòd's measure could ever be raised. Those who held it fixed kept the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag. Those who said a larger flock might be fed a larger handful were called the Fed Hawk, and they settled at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western port of that name. In 880 DE they petitioned the council to raise the handful by a quarter for the northern hearths. The council refused. It was the first recorded request to change the Small-Burning Law, and the custody-book records their teaching as an error, at length.

The mountain took its own toll. In 890 DE a second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brought down a gallery of the vein and killed fourteen labourers, and the vein-house closed it and set a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names. The last shepherds left the high pastures of Doire uaine. They said it was for the grazing, and every one of them who was asked also mentioned the Marbh-bheò.

Two findings of these years sit uneasily in the record. In 940 DE quarrymen north of the capital broke into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings, long lost, and found a stair cut in the rock going down past the light of their lamps. The custodians had the entrance walled up. The one quarryman who went down is not recorded as saying what he saw. Twenty years later Ailean mac Dhùghaill of the deer school measured the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and wrote that its altar faced the central mountains and not the sea, and he declined to guess who had set it so. By 972 DE he had finished his tables of the three old ruins and concluded that he could not say whether one people had built all three. His tables are the reason later scholars could not say either. He had measured too carefully to leave any room for guessing.

Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill was crowned in 980 DE, the first ruler whose household accounts survive whole. On 15 an Dùbhlachd 1000 DE the vein-house marked the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the ore on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, with the queen present. The record says the flame burned the colour of the vein and that the crowd went home without a word.

## VIII. Of Things Forgotten, and the Brothers' War

In its eleventh century the island began, visibly, to lose its skills. The dyers of Baile ghorm had made a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own, and it was the feast-day dress of the seven houses. In 1100 DE the last dyer who knew the mordant died without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers, and the blue that came after was the ordinary blue of the rest of the island.

A sickness that closed the throat, the swallowing cough, broke out at Muileann dhomhain in 1040 DE and killed nearly a third of the town. When it reached Seann Bhral the townsfolk shut their own harbour and kept the shared-meal custom by leaving food at the gate. Queen Beathag Fhionn, daughter of Mòrag Ruadh, closed the coast road between the two towns and set reeves at the fords, and the cough went no further west. Her son Ailean followed her, the first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.

Ros fhionn's harbour silted behind a shifting bar, and its salt-masters moved their trade to Caol gharbh. The carts stopped crossing Drochaid Ros fhionn, and the bridge-keeper's office was abolished. Fishers of the thinned north-west reported the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, close enough to foul their nets, and the few boats left there drew further in.

In 1170 DE Raghnall mac Chaluim of the deer school at Dùn thais set out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses lived on average a few years longer than the tenants of their lands, and asked whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The record notes the finding with unease and without an answer. The council forbade the copying of the table and closed the house at Dùn thais for a generation. Raghnall's own copy went into the vein-house and was entered in its inventory.

In 1227 DE King Ailean mac Raghnaill died leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, each of whom had been told he was the heir. Four years later Alasdair Bàn's men seized Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar took it back. The houses divided four to three, and the Brothers' War, Cogadh nam Bràithrean, took its name from that battle. Alasdair's ships burned the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire took the rope stores and the granary, and the town had to beg its bread from Cathair mhòr. In 1235 DE Iain Ciar beat Alasdair below Muileann ghlas, took him alive and let his captains go home. The field comes into the record again two ages later.

The brothers made peace in 1237 DE at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands, the road-house where the ox-teams waited out the snow. Alasdair gave up his claim for the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. He kept the peace he had made and died there. Iain Ciar was crowned. Because he had seen Ceann mhin beg for bread, he ordered every shire seat to keep a year's grain against the next war. The law was kept while he lived and lapsed within a few years of his death, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand. His clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh wrote the account of the war. It praises the king at every turn and is the only account that survives, which later readers have found inconvenient.

The road-houses come back into the record here, and the keepers are glad of them. In 1280 DE the crown chartered the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit and made their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers met once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts. At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the high northern road a party of reeves was snowed in for a whole season and lived on pickled spinach and fire milk. Their complaint to the charter-roll is recorded in full.

In 1320 DE Seumas mac Iain of Seann Skell tried to rebuild a deep-keeled hull from what was still remembered of the Sundering fellowship's lore on the strand. It filled and sank at its launch, and the Scorpion's priests preached on it for a year. Twenty years later Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a folk-collector of the royal household, took down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words meant nothing to anyone who sang it. It is the only record of the fleet's techniques that survives in any form. Its first lines can still be understood:

> *Druim fon aisne, aisne fon chlàr,*
> *clàr ri clàr is an cuan fodhpa.*
> Keel under rib, rib under plank,
> plank to plank and the sea beneath them.

After that the song goes on in words no one can read. The rope-makers who kept it were of the Scorpion by then, and sang it anyway.

## IX. Of the Last Lamps

The last four centuries of the age are the longest stretch in the record, and they have the least to tell. The keepers will not pretend otherwise.

The Wolf divided over whether Clach might be prayed to for the dead, and its two houses, at Inis thais and Baile gheal, were not reconciled in this age. Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill was crowned in 1390 DE, the first queen in more than three centuries. The record notes that she was small, and that no one said so twice. In 1410 DE she had the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth in her presence, the first renewal of that oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swore last.

More was forgotten. The potters of Muileann gheal made a grey-green glaze no other kiln could match, and the custodian houses bought it for their tables. The secret stayed in one family, and in 1470 DE the last of them died without passing it on. The smiths of Dùn dhearg lost the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded, and later Dùn dhearg blades were ordinary. In the east, charcoal-burners found again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tellings, with the same cut stair as the first. The custodians walled it up as well, and the scribe cross-referenced the two entries.

At Àth shean the granary found that its firlot had worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and had been for generations. The reeve corrected the accounts as far back as anyone could reckon.

Sìleas Òg, named for the queen of the firlot, was crowned in 1490 DE, the first ruler to visit every shire seat. She ordered a new count of the households holding the right to the ore. It was smaller than any before it, because the right had narrowed into fewer and larger households, and she had it entered without comment. In 1520 DE Clann Choinnich asked leave to burn the ore beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, arguing that it burned hotter than charcoal. The council refused. It was the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship. The keepers know where that request leads in the next age, and here they only record it.

Ailean the Fourth had the shortest reign in the king-list. His sister Mòrag nic Ailein, who followed him, reigned forty years, and her entries record nothing but good harvests and the rite. In 1551 DE the priests of the Scorpion met in synod at Seann Skell, restated the rule of sight-of-land, and added a prayer to be said at the harbour mouth:

> *A Chnut, cùm an cuan dùinte.*
> Cnut, keep the sea shut.

The library that keeps this record begins in these years. In 1620 DE Beathag nic Thòmais, a mill-owner's widow of Muileann chaol, began buying old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them, and kept them in a loft over her mill. A mill in the same town soon began making paper from rags, the first on Rodos, and the custody-book was copied onto paper for the first time. Among her papers were the three copies of the landfall report. She died in 1660 DE and left the loft to the town on condition that nothing in it was burned. The town kept that condition and very little else of her wishes.

The crown sent a reeve to list the households of the north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr, and he counted fewer households than harbour berths. Tormod mac Ruairidh, crowned in 1670 DE, reigned for more than fifty years. In 1675 DE the Scorpion's priests at Seann Skell began saying their prayer to keep the sea shut on the same day as the empty-harbour rite, so that the two were kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side was pleased.

In 1710 DE a visiting scribe found the empty-harbour rite at Seann Skell kept by the harbour priests and a few old families, and wrote that no one there could say on which day the fleet had actually sailed. The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and reopened more than once since the table of years, opened again in 1720 DE on condition that the question of longer lives was not raised. The scholars accepted and argued about the vein instead.

Tormod's daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid, crowned in 1727 DE, made a progress round every shire seat. Her clerks wrote down the grievances of each shire, and she answered none of them in writing. On the eastern road An Taigh-òsta Grianach fed her company on pan-fried spinach and black wine, and its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, was excused her road dues for a year. It is the last warm entry of the age. In 1737 DE Clann Choinnich asked again to burn the ore for the silver smelt, this time with three of the seven houses behind it, and Gormshuil's council refused by one voice. The record gives the name of the member who changed his vote, and does not give his reason. In 1752 DE the vein-house counted the households of the right for the last time in this age. There were fewer than ever before, and they were larger, and three of the seven houses now held more than half the right between them.

In 1755 DE a worked timber came ashore at Ceann mhòr on the empty north-west coast. It was longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith on Rodos recognized. It was carried to Seann Skell and shown to the Scorpion's priests, and they burned it. The record does not say what was said over it.

By then fewer and fewer houses on the Seann Skell waterfront kept the night of lamps, and at last none did. An old woman set a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe recorded that it was she who kept it and not the town. On 17 an t-Sultain 1764 DE eleven people kept the empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail. The harbour scribe entered their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing else.

Clann Choinnich did not bring its silver petition again, because the member who had turned the vote had died. The petition lay in the vein-house unanswered, and the record of the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept. Eighteen centuries after a queen at Cathair dhearg said she would keep no one back, Rodos had kept the vein and kept the law, and had let go nearly everything else the fleet had meant: the keel, the stars, the far coast and all but eleven keepers of the rite. The houses were fewer and richer. The north-west was nearly empty. The prayer to keep the sea shut had been said for two hundred years, and no one had tried the sea. Then sails came in over that water from the far side, and they were not Rodian sails. The people under them had crossed the water the Rodians once crossed. Whether any of them came down from those who chose to go, no one on Rodos knew then and no one knows now. The Age of Strangers begins with their coming, and the next book tells it.


# The Fourth Book: An Aois Choigreach, the Age of Strangers

> *Thàinig na coigrich air an t-sàl, agus dh'fhàg iad an cnoc falamh.*
>
> The strangers came over the brine, and they left the hill empty.
>
> — a line sung in the camps, as the copyists at Muileann chaol set it down

*Here is told the history of Rodos from the Crossing to the Severance: the hundred and fifty years in which the island was ruled, first by leave and then without it, by people from over the western sea. It is drawn from the rolls of the custodians, most of which survive only in the copies kept in the cellars of Muileann chaol; from the letter-books of the humans' Administration, left behind when the Residency was emptied; from the daybooks of the beacon-keepers; and from the songs of the camps. Where these witnesses disagree, both are given. Where they are silent, this account is silent also.*

## Of the Three Ships and the Leave to Stay

The age begins with the Crossing, on 5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE, when the humans first made landfall on Rodos. The roll of Cuan shean, which is the fuller witness, does not enter their ships until the thirteenth of that month: three hulls out of the west riding at anchor off the town, the first of their size seen from any shore of the island since the fleet of the Sundering went out sunwise from the harbour and did not come back. Where the strangers were in the days between, the rolls do not say.

Their master was a captain whom the record calls Edmund Harrow. He came ashore without arms and with eleven men, and asked by signs for water. The custodians of Cuan shean gave it. They would give no more on their own word, for no custodian living had been asked such a thing, and they sent inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers were fed on the beach and not allowed beyond the dunes.

On 11 am Faoilleach 1781 DE the Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which had sat in the crown's place since the crown fell vacant at the close of the Age of Sundering, under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein, confirmed the strangers' leave to stay. The council roll records the vote as unanimous. A later hand has written in the margin that three custodians were absent. Who they were the margin does not say; but the chroniclers have kept the note, for it is the first of many places in the record of this age where what was written and what was so are not quite the same.

Soon after, the old sailors of Cuan shean began to say that the strangers had come in from the same quarter of the sea into which the Sundering fleet had sailed. The council forbade the remark in its hall. It was written down anyway, and it was never answered, and this account will not answer it either. Whether the humans are children of the departed, or of another people of those waters, or of no one the Ròdaich ever knew, is not known on Rodos.

The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdach scribe set the word down. From the first season the record calls it *an Tìr Thall*, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans; and so they are called in this history.

Then came the season of words. The humans' clerics and the custodians sat together to build a common vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed in that season has come down whole. The humans' cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept word-lists side by side. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's was lost, and only its first leaf is known, from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken ore. Her copyist noted a thing that the chroniclers have since set at the head of the whole age. The humans had a single word for the black ore of the vein, and it was the word for the fuel they burned at home. No Ròdais word in either list answered to it. And the humans did not ask for one.

## Of the Years of Fair Exchange

It must be set down plainly, because what came after has cast its shadow back over it, that the first years were good. The exchange was reciprocal. The island had been alone for eighteen centuries and lacked much that the humans had; the humans lacked much the island could spare. For a few years the arrangement looked as if it would last, and the chroniclers do not think those who trusted it fools.

The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour: iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper, against wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. Its first tally-book, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly across its first year. The smiths of Cathair dhearg learned in a single winter to temper the humans' bar-iron, and within a few seasons the old bronze hoes were melted down for bells. The salt-pans of Seann Warr sold to Pike by the barrel, the first Ròdach trade the humans came back asking for twice.

Harrow sailed west and came back with four ships instead of three, bringing carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island had. The surgeon, Jonas Tull, set the leg of a Cuan shean fisherman whom the town had given up for lame, and the custodian entered it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.

In 1784 DE the small port of Baile dhìreach, on the south-west coast, took Ròdaich and humans under one council of six, three of either people, with a founding compact written twice, once in each tongue: the only such compact on record in the age. It was chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook, and its harbour dues went half to the custodians and half to the humans' post. At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council entered the marriage in both its books. The custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, sent none. Later history did not repeat the experiment, and this book will come back to that marriage when it reaches the years in which the humans' law found a use for it.

In 1785 DE a human supply ship struck the western reefs in fog and nine of her crew were drowned; her master had been sailing, the letter-books complain, by a chart drawn from memory on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires. The human navigators asked for beacons, and the Ròdaich engineers agreed, not yet understanding what the request would enable. The navigator James Fenn and the Ròdach mason Torcall Clachair walked the coast together to choose sites for the new beacons, and marked the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives. Torcall's cairns, for the most part, do not.

## Of the Treaty in One Tongue, and the Company

In 1787 DE the terms of the humans' presence were set down in writing for the first time, in the humans' tongue only, and nobody on the Ròdach side is recorded objecting. The treaty was signed on 7 an Cèitean 1787 DE in the council hall at Cathair dhearg, by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians and by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner, for the Administration. Tormod could not read the tongue in which it was written. The record does not say who read it to him.

Pell built a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and called it the Residency, and from it the humans governed Rodos for a hundred and forty years. Harrow went back to the sea, and with Pike he formed a trading house licensed by the Administration, known on Rodos simply as the Company. Its charter gave it first refusal on "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield." Its first building of its own was a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, up the coast, to keep its tools from the harbour thieves. The chroniclers ask the reader to remember that warehouse.

The strangers' fever came ashore at Cuan shean with a crowded ship in 1788 DE and ran down the west coast. Ninety-one Ròdaich are recorded dead, and eleven humans. The custodians closed Cuan shean to ships for a season, and Pell protested in writing.

In 1789 DE the Company sent two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital, the country of Muileann chrom. They came back with sacks of broken ore and word that the black seam ran "further than can be walked in a day." The custodians demanded the ore back, to be laid in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returned half. The roll records the other half as "carried west."

In 1790 DE trade became arrangement. Under the first extraction contracts Ròdach labour began to mine the vein at a scale no reverent tradition had ever used. A crew of thirty opened the first pit at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil, and the chroniclers set beside it the plain fact that the custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all. The Company built an ore quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, and paid the fishermen for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight. Wren finished his grammar of Ròdais for the Mission, careful and accurate in most particulars, rendering the word for the custodians of the vein as "keepers of the coal." The Mission raised a chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain and hung in it the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians asked that it not be rung before the fishing fleet was out.

In 1793 DE one settlement refused to sign. It was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer survives only in the Company agent's paraphrase: that the hill was not hers to sell and not his to buy. Doire mhòr was not punished. The Company opened its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and ran its cart-road around Doire mhòr's fields rather than through them. The annals add two words: *for now*.

The first of the new beacons was finished in 1794 DE on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg, a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower and paid for by the Company; Torcall Clachair built it and Fenn set its lens.

In 1796 DE the humans brought in their coin, for convenience, they said, alongside the barter of the island: the mark and its hundred pence, struck at Ros dhomhain from metal shipped in from an Tìr Thall, with a ship on one face and nothing Rodian on either. At the capital the custodians' clerks began to keep two sets of books, and complained of it in both. Within ten years the mark was the only thing that would buy anything that came across the sea.

Wren spent a winter at Dùn thais among the masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. He asked them why the vein should be holy. They asked him why his fuel should be burned. Neither account records a winner.

The Harbour Articles, written like the treaty in the humans' tongue alone, fixed the dues at Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour, and this time two custodians refused to sign. The council granted the Administration upland grazing in the north-west around Muileann àrsaidh for human families who would not work in the pits. The grant was for grazing. The families built houses of stone.

Tormod mac Ailein died at Cathair dhearg in 1799 DE, and the council chose Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh to follow him, a man who had never met a human before the Crossing and had dealt with little else since. In 1800 DE Edmund Harrow's ship did not come home from the western crossing. The Company passed wholly to Pike, and the letter-books mourned Harrow as the man who found Rodos.

## Of the Lapse of the Law, and the First Steward

The Small-Burning Law had been kept since the Holy Age: that the vein be cut and burned sparingly, and that what the hill could give in a year be counted and not exceeded. The Age of Sundering ended with it still kept. Within a generation of the Crossing it was gone. No repeal is recorded. It stopped being enforced when it stopped being profitable to enforce. At Dùn dhearg the custodian Fionnghal nic Artair wrote to the council the only defence of the Law that survives. It argues that the Law had never been about the ore, but about the people who would become whatever the burning made them.

At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preached that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them, and his sermon was the first Ròdach text the Company's agents were told to confiscate. At Muileann chrom the Company burned ore by the cartload to drive its pumps, and when Coinneach Glas's council asked that the tally be observed, it received a copy of the Company's accounts instead.

Pell went home in 1803 DE and did not return. Henry Maddox came in his place, with instructions to double the yield and a letter promising him a share of it. In 1804 DE a gallery at Cnoc fhiadhaich, driven forward faster than any Ròdach crew would have chosen and without the timbering the crews had asked for, fell in and killed eleven. The custodians' roll names all eleven. The Company's report names none, and calls the gallery "unsound ground." A dry cough ran through the camps and killed thirty-eight, most of them boys who broke ore at the pit-mouth; the Mission's surgeon called it a winter complaint, and it lasted through the summer.

The second beacon was lit at Baile ìseal on the eastern shore, Torcall Clachair directing from a chair at the foot of the headland, too old now to climb. The Company founded a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, the first settlement on Rodos built for no purpose but the pit, and dammed the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash its ore. No order for that is recorded. Beathag Dhubh's people carried water by hand for two summers and then began to leave. In 1809 DE the hill villages lost their oats to rain that no one was home to cut ahead of, and the Company sold meal for marks, and the villages had few.

From 1810 DE the mountain was worked by the ton. The Company was rechartered in an Tìr Thall under a new name the Ròdaich never used, and its agents at Ros dhomhain outnumbered the Administration's clerks four to one. Ore barges loaded at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, where the old canoe landing was widened with cut stone and its shrine moved uphill; within a few seasons the green river ran black with slurry, and the salmon at its mouth failed, and the fishermen kept its name and used it bitterly. Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdach town drawn on paper before it was built. On the ore road the old carters' house at the halfway stage was rebuilt and kept its name, An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, and its keeper Seònaid Bhàn took marks and barter both, the only keeper on the road who would. Seann Toll was made an ore port, and its fishing boats moved to the next cove.

In 1815 DE a Ròdach was given authority over Ròdach miners, answerable to human masters, and the chroniclers count it the first fracture within Ròdach society itself. He was Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader since the first contract. The Company gave him its staff and a house with a slate roof, and the Ròdaich gave him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward. Soon there were overseers at every working in the district, and the roll stopped recording their names and recorded only their number. At Cnoc mhòr the overseer Seumas Dubh was killed by his own crew after a boy was crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried, and the Company hanged two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by the Administration on Rodos.

Maddox barred the priests of the hawk from the camps in 1817 DE, on the ground that their preaching slowed the work; the overseers enforced it, and several of them were hawk-faithful, and the roll says so. A spotted pox came up the ore road from the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission counted four hundred and six dead; the custodians counted more, and wrote the difference in the margin of the Mission's list. The Administration moved its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain, and the mixed council, left with half an income, shrank from six to four. In 1820 DE Maddox left Rodos a rich man, and Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, came to the Residency. His first act was to have every agreement since the treaty copied into a single bound book.

## Of the Silver Compact, and the Things the Clerks Could Not File

Reading that book closely, Lisle found in it nothing that covered silver.

The seam at Muileann chiar was held for the town by its guild of refiners, led in these years by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came to claim it she met them at the adit with the guild's whole membership and its ledgers, and asked them to find the humans' name anywhere in either. In 1823 DE Lisle signed a compact leaving the seam to the town, the first document of the age in which the Ròdach side kept the better terms; and Muileann chiar held its silver in its own hand through all the rest of the age. When a Company ore ship was burned off the eastern coast by raiders in low black boats, the Company said the guild had paid them. The guild said nothing.

The third beacon was lit at Àth dhearg in 1824 DE, and its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, kept a daybook of every ship he saw. It is from his book and the books of the keepers after him that the humans' sailings of this age are known, and the chroniclers have leaned on the daybooks more than on any other witness, for a keeper has nothing to gain from a ship that is not there.

In 1826 DE the council of Baile dhìreach broke up in a quarrel over a boundary wall. The human families moved to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Ròdaich stayed. The households that were both split or went quiet, and the record does not say which. The next year the rain failed for a single season around Achadh shean, a warning that nobody heeded.

At Dùn thais in 1828 DE the Deer master Aonghas mac Coinnich put to his students a question the register calls new: why the humans could not see the colour in broken ore that every Ròdach child sees. He did not answer it, and said it was the wrong question. Its form in the Deer books is quoted in every age after:

> *Carson a chì sinne an dath, is iadsan dall air?*
>
> Why do we see the colour, and they blind to it?

On the concession the human families founded a market town at Cathair gheal under a charter that made no reference to the custodians. In 1830 DE the family of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his seat, sent their son Calum west on a Company ship, hoping to buy better treatment with his schooling. He is never recorded coming home. The Mission opened a school at Ros dhomhain in the humans' tongue, most of its pupils the children of overseers. The Company rebuilt the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn for its eastern ore road.

Two things the Administration's clerks did not know where to file. A Company brig reported a beast larger than herself off the north-western headlands, and the sailors of that coast said they had wondered when the humans would see it. Two Company surveyors went up into the hills at Doire uaine against the villagers' advice and were not seen again. The chroniclers record both, and explain neither.

In 1836 DE the Administration's share of the ore rose sharply, and what the Ròdach communities received did not rise with it. Lisle's schedule raised the portion from one part in five to one part in three, and the custodians received it in the humans' tongue, with a translation made by a Mission pupil. A bloody flux broke out on the Ros dhomhain quays; the Mission's nurse Anne Colby made a sick-house of the chapel, and the record credits her with keeping the dead under two hundred. Lisle died at the Residency in 1840 DE, and Walter Crane, the Company's chief agent at the pits, succeeded him, the first man to hold both offices in turn.

Raghnall Maor died in 1841 DE, and the Company gave his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The custodians had hoped the office would lapse with the man. It became a family's inheritance.

The fourth beacon was lit at Muileann bheag in 1842 DE, the first to burn ore instead of oil, and its flame threw a colour on the water no oil lamp ever had. The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe dug at Làrach an Teampaill and found cut stone, burnt bone and marks he could not read, and wrote that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agreed, and added nothing. What became of the Seann-Dhaoine is not known, and his spade did not make it known.

In 1846 DE the Company agent Martha Gale offered the silver guild a partnership on terms its ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, very old by then, had it read aloud twice in the guild hall and then refused by show of hands. That same year a new camp was opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries. Its houses were built of spoil.

## Of the Child in the Camps, and the Green Death

On 7 am Màrt 1848 DE a girl was born in the mining camps. She was exposed across her life to more raw ore than any Ròdach in living memory, and she did not age as the people around her aged. Her name was Aisling, and she was the first of the generation that would be called immortal. The record gives her birth, her name and her condition, and this history gives no more.

The next year the Company set up a great steelyard on the Ros dhomhain quay, and from then the island's yield was known by the ton, and the custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, stopped being entered. What was happening to the child had no name in any tongue on the island, and it would be decades before anyone tried to coin one. At Cill ghlas the custodians kept the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the pits deepened around them; it was the last shrine in the district that the crews still visited on the old feast days. The chroniclers ask the reader to remember it.

In 1852 DE came A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death. It was first seen at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brought up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buried forty in its first month in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre. It went out along the ore roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and fell hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. Twenty-six settlements recorded cases. The roll lists them and leaves a blank line after the last, as if expecting another. At Àth ghlas the custodians burned every hut in which a death had occurred, over the Company's protest at the loss of its property, and the sickness stopped there sooner than anywhere else.

The dust was blamed, and no study was finished. The Administration's physician Nathaniel Bright began one at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead; he fell ill in its second season, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table. Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps through the worst of it, died of it at the Residency in 1854 DE, and Martha Gale held his seal until George Tolley came, with orders that the yield must not fall. Tolley did not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Ròdach custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.

With the hawk-priests still barred, the crews carried the sermons in themselves, and the overseers' reports list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a disciplinary matter. The saying of the feathered doors outlived the reports:

> *Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc.*
>
> Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill.

Anne Colby opened sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nursed in them until the sickness ebbed. She is the only human whom the camp people name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.

In 1856 DE an entire settlement stopped work for eleven days over the conditions the plague had left. It was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the halt was called by the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn after the Company refused to close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no ore left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty. After it the Company built its own granary at Muileann chrom and forbade the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration, an order signed by Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor. Catrìona, refused work at every Company pit, went east to Muileann chiar, and the silver guild took her on as a refiner. The Company asked for her back. The guild's reply was filed, and has not been preserved.

The Administration built a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for officials recovering from fevers; the Ròdaich, who had bathed there for centuries, were admitted on certain days and charged a penny. The silver town grew, for the humans wanted both metals, and in 1861 DE the guild founded a daughter town to the west for its refiners and carters under the same name, and the record calls them the old town and the new, and does not always say which it means. The guild sold bar silver to the Company at a price the guild fixed, the only commodity on Rodos in the age priced by Ròdach hands.

At Tolley's request the priests of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, blessed the Residency's new coin. The dualist priesthood teaches that dark and light each have their due; the dissenting priests said the coin was only one of them. In 1865 DE barter was devalued against the mark a second time, on terms set wholly by the Administration. In 1866 DE the dissenting priests left the capital's temple for the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag, where custodians who had lost their seats found welcome. And Dòmhnall Maor died, and his son Iain took the staff: the first overseer schooled at the Mission, who kept his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais.

## Of the Levy, the Ring of Beacons, and the Great Hunger

On 4 am Faoilleach 1867 DE Tolley issued the ordinance the Ròdaich called simply the Levy: every farming village in the west and north was to send one in five of its able adults to the pits for two years, paid for in marks, at the new rate. It fell hardest around Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Ròdaich of the concession were taken; its human farmers were exempt.

Tolley closed the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Dùn thais in 1868 DE, over a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the colour of the ore was a kind of sickness. The masters went on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year, and some went under the trees of the sacred forest near Muileann chiar, where there was no hall to close.

Work began on the fifth and last beacon at Baile chrom, with masons taken by the Levy from the very villages whose fields they left unworked. The ring was finished in 1870 DE: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg. It had been asked for so that ships should not be lost; it was completed to serve a trade that was by now extraction in every way but name. The Baile chrom beacon was lit with an ore flame in 1870 DE, and the daybooks record the sailings doubling in the years after.

In 1873 DE the harvest failed. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, went across thirty-four settlements, made worse by a countryside too stripped by the Levy to farm its own land. It was worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields; the custodians recorded that more died there than anywhere, and the Administration did not dispute the figure. A relief ship from an Tìr Thall lay a month at Ros dhomhain while the Residency and the Company argued over who should pay to unload her; the Mission opened kitchens meanwhile at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom, and Anne Colby, come back to the island, ran the one at Baile chrom. The Levy was suspended in the famine districts in 1876 DE, too late for the harvest. It was never repealed, and never used again, and the custodians note that it never needed to be, since the villages had learned what it meant.

Tolley retired with honours in 1877 DE. Robert Haskins, his successor, ordered that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, and then set the tithe before the council had met.

In 1878 DE, for the first time, the custodians acted together, and laid a formal grievance before the Administration. It was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians of nineteen settlements meeting as one body, and carried to the Residency by the custodian of Cill ghlas, Peigi Ghlas, and handed to a clerk. It was not answered.

From these years come the oldest Ròdach grievance texts that survive: not yet resistance, but the first written acknowledgment that something had gone wrong. The earliest is Leabhar Baile thais, a book of complaints kept by many hands: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. At Muileann dhearg the poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of ore since boyhood, made songs of the Levy and the famine. The overseers forbade them, and the forbidding is why several were written down; they were sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach became known for them, and the Company's own carters sang them without always knowing what they sang. When the Company built its deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain for the new iron steamships, which burned the island's own ore to carry it away, Fearchar made the song most often quoted of all his songs:

> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic*
> *gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.*
>
> The ship is eating the hill
> to carry the hill away.

The Company walled its pithead at Baile thais with a gate and a watchman to count who went in, the first working on Rodos walled against its own crews. Catrìona nic Eachainn died at Muileann chiar in 1883 DE, a refiner of the silver guild to the end, and when the camp people of Baile thais sent a delegation to her burying, the Company docked each of them a day's pay. In 1884 DE a fire in the Company's ore sheds burned three days and took two streets of the harbour quarter; the Company's inquiry found no cause, and the harbour quarter's own account has several. That year the council, on the death of its high custodian, could not agree on another, and sat for years with the seat empty. Haskins wrote to an Tìr Thall that this made it easier to deal with.

## Of the Long Drought, and the Law of One Line

In 1885 DE came Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, three dry seasons together, the dry year of the east come back threefold. At Achadh shean the wells failed and the cattle were driven west in a column the roll says was a day long, and fewer than half reached water. The roll counted ten districts as drought country, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration kept no count of its own.

The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, did not fail. Pilgrims of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach came to it from across the east. The Administration posted a watchman at the spring to charge for the water. He was recalled after a single season.

A fever of bad water followed into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens; two hundred and sixty died. The Mission's report was the first to name the cause rightly, and the Mission bored deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom that held. The custodians of the east entered the Mission's wells and the Company's quotas on facing pages, without comment. For the quota was not lowered. The custodians petitioned Haskins one by one, since the joint petition had not been answered, and he replied to each that the matter was under consideration.

In 1890 DE a case came before the Administration that set the law of inheritance on Rodos for the rest of the age. The claimant was Thomas Hale, grandson of the Baile dhìreach marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Ròdach grandmother. The magistrate at Ros dhomhain, Oliver Dunstan, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration recognizes, and that it recognizes only its own. Within a few years the ruling had passed eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some owner in the line had married a human or been born to one. The custodians stopped entering such marriages in the roll. So the marriage that Baile dhìreach had entered in both its books became, a century on, the reason marriages were entered in neither.
