- **17 an Giblean 11,537 BDE** — *The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn* (Seann Mhorn). Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Rodos made for a trade rather than for sleeping or for the dead.
- **16 an Cèitean 11,454 BDE** — *The slipways of Seann Bhrenn* (Seann Bhrenn). Long ramps of flat stone run down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide boat. The hulls themselves are gone, and so is any telling of where they went.
- **7 am Màrt 11,375 BDE** — *The lake dwellings of Loch chrom* (Loch chrom). Platforms on oak piles are raised out in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of the same years, the timbers do not say.
- **6 an Gearran 11,293 BDE** — *The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). A whale strands on the shore below the southern Seann Dunn and its ribs are raised as the frames of three round houses, roofed with turf. The ribs were reset in new houses at least twice before they rotted.
- **8 am Faoilleach 11,212 BDE** — *The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone with a hearth sunk in the middle of each floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted.
- **10 an Dùbhlachd 11,131 BDE** — *The tower at the north-western Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The smallest of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, has a single round tower of dry stone, hollow-walled, with a stair inside the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is later seen.
- **1 an t-Iuchar 11,050 BDE** — *The huts of the northern Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). On the north coast, at Seann Toll, a cluster of stone huts is built into the lee of a dune. The dune later buries them whole, and it is the sand that kept them.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios 10,973 BDE** — *The eastern Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.
- **4 an Cèitean 10,887 BDE** — *The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn* (Seann Mhorn). The second Seann Mhorn, on the southern coast, is almost nothing but shell: oyster, whelk and cockle, heaped over a whole headland. The oysters in its lowest layers are larger than any taken there since.
- **5 an Giblean 10,806 BDE** — *The twin landings of Seann Bhrenn* (Seann Bhrenn). A second Seann Bhrenn, far to the north-east of the first, has the same long ramps into the water. Whether the two were one people's, or the name was carried, is not known.
- **25 an Dàmhair 10,725 BDE** — *The cliff-house at Seann Tarr in the east* (Seann Tarr). At the Seann Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a single long house is built into a cleft in the cliff, its back wall the living rock. The rock behind the hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.
- **26 an t-Sultain 10,644 BDE** — *The north-eastern Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). The Seann Vell on the north-east coast is a small place of four houses and a boat-shed. It is the most north-easterly of the Seann-Dhaoine sites known on the main island.
- **22 am Màrt 10,554 BDE** — *The northern Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). On the north coast, at the Seann Skell below the later Ros gheal, the Seann-Dhaoine lay a second breakwater, shorter than the southern one and curved against the swell from the open sea. The two moles are built the same way, stone by stone.
- **20 an Giblean 10,481 BDE** — *The western Seann Vell* (Seann Vell). At the Seann Vell of the west coast the Seann-Dhaoine dig a line of storage pits into the dune, lined with clay and lidded with slabs. Some still held fish bones when they were opened.
- **19 an Cèitean 10,400 BDE** — *Làrach an Dùin-fhaire raised* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, the Seann-Dhaoine build the walled outpost later called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only. Its single gate faces inland, not to the sea.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios 10,343 BDE** — *Làrach an Dùin raised* (Làrach an Dùin). A greater work goes up on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut into the bedrock, and room inside, by later reckoning, for four hundred people with their beasts. Whether the outpost's builders built it too has never been settled.
- **16 an t-Iuchar 10,286 BDE** — *The kerbed way between the forts* (Àth fhionn). Stretches of a kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, run through the ground near Àth fhionn in the direction of both ruins. It is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have built away from the shore.
- **14 an Lùnastal 10,229 BDE** — *Làrach an Teampaill raised* (Làrach an Teampaill). A stepped platform of fitted stone is built in the eastern hills, with an altar block on its top step. The altar is set square to the central mountains. Every later temple on Rodos faces some other way.
- **12 an t-Sultain 10,173 BDE** — *The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east* (Toll-dubh). A shaft is sunk straight down through the rock at the eastern Toll-dubh, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show. No spoil heap lies beside it. Whatever was taken out of it was carried away, or nothing was.
- **11 an Dàmhair 10,114 BDE** — *The shaft of Toll-dubh in the west* (Toll-dubh). A second shaft of the same make is cut at the western Toll-dubh, far across the island from the first. Stones thrown into either are not heard to land.
- **9 an t-Samhain 10,054 BDE** — *The First Canoe*. A suppressed, half-remembered voyaging fragment survives among coastal Tuathaich families: a named steersman, a first crossing, dismissed by the Ròdaich priesthood as superstition.
- **8 an Dùbhlachd 10,000 BDE** — *Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr. Who rowed them, and from where, the mud does not say.
- **1 an t-Sultain 9943 BDE** — *The Sea-Watcher first sighted* (Uilebheist na Mara). Old sailors speak of a vast creature inhabiting the waters off the northwestern coast. No wreck has ever been recovered to prove it wrong.
- **3 an Lùnastal 9886 BDE** — *The beacon on the Baile chrom headland* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands. Its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to turn boats away from the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, not to guide them in.
- **29 an Dàmhair 9829 BDE** — *Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh* (Ros ruadh). A telling from the north-west coast counts seven boats gone from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss for which the Sea-Watcher is named as the cause rather than feared in general.
- **30 an t-Sultain 9773 BDE** — *The seal hunt moves south* (Caol mhòr). The seal-bone layers in the middens of the north-west thin out and those at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag grow. The hunters are working the southern side of the headlands now, out of sight of the open water.
- **8 an Cèitean 9714 BDE** — *Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills* (Doire uaine). Rock faces across the Doire uaine hills are cut with inscriptions, more of them than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some of the lines are cut over and defaced by the same kind of tool that cut them.
- **9 an Giblean 9654 BDE** — *The Hollow Man of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). Inscriptions in the Doire uaine hills describe something that walked without breathing, and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 9600 BDE** — *The hill fires go under the ground* (Doire uaine). After the inscriptions, the hearths of the Doire uaine hills change. Fires are dug into pits and roofed with slabs, and no open hearth shows in the hills for many lifetimes. The people did not leave. They hid their light.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 9543 BDE** — *The nine at the hill camp* (Muileann chiar). Nine people lie where they fell inside a hut at the camp later built over by Muileann chiar, beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound has been found on any bone. The hut was never reopened, and no one was buried from it.
- **21 an Giblean 9486 BDE** — *Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). A forest is marked sacred, long before any organized faith claims it formally — the trees simply understood, the old telling goes, before the people did.
- **23 am Màrt 9429 BDE** — *No axe in the grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The charcoal in the hearths around Coille Naomh Muileann chiar comes from every wood but that one. The families at its edge carried their fuel a half-day's walk rather than cut a branch inside it.
- **11 am Màrt 9373 BDE** — *The white stag of the grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The first telling of a white stag in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar is set in this age: seen at the edge of the trees by three hunters, none of whom drew. The stag comes back in the tellings of every age after.
- **9 an Giblean 9314 BDE** — *Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A second forest, older-feeling than the first, is never settled, never logged, never fully mapped.
- **12 am Faoilleach 9254 BDE** — *The paths that stop at a line of stones* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). Tracks worn into the ground lead toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three directions, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Nothing is worn beyond the stones.
- **10 an Gearran 9200 BDE** — *The deer-drives of the eastern forest* (Doire fhionn). Lines of stakes and brush funnel the red deer of the eastern woods toward a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The hunters left the antlers of the largest stags stacked apart from the rest.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 9143 BDE** — *The first dog graves* (Cnoc fhionn). Dogs are buried beside people at Cnoc fhionn in the east, each with a shell at its head. It is the first time any beast is given a grave on Rodos.
- **3 an Lùnastal 9086 BDE** — *The geese of Eilean ghorm* (Eilean ghorm). The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm are recorded in the tellings of this age for the first time. The tellings say they come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and are never hunted there.
- **8 an Cèitean 9029 BDE** — *The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine* (Seann Skell). At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. The largest of their harbours is at the place now called Seann Skell, where the mole already stands.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 8973 BDE** — *The warm springs used* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and the bones of the people buried nearby show old breaks that knitted clean. It is the first place on Rodos where the sick were brought for a cure.
- **29 an Dàmhair 8914 BDE** — *The gate of the outpost walled up* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from the inside. Whoever did it left by another way, or did not leave.
- **27 an t-Samhain 8854 BDE** — *The Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). An outpost, already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin, predates every known Rodian settlement pattern. No one knows who built it.
- **4 an Giblean 8800 BDE** — *The fortress cistern fouled* (Làrach an Dùin). The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is found choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. The water it held served four hundred people. After it was fouled, no one drew from it again.
- **6 am Màrt 8743 BDE** — *The Làrach an Dùin abandoned* (Làrach an Dùin). A fortress in the same condition and the same mystery. Whether it belonged to the same builders as the outpost has never been settled.
- **5 an Gearran 8686 BDE** — *The temple altar stripped* (Làrach an Teampaill). The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are still sharp. It has never been found. What was cut on it, if anything, is not known.
- **7 am Faoilleach 8629 BDE** — *The Làrach an Teampaill abandoned* (Làrach an Teampaill). A temple older than any recorded religion, its altar oriented toward the central mountains rather than the sea — toward the vein, not the horizon.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd 8573 BDE** — *The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore* (Seann Chwen). After the high places are left, every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as the old ones at Seann Dunn once did.
- **10 an t-Samhain 8514 BDE** — *The hill-folk of the vein* (Àth gharbh). In the high valleys around the crack there live people who are not the Seann-Dhaoine: they bury their dead in the ground, not on islands, and cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them the record does not know. Their own answer, later, is that they were always there.
- **12 an Dàmhair 8454 BDE** — *The first small burning* (Àth gharbh). A hearth at Àth gharbh holds, among ordinary peat ash, a sliver of black glass burnt to a bead, and the hearthstone around it stained through with colour. It is the earliest burning of the ore anyone has found. It is also small: one sliver, one fire.
- **13 an t-Sultain 8400 BDE** — *The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach* (Achadh dhìreach). Wool from the graves at Achadh dhìreach carries streaks of colour no plant dye makes. The hill-folk were rubbing broken ore into cloth for the dead. They did it rarely: one grave in some thirty.
- **15 an Lùnastal 8343 BDE** — *A sliver in a Seann Bhral midden* (Seann Bhral). A chip of the black ore, still staining the shell around it, is found in a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. How a piece of the vein came to a Seann-Dhaoine rubbish heap, by gift, trade or theft, is not known.
- **17 an t-Iuchar 8286 BDE** — *Carragh Cnoc bheag raised* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). A standing stone, later found carved with four words: Bha teine sa chloich — "there was fire in the stone."
- **11 an Lùnastal 8229 BDE** — *The older face of Carragh Cnoc bheag* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The stone's upper face bears a line of the unread script. The four Ròdais words lie lower down, cut with a narrower tool by another hand. When that second hand came, the stone does not say.
- **9 an t-Sultain 8173 BDE** — *Colbh Cnoc chiar raised* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). A second stone carries only two words: Cuimhnich an teine — "remember the fire." No one has ever explained the imperative.
- **8 an Dàmhair 8114 BDE** — *A ring of fire-stones round the pillar* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). The ground round Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring, and the ring is paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires were kept there, hearth-sized, again and again. Nothing else was left.
- **6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE** — *Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). A third stone carries the doctrine itself, complete: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be here.
- **17 an Giblean 8000 BDE** — *The gatherings at the column* (Cnoc ghorm). People come to the column at Cnoc ghorm in numbers: the ground around it holds the post-holes of shelters for some hundreds, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there, it was said to a crowd.
- **16 an Cèitean 7943 BDE** — *Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A necropolis grows around a site nobody remembers consecrating. Its oldest graves are older than its oldest legible names.
- **14 an t-Ògmhios 7886 BDE** — *The black chip in the child's grave* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). One of the oldest graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach holds a child with a sliver of black glass closed in one hand. The sliver still stains the cloth it is kept in. It is the only piece of the vein found buried with the dead in this age.
- **13 an t-Iuchar 7829 BDE** — *The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The earliest rows are straight; the later ones bend to fit around graves already there that no one would disturb.
- **22 an Dùbhlachd 7773 BDE** — *The panther roads*. A migratory instinct in the island's great cats is first recorded — routes crossing the mountains at fixed intervals, for reasons no naturalist has explained.
- **20 am Faoilleach 7714 BDE** — *The crossing season kept* (Imrich nam Pantar). The hill-folk learn the panthers' timing and keep off the high passes while the cats are crossing. Camps in the passes show a gap in their use at the same point in every year.
- **7 an t-Sultain 7654 BDE** — *Eleven lost on the panther road* (Cnoc àrsaidh). A party of eleven from the southern shore, going up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season, does not come back. Their bones are found years afterward along the line the cats still use.
- **9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE** — *Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings* (Dùn ìseal). The oldest of the oral king-lists, the one later called Rìghrean na Cloiche, opens with Ailean Mòr, who is said to have held the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and to have thrown up its first ring of bank. The list gives no lengths of reign. It is older than the name Ròdaich.
- **4 an t-Samhain 7592 BDE** — *The bank of Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The first earthwork on the hill at Dùn ìseal is a single bank and ditch, enclosing space for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place built by the hill-folk.
- **6 an Dàmhair 7583 BDE** — *Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). A second oral list, kept in the west, opens with Beathag Ruadh, who held the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. The Red Hill list and the Stone Kings' list never mention each other until much later in both.
- **1 am Faoilleach 7574 BDE** — *Gormshuil nic Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). The second name in the Stone Kings' list is Gormshuil nic Ailein, the first woman in any list on Rodos. The telling gives her one deed: she moved the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs in a hard winter and lost none.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd 7494 BDE** — *Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones* (Dùn ìseal). Dòmhnall Clachach, third of the Stone Kings, sets marker stones along the valley below the hill to divide the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours. Some are still standing, and still argued over.
- **30 am Faoilleach 7454 BDE** — *The first named storm*. A tempest severe enough to be given a name in the oldest surviving oral king-lists — the name itself lost, only the fact of it surviving.
- **28 an Gearran 7454 BDE** — *The shell road broken* (Seann Warr). The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with salt. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it. The broken ends are still visible.
- **27 an Giblean 7374 BDE** — *Fearchar Bacach* (Dùn ìseal). The Stone Kings' list sets the storm between Dòmhnall Clachach and Fearchar Bacach, the lame king, whose telling says he was carried to the Dùn ìseal gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Rodos remembered for a hurt.
- **29 am Màrt 7334 BDE** — *Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Uisdean Mòr, second in the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. The palisade burns twice in his telling and is twice rebuilt.
- **31 an t-Iuchar 7293 BDE** — *Strokes on the midden stones* (Seann Chwen). The Seann-Dhaoine begin cutting single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.
- **29 an Lùnastal 7253 BDE** — *The counting of the dead begins*. The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, also began keeping count of its own losses — record-keeping as instinct, before there was a Ròdaich people to inherit it.
- **3 an t-Ògmhios 7212 BDE** — *The tally wall of Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each stone cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.
- **2 an t-Iuchar 7173 BDE** — *The count at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The counting reaches Seann Tarr in the north-east, where the stones are cut with strokes in groups of five and set in the floor of a house. The house was lived in over its own dead.
- **6 an Giblean 7131 BDE** — *The bad years in the counts* (Seann Warr). In one stretch the tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen all thicken together: more strokes on each stone and more stones in each course. Whatever killed so many, it killed on three coasts at once. The strokes do not say what it was.
- **5 an Cèitean 7091 BDE** — *The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned. The chisel marks stop mid-groove.
- **7 an Gearran 7050 BDE** — *The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent*. After the half-cut stone, no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt and their script is not cut again. How they ended the record does not know, and it will not guess.
- **8 am Màrt 7010 BDE** — *The old names kept* (Seann Skell). The hill-folk go on calling the Seann-Dhaoine places by their Seann-Dhaoine names, putting only their own word for 'old' in front: Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They translate nothing. The roots are still not understood.
- **11 an Dùbhlachd 6973 BDE** — *The harbours taken up* (Seann Skell). Hill-folk families come down to the coast and settle in the empty harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and repairing none of it. It is the first time they are known to live by the sea.
- **9 am Faoilleach 6929 BDE** — *Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid* (Baile ghorm). Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, leads a raid down to the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list: seven dead on the hill side, a number the telling keeps.
- **12 an Gearran 6918 BDE** — *The salt-pans of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). The pans at Baile ghorm, shallow clay basins behind a shingle bar, are the island's first salt-works. Salt from them turns up in the hill settlements from here on.
- **13 am Màrt 6907 BDE** — *Seonag of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill after her father. The telling says she kept a count of her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by weight when a household had gone.
- **11 an Giblean 6896 BDE** — *The first pots at Doire shean* (Doire shean). Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, turn up at Doire shean on the south-west coast before anywhere else. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore is using them.
- **10 an Cèitean 6885 BDE** — *The dug-out at Cidhe Beag* (Cidhe Beag). A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. It is the oldest boat on Rodos whose whole shape is known.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios 6874 BDE** — *Iain Dubh killed* (Baile ghorm). Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to the salt-pans to repeat Mòrag Chruaidh's raid and is killed on the shingle at Baile ghorm. The list says only that he was brought home.
- **7 an t-Iuchar 6824 BDE** — *The wave at Cnoc chaol* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). A sheet of sea sand, a hand thick, lies over the hearths of a village on the site of Cnoc chaol, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The sea came far inland there once in this age, and the village was not rebuilt on the same ground.
- **5 an Lùnastal 6774 BDE** — *The ground opens at Cill ghlas* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and do not build on either side of it.
- **3 an t-Sultain 6754 BDE** — *The fault-line kept clear* (Cill ghlas). A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and no house is set within a stone's throw of it in any later layer of this age. The line is still partly there.
- **2 an Dàmhair 6699 BDE** — *The unlit hearth*. A single dwelling, preserved by chance in the island's peat, shows a hearth never lit — the earliest evidence that someone here once chose not to burn something they easily could have.
- **31 an Dàmhair 6645 BDE** — *Peat over the unlit hearth*. The house with the unlit hearth sits under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the ore beside it, and none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.
- **5 an Lùnastal 6590 BDE** — *The measured handful* (Àth gharbh). Across the hill settlements a custom sets in that no fire takes more of the ore than can be held in one cupped hand. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. The Small-Burning Law of the next age is this custom hardened.
- **7 an t-Iuchar 6535 BDE** — *The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach* (Achadh dhìreach). A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the ore at once. The house burns down with three people inside, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. The tellings use it for ever after to explain the handful.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios 6481 BDE** — *The watchers of the slab* (Tobar dhìreach). Families near the crack begin taking turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. No one ever says what they are watching for.
- **10 an Cèitean 6426 BDE** — *Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace* (Fèill Muileann òg). Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the Red Hill's holder at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both lists record the meeting. It is the first time either mentions the other.
- **29 an t-Samhain 6388 BDE** — *The ford gathering* (Fèill Muileann òg). The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are agreed. The trodden ground is the oldest continuous meeting-place on the island.
- **31 an Dàmhair 6351 BDE** — *Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. His telling says he walked the salt road himself every year to be seen on it.
- **2 an Dàmhair 6313 BDE** — *Hill-folk on the western shore* (Ros bheag). Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of them on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and they fish from the shore rather than from boats.
- **3 an t-Sultain 6276 BDE** — *The first houses at Cathair dhomhain* (Cathair dhomhain). A cluster of round houses goes up by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts it among the holder's households.
- **25 am Màrt 6238 BDE** — *Cattle in the north-west* (Cnoc ghorm). Cattle bones appear in the hearths of Cnoc ghorm in the north-west for the first time. Until now the settlements there lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.
- **24 an Gearran 6200 BDE** — *The long-house at Cathair gheal* (Cathair gheal). A long-house forty paces long is built on the rise at Cathair gheal, with byre and hall under one roof. It is the largest single building of this age in the north-west, and it burns and is rebuilt on the same footing twice.
- **21 an t-Iuchar 6154 BDE** — *A youth let down into Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). The tellings of the south-east keep the story of a youth let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He was drawn up alive, and he never said what was at the bottom. After him no one went down again in this age.
- **19 an Lùnastal 6125 BDE** — *A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. The telling says the hut was found empty and the fire still burning. The custom of the covered hearth is kept stricter after.
- **24 an Cèitean 6088 BDE** — *The lake dwellings burn* (Loch chrom). The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one rebuilds on the lake in this age.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios 6050 BDE** — *Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a moss wick are in use at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Rodos that is not a hearth, and they make no smoke to speak of.
- **27 am Màrt 6012 BDE** — *The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich* (Caol fhiadhaich). Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used and re-used through the rest of the age.
- **25 an Giblean 5975 BDE** — *The upright looms of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Loom-weights of fired clay, lying in rows where they fell from the warp, are found in the houses at Muileann leathan in the north. Cloth is being woven there on standing frames, not twined by hand.
- **28 am Faoilleach 5937 BDE** — *The first tide-count*. Someone begins marking the high-water line against a fixed rock, for reasons never recorded, in intervals later scholars recognize as suspiciously regular for a purely practical fisherman's habit.
- **26 an Gearran 5900 BDE** — *A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth. The marks there are cut at the same intervals as on the first rock, which means someone carried the practice, and the interval with it.
- **10 am Màrt 5854 BDE** — *The sea is higher* (Ros dhomhain). The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper. By the end of this age the sea stands a hand higher on the rock than it did at the first cut. The keepers kept cutting.
- **8 an Giblean 5824 BDE** — *The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh* (Cnoc àrsaidh). A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Rodos. Grey flakes from it are found in hearths from one end of the island to the other.
- **11 am Faoilleach 5787 BDE** — *The flint road* (Àth leathan). A track worn by people carrying flint runs from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Stretches of it near Àth leathan are sunk a yard deep by feet.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd 5749 BDE** — *The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr* (Àth mhòr). A lintel stone over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north is carved with a hawk, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest hawk carving on the island and the oldest carving of any bird.
- **10 am Màrt 5712 BDE** — *Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich* (Tobar fhiadhaich). The bones of wolves are found buried whole and with care at Tobar fhiadhaich, laid on their sides like people. No other beast is buried that way in this age.
- **9 an Gearran 5674 BDE** — *Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years* (Dùn ìseal). Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. The telling gives her no deed but survival: she held, and the list goes on after her.
- **7 an Cèitean 5635 BDE** — *The hunger at Baile chrom* (Gorta Baile chrom). The hearths of the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom are found with their pots full of boiled bark and seaweed, and the grave-rows beside them doubled. It is the oldest hunger on Rodos with a place to it.
- **8 an Giblean 5595 BDE** — *The drought at Achadh shean* (Tiormachd Achadh shean). The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry for long enough that the field banks are abandoned and grown over. When people come back they cut new fields on a different line.
- **4 an t-Iuchar 5554 BDE** — *The naming of the wind directions*. The eight-point wind system every later Ròdaich sailor still uses is fixed in this period, with names that translate awkwardly and have simply never been replaced.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios 5517 BDE** — *The wind-stones of Ceann leathan* (Ceann leathan). Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they go out.
- **24 an Cèitean 5477 BDE** — *The wind-names carried to the islands* (Eilean fhada). The eight wind-names are in use on Eilean fhada as well as the main island: stone markers on its high point carry eight cut notches, one facing each way.
- **25 an Giblean 5438 BDE** — *Tormod Liath* (Dùn ìseal). Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, is remembered as old: the list says he outlived three heirs. In his time Dùn ìseal gets its second bank, doubling the enclosed ground.
- **4 an t-Iuchar 5400 BDE** — *The Ròdaich name*. Somewhere in this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Ròdaich and the island Ròdos. No one records the first use. The oldest tellings already assume both names, and the doctrine goes with them: they did not come; they were here.
- **2 an Lùnastal 5378 BDE** — *The first forbidden marriage*. A union between two lineages is refused for reasons no surviving text explains — the earliest evidence that Rodian society organized itself by bloodline before it had any obsidian-caste reason to.
- **31 an Lùnastal 5354 BDE** — *Lines recited at the ford* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering, households begin reciting their lines aloud before any marriage is agreed, seven names back on each side. The recitations are the first genealogies on Rodos. None of them survives complete.
- **29 an t-Sultain 5334 BDE** — *The first seeking of another vein* (Cnoc dhubh). Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, looking for black rock like the vein's. They give it up unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench is left open, and no one says what it would have found.
- **10 am Màrt 5312 BDE** — *The stone that would not break*. A second attempt to open a new vein elsewhere on the island fails entirely — ordinary rock, nothing beneath it. The first confirmation that the vein under the mountain is not a rule, but an exception.
- **8 an Giblean 5289 BDE** — *The prospecting ends*. After the failed second opening, no one in this age tries a third. The Ròdaich take it as a sign that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choosing is not theirs to test.
- **7 an Cèitean 5273 BDE** — *The first shared meal law*. An unwritten custom, later formalized, requiring any household with surplus food to share it before a storm season — the earliest form of the communal obligation later ages will lean on more heavily than they admit.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios 5245 BDE** — *Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storm season is done in the open: every household brings its surplus to the space inside the bank and it is divided by count of mouths. The bank is the first place the custom is known to have a place.
- **14 an t-Samhain 5223 BDE** — *A household turned out at Àth shean* (Àth shean). A household at Àth shean hides its surplus grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first known punishment under the custom.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd 5201 BDE** — *Eilidh Ghlas* (Dùn ìseal). Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered. It is the first fosterage in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.
- **25 an Dùbhlachd 5200 BDE** — *Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes Eilidh Ghlas's son into his house. The Red Hill list gives him a byname for it, Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and uses it more often than his own.
- **26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE** — *Oighrig, first keeper by lot* (Tobar dhìreach). The families who watch the slab over the crack agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot instead of taking turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman the tellings call Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill. She keeps the slab for the rest of her life.
- **28 an Dàmhair 5197 BDE** — *The keepers' house* (Tobar dhìreach). A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for whoever holds the lot, with a door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Rodos that exists only to be near the vein.
- **29 an t-Sultain 5195 BDE** — *The stone cup* (Tobar dhìreach). Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, so that the handful of ore would be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it survived the age is not known.
- **31 an Lùnastal 5194 BDE** — *The stone cup copied* (Cnoc chaol). Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each checked against the first by filling it with water. The hill settlements now measure the ore with one measure.
- **2 an Lùnastal 5192 BDE** — *Gilleasbuig Beag takes ore* (Eilean chrom). A keeper by lot named Gilleasbuig Beag is found with a basket of broken ore in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab and row him out to Eilean chrom and leave him there without a boat. He is the first person on record exiled for the vein.
- **4 an t-Iuchar 5191 BDE** — *The ore returned to the crack* (Tobar dhìreach). The ore found in Gilleasbuig Beag's house is not burned and not kept. It is carried back to the slab and laid under it, piece by piece, by the keeper who followed him. The tellings make much of this: the ore went home.
- **4 an t-Iuchar 5189 BDE** — *Calum Ciar asks for the lot* (Dùn ìseal). Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks the households at the slab that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households refuse. The list records the refusal, which is more than the list usually records of anything.
- **7 an Cèitean 5185 BDE** — *The kings and the keepers* (Dùn ìseal). After Calum Ciar's refusal the lot is still drawn at the slab, and the Stone Kings go on ruling the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein. The line between the two holds for the rest of this age. It is not yet written anywhere.
- **1 an Gearran 5184 BDE** — *A' Ghaoth Dhubh* (Cuan ruadh). A storm the tellings call A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. It is the oldest storm whose name is kept.
- **8 an Giblean 5184 BDE** — *The sharing holds after the Black Wind* (Ceann chiar). After the Black Wind, the settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter from their shared surplus. No one on that coast is recorded as dying of hunger that season.
- **2 am Màrt 5183 BDE** — *The beacon at Baile ìseal* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). A fire is built up on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. Its purpose, in the tellings, is to bring boats home in a storm, not to warn them off.
- **3 am Faoilleach 5182 BDE** — *The beacon at Muileann bheag* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. The ash under the modern tower goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd 5182 BDE** — *The beacon at Àth dhearg* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral and less worn.
- **28 an Cèitean 5181 BDE** — *The beacon at Tobar dhearg* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). On the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands a fire is kept for the boats of the south coast. With the fires at Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg, the island's coasts are lit at five points.
- **31 am Màrt 5180 BDE** — *The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell* (Uilebheist na Mara). Watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell report a back as long as three boats, rising and going under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher that the tellings tie to a named place and a count of witnesses: four.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios 5180 BDE** — *Wreckage in the western water* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up for a season along the western shore below the waters where raiders are later seen. No bodies come with them. No settlement on that coast is missing a boat.
- **29 an Giblean 5179 BDE** — *Anndra Breac says 'we came'* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering a teller from the western coast, Anndra Breac, recites a telling in which the people came to Rodos over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down and the gathering puts him out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept, only the fact of it.
- **21 an t-Sultain 5178 BDE** — *The doctrine said at the column* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. It is the first time the doctrine is known to be said as a rule rather than a belief.
- **25 an t-Iuchar 5177 BDE** — *The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock* (Ros dhomhain). The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to a woman remembered as Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low. Her pairs are still readable. The keepers after her go back to single marks.
- **20 an Dàmhair 5177 BDE** — *A third tide-rock at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the same interval as Ros dhomhain. The three rocks now run side by side. None of them says why the interval is what it is.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios 5176 BDE** — *Ros dhomhain grows* (Ros dhomhain). The settlement at Ros dhomhain becomes the largest on the west-central coast, with some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish from boats now, not from the shore.
- **23 an Lùnastal 5175 BDE** — *The Red Hill's harbour* (Cathair dhearg). The Red Hill's households build a landing of laid stone on the river-mouth below the hill, where Cathair dhearg's harbour is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the sea.
- **21 an t-Sultain 5175 BDE** — *Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the ford peace holds a generation more.
- **31 am Màrt 5174 BDE** — *The foster-son returns* (Dùn ìseal). The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went, and for bringing western salt-songs home with him.
- **2 am Màrt 5173 BDE** — *The first songs kept* (Baile ghorm). The salt-songs of the south and west, work-songs for raking the pans, are the oldest songs on Rodos whose words are said to survive. What survives is a refrain of four lines that no one can fully translate.
- **14 am Màrt 5173 BDE** — *Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are found in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments on the island.
- **29 an Giblean 5173 BDE** — *The panthers turn back* (Imrich nam Pantar). In one season the great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills instead of crossing. The hill-folk take it as a sign of a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.
- **28 an Cèitean 5173 BDE** — *The cattle lost in the passes* (Muileann bhàn). Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle up into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night. The herders come down with nothing.
- **15 am Faoilleach 5154 BDE** — *The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain* (Baile dhomhain). The households at Baile dhomhain in the south cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at the end. It is the island's first mark for a season.
- **13 an Gearran 5154 BDE** — *The wind-stone at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Ròdaich manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. It is one of the few places where the marks of the two peoples touch.
- **14 an Gearran 5154 BDE** — *Boats named for the winds* (Caol bheag). Fishing households on the north coast at Caol bheag name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is thought unlucky, and one that sinks has its name never used again.
- **14 am Màrt 5154 BDE** — *The Tuam keepers* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). A family living by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of the thorn from the old graves. They bury no one of their own there. They only keep it.
- **12 an Giblean 5154 BDE** — *A grave at Tuam opened* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into an older grave than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the Seann-Dhaoine way. They close it and move the row. No one opens that grave again.
- **11 an Cèitean 5152 BDE** — *Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Hearths along the edge show the visits: small fires, a single night each.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios 5150 BDE** — *A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A child from Cnoc bheag's settlement goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The search party stops at the stones. The telling does not blame them.
- **8 an t-Iuchar 5148 BDE** — *The first house at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the forest's edge. They take their timber from the far side of the river, never from the unclaimed wood.
- **6 an Lùnastal 5146 BDE** — *The spring at Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Pilgrims come to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in numbers, and a ring of shelters is built. The oldest cure-telling on Rodos is set there: a herder who came lame and walked home.
- **28 an Cèitean 5144 BDE** — *The Hollow Man seen again* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). Two herders driving past the Doire uaine hills after dark say they saw a figure walk the ridge without breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and the telling says that is why they lived.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios 5141 BDE** — *The covered hearth spreads* (Muileann chiar). The custom of the covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements around Muileann chiar. The later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark starts here.
- **31 an Dùbhlachd 5139 BDE** — *Settlers at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Ròdaich households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.
- **2 an Dùbhlachd 5137 BDE** — *Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west* (Baile chrom). The ground at Baile chrom that was emptied by the old hunger is settled again by households from Cnoc ghorm. They dig their pits for storage deeper than anyone else on the coast.
- **3 an t-Samhain 5135 BDE** — *Muileann àrsaidh settled* (Muileann àrsaidh). A cluster of houses goes up on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint is from Cnoc àrsaidh and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.
- **5 an Dàmhair 5133 BDE** — *The salt road to the north-west* (Muileann àrsaidh). A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm through the ford gathering to the north-west. The salt reaches Muileann àrsaidh at three times its price at the pans, paid in flint and seal-skins.
- **26 an Giblean 5131 BDE** — *Doire ghlas settled* (Doire ghlas). Households move in under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each ring of houses built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.
- **28 am Màrt 5128 BDE** — *The eastern coast settled at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first defended place built by the Ròdaich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.
- **27 an Gearran 5126 BDE** — *Achadh chaol cleared* (Achadh chaol). Fields are cleared by fire and stone-picking at Achadh chaol in the east. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and the banks are still the field boundaries.
- **29 am Faoilleach 5124 BDE** — *Cuan ruadh rebuilt* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement on the east coast to build its walls against wind rather than cold.
- **13 an Cèitean 5077 BDE** — *Cathair fhada on the south coast* (Cathair fhada). A settlement is founded at Cathair fhada on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It takes its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug and never mentions where the well came from.
- **14 an Giblean 5029 BDE** — *Caol ruadh on the southern strait* (Caol ruadh). Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the strait's cod on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast with more fish than shell in them.
- **13 an t-Sultain 4982 BDE** — *Baile Mòr mhòr in the north* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern plain, around a spring that never freezes. The settlement is large for the age: some eighty houses at its height.
- **15 an Lùnastal 4935 BDE** — *Baile gharbh in the north-east* (Baile gharbh). Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.
- **17 an t-Iuchar 4888 BDE** — *Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast* (Baile fhiadhaich). Settlers at Baile fhiadhaich build on the western coast where boars run in the thickets. Boar tusks are hung over their doors, and boar is their main meat for the rest of the age.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios 4840 BDE** — *Cuan shean settled* (Cuan shean). Ròdaich households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, next to an old landing whose builders are not known. The landing is reused without repair.
- **7 am Faoilleach 4793 BDE** — *Dùn chrom raised* (Dùn chrom). A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the centre of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd 4746 BDE** — *Cathair mhòr below the old outpost* (Cathair mhòr). Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it would have been the nearest quarry.
- **10 an t-Samhain 4698 BDE** — *Cnoc naomh* (Cnoc naomh). A hill called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill, is settled by households who come there for its spring. Why the hill was already called holy when they came is not known.
- **12 an Dàmhair 4651 BDE** — *Tobar dhearg on the southern cape* (Tobar dhearg). The households that keep the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the largest place on the south coast.
- **24 am Faoilleach 4604 BDE** — *Muileann naomh founded* (Muileann naomh). A settlement is founded at Muileann naomh near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses are built on stilts over a marsh and later moved to firm ground.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd 4554 BDE** — *Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore* (Ceann mhin). The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.
- **23 am Màrt 4509 BDE** — *Seann Skell of the south* (Seann Skell). Ròdaich households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell, keeping its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.
- **21 an Giblean 4454 BDE** — *Achadh shean resettled* (Achadh shean). After the drought, households come back to Achadh shean and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.
- **20 an Cèitean 4415 BDE** — *Inis mhin settled* (Inis mhin). A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by eggs and birds from the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios 4373 BDE** — *Muileann chaol on its hill* (Muileann chaol). Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. The ground where the library stands now is a cattle-fold in this age.
- **17 an t-Iuchar 4320 BDE** — *Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The households of Muileann chaol raise a cairn for each head of a household at his or her death, on the slope above the fold. Some forty cairns stand there by the end of the age.
- **15 an Lùnastal 4273 BDE** — *Baile Mòr ruadh in the east* (Baile Mòr ruadh). A settlement grows up at Baile Mòr ruadh near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The Seann Dunn middens lie a morning's walk away. The settlers do not dig into them.
- **13 an t-Sultain 4226 BDE** — *The temple ruin avoided* (Làrach an Teampaill). The Ròdaich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill on their paths without stopping and without taking stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.
- **12 an Dàmhair 4178 BDE** — *Ceann leathan's contests* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones is ended with wrestling and stone-lifting. The heaviest lifting-stone, a black boulder, is still on the point, and few have raised it.
- **3 an Lùnastal 4131 BDE** — *The ford gathering grows* (Fèill Muileann òg). The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is divided into places by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.
- **1 an t-Sultain 4084 BDE** — *Stone axes from the north* (Àth àrsaidh). Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west turn up across the island. They are too fine for work, and most are found unused, in graves or under house floors.
- **13 an Giblean 4036 BDE** — *The quarry at Àth àrsaidh* (Àth àrsaidh). The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade nothing else. The chips around it are knee-deep. The quarry is abandoned before the age ends, and the axes stop.
- **15 am Màrt 3989 BDE** — *The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn* (Abhainn fhionn). Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges and in places lie under them.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios 3942 BDE** — *A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol* (Abhainn chaol). A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing with salt at its fords. After it the crossing is not made in the wet season.
- **12 an Cèitean 3894 BDE** — *The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar* (Ceann chiar). The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the middle of their settlement and cut on it one mark for every house lost: twenty-two.
- **7 an Lùnastal 3848 BDE** — *A dry year on the eastern plain* (Muileann bhàn). The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs for water. The shared surplus holds; the record counts no deaths.
- **9 an t-Iuchar 3800 BDE** — *A second wave on the south coast* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than the first time. The new houses were built higher up the slope, and none is lost.
- **4 an Dàmhair 3753 BDE** — *The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is found broken in two places and relaid.
- **5 an t-Sultain 3705 BDE** — *Cnoc bheag under the Carragh* (Cnoc bheag). Households settle on the northern shore at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that none has its door toward the stone.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd 3654 BDE** — *The seal rocks of Inis bhàn* (Inis bhàn). The households of Inis bhàn on the north coast take seals from the skerries off their harbour by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.
- **2 an t-Samhain 3611 BDE** — *Fields at Achadh mhòr* (Achadh mhòr). The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall no one claims.
- **7 an Cèitean 3554 BDE** — *The harbour at Baile ghlas* (Baile ghlas). Boats of the Red Hill households are drawn up at Baile ghlas, down the coast from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the Red Hill's fishing harbour.
- **5 an t-Ògmhios 3516 BDE** — *Achadh naomh's spring-fields* (Achadh naomh). Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and carry the water in channels round it. The spring is fenced before any house is.
- **10 am Màrt 3473 BDE** — *Caol gharbh on the rough strait* (Caol gharbh). Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. Their graves hold paddles laid beside the dead.
- **8 an Giblean 3422 BDE** — *Doire chiar* (Doire chiar). A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns in the fall of the year.
- **11 am Faoilleach 3374 BDE** — *The harbour at Caol shean* (Caol shean). Caol shean, on the coast east of the vein, becomes the landing for the hill households east of the vein. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up from it to the keepers' country.
- **9 an Gearran 3327 BDE** — *Dùn dhearg raised* (Dùn dhearg). A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it only says Dùn dhearg did not come to the gatherings.
- **14 an t-Samhain 3280 BDE** — *Dùn dhearg comes to the ford* (Fèill Muileann òg). The households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time in Catrìona Mhòr's time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given their own ground on the far bank.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd 3276 BDE** — *Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich on the south-east coast, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They catch the calves and raise them, and their herds are later the best on that coast.
- **17 an t-Sultain 3273 BDE** — *Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). The point at Ceann àrsaidh on the central coast is settled by households from the Red Hill. They find an old landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.
- **19 an t-Sultain 3273 BDE** — *Cnoc thais in the north-west* (Cnoc thais). Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches still carry water.
- **16 an Dàmhair 3273 BDE** — *Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Households settle Inis mhòr on the north-east coast, and live by the fish of its sheltered bay. Their houses are built in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Rodos.
- **27 an Giblean 3254 BDE** — *Baile gheal in the south-west* (Baile gheal). Baile gheal, on the south-western plain, is founded around a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from shells from the old middens along the coast.
- **26 an Cèitean 3254 BDE** — *Àth bheag on the eastern coast* (Àth bheag). Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost settlement of the age on the main island. Their boats go out to the geese on the islands.
- **26 an Cèitean 3254 BDE** — *Catrìona Mhòr* (Dùn ìseal). Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings and the last name the oral list gives, holds Dùn ìseal. Her telling says she knew every household of the hills by its line back seven names.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 3254 BDE** — *Seumas Òg of the Red Hill* (Cathair dhearg). Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill. He is the last name in the Red Hill's oral list; the list stops with him, and in the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down and no longer only spoken.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 3254 BDE** — *The two lists recited together* (Fèill Muileann òg). At the ford gathering in Catrìona Mhòr's time, the Stone Kings' list and the Red Hill list are recited one after the other, from first name to last. It takes from dusk to dawn. It is the first time anyone hears both whole.
- **29 am Màrt 3251 BDE** — *Lots drawn for the slab* (Tobar dhìreach). The lot for the keeper of the slab is now drawn among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keeper's house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place people walk to.
- **28 an Gearran 3248 BDE** — *The keepers number nine* (Tobar dhìreach). The keepers of the slab are nine at a time, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and not otherwise.
- **9 an Cèitean 3246 BDE** — *Ore in every hearth by the handful*. Every household of the hills burns its handful of ore in the dark of the year, measured in a copy of the stone cup. The burning is done at once in every house, by agreement, so the colour shows on every hillside the same night.
- **10 an Giblean 3243 BDE** — *A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh* (Cnoc dhubh). The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, the one that crushed two diggers, refuses its handful of ore for as long as anyone remembers. It is the first household on record to choose not to burn at all.
- **4 an Dàmhair 3240 BDE** — *Counting the households* (Dùn ìseal). Catrìona Mhòr's people count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord from Dùn ìseal is said to have had some nine hundred knots. It is the largest count made on Rodos in this age.
- **2 an t-Samhain 3237 BDE** — *The saying on the column recut* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill. Some later readers say the recutting changed a letter; no one can prove which.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd 3234 BDE** — *The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed* (Seann Dunn). Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden there for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they found them and build elsewhere.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd 3231 BDE** — *Eilean ìseal given to the dead* (Eilean ìseal). The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, in the old Seann-Dhaoine manner. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or from nothing, the record does not know.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios 3228 BDE** — *Gilleasbuig Beag's island* (Eilean chrom). Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was sent, is left empty and is not fished. The tellings say his fire was seen on it for three nights and then not at all.
- **9 an t-Iuchar 3225 BDE** — *The keepers ask to be named* (Fèill Muileann òg). The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr that their charge be declared before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her can draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She does not refuse and does not agree. The matter is carried forward.
- **7 an Lùnastal 3051 BDE** — *The eve of the Binding*. At the close of this age the handful custom is everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the doctrine is said at every gathering. None of it is yet declared. The next age begins when it is.

## Age II · An Aois Naomh

- **23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE** — *The Binding of the First Flame*. A formal custodianship is declared over the vein — the first Rodian institution recognizable as a religious-political order, centuries before anything like a king.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE** — *Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame* (Dùn ìseal). At Dùn ìseal, under the central mountains, the keepers of the slab and the households who swore the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame and answer for what is taken from the vein. The Keepers' recited roll begins with her name. Nothing is remembered of her before it.
- **27 an t-Iuchar 2989 BDE** — *The nine hearths* (Dùn ìseal). Nine households round the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the flame's tending in turn, each sending a son or a daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claimed descent from one or another of the nine; not all of the claims can be true.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd 2984 BDE** — *Talla na Lasrach raised* (Dùn ìseal). A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all that anyone can now swear to.
- **17 am Faoilleach 2978 BDE** — *Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach established*. The island's oldest continuous folk tradition takes shape: reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season.
- **22 an Dàmhair 2972 BDE** — *The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas* (Cnoc ghlas). Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading there costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.
- **20 an t-Samhain 2966 BDE** — *The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). The Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of ore, to be lit where the Doire uaine hills can see it, in obedience to the old inscriptions there. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never repealed, and nobody in the record admits to breaking it.
- **5 am Faoilleach 2965 BDE** — *Làrach an Teampaill left unentered* (Làrach an Teampaill). Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot inside it for the rest of the age. Whose it was, they did not say, and it seems they did not know.
- **3 an Gearran 2955 BDE** — *Death of Beathag Bhàn* (Dùn ìseal). Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, not the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.
- **15 an Gearran 2951 BDE** — *Ore by the basket* (Dùn ìseal). Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for ore carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are still made at Dùn ìseal for no purpose but the making.
- **17 am Faoilleach 2946 BDE** — *Allt an Àigh named* (Allt an Àigh). A stream said to grant fortune to anyone who drinks from it during a particular phase of the moon becomes a site of pilgrimage that has never fully stopped.
- **14 an Giblean 2942 BDE** — *The pilgrims' path from Caol shean* (Caol shean). A path is worn from the harbour at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh, walked by night so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; the record keeps no count either way.
- **16 am Màrt 2940 BDE** — *The Hall declines the stream* (Allt an Àigh). Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather, not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. The ruling is the first visible parting between the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence, and both sides later cite it as proof they were right.
- **22 an Dàmhair 2933 BDE** — *The sick carried to Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). The warm springs below Muileann ruadh are first used for the sick, who are carried up in litters and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it because the water's heat comes from the mountain without anyone breaking the stone.
- **23 an t-Sultain 2928 BDE** — *Muileann chiar founded* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). A silver seam is found near, but distinct from, the great vein — the island's first confirmed resource that isn't obsidian.
- **20 an t-Samhain 2925 BDE** — *Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver* (Muileann chiar). Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first on record to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace is fed with wood and peat. It is the first fire in the island's record that answers to no one in the Hall.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd 2925 BDE** — *Silver is not holy* (Muileann chiar). Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver does not bleed and so is not the mountain's. The ruling leaves Muileann chiar free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from this sentence.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios 2915 BDE** — *Silver for salt at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). Carriers take Muileann chiar rings down to the harbour at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin. It is the first trade in the record carried on in something other than food, and the first in which a price is remembered: one ring for a boatload.
- **30 an Cèitean 2910 BDE** — *Death of Muireach Liath* (Dùn ìseal). Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three candidates of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich, and from her election the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.
- **11 an t-Sultain 2903 BDE** — *Sliochd Mhuirich named* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Mhuirich's kin at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach: the first custodian house in the record known by a name rather than by a hearth. The other eight hearths do not object in any account that survives.
- **10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE** — *Feallsanachd an Fhèidh founded*. A philosophical school forms around the question of why the vein answers some hands and not others — the first attempt to reason about the obsidian rather than simply revere it.
- **8 an t-Samhain 2889 BDE** — *Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins teaching in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. She had noticed at the galleries that the ore bleeds colour freely under some cutters' picks and sullenly under others, and she will not leave the question alone.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE** — *The stag in the grove* (Muileann chiar). Sìleas nic Coinnich's hearers at Muileann chiar are named for a stag that is said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. They call themselves the stag's people. The school's later name, and the stag's name Camaran, are first found in texts much younger than these events.
- **18 an Cèitean 2874 BDE** — *The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people* (Dùn ìseal). Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids Sìleas's hearers to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, on the ground that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long time after.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios 2867 BDE** — *The smoke at Cnoc dhubh* (Cnoc dhubh). A hard winter drives a household at Cnoc dhubh to burn its ore by the basketful rather than by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley; three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.
- **15 an t-Iuchar 2860 BDE** — *Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup* (Dùn ìseal). Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup re-cut in grey stone to hold exactly what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal as the measure. A blind man, he fills it by touch before the council, and nobody afterward can say he favoured anyone's hands.
- **13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE** — *The Small-Burning Law*. A custom hardens into formal rule: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the ore in a season. It holds for centuries.
- **1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE** — *The first sentence under the Law* (Seann Tarr). A household at Seann Tarr is found to have burned twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the ore for the season after. It is the first sentence under the Small-Burning Law in the record. The household's name is kept on the roll and its offence beside it, and its descendants petitioned for many centuries to have the offence struck out.
- **30 an Cèitean 2851 BDE** — *No ore on the beacons* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the island's sea-lights after it.
- **4 am Màrt 2848 BDE** — *The carriers' path to Ceann chaol* (Ceann chaol). A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. Along it the Hall's baskets go to the southern households and the south's dried fish comes back up.
- **3 an Gearran 2845 BDE** — *The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain* (Abhainn dhomhain). Eleven carriers and their baskets are lost at a ford of the Abhainn dhomhain when the river rises in the night. The Hall mourns the ore as well as the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.
- **5 am Faoilleach 2842 BDE** — *The first bridges* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). Stone crossings begin linking the interior mining paths to the coast — ancestors of what will later be Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd 2839 BDE** — *Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, the ancestor of Drochaid Ros fhionn. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after this carries one, and a bridge without one is not trusted.
- **8 an t-Samhain 2836 BDE** — *The masons' custom* (Ros dhomhain). The bridge-masons form a fellowship with its own oath, sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, none to be paid for in ore. Its lodge is kept near the western crossing in the country of Ros dhomhain.
- **10 an Dàmhair 2833 BDE** — *The tavern roads begin* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). The first waypoint houses appear along the mining roads — ancestors of Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and the rest of the circuit.
- **11 an t-Sultain 2830 BDE** — *Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). The first keeper of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach is Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean. She serves carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, a dish the house has never stopped serving.
- **13 an Lùnastal 2827 BDE** — *The house at the middle of the road* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at each end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.
- **22 an Dàmhair 2824 BDE** — *The road-peace* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first recorded at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made.
- **23 an t-Sultain 2821 BDE** — *Seann Mhorn resettled* (Seann Mhorn). Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue. They say the old name came with the stones. It is the first such name the record shows being taken over rather than replaced.
- **20 an Dàmhair 2818 BDE** — *Seann Warr resettled* (Seann Warr). On the western coast, the harbour called Seann Warr is resettled in the same way, by families walking the new road from the mountain. They find house-footings there already and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.
- **23 an Lùnastal 2815 BDE** — *Death of Fionnlagh Dall* (Dùn ìseal). Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. By his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.
- **18 an t-Samhain 2815 BDE** — *Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The bearers take eleven days over the road with Fionnlagh Dall's body and lay it among graves older than any name at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. The Keepers who follow him cannot agree why he asked it, and the record gives two answers without choosing.
- **21 an t-Sultain 2810 BDE** — *The mausoleum consecrated*. Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first formally recorded burial — an unclaimed necropolis becoming a claimed one.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios 2805 BDE** — *The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach* (Cnoc dhìreach). A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial there. They are paid in ore by the Hall, one handful each a season, the only payment in ore the Law ever allowed.
- **25 an t-Iuchar 2611 BDE** — *Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame* (Dùn ìseal). For the first time the nine hearths choose a Keeper outside the house of Muireach: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich accepts it at Dùn ìseal after a season of refusal, on condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.
- **29 an Giblean 2607 BDE** — *The Four Houses sworn* (Dùn ìseal). Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the Keepers' office is bound to four custodian houses: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council but not their claim to the flame. Most of the island's later nobility descends, or says it does, from one of the four.
