- **28 an Cèitean 2603 BDE** — *The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the bay. The shrine keeps a lamp of ore burning at the Law's measure, and the other houses complain that Seann Dunn's measure is always fullest.
- **2 am Màrt 2599 BDE** — *The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Sliochd Raghnaill takes Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast for its seat, the same town whose household was the first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats rather than galleries and grows rich on the fishing.
- **31 am Màrt 2595 BDE** — *Round Eilean dhubh* (Eilean dhubh). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage in the record undertaken to see a coast rather than to fish it. The steersman is named in the house's songs as Tormod Ruadh. He brings back no report beyond rock, birds and the fact of having gone.
- **26 an t-Sultain 2591 BDE** — *The outlaws of the north-west waters* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence begin to take to boats and live off the north-western waters, raiding the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.
- **28 an Lùnastal 2587 BDE** — *The boat lost off the north-west* (Uilebheist na Mara). A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast, and the two men who swam home say something rose under it. The boat's village keeps a wake for it each year thereafter. Nothing further is recorded of the thing they saw.
- **23 an t-Samhain 2583 BDE** — *The fire at Baile chrom relit* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The fishers of Baile chrom relight the old beacon on the point after the loss, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile chrom.
- **25 an Dàmhair 2579 BDE** — *Seann Bhrenn resettled* (Seann Bhrenn). On the northern coast the harbour of Seann Bhrenn is resettled by fishers from the mountain's north side, who keep its old name as the western settlers had kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.
- **20 am Faoilleach 2575 BDE** — *The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh* (Cathair naomh). The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the largest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it is still growing.
- **22 an Dùbhlachd 2571 BDE** — *The panthers let pass* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats' crossing of the mountains is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept because it costs the carriers only time.
- **19 am Màrt 2558 BDE** — *The granaries of Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old unwritten custom of sharing asks. The granaries give the house the thing the Hall never had: people who owe it food.
- **18 an Gearran 2544 BDE** — *Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass and by little else.
- **16 an Cèitean 2531 BDE** — *The reverent centuries*. Generation after generation mines the same modest quantity, burns the same modest quantity, and nothing about the population changes. This is the last age in which that remains true.
- **17 an Giblean 2517 BDE** — *Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame* (Seann Dunn). The first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid is Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn. He is remembered for keeping the flame longer than any Keeper before him and changing nothing while he did.
- **5 an t-Sultain 2504 BDE** — *The shepherds of Achadh chaol* (Achadh chaol). Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits on the council at Dùn ìseal for a single season, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.
- **4 an Dàmhair 2490 BDE** — *The Keepers' count of the old places* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people, and they return with Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place. It does not say who built them, and the Keepers ruled that it should not guess.
- **2 an t-Samhain 2477 BDE** — *The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old obelisk above their town so that cattle will not rub against it. The ring is renewed by every generation afterward; the stone is never moved.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd 2463 BDE** — *The bath-house at Muileann ruadh* (Muileann ruadh). A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their carriers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, the first office it creates that has nothing to do with the ore.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd 2450 BDE** — *The silver weights of Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar). The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the smallest the weight of a barley-corn and the largest of a newborn lamb, and every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them. For the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.
- **28 am Faoilleach 2436 BDE** — *The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn* (Cnoc bhàn). A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and takes cutters again after the long exclusion. Its teachers keep Sìleas nic Coinnich's question in the form she left it: why does the ore bleed for one hand and not another.
- **26 an Gearran 2423 BDE** — *Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people* (Dùn ìseal). Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, on oath to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's record calls it a reconciliation. The school's own memory calls it a truce.
- **27 am Màrt 2418 BDE** — *Cathair mhòr walled* (Cathair mhòr). The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone around their headland town, the first town wall in the record. Nobody in the record says what they feared.
- **16 am Faoilleach 2413 BDE** — *Ceann leathan's fish-market* (Ceann leathan). Ceann leathan becomes the market for the southern fishing, trading dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks, and several sticks survive in the collection at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted objects there.
- **14 an Gearran 2408 BDE** — *The shrine at Inis thais* (Inis thais). A shrine is raised at Inis thais on the western coast to the ancestors lost at sea. Its keepers burn their season's handful of ore on the shore rather than indoors, so that the drowned can see it.
- **29 an Giblean 2403 BDE** — *Cuan shean's salt-pans* (Cuan shean). The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and preserves the fish of half the island.
- **31 am Màrt 2398 BDE** — *Baile fhiadhaich on the western heath* (Baile fhiadhaich). Baile fhiadhaich is founded on the western heath by salt-carriers from Cuan shean, on a stream that runs all summer. The heath round it is not worth ploughing, and its people keep goats.
- **2 am Màrt 2393 BDE** — *The sunny house* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south and is known from the first for its warmth, which is the only thing its name has ever meant.
- **1 an Gearran 2388 BDE** — *Cnoc leathan's market* (Cnoc leathan). Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.
- **23 an Lùnastal 2383 BDE** — *The fall in the high gallery* (Dùn ìseal). A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak in every gallery afterward, the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.
- **25 an t-Iuchar 2364 BDE** — *Cathair dhomhain founded* (Cathair dhomhain). Carriers who had settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and call it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly and its people are proud of it.
- **26 an t-Ògmhios 2344 BDE** — *A fishing town at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). The Red Hill's old settlement, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot where the Abhainn dhomhain meets the sea, on the ground later called Cathair dhearg. Its red stone gives it its name. At this time it is a place carriers pass through on their way to somewhere else.
- **28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE** — *Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh* (Dùn dhearg). At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. He is the first person in any record so called. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein and is careful to say so to the Hall.
- **9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE** — *The division of keeping* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division: the Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries; the Keeper may not raise spears. The division is the frame of Rodian government for the rest of the age.
- **11 an Lùnastal 2285 BDE** — *Goraidh Mòr's hall* (Dùn dhearg). Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes were still visible when the Library's surveyors walked the hill, and were measured and drawn then.
- **22 an t-Sultain 2280 BDE** — *The first road-toll* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay for the road-guards and the upkeep of the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses collect it. They also keep a share of it, and the record says so.
- **21 an Dàmhair 2245 BDE** — *Mòrag of the Roads* (Dùn dhearg). Goraidh Mòr's daughter Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after him. She is remembered as Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for walking every carriers' road on the island in her first years and ordering the bad stretches remade.
- **26 an t-Iuchar 2218 BDE** — *The golden house* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler rather than a family.
- **24 an Lùnastal 2205 BDE** — *The bridge-foot rebuilt* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone at Mòrag nan Rathad's order, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign in its keystone is Ailean Clachair's, recut. From this rebuilding the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.
- **16 am Faoilleach 2165 BDE** — *Dòmhnall Crùbach* (Dùn dhearg). Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and he governs through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow powerful in his reign.
- **14 an Gearran 2136 BDE** — *The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). The keepers of the waypoint houses round the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the collection of the road-toll into their own hands in Dòmhnall Crùbach's reign and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgment is generous to themselves, and the rolls record the sums.
- **19 an t-Samhain 2120 BDE** — *Baile àrsaidh on the western heath* (Baile àrsaidh). Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the dry heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh there, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions are thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and neighbours find the custom strange.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd 2120 BDE** — *The storm at Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.
- **15 am Màrt 2085 BDE** — *The stag-letters* (Muileann chiar). At Muileann chiar in the far east, the teachers of the stag's people turn the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters on Rodos in use by the Ròdaich. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.
- **12 an Cèitean 2085 BDE** — *The letters set against the obelisk* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). Stag-scholars carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and compare them with the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write down that the stone's writers were not their teachers, the first thing the Ròdaich ever put in writing about the old people.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios 2085 BDE** — *Sìleas Dhonn* (Dùn dhearg). Sìleas Dhonn, Dòmhnall Crùbach's niece, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are made to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.
- **14 an Gearran 2008 BDE** — *The lords of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, headed by Lachlann Ciar, begins to take the road-toll for itself and send none of it to Dùn dhearg.
- **12 an Cèitean 2005 BDE** — *Iain Garbh* (Dùn dhearg). Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls from Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.
- **13 an Giblean 2000 BDE** — *The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg* (Muileann òg). Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and his men burn the toll-house at Muileann òg that Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. It is the first war in the record between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. The Hall refuses to bless either side.
- **19 an t-Samhain 1999 BDE** — *Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses Iain Garbh's messengers at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying the flame does not warm men who are going to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.
- **21 an Dàmhair 1998 BDE** — *The fight at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). The men of Caol leathan meet Iain Garbh's levies at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before giving way. Forty are dead on both sides. The ford is called by the carriers for a long time afterward the ford of the forty.
- **16 am Faoilleach 1997 BDE** — *Baile ghlas burned* (Baile ghlas). Retreating toward Caol leathan, Lachlann Ciar's men burn Baile ghlas so that Iain Garbh's levies will find no grain. The town's people walk to Cathair dhomhain and many never return.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd 1996 BDE** — *Baile chiar holds* (Baile chiar). Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate against both armies in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither side attacks it.
- **2 an t-Samhain 1994 BDE** — *The siege of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Iain Garbh closes Caol leathan from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea and he cannot close the harbour. His levies begin to go home for the harvest. The siege ends without an assault.
- **4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE** — *The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. The War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.
- **12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE** — *The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, which they keep at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages will read more into the stone than they did.
- **14 an Dùbhlachd 1963 BDE** — *Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt* (Caol fhiadhaich). Caol fhiadhaich, on the south-western shore, which had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege, is given a share of the western tolls by Lachlann Ciar in thanks. The town builds a harbour wall with it.
- **15 an t-Samhain 1955 BDE** — *Death of Iain Garbh* (Dùn dhearg). Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona has him buried in the hall's floor and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.
- **17 an Dàmhair 1953 BDE** — *Catrìona Ghlic* (Dùn dhearg). Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg and sends her own son to sit with the flame for a season, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. The Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again by the end of her reign.
- **8 an Cèitean 1918 BDE** — *The house on the northern road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.
- **9 an Giblean 1914 BDE** — *The house in the cold pass* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). A stone house is built high in the pass on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. Its keepers are paid by the Hall in grain and by the crown in cloth, and complain of both.
- **11 am Màrt 1910 BDE** — *Inis mhòr grows* (Inis mhòr). The harbour at Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people petition Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.
- **10 an Gearran 1844 BDE** — *Muileann shean on the northern road* (Muileann shean). A mill is built at Muileann shean, on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The miller is paid by the Hall in grain, and pays the rìgh's toll in flour.
- **1 an t-Sultain 1779 BDE** — *The unrecorded rulers* (Dùn dhearg). Between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar, the later king-list sets eleven names at Dùn dhearg, of which nothing is known but the names and the order. The Keepers' roll for the same years gives five Keepers, and their names also are all it gives.
- **3 an Lùnastal 1713 BDE** — *Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters* (Muileann chiar). Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life.
- **22 an t-Iuchar 1700 BDE** — *Ealasaid Chiar* (Dùn dhearg). Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She orders him to set down the names of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him, in order.
- **20 an Lùnastal 1684 BDE** — *The first written king-list*. Rulers begin to be recorded by name rather than remembered by story — a shift the later succession records will inherit directly.
- **18 an t-Sultain 1668 BDE** — *The contents of Tormod's roll* (Dùn dhearg). Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, begins with Goraidh Mòr and runs to Ealasaid Chiar. Its earliest names come from the reciters and the later ones from living memory, and he marks which are which. The roll disagrees with the Keepers' recited roll in three places, and Tormod writes down both readings without choosing.
- **17 an Dàmhair 1648 BDE** — *The Keepers' roll written down* (Dùn ìseal). Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their recited roll set down in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. Its first name is Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.
- **15 an t-Samhain 1430 BDE** — *The watchers of the dark wood* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). A small company settles on the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood nobody had ever cleared, and keeps watch there for a black horned beast they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of the watchers' own accounts are older than the later faith that claims them.
- **14 an Dùbhlachd 1420 BDE** — *The wood-watchers in the stag's grove* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a teaching-place. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.
- **12 am Faoilleach 1415 BDE** — *The stag's people claim the dark wood* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). In answer, the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying the first stag had come from there. Each side now claims both woods, and in each wood the two companies meet and do not speak.
- **10 an Gearran 1403 BDE** — *The holy-wood dispute*. The first recorded conflict between rival religious claims to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag — settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner.
- **11 am Màrt 1395 BDE** — *The boundary stones of the woods* (Dùn dhearg). The division of the woods is made at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath: the stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at both woods' edges with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones survive.
- **9 an Giblean 1385 BDE** — *Calum Liath's surveyors* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark how it thickens and thins. The work takes the cutters out of the ore-season for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.
- **27 an t-Samhain 1380 BDE** — *The measuring of the vein*. The first attempt to estimate how much obsidian the mountain holds. The estimate will prove wildly optimistic.
- **26 an Dùbhlachd 1380 BDE** — *The reckoning of the cords* (Dùn ìseal). Calum Liath's reckoning, cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal, holds that the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It was read out at the council and received in silence, which the Hall took for assent.
- **22 an Gearran 1355 BDE** — *The deaths in the lower gallery* (Dùn ìseal). Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been in the galleries less than a season. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.
- **24 am Faoilleach 1345 BDE** — *The apprentice-binding custom*. Young Rodians are first formally bound to a master custodian of the vein for seven years before being trusted near the ore themselves — the origin of every later mining guild's structure.
- **21 an Giblean 1345 BDE** — *Oighrig Bhàn's first bound* (Dùn ìseal). Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before touching the vein. Four of the twelve are later Keepers, which is the custom's best argument for itself.
- **23 am Màrt 1325 BDE** — *The stag's people take apprentices* (Cnoc bhàn). The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn adopts the seven years for its own cutters and adds a teaching to it: an apprentice keeps a written account of every strike, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.
- **9 an Giblean 1325 BDE** — *The long reign of Fearchar Òg* (Dùn dhearg). Fearchar Òg, who made the division of the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered for nothing so much as for dying old. The list gives him a byname, Òg, the young, from his accession as a boy, and it stuck.
- **8 an Cèitean 1325 BDE** — *The silver tokens* (Muileann chiar). Fearchar Òg's clerks begin paying the road-guards in small silver rings of Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first time a ruler on Rodos pays in metal. The rings travel further than the guards do.
- **20 an Cèitean 1325 BDE** — *The toll-house at Àth ghlas* (Àth ghlas). A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. It is the first toll-house on the island with a keeper sent from the rìgh's hall rather than chosen locally.
- **18 an t-Ògmhios 1325 BDE** — *The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The road-guards of the south begin meeting at Ceann leathan each year to fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose; the field it used is the one where Còmhrag Ceann leathan is later fought. The first winner the record names is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 1325 BDE** — *The fair at Muileann òg* (Fèill Muileann òg). Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town, and a fair is held there each harvest for the western and southern roads to trade. The fair is the ancestor of Fèill Muileann òg.
- **3 an Lùnastal 1325 BDE** — *The landing on the Abhainn uaine* (Cidhe Beag). A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that grain from the lowlands can go upriver in boats rather than on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg and lose.
- **11 am Màrt 1305 BDE** — *The river-boats* (Abhainn uaine). Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. Boatmen become a fellowship of their own, with an oath sworn on a paddle, and they compete with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.
- **8 an Cèitean 1305 BDE** — *The boatmen of Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its boatyards build the flat hide boats for every river on the island.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 1305 BDE** — *Beathag Mhòr* (Dùn dhearg). Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. She is the first ruler the list calls banrìgh, queen, rather than rìgh with a woman's name after it, and the change of word is the list's own.
- **12 am Faoilleach 1280 BDE** — *The hall moves to Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, so as to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the house of Ìomhar's graves. Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Rodos from this reign onward, whatever else changes.
- **10 an Gearran 1280 BDE** — *Dùn dhearg after the move* (Dùn dhearg). Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves refuse to send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in any hand but their own.
- **22 an Gearran 1280 BDE** — *The red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built of the red stone that gives the town its name, on the rise above the harbour. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign into its lintel as if it were a bridge.
- **23 am Màrt 1280 BDE** — *Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhomhain). The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, resents the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls, and the two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.
- **9 an Giblean 1280 BDE** — *Disputed hands* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more disputes over which households hold a right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Oighrig Bhàn's successor as Keeper, Dùghall mac Raghnaill, asks the queen for a counting.
- **11 am Faoilleach 1255 BDE** — *Beathag Mhòr orders the count* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write; the Keepers are to judge.
- **9 an Gearran 1255 BDE** — *The waypoint houses as counting-houses* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The census-takers use the waypoint houses as their stations, since every household on the island is within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost. The census is later remembered in the houses as a good year.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios 1255 BDE** — *The census of hands*. The first attempt to count, island-wide, how many households hold a customary right to burn obsidian at all — proof the reverent tradition was already being formally rationed, not simply assumed.
- **21 an t-Iuchar 1255 BDE** — *The count of hands* (Cathair dhearg). The census rolls kept at Cathair dhearg give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused households are written on a separate roll, and it is the separate roll that later generations went looking for when they wished to prove an ancestor's standing.
- **19 an Lùnastal 1255 BDE** — *The refused of Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). Most of the refused households on the north-eastern coast are fisher-families around Seann Tarr who had never burned ore at all and now found they had no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses it. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.
- **17 an t-Sultain 1255 BDE** — *The light at Baile ìseal* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.
- **16 an Dàmhair 1255 BDE** — *The light at Muileann bheag* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt, the ancestor of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.
- **14 an t-Samhain 1255 BDE** — *The light at Àth dhearg* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). The old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg is rebuilt by Sliochd Raghnaill, to mark the passage in toward Seann Tarr. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd 1255 BDE** — *Death of Beathag Mhòr* (Dùn dhearg). Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and, by her own order, is carried back to Dùn dhearg to be buried among the house of Ìomhar. The procession between the two is the longest royal journey in the record to this point.
- **24 an Cèitean 1254 BDE** — *Ruairidh Liath* (Cathair dhearg). Ruairidh Liath, Beathag Mhòr's son, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is already grey when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's joke, the only one it makes.
- **19 an Lùnastal 1234 BDE** — *The Silver Feud begins* (Muileann chiar). Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers that silver is not holy and so not the crown's either, citing Muireach Liath's ruling. They close the workings rather than pay.
- **17 an t-Sultain 1233 BDE** — *The closing of the silver* (Muileann chiar). For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the carriers' tolls go uncollected on the eastern road. The record calls it the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.
- **16 an Dàmhair 1230 BDE** — *The Keeper's judgment on the silver* (Dùn ìseal). Asked by both parties, the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that Muireach Liath's words stand: silver is not the mountain's. But he rules too that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels on. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair reopens the workings, and both call it a victory.
- **14 an t-Samhain 1229 BDE** — *The Muileann chiar weight made law* (Muileann chiar). As part of the settlement, the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the island's roads. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.
- **25 an Giblean 1210 BDE** — *The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg* (Muileann dhearg). The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the work from the silversmiths. They go on casting bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold exactly the Law's measure.
- **24 an Cèitean 1209 BDE** — *Seonag Chrom* (Cathair dhearg). Seonag Chrom, Ruairidh Liath's granddaughter, rules at Cathair dhearg. She has the clerks' office there given a room of its own in the red hall and a stipend in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year rather than reign by reign.
- **22 an t-Ògmhios 1138 BDE** — *Inis bheag's school of letters* (Inis bheag). At Inis bheag on the northern coast a teacher of the stag's people begins teaching letters to fishers' children who will never cut ore. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll records it with the remark that fish do not need reading.
- **21 an t-Iuchar 1066 BDE** — *Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi nic Tormoid, a descendant of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is the first clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg whose own hand can be told apart from the others in the surviving copies. Her entries are short and she never gives a reason when a fact will do. Much of what this record knows of the middle of the age is in her hand or copied from it.
- **30 an Dùbhlachd 995 BDE** — *The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell on the northern coast, fowler families keep a hawk in each household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, saying that the flame is a hunger and should be fed the way a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd.
- **28 am Faoilleach 923 BDE** — *The hawk-rite spreads along the north coast* (Inis ìseal). The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell east to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag on the northern shore. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time the Hall says so about any rite.
- **1 am Faoilleach 852 BDE** — *The sting-oath at Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). The custom of swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, where the harbour court adopts it for every oath of trade. A merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours for the rest of the age.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd 780 BDE** — *The wolf-stone at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the shrine's keepers begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz and was carried from the mountain on a sledge, which cost more than the shrine.
- **28 an Gearran 709 BDE** — *The strike-books compared* (Cnoc bhàn). A teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, Donnchadh mac Iain, reads through generations of apprentices' strike-books and finds that the ore bleeds brighter for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever house they come from. He argues from it that the vein answers practice. The house's elders answer that the vein answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.
- **30 am Faoilleach 699 BDE** — *Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it a copying, which it was.
- **7 an t-Sultain 682 BDE** — *The founding of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh's rival school*. A breakaway sect argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over in a very different form.
- **9 an Lùnastal 669 BDE** — *The school at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain's school at Muileann chaol keeps its own strike-books and adds a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag argue by letter for the rest of the age, and the letters are kept by both.
- **4 an t-Samhain 633 BDE** — *The Hall hears the two schools* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll notes the hearing and the refusal. It was the most-cited refusal in the Hall's history.
- **6 an Dàmhair 623 BDE** — *What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). Stag-scholars from Muileann chaol visit Calbh Cnoc ghorm and find they cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them that the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. Neither the stone nor the saying is explained in any later hand.
- **21 an Lùnastal 613 BDE** — *The digging at Làrach an Dùin* (Làrach an Dùin). Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold. They find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 608 BDE** — *Baile ghorm's penance* (Baile ghorm). The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm pay their penance by keeping the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach in repair. The road is still called the diggers' road in the southern hills.
- **16 am Faoilleach 593 BDE** — *Lachlann Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered for his granaries, which he builds in every province seat that will take one, and for a law about them.
- **14 an Gearran 588 BDE** — *The shared-meal law written* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh set the old unwritten custom down as law at Cathair dhearg: any household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors wrote it into the rolls in full. It is the first law in the record made by rìgh and Keeper together.
- **19 an t-Samhain 574 BDE** — *The granary of Cnoc mhòr* (Cnoc mhòr). Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.
- **18 an Dùbhlachd 564 BDE** — *The common granaries of the mountain* (Muileann chiar). Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.
- **12 an Cèitean 554 BDE** — *The granary at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). A common granary is built inside the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first put behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns send dried fish to it as their share, since they have no grain to send.
- **10 an t-Ògmhios 544 BDE** — *Raiders in the eastern waters* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Boats of outlaws begin raiding the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest are not caught.
- **15 am Màrt 538 BDE** — *Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn, Lachlann Bàn's daughter, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children. The houses begin to count their claims before her reign is half done.
- **13 an Giblean 527 BDE** — *The late snow on the high passes* (Cnoc ghlas). The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas report snow lying on the high passes long past the time the galleries should open. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety. The mountain households wait.
- **5 an t-Sultain 527 BDE** — *The poor season in the mountain* (Muileann chiar). The galleries open late and close early, and the ore carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade. By the end of the season they are eating their seed.
- **4 an Dàmhair 526 BDE** — *The first recorded famine averted*. A poor mining season nearly starves three settlements before the shared-meal custom, formalized a generation earlier, holds and prevents it — the tradition's first real test.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd 526 BDE** — *The granaries opened* (Muileann gheal). Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal, and when they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice. The carriers carry it for no fee. No one in the three settlements is recorded as having died of hunger that winter.
- **18 an Dàmhair 525 BDE** — *Àth dhìreach after the poor season* (Àth dhìreach). At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought the grain up are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them died old, and the right with him.
- **16 an t-Samhain 525 BDE** — *The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain* (Dùn dhearg). The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had refused Cathair dhearg their accounts for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. Peigi nic Tormoid's successor notes that they did not.
- **19 an t-Sultain 488 BDE** — *Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg without an heir of her body, and the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it, ends with her. The red hall is shut and its clerks keep it.
- **10 an Giblean 486 BDE** — *The four houses meet* (Dùn ìseal). The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, since no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, will not claim at all.
- **12 am Màrt 483 BDE** — *The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Seann Dunn). The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair accepts on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the kings' burying-place.
- **11 an Gearran 482 BDE** — *Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in his own house's hands and has the king-list recopied from the beginning, with a line drawn under Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.
- **13 am Faoilleach 462 BDE** — *The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged* (Seann Dunn). Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. Its ore-lamp is still said by the other houses to burn fuller than the measure, and a Keeper's cutter is sent to check it every season.
- **27 an Giblean 458 BDE** — *Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Dùn dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as agreed. His son Tormod Òg succeeds him without a meeting of the houses, and nobody asks for one.
- **29 am Màrt 439 BDE** — *The gap in the list* (Cathair dhearg). Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh the king-list kept at Cathair dhearg gives the names of nine rulers of the house of Tormod with their years and little else. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors were diligent and brief; in these reigns the rolls record mostly harvests, tolls and repairs to bridges.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios 423 BDE** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, since carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is recut again in the keystone. The span stands on the same piers as Mòrag nan Rathad's.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 408 BDE** — *The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn is repaired after a flood takes its eastern approach. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone and leave it untouched.
- **21 an Lùnastal 393 BDE** — *The bridge at Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western one without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.
- **19 an t-Sultain 377 BDE** — *The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). A bridge is built at the harbour town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing in the lowlands. The masons' roll lists the names of the forty who built it, all of them of Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin, who had learned the trade because the boats were idle.
- **18 an Dàmhair 362 BDE** — *The bridge at Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. The keystone carries the hearth-sign and, beside it, the first mason's mark in the record: the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it.
- **16 an t-Samhain 347 BDE** — *The far-off house* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It has become so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and the name comes from the saying.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd 331 BDE** — *Fire-water on the northern road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). The house on the northern road on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe begins serving a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule it is not a burning and not their concern. The house's trade doubles.
- **13 am Faoilleach 316 BDE** — *Caol mhòr in the north-west* (Caol mhòr). Fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to collect them. The record for the north-west in this age is thin, and most of it is complaints about that.
- **4 an t-Samhain 300 BDE** — *Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins trading seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. The seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Rodos for many generations.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd 285 BDE** — *The high pastures of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.
- **30 am Faoilleach 270 BDE** — *Inis mhin on the northern shore* (Inis mhin). Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, is recorded in the rolls for the first time, when its headman comes to Inis mhòr's wool-fair to complain about the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and is the town's whole record for the age.
- **28 an Gearran 254 BDE** — *The raid on the western strands* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.
- **29 am Màrt 239 BDE** — *The second sighting* (Uilebheist na Mara). Two boats from Baile chrom report something vast moving under them in the north-western water, the second sighting in the record. One boat does not come home. The wake kept in Baile chrom for the first loss is kept for both.
- **27 an Giblean 224 BDE** — *Round the islands* (Seann Tarr). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr and make the round of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is recorded as wanting to.
- **26 an Cèitean 208 BDE** — *Summer herders on Eilean ruadh* (Eilean ruadh). Families from the coast begin taking sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bringing them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders reuse.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios 193 BDE** — *Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler since Mòrag nan Rathad to walk the whole road circuit, and she does it twice.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 190 BDE** — *Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The house's keepers still tell it.
- **21 an Lùnastal 186 BDE** — *Anna Ruadh at the sunny house* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). On the eastern road Anna Ruadh stays at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and grants its keepers the right to a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan. It is the only waypoint house on the island with a royal charter.
- **12 an t-Ògmhios 183 BDE** — *Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the fishers' dispute with the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The ruling doubles the fish going inland and halves its price at Dùn ìseal.
- **11 an t-Iuchar 180 BDE** — *The contest at Ceann leathan in stone* (Ceann leathan). Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field and a silver ring from the red hall as its prize. The contest draws fighters from across the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 177 BDE** — *A wood-watcher in the red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. It is the first sign of the wood-watchers' rite in the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal and receives no answer that the rolls record.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios 173 BDE** — *Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers* (Cathair dhomhain). The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of keeping the Law strictly, refuses to take a wood-watcher, and its people say the capital has given its omens to people who sit in trees. The rivalry of the two towns takes a religious turn it never loses.
- **26 an Cèitean 170 BDE** — *Death of Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg with the house of Ìomhar and her own house's kings. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.
- **27 an Giblean 167 BDE** — *Coinneach Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin copying the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws, and several of those copies survive where the originals do not.
- **16 an t-Samhain 164 BDE** — *Seumas Bàn keeps the flame* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. He finds, on reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal, that more than half the Keepers of the age have been of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survived.
- **18 an Dàmhair 161 BDE** — *The rites counted at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn has the Hall's clerks list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that claims the vein, so the council can know what it is keeping. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks note that the list would not have been needed a thousand years before.
- **19 an t-Sultain 159 BDE** — *The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter* (Seann Skell). The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell refuse the Hall's cutter who comes to check their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. It is the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright.
- **21 an Lùnastal 156 BDE** — *The wolf-sworn build a hall* (Caol leathan). The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own around the white wolf-stone at the town gate and take oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. They say one god watches the whole island as the guard watches the road.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd 153 BDE** — *The sting-oath at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell on the western coast the harbour court's sting-oath becomes a creed: its keepers say that one power stings the liar wherever he is, and that the scorpion is only its sign. The Hall's roll records it as a new teaching. It is the first on the island to call itself the only true one.
- **4 an t-Samhain 150 BDE** — *Seann Vell swears on the sting* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship rather than for swearing on.
- **13 am Faoilleach 147 BDE** — *The dark wood keeps its own rite* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag stop sending to the Hall for judgment of their disputes and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same.
- **11 an Gearran 144 BDE** — *The naming of the nine faiths' common ancestor*. A single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name — the moment 'Rodian belief' stops being one thing.
- **16 an t-Samhain 141 BDE** — *The council divided by rite* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he now keeps the flame for eight peoples who each think they are its only keepers. The seating is kept for the rest of the age.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd 139 BDE** — *Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims* (Allt an Àigh). Whatever their rite, pilgrims go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon, the one custom on the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. The path from Caol shean is repaved by pilgrims of four different rites in the same season.
- **19 an t-Sultain 136 BDE** — *The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the provincial rolls. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.
- **18 an Dàmhair 133 BDE** — *Cnoc dhìreach's weavers* (Cnoc dhìreach). The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, the one on the carriers' road south of the springs and not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth the carriers wear on the high passes. The two Cnoc dhìreachs are told apart in the rolls by that cloth.
- **23 an t-Iuchar 130 BDE** — *The dyers of Muileann bhàn* (Muileann bhàn). The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of the whole mountain country begins to be dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.
- **21 an Lùnastal 127 BDE** — *Muileann dhomhain's mill* (Muileann dhomhain). A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the mountain districts' common granaries. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, which the rolls record as fair.
- **26 an Cèitean 124 BDE** — *The flood at Àth chiar* (Àth chiar). Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar and carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district, built on a rise, is untouched and feeds the town through the winter.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios 121 BDE** — *The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin laying oyster-beds in the shallows, a practice they say came with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll records the claim and marks it doubtful.
- **20 an Gearran 119 BDE** — *Seann Vell's harbour* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the trade of the southern fishing and the Muileann chiar silver brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.
- **22 am Faoilleach 116 BDE** — *The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil from the north-west carried the whole length of the island.
- **19 an Giblean 113 BDE** — *Muileann naomh's mill-shrine* (Muileann naomh). At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, the miller keeping the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who inspects it finds the measure kept and the flour good.
- **21 am Màrt 110 BDE** — *Dùn thais walled* (Dùn thais). Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled and a temple of the stag's people is raised in it, the first built in stone rather than kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios 107 BDE** — *The wool-fair of Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair each shearing that draws buyers from the whole northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.
- **18 an Cèitean 104 BDE** — *Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows large enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses do not like it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.
- **13 an Lùnastal 101 BDE** — *The northern boats at Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, meant for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.
- **15 an t-Iuchar 99 BDE** — *Drought at Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and the district's common granary is emptied by spring. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the following harvests.
- **10 an Dàmhair 96 BDE** — *Baile chaol's repayment* (Baile chaol). The rolls at Baile chaol record Achadh shean's repayment of the drought grain, measure by measure, down to the last. The clerk adds that it is the first such debt in the rolls repaid in full.
- **11 an t-Sultain 93 BDE** — *The panthers late* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats' crossing of the southern road comes late and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers call it a sign of a hard winter and are right. The Keepers note it without comment.
- **13 an Lùnastal 90 BDE** — *The watch-tower at Baile ruadh* (Baile ruadh). A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands. It is manned by Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin by turns, and it is the only tower of war the age built.
- **11 an t-Sultain 87 BDE** — *Cuan ruadh's boats* (Cuan ruadh). The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.
- **10 an Dàmhair 84 BDE** — *The drowned-feast at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours north as far as Seann Warr.
- **8 an t-Samhain 81 BDE** — *The potters of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin firing a hard red ware from the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it are found on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.
- **19 an Giblean 79 BDE** — *Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. The red ware of the western road is made there for the rest of the age.
- **18 an Cèitean 76 BDE** — *Cathair fhada founded* (Cathair fhada). Cathair fhada is raised on the southern coast by families moving out of the crowded harbours round Cathair dhearg. Its founders bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.
- **16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE** — *Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine* (Cnoc naomh). The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.
- **15 an t-Iuchar 70 BDE** — *Mòr nic Coinnich crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Her name is the last written in the king-list of the Holy Age.
- **2 an Giblean 60 BDE** — *The Hall's roll at the close of the age* (Dùn ìseal). At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds the names of one hundred and forty Keepers from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list the names of more than ninety rulers from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law has not been changed in a word since Fionnlagh Dall's stone cup. The cup is still on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.
- **1 an Cèitean 50 BDE** — *The last age of even population*. Chroniclers later look back and note, with some unease, that this is the final stretch of Rodian history in which no single family held meaningfully more years of life than any other.

## Age III · An Aois Scaraidh

- **6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE** — *Land is found*. Word returns of a land across open water, unpeopled by anyone resembling the Ròdaich. No record survives of who found it first.
- **9 an t-Samhain 39 BDE** — *The report heard at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). The report of the far land is repeated at Cathair dhearg in the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, by three separate crews from the western harbours, none of whom claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three accounts and notes that they agree on the coast and on nothing else.
- **8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE** — *The Choosing*. A vote — or something the later chronicles call a vote — decides who will go. Volunteers only. No lots are drawn, no conscription recorded.
- **12 an t-Sultain 38 BDE** — *The roll of the willing* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell the harbour scribes open a roll for those who mean to go, entered by household rather than by name. The roll is kept on boards in the harbour-house, and a later hand notes that entries were struck out as often as they were added.
- **11 an Dàmhair 38 BDE** — *The queen neither commands nor forbids* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag declares that the crown will neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back. Her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell within the season.
- **14 an Lùnastal 37 BDE** — *The custodians count the cost* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal, reckons which of the households holding the customary right to burn the ore have entered the roll. The custody-book puts it at nearly one household in five, and adds that the reckoning was made twice because the first figure was not believed.
- **16 an t-Iuchar 35 BDE** — *The ships are built*. The island's shipwrights, used to modest coastal craft, build vessels meant to survive open water for the first time in Rodian memory.
- **14 an Lùnastal 35 BDE** — *Alasdair Saor lays the first keel* (Seann Skell). On the strand below Seann Skell, the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull ever built on Rodos. The island's craft until then were sewn-plank coasters that never slept out of sight of land.
- **26 an Lùnastal 35 BDE** — *The oaks of Doire fhionn* (Doire fhionn). The oak grove that gave Doire fhionn its name is felled for the fleet's keels and carried down to the coast by ox-sled. The grove never regrew, and the village kept a name it no longer had a reason for.
- **24 an t-Sultain 35 BDE** — *The shipwrights' fellowship bound* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor takes the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into a single fellowship, binding each apprentice for seven years in the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.
- **12 an t-Sultain 34 BDE** — *The trial hull lost off Inis àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The first finished hull is sailed out past Inis àrsaidh to be tried in open water and founders in a following sea. Eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor changes the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the changed pattern.
- **11 an Dàmhair 32 BDE** — *The rope-walks of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and turns its hemp fields over entirely to cordage for the fleet. The town's rope trade outlasts the Sundering by some centuries.
- **9 an t-Samhain 31 BDE** — *The sail-cloth levy* (Baile àrsaidh). Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh is asked for a set length of close-woven cloth for sails, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many households paid does not.
- **20 an Giblean 27 BDE** — *The star-lore taught at Cuan ruadh* (Cuan ruadh). Old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors on the island who had ever kept a course by night, teach the fleet's pilots to hold a heading by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part has not survived.
- **19 an Cèitean 22 BDE** — *The volunteers name their leaders* (Seann Skell). The households on the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose their own leaders: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein. The custody-book records the choice and nothing of how it was made.
- **17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE** — *The handful for the new hearth* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house rules on whether departing custodians may carry the ore. Each ship may take one sealed measure, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. The ruling is the only text in the custody-book addressed to people who were leaving.
- **16 an t-Iuchar 10 BDE** — *The west quay lengthened* (Seann Skell). The west quay at Seann Skell is lengthened with dressed stone so that the deep hulls can lie alongside it at low water. Masons are brought from the capital to do the work, and the new stones are the ones the later rite would be held on.
- **20 an Gearran 2 BDE** — *The provisioning debate*. A dispute over how much of the island's stored grain the departing ships may take nearly cancels the whole expedition. It is resolved, unrecorded how, within a season.
- **21 am Màrt 2 BDE** — *Àth shean shuts its granaries* (Àth shean). During the dispute over the fleet's grain, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, Tormod mac Coinnich, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them. The watch is kept until the matter is settled, and Tormod is not recorded as holding office afterward.
- **3 an Giblean 2 BDE** — *Grain down Abhainn dhomhain* (Abhainn dhomhain). Once the dispute is settled, grain barges are sent down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital and on by coast to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts the barges passing and makes the count forty-one.
- **2 an Cèitean 2 BDE** — *The fleet assembled* (Seann Skell). The fleet lies at Seann Skell complete. The custody-book gives it as nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin corrects this to twenty-one, and no one since has been able to settle which is right.
- **18 an Giblean 1 DE** — *The night of lamps* (Seann Skell). On the last night before the sailing, every house along the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning until morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering recorded as a custom, and the town kept it long after the reason was a story.
- **19 an Giblean 1 DE** — *The Setting-Out*. The volunteers depart. The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor.
- **19 an Giblean 1 DE** — *The sunwise turn* (Seann Skell). Before making for open water the fleet goes once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The record ends at the harbour mouth.
- **22 am Faoilleach 5 DE** — *The years counted from the turn* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes adopt it only a generation later.
- **27 an Dàmhair 5 DE** — *A report reaches Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). A report of the fleet reaches Seann Skell. The custody-book does not say how or by whom it came, only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water and missing its end.
- **24 an Dùbhlachd 5 DE** — *Two landfalls*. What fragmentary report ever returns describes two separate coasts reached, not one — the seed, in this telling, of two later peoples rather than one.
- **1 an Lùnastal 7 DE** — *Mòrag's line struck* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag removes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Rodos. The act is entered without comment between a grain ruling and the repair of a bridge.
- **3 an t-Iuchar 14 DE** — *The thinning*. Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing required fades across the departed's own children. By the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Rodos would recognize.
- **28 an t-Sultain 14 DE** — *The custodians' second reckoning* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house counts again the households that hold the right to the ore. The loss is set down as one hand in five, and beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein itself answers no differently for those who stayed.
- **1 an Lùnastal 15 DE** — *The Mourning Custom*. Rodos formalizes a mourning rite for the departed that is not quite grief and not quite celebration — reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.
- **27 an Dàmhair 15 DE** — *The white sorrow first kept at court* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag keeps the new mourning for her sister in undyed wool, with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and by the next generation it is kept in every harbour town on the island.
- **7 am Faoilleach 16 DE** — *Population correction*. With a portion of the obsidian-bonded population gone, Rodian society reorganizes around a smaller, more concentrated custodian class — the shape every later aristocracy inherits.
- **4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE** — *The seven houses of custody* (Muileann dhearg). The remaining custodian households are regrouped into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. The division is the first in the record to treat the right to the ore as something inherited by house rather than earned by apprenticeship.
- **28 an t-Iuchar 16 DE** — *Death of Queen Beathag* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Rodos to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.
- **25 an t-Samhain 22 DE** — *The empty harbor rite*. A ceremony develops around the specific dock the ships departed from, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can precisely date anymore.
- **24 an Dùbhlachd 25 DE** — *The harbour at half trade* (Seann Skell). Seann Skell's harbour-master records his berths at half their former use. The fishing households that had crewed the fleet are simply gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean lay off hands for the first time.
- **8 an Gearran 26 DE** — *The second silence*. A rumor of a second, smaller crossing — fewer ships, no surviving record of a destination — is neither confirmed nor denied by anything that survives.
- **5 am Màrt 28 DE** — *The watch at Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). Fishing families at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, taking turns by household. The watch lapses within a generation, and no sail is recorded.
- **13 am Màrt 28 DE** — *The renaming of the west quay*. The dock the ships departed from is given a new name specifically so ordinary trade could resume using the old one without the association — an early, quiet act of managed forgetting.
- **15 an Lùnastal 28 DE** — *Cidhe an Diosail* (Seann Skell). In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.
- **21 an Lùnastal 28 DE** — *Roghnaich takes its narrow sense*. In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to appear with no object at all, meaning to have chosen the crossing. Scribes of the next century use it this way without explaining it, which is the surest sign it had become ordinary speech.
- **31 an Lùnastal 28 DE** — *The first generation to never see the sea empty*. Children born just after the Setting-Out grow up never having known the harbor with those particular ships in it — the exact moment departure stops being an event and starts being a fact of history.
- **8 an t-Sultain 28 DE** — *Death of Alasdair Saor* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.
- **27 an t-Ògmhios 45 DE** — *The closing of the shipwrights' guild*. With no more ocean-crossing vessels needed, the guild that built the Sundering fleet quietly dissolves — its techniques half-forgotten by the time anyone thinks to need them again.
- **29 an Cèitean 46 DE** — *The keel-moulds burned* (Seann Skell). The patterns and moulds of the dissolved fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are broken up and burned as firewood during a hard season. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed, not of what was in it.
- **30 an Giblean 70 DE** — *The mountain divided among the houses* (Muileann dhearg). The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms the Small-Burning measure for each of them. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.
- **14 an t-Iuchar 70 DE** — *The coppice law of Doire fhionn* (Doire fhionn). With the great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.
- **12 an Lùnastal 70 DE** — *The lamps kept at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, which the priests do not correct.
- **9 an Dàmhair 70 DE** — *Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is a list of the ore burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first.
- **7 an t-Samhain 86 DE** — *Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned* (Cathair dhearg). King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and uneventful reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.
- **6 an Dùbhlachd 110 DE** — *The silversmiths of Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). The silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is worked into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses.
