- **4 an Dàmhair 1929 DE** — *The families of Baile dhìreach* (Baile dhìreach). At Baile dhìreach the descendants of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, are asked by each side which they are. The record says most of them refused to answer, and that neither side forced them.
- **20 an Dàmhair 1929 DE** — *The last ship from the west* (An Cuan Siar). The last ship recorded arriving from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and she sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.
- **1 an t-Samhain 1929 DE** — *The truce of Àth àrsaidh* (Àth àrsaidh). Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession. They agree a truce: the humans remaining on Rodos to withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, the council to leave the concession towns standing.
- **2 an t-Samhain 1929 DE** — *Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns* (Baile Mòr ruadh). Baile Mòr ruadh, the largest town of the north-west, is named in the truce as the place where the columns will be received. Its Ròdaich people are given the choice of staying or going south. The record gives the numbers of each and they are close.
- **20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE** — *The columns go north* (Cuan shean). The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and that none was helped.
- **30 an t-Samhain 1929 DE** — *The columns at Àth chrom* (Àth chrom). The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on the way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and the count is the last the Ròdaich make of the humans on Rodos in this age.
- **1 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE** — *Àth leathan* (Àth leathan). At Àth leathan, on the last stage before the northern territory, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town record that the humans asked the name of the place, and that the name was written down by several of them.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE** — *The ship that sailed west* (Cuan shean). Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails west from Cuan shean with his officials in the last ship on the island that could make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom records her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Rodos records her arriving anywhere.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE** — *The beacons relit* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, continue to be kept, with nothing in them.
- **29 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE** — *The rolls sent to Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The custodians send what survives of the age's rolls, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.
- **1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE** — *The Severance*. The war ends with the crossing itself closed. Whatever let humans reach Rodos shuts. The humans still on the island are shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in its immediate wake.

## Age V · An Aois Ùr

- **22 am Màrt 1930 DE** — *The Tuathaich homeland fixed*. Human descendants stranded by the Severance are formally settled in the island's north — a confinement, not a homecoming, though later generations will simply call it home.
- **3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE** — *The Severance companies stood down* (Cathair dhearg). The war-companies that fought the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls are handed to the council rather than burned, and the companies are never formally abolished; they survive as names on a list.
- **31 an t-Iuchar 1930 DE** — *The boundary stones set* (Caol mhòr). Stones are set on the roads running north to mark where the Tuathaich territory begins. No wall follows them. Many still stand at the roadside, and nobody has been paid to move them.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd 1930 DE** — *The hungry year at Doire ghlas* (Doire ghlas). Cut off from the stores that used to come over the water from an Tìr Thall, the northern settlements go short of grain in their first year alone. Tuathaich memory, taken down long afterwards, puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. No Ròdaich count was made.
- **11 an t-Ògmhios 1931 DE** — *The human counting-houses emptied* (Ros dhomhain). Council clerks enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off everything written. What the raids of the war left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, because few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.
- **10 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE** — *The north-west ports without a master* (Inis àrsaidh). At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh, the humans' harbour officers leave with the last ships before the crossing closes, taking their keys. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks on the harbour stores and share out what they find by household.
- **27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE** — *Rìoghachd Ròdais declared* (Cathair dhearg). The state formally restyles itself a kingdom in form, whatever it remains in function — the same contradiction its own records still carry today.
- **25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE** — *The Moot at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Tuathaich householders from the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose a speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Ròdaich law. It meets anyway and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from this meeting to the present.
- **23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE** — *The council of the kingdom seated* (Cathair dhearg). A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest continuous record of the state in this age.
- **11 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE** — *The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over* (Ros dhomhain). The customs sheds the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the kingdom's largest port, pass to Ròdaich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff in force for want of another and translates it line by line over the following years.
- **19 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE** — *The ship sent west* (An Cuan Siar). The council sends a ship out past the western capes to look for the crossing the humans used. It comes back after a month of open water and reports nothing: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent.
- **7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE** — *Niall crowned* (Cathair dhearg). The first ruler of the restored kingdom takes the throne at Cathair dhearg — the opening name in the line the state's own chronicles keep unbroken from here forward.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE** — *A saying enters speech* (Cathair dhearg). The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-over of power. Its first written use is in a Cathair dhearg tavern ledger, set against a debt settled without argument.
- **23 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE** — *The shires drawn* (Cathair dhearg). The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only complete ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and does not say so.
- **4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE** — *The maoir appointed* (Ceann mhòr). A maor is appointed to each shire to collect the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Ròdaich, lodged in the seat towns; at Ceann mhòr the maor's house is the old human magistrate's, and the townspeople call it by the old name.
- **21 am Faoilleach 1933 DE** — *The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr* (Baile Mòr mhòr). The first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, Coinneach mac Ailein, holds his court under the market roof of the town, since the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps the court there after the new courthouse is built, and so do his successors.
- **2 an Gearran 1933 DE** — *Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol*. The Great Wave strikes the southern coast without warning, devastating Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night — the first disaster the new state responds to on its own terms.
- **24 an t-Samhain 1933 DE** — *The dead of the Great Wave counted* (Cuan dhearg). Relief parties from Cathair dhearg reach Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over nine hundred. The harbour at Cuan dhearg is gone. Its boats are found in the fields behind the town.
- **6 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE** — *Achadh mhin under salt* (Achadh mhin). The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury, the first relief the restored kingdom ever grants.
- **23 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE** — *Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill* (Cnoc chaol). Cnoc chaol is rebuilt on the slope behind the old town, out of the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townspeople call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.
- **4 am Faoilleach 1934 DE** — *Tonn* (Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol). The accounts gathered from survivors by the relief parties use 'tonn', wave, for anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.
- **1 an Giblean 1934 DE** — *The wave's reach on Eilean mhin* (Eilean mhin). The Great Wave also crosses the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where no one then lived year-round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.
- **30 an Giblean 1934 DE** — *The old human coinage withdrawn*. Every remaining piece of human currency is formally demonetized. A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with obsidian-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year.
- **9 an Dàmhair 1934 DE** — *The mint at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from obsidian dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.
- **7 an t-Samhain 1934 DE** — *The northern savings voided* (Caol mhòr). Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. With its withdrawal those savings are worth their metal by weight and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.
- **2 an Gearran 1935 DE** — *Joseph Marlow's ploughshares* (Doire mhin). At Doire mhin in the north a smith named Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, which he sells back to them at the cost of the charcoal. Tuathaich songs still name him.
- **3 am Màrt 1935 DE** — *The coin at Inis thais* (Inis thais). At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is short for most of the year and the town's merchants trade in chits written on the Wolf house's paper. The chits are redeemed at the Wolf house door when the coin arrives, and the house keeps a tenth.
- **18 an Giblean 1935 DE** — *Creideamh nan Ròdach formalized*. The Obsidian Rite becomes organized doctrine rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched.
- **30 an Giblean 1935 DE** — *The first high custodian of the Rite* (Seann Skell). Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Creideamh nan Ròdach and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the Rite's largest house stands. His first charge is a written order of worship. There had never been one.
- **17 an Cèitean 1935 DE** — *The Hawk houses refuse* (Cnoc bheag). The houses of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig around Cnoc bheag decline the new order of worship, holding that the Rite's older form needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. The long quarrel between the two forms of the Rite begins here.
- **29 an Cèitean 1935 DE** — *The Wolf houses stand aside* (Baile Mòr fhionn). The houses of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh in the south-west, whose god Clach is not the Rite's, are asked to send witnesses to the formalizing of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter saying they wish it well.
- **2 an Gearran 1936 DE** — *The Moot's schoolhouse petition* (Caol mhòr). Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Ròdais and that it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.
- **26 an Gearran 1936 DE** — *The capital's faith and the court* (Cathair dhearg). The house of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, as it had been before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks for a share of the keeping and is refused.
- **30 an t-Iuchar 1936 DE** — *The first post-Severance census*. The state counts its own population for the first time since reclaiming the island — and quietly notes, without further comment, exactly how few obsidian-touched individuals actually exist.
- **15 an Lùnastal 1936 DE** — *The count taken from the road* (Doire ghlas). Ròdaich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road, without entering most houses. The Moot keeps its own tally the same year. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side keeps its own.
- **23 an Lùnastal 1936 DE** — *The circuit justices* (Cathair dhomhain). Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, the first of them Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit covers eleven shires of the south-west and takes most of a year to ride once.
- **3 am Màrt 1937 DE** — *Muileann bhàn's waterworks* (Muileann bhàn). Muileann bhàn, on the southern plain, builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn how it was done.
- **10 an t-Sultain 1937 DE** — *The Leòid ruling* (Seann Bhral). Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, while the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age that follows.
- **9 an Dàmhair 1937 DE** — *The ore line repaired* (Muileann chrom). The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places during the Severance war, is repaired as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.
- **17 an Dùbhlachd 1937 DE** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt under the humans, is re-dedicated with a Ròdais name-stone. The humans' stone is not removed. It is turned to face the river.
- **15 am Faoilleach 1938 DE** — *The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, since the vines have broken too many stones to find room. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.
- **13 an Gearran 1938 DE** — *Creideamh nan Tuathach persists*. Tuathaich communities keep their own folk-shamanic tradition alive in the north — including, quietly, the First Canoe fragment the Ròdaich priesthood still calls superstition.
- **14 am Màrt 1938 DE** — *The Grey Night kept openly* (Baile chrom). At Baile chrom in the far north-west, the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the rites of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open for the first time since the Severance. The cult keeps one night of silence in the year for Sìne, the Peaceful Goose. Outsiders are not told which night it is.
- **12 an Giblean 1938 DE** — *The Scorpion houses of the north* (Cnoc ghorm). Most Tuathaich towns keep the worship of Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion, as the Ròdaich of the west coast do; how the settlers came to it the record does not say. A house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe is built at Cnoc ghorm, the largest in the north.
- **29 an Giblean 1939 DE** — *The school of the Scorpion at Cnoc ghorm* (Cnoc ghorm). The Scorpion house at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests, teaching in the humans' tongue and reading the Scorpion's scripture in the Ròdais text the west-coast houses use. It is the only place in the north where both are taught.
- **11 an Cèitean 1939 DE** — *The border wall proposed*. A formal boundary between Ròdaich and Tuathaich territory is proposed for the first time. It is rejected — not out of principle, records suggest, but because it's considered unnecessary. The two populations are already staying apart on their own.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios 1939 DE** — *The minute on the wall* (Cathair dhearg). The council minute that rejects the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' It is initialled by five of the twelve councillors, and the other seven did not sign against it.
- **8 an t-Iuchar 1939 DE** — *The Allt an Àigh walk* (Allt an Àigh). Followers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach keep up their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water the old tales say brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite discourage the walk and do not forbid it.
- **11 an Gearran 1940 DE** — *The walkers at Achadh gharbh* (Achadh gharbh). The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, which by the end of the decade holds names from fifty shires.
- **15 an Cèitean 1940 DE** — *Extraction resumes at full scale*. The mine's post-Severance yield matches, then exceeds, its colonial-era output. Nothing about the method changed. Only who profits did.
- **23 an Cèitean 1940 DE** — *The Sloc Mòr concession* (Achadh dhomhain). The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The terms give the Crown a fifth of the yield. They are the humans' terms with the names changed.
- **18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE** — *The night-shift kept* (Cnoc fhiadhaich). The council declines to end the continuous working of the vein, day and night, that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest and then bless the shafts.
- **14 am Màrt 1941 DE** — *The pit towns fill* (Muileann dhearg). Ròdaich families from the hungry east move to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years, and its hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and enlarged twice in the same span.
- **6 an Lùnastal 1941 DE** — *Baile thais grows on the ore road* (Baile thais). Baile thais, where the ore road from the central mountains meets the east coast, takes on carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its population doubles in a decade, and the town is given a shire court.
- **4 an t-Sultain 1941 DE** — *Raiders off Cathair gheal* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Ships that no longer fly any flag, some crewed by men who once served the human administration, begin raiding the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first and are not defended.
- **3 an Dàmhair 1941 DE** — *The ore line reaches the Sloc Mòr* (Achadh dhomhain). The repaired railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first ore train from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg runs under the kingdom's name and on the humans' rails.
- **25 an Cèitean 1942 DE** — *The quarry at Achadh dhomhain* (Achadh dhomhain). The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a black-veined grey stone, is cut and sold as building stone under the house of Mac Ùisdein's quarry-mark. It is used for public buildings across the south for the next forty years.
- **8 an t-Iuchar 1942 DE** — *The shunting yards at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where ore trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The yard's families, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted separately by the Board and live apart in rows by the lines.
- **21 an t-Sultain 1942 DE** — *The guild system restored*. The old apprentice-binding custom from the Holy Age is revived in modified form, now explicitly reserved for Ròdaich applicants only.
- **20 an Dàmhair 1942 DE** — *The Guild of Hewers chartered* (Achadh dhomhain). The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is taken with a hand on a piece of ore. Its rolls are open to Ròdaich only, as the charter requires.
- **29 am Faoilleach 1943 DE** — *The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.
- **28 am Màrt 1943 DE** — *The indentures broken* (Cuan shean). At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral, Tuathaich boys already bound to Ròdaich masters are released from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labour, outside the guilds and their wages.
- **26 an Giblean 1943 DE** — *The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the southern coast east of the capital, take a guild charter and a monopoly of supplying the Crown's patrol boats. The monopoly outlasts the patrol boats.
- **23 an t-Ògmhios 1943 DE** — *The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the ore lamps used in every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp and is the only guild mark the humans' traders had ever copied.
- **6 am Faoilleach 1944 DE** — *The weavers of Baile chiar* (Baile chiar). The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth, woven from southern wool, undersells the northern cloth at the fair until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.
- **14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE** — *Agnes Pike's school* (Doire ghlas). Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with Moot money and without the council's leave. Within a decade there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never closes them.
- **19 an t-Iuchar 1944 DE** — *The Cill ghlas district reopened* (Scàineadh Cill ghlas). The mining district closed since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. The first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line, on the surveyors' word.
- **27 an t-Iuchar 1944 DE** — *The Leòid circuit in the north* (Ceann mhòr). Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. She finds for the Crown in fifteen, citing her own ruling.
- **2 an Giblean 1945 DE** — *Eilidh nic Leòid dies* (Cathair dhomhain). Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound as a single book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.
- **1 an Cèitean 1945 DE** — *Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). A great library is established at Muileann chaol — the institution that will eventually keep the most complete surviving record of everything in this chronicle.
- **28 an t-Ògmhios 1945 DE** — *Ailean Leabhar, first keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is appointed the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what survived of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.
- **3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE** — *A chur san Leabharlann* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Within a few years, 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything made settled and beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is recorded as disliking the phrase, on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it.
- **30 an Cèitean 1946 DE** — *The first readers* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The library's first reading room opens to anyone who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader entered in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, asking for the humans' plans of their hulls.
- **27 an t-Iuchar 1946 DE** — *The bath-house at the hot springs* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year lists four hundred men by name and shift.
- **25 an Lùnastal 1946 DE** — *The keepers of the five lights* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Ròdaich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the keeper is a Ròdaich man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant tells him to report what he sees on land as well as at sea.
- **22 an Dàmhair 1946 DE** — *The Muileann chaol town grows* (Muileann chaol). Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle in Muileann chaol around the library. The town takes a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.
- **23 an t-Sultain 1947 DE** — *The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach* (Tobar dhìreach). A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For the next half-century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.
- **20 an t-Samhain 1947 DE** — *The first royal chronicler appointed* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). A formal office is created specifically to maintain the kingdom's records — the direct ancestor of the archive this very document draws from.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd 1947 DE** — *Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol, not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.
- **25 am Màrt 1948 DE** — *The first chronicle circuit* (Àth àrsaidh). Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one; few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.
- **2 an Giblean 1948 DE** — *The chest from Inis bheag* (Inis bheag). The chronicle clerks at Inis bheag on the north-east coast are shown a parish book going back before the humans' coming, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied and not taken.
- **20 an t-Sultain 1948 DE** — *Boats lost off Cuan bheag* (Cuan bheag). A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.
- **28 an t-Sultain 1948 DE** — *The thing off the north-west cape* (Uilebheist na Mara). Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh report a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill records the report and adds that the same waters are where the raiders shelter.
- **9 an Gearran 1949 DE** — *The Eilean dhubh sheep-count* (Eilean dhubh). A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks on Eilean dhubh, the largest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.
- **10 am Màrt 1949 DE** — *Cathair gheal arms its boats* (Cathair gheal). The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders out of the bay. The council, asked for help twice, had sent none. It later fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.
- **8 an Giblean 1949 DE** — *The market cross at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr, paid for by the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and ore markets are moved to its foot.
- **7 an Cèitean 1950 DE** — *The Wolf house at Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). The Wolf house at Caol leathan, the largest of the faith, is rebuilt with a tower from which a bell rings at the hours. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.
- **16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE** — *Fèill Muileann òg established* (Fèill Muileann òg). An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering, drawing trade from every province the state controls.
- **14 an t-Samhain 1950 DE** — *Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules* (Fèill Muileann òg). The first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, Oighrig nic Mhathain, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods sold only through Ròdaich factors. The rules are read aloud at each fair's opening to this day.
- **26 an t-Samhain 1950 DE** — *The fair's road* (Dùn chrom). The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the fair's carts, passing Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it.
- **2 an Lùnastal 1951 DE** — *Dùn chrom's gate-toll* (Dùn chrom). The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townspeople call it the fair's wall, and the fair's carters call it something else.
- **31 an Lùnastal 1951 DE** — *Niall dies; Brìghde crowned* (Cathair dhearg). His daughter succeeds him without contest — mortal succession within an immortal-adjacent aristocracy, unremarkable at the time, unusual in hindsight.
- **29 an t-Sultain 1951 DE** — *The chronicler's use of the saying* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall', the first time the saying appears in the royal record. It is the only idiom she allows into the chronicle in her whole tenure.
- **28 an Dàmhair 1951 DE** — *The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where the ancestors of forty families are named aloud each year by their living heads. The list is copied to the library the next year and grows by a few names every year after.
- **25 an Gearran 1952 DE** — *Cuan ruadh's harbour light* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has no lighthouse of the five, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole, lit with ore bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board declines to take it on.
- **4 am Màrt 1952 DE** — *Còmhrag Ceann leathan established* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). A brutal annual melee tournament begins at Ceann leathan, ostensibly a martial tradition, increasingly a release valve for a population with fewer and fewer other outlets.
- **22 an Lùnastal 1952 DE** — *Calum Ruadh* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The first champion of the Còmhrag the record remembers is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer from Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to carry arms in any shire.
- **30 an Lùnastal 1952 DE** — *Ceann leathan's inns* (Ceann leathan). Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the Còmhrag crowds. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.
- **10 am Màrt 1953 DE** — *The ore-ships of Ros gheal* (Ros gheal). Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of the dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.
- **7 an t-Ògmhios 1953 DE** — *Splatter and Dodge's generation born*. A cluster of births in the Class-08-adjacent shunting families — the generation that will grow up to become Dubhan's closest allies, Seachran and Brean among them.
- **6 an t-Iuchar 1953 DE** — *Seann Bhral in the south* (Seann Bhral). Seann Bhral on the south coast, not to be confused with its namesake in the west, becomes the kingdom's largest fishing port, landing more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.
- **4 an Lùnastal 1954 DE** — *The circus at Seann Chwen* (An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn). The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what the acts were meant to show. Neither, the clerk adds, could the crowd, which came back the next night.
- **2 an t-Sultain 1954 DE** — *The Scorpion at Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, refuses to admit Tuathaich worshippers from the north who come for its feast. Its keeper says the god is the same and the house is not.
- **11 an Gearran 1955 DE** — *The northern Scorpion feast* (Cnoc ghorm). Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich worshippers of the Scorpion hold the feast at Cnoc ghorm instead. It is kept there every year after, and the northern feast is larger than the western within a generation.
- **12 am Màrt 1955 DE** — *The Depletion first acknowledged*. Survey reports begin quietly noting the vein's declining yield. The state does not act on them for years.
- **9 an Cèitean 1955 DE** — *Iain Mapa's survey* (Achadh dhomhain). The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measurements of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to the east and south. The Board files the survey without circulating it, and Iain Mapa is moved to the silver works at Muileann chiar.
- **4 am Faoilleach 1956 DE** — *The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). The Mine Board, which had sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. Its surveys are kept there, not sent to the library, by the Board's own rule.
- **15 an t-Ògmhios 1956 DE** — *The Grey Night forbidden* (Baile chrom). A Ròdaich magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night cult as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil moves indoors and goes on.
- **9 an t-Iuchar 1956 DE** — *The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened* (Cuan dhearg). The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is reopened with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.
- **13 am Faoilleach 1957 DE** — *Achadh mhin resettled* (Achadh mhin). The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old boundaries from the humans' survey.
- **11 an Gearran 1957 DE** — *Eòghan crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Brìghde's reign ends young — no cause is recorded publicly. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne amid the first real succession tension the restored kingdom has faced.
- **16 an t-Samhain 1957 DE** — *The succession entry* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the fact and nothing more. The chroniclers who followed Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.
- **15 an Dùbhlachd 1957 DE** — *Dissent recorded in council* (Cathair dhearg). For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.
- **12 am Màrt 1958 DE** — *Inis bhàn's fire* (Inis bhàn). Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the north-central coast and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.
- **9 an Cèitean 1958 DE** — *Dubhan born*. Born mortal, into the exact confinement the Severance created, decades after the war that closed the island to the people his line descends from.
- **7 an t-Ògmhios 1958 DE** — *The Tuathaich schools counted* (Doire ghlas). The Moot counts eleven schools in the north teaching in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is among the three.
- **10 an Giblean 1959 DE** — *The stone house of Mac Ùisdein* (Cathair mhòr). Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the largest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.
- **26 an Cèitean 1959 DE** — *The northern fishing grounds* (Caol mhòr). Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are reserved to Ròdaich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, which the raiders also work.
- **24 an t-Ògmhios 1959 DE** — *Doire shean's harbour* (Doire shean). Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Wolf country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The Wolf house lends the money and takes the harbour dues.
- **3 an Giblean 1960 DE** — *Trenches at Làrach an Dùin* (Làrach an Dùin). Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Ròdaich building and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar orders the finds catalogued as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.
- **7 an Dàmhair 1960 DE** — *Làrach an Teampaill measured* (Làrach an Teampaill). The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east but do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.
- **29 am Màrt 1961 DE** — *The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). A scribe of the library copies the inscription on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It matches no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk is fenced.
- **27 an Giblean 1961 DE** — *A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The Ròdaich keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reports to the council that the Grey Night cult keeps its vigil in the dark of the lighthouse's own shadow. The council takes no action.
- **26 an Cèitean 1961 DE** — *Salt-pans of Àth bheag* (Àth bheag). Salt-pans are dug on the flats below Àth bheag on the east coast, and within a few years the town supplies the whole eastern seaboard. The salt is carried inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal.
- **1 am Faoilleach 1962 DE** — *Cathair fhada's grain-store* (Cathair fhada). Cathair fhada on the southern plain builds a Crown grain-store large enough to feed the south for a season. It is filled from the south's own harvests, and first opened in the dry years at Achadh shean.
- **30 am Faoilleach 1962 DE** — *The second post-Severance census*. The gap between Ròdaich and Tuathaich living standards is, for the first time, measured rather than simply observed. The report is not made public.
- **28 an Gearran 1962 DE** — *Walter Hale dies* (Caol mhòr). Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies at Caol mhòr. The Moot chooses Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, to follow him. She is the first woman to hold the chair.
- **30 am Faoilleach 1963 DE** — *The census clerks' private note* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). One of the census clerks, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, leaves among her papers a note that she had asked to see the gap report and been refused. The note reached the library with her papers after her death and is the only mention of the report outside the council.
- **11 an Gearran 1963 DE** — *The Tuathaich doctors* (Àth àrsaidh). The Moot pays for two Tuathaich women to be taught medicine by a Ròdaich physician at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them in defiance of his guild. He is struck from the guild's rolls. They practise in the north for forty years.
- **12 am Màrt 1963 DE** — *The Abhainn ìseal floods* (Abhainn ìseal). The Abhainn ìseal, the longest river on the island, breaks its banks along its lower reach, carrying away three bridges and a stretch of the ore line's embankment. The line is closed for most of a year and the ports live on stored ore.
- **26 an Cèitean 1964 DE** — *The Hawk houses' own custodian* (Inis ìseal). The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag name a custodian of their own, Raonaid nic Iain, and seat her at Inis ìseal. The high custodian at Seann Skell refuses to recognise her. The houses carry on as if he had.
- **29 an t-Samhain 1964 DE** — *Raonaid nic Iain at Inis ìseal* (Inis ìseal). Raonaid nic Iain, custodian of the Hawk houses, writes out the Hawk's order of worship, which had been said and never written. The Hawk houses read it aloud once a year and keep the written copy locked away.
- **27 an Giblean 1965 DE** — *Six dead at the Còmhrag* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). Six fighters die at the Còmhrag, the most in any year yet. The custodians of the Rite petition for it to end. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lives off the crowds, refuse.
- **6 an Dàmhair 1965 DE** — *The circus at Ceann leathan* (Ceann leathan). An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches at Ceann leathan in the year of the Còmhrag's six dead and plays to the crowds who stay on after the melee. The fair-wardens are said to have paid it to come.
- **4 an t-Samhain 1965 DE** — *The ore line reaches Ceann leathan* (Ceann leathan). The railway is carried through to the port of Ceann leathan, so that ore can be shipped from a second harbour. Ceann leathan's quays are rebuilt for ore ships, and the town outgrows its walls.
- **1 am Faoilleach 1966 DE** — *Ros bheag's shipyard* (Ros bheag). Ros bheag on the west coast opens a shipyard for ore-ships, so that the western ports need no longer send to Ros dhomhain for hulls. The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain protest to the guild court and lose.
- **19 an t-Sultain 1966 DE** — *The silver at depth* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). The silver seam at Muileann chiar, which the Ròdaich kept from the humans, is found richer at depth than anyone expected. The town's old silver guild takes a charter under the restored custom. Iain Mapa, working there since the Board moved him, measures the new faces.
- **3 an Dùbhlachd 1966 DE** — *Dùn thais in the west* (Dùn thais). Dùn thais on the west coast is granted the right to hold its own court of the sea, deciding salvage and wreck along its shore. Its first session awards a raider's hulk to the fishermen who drove it aground.
- **8 an t-Ògmhios 1967 DE** — *Dùn thais in the east* (Dùn thais). Its namesake Dùn thais in the east, seat of its own shire, builds a covered market for the hill farms. The two towns' courts are confused in the royal record for a decade until Tormod Pinn marks them west and east.
- **18 an Dàmhair 1967 DE** — *The dead and not dead of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). Herders near Doire uaine refuse to graze the hills above the town, where old inscriptions tell of a thing that is dead and does not rest. A shepherd goes missing there. The magistrate records wolves.
- **23 an t-Ògmhios 1968 DE** — *The fall at Muileann dhearg* (Muileann dhearg). A gallery of the reopened Cill ghlas district gives way under Muileann dhearg, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers die. It is small beside the Rending. It is the same fault.
- **1 an t-Iuchar 1968 DE** — *The mine-safety reforms*. New excavation rules are introduced after a smaller echo of the old Scàineadh Cill ghlas collapse. They apply to Ròdaich workers. Enforcement in Tuathaich-adjacent sites is inconsistent, records suggest deliberately so.
- **19 an Dùbhlachd 1968 DE** — *The timber at Àth leathan* (Àth leathan). At the pits around Àth leathan, where Ròdaich overseers work Tuathaich hands, the new timbering rules are posted and not paid for. The overseers' books, which reached the library later, show the timber ordered and never delivered.
- **3 an t-Sultain 1969 DE** — *Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Ailean Leabhar dies at Muileann chaol, and Mòrag nic Coinnich becomes keeper of the library. She begins the practice, kept ever since, of writing each item's source beside the item itself.
- **2 an Dàmhair 1969 DE** — *The pit families of Achadh dhomhain* (Achadh dhomhain). After the fall at Muileann dhearg, forty hewers' families leave Achadh dhomhain for the fishing ports of the south. The Guild of Hewers binds sixty apprentices to fill the rolls. None of them are Tuathaich.
- **31 an Dàmhair 1969 DE** — *Fire at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). Fire runs through the stalls of the fair at Muileann òg. The fair's court sits in a field the next day and the fair goes on. Oighrig nic Mhathain, toll-mistress since the first fair, dies of her burns.
- **29 an t-Samhain 1969 DE** — *The Tuathaich wool carts* (Muileann leathan). The Rail Board refuses to carry goods consigned by the Moot, citing the fair's rule on factors. The wool of the north goes south to Muileann òg by cart, a week on the road, and is sold by factors when it arrives.
- **26 am Faoilleach 1970 DE** — *The Tuathaich carters' road* (Àth fhada). The carters taking northern wool to the fair go by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and the old road down to Inis àrsaidh, and the Tuathaich villages on the way open inns for them. The road is called the Carters' Road in the north and nothing in the south.
- **2 an t-Iuchar 1970 DE** — *Dubhan's childhood*. He grows up watching an eternally young caste hold every real advantage on an island his own ancestors were pushed to the edge of. The obsidian was never his to inherit.
- **28 an Dùbhlachd 1970 DE** — *The Moot's pit register* (Caol mhòr). The Moot at Caol mhòr begins a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, since no Ròdaich book counts them. Mary Coyle's clerks enter the first year's names from the families' own word. The register is kept to the present and has never been sent south.
- **5 an Cèitean 1971 DE** — *Ros mhòr's boatyard* (Ros mhòr). A boatyard is opened at Ros mhòr in the north by Tuathaich boatbuilders turned out of the guild yards. Its boats are built to the humans' old lines and are faster than anything in the south.
- **31 an t-Iuchar 1971 DE** — *Tormod Pinn* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lays down the office of royal chronicler. Her successor, Tormod mac Sheumais, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, keeps the record for more than twenty years and writes more of it than anyone before or since.
- **25 an Giblean 1972 DE** — *Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's last entry* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Her last entry as chronicler is a list of what the record does not hold: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, the Board's surveys. Tormod Pinn copies the list into the front of his first book and does not add to it.
- **3 an Cèitean 1972 DE** — *Dry years at Achadh shean* (Tiormachd Achadh shean). Dry years return to the country around Achadh shean, where the Long Drought settled in the humans' time. This time the council sends grain up the ore line and pays for it out of the Sloc Mòr's share. Nobody dies of hunger in the shire, and the chronicler records the fact.
- **6 an t-Samhain 1972 DE** — *The wells of Siorrachd Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). The maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean has twelve wells dug to the rock along the drove road, each marked with the shire's name and the council's. Four of them are still drawn from.
- **9 am Faoilleach 1973 DE** — *Grain by the ore line* (Achadh shean). The grain for Achadh shean comes from the store at Cathair fhada and goes by the ore line for the first time. The Rail Board charges the council for the carriage.
- **7 an Gearran 1973 DE** — *Raiders at Baile ìseal* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Raiders land near Baile ìseal on the far east coast and burn the salt-sheds that serve Àth bheag. The kingdom's patrol boats arrive two days later and find the sheds cold.
- **12 an t-Samhain 1973 DE** — *Murchadh mac Coinnich's log* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). Murchadh mac Coinnich, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, begins entering every unlit ship he sees in the lighthouse log with its heading and the hour. His logs, kept for most of his life, are the fullest record of the eastern raiders the library holds.
- **9 am Faoilleach 1974 DE** — *The pirates' names* (Àth bheag). Murchadh mac Coinnich's log names the eastern raiders' ships as the fishermen of Àth bheag name them, since the raiders fly no flag. The names pass into the royal record from his log.
- **11 an Dùbhlachd 1974 DE** — *The Còmhrag at its height* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The Còmhrag draws its largest crowd yet to Ceann leathan, and the fair-wardens build timber stands along the three sides of the field. The champion is Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas, the first woman to win it. She does not fight again.
- **14 an Dàmhair 1975 DE** — *The Hawk port of Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Cnoc bheag, the largest town of the Hawk country, passes Cathair mhòr in population. Its harbour takes the grain of the north-central coast and its Hawk house is the richest of any faith outside the capital.
- **12 an t-Samhain 1975 DE** — *The Feallsanachd an Fhèidh revival*. The old philosophical school, dormant since the colonial period, reopens — its founding question, why the vein answers some and not others, suddenly urgent again as the vein itself starts running short.
- **11 an Dùbhlachd 1975 DE** — *Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The revived school's first teacher is Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain, who lectures in the sacred wood near Muileann chiar in the east, where the Fèidh had last met under the humans. Her opening question is the school's oldest, put plainly: why the vein answers some hands and not others.
- **9 an t-Ògmhios 1976 DE** — *The Fèidh in Siorrachd Baile gharbh* (Baile gharbh). Houses of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh in Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, dormant since the humans' time, reopen at Baile gharbh and Àth fhada. Their teachers walk to the sacred wood to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain and walk back.
- **5 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE** — *The school at Caol shean* (Caol shean). The Fèidh school takes a house at Caol shean, the largest town of its faith on the east coast, and begins to teach in the wet months, when the wood is too sodden for lectures. Its students copy the census note on the obsidian-touched and debate it openly.
- **13 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE** — *The Hawk given a place* (Cnoc bheag). A council of the Rite at Seann Skell offers the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag a place under the high custodian with their own order of worship. The Hawk houses accept the place and keep their order. The quarrel is quieter after this. It is not over.
- **7 an Gearran 1977 DE** — *The north-eastern harbours* (Caol chrom). Caol chrom and Caol gharbh on the north-east coast combine their harbour dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them. It takes eight years to build and is still the longest on the island.
- **23 an Giblean 1977 DE** — *Daniel Frayne's copying school* (Muileann leathan). At Muileann leathan in the north, a clerk of the Moot named Daniel Frayne teaches young Tuathaich to copy and bind books, since the guilds that do it in the south will not take them. The bindings of Muileann leathan are later found in Ròdaich libraries without their makers' names.
- **22 an Cèitean 1977 DE** — *The Abhainn uaine ferries* (Cidhe Beag). The boat-landing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine is licensed as a ferry, carrying passengers and small freight down the river toward the coast. Its first licensee is an old boatman who had worked the landing without a licence for forty years.
- **24 am Faoilleach 1978 DE** — *Loch chrom* (Loch chrom). Fishermen on Loch chrom, the island's only lake of any size, are given a licence to net its trout, which had been kept for the Crown's table. The Crown's table is supplied first each year.
- **22 an Gearran 1978 DE** — *The pillar at Cnoc chiar* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). Students of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh try to read the pillar near Cnoc chiar by setting it against the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm. They find signs in common and no meaning. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that nobody living can hear it.
- **23 am Màrt 1979 DE** — *Flood at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). A storm tide floods the lower town at Inis chrom on the south-west coast, drowning the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town rebuilds both on piles, which is how they stand now.
- **21 an Giblean 1979 DE** — *Cnoc leathan's schools* (Cnoc leathan). Cnoc leathan in the east opens a school in every one of its six parishes, paid from the shire's dues, the first shire to do so. The council asks how it paid for them and is shown the accounts.
- **20 an Cèitean 1979 DE** — *Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan* (Cathair mhòr). Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr concession, borrows against the house's share to pay for a search for a second vein. The Mine Board lends its surveyors. The Crown lends its name.
- **13 an Giblean 1980 DE** — *The Feallsanachd on the search* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes to the Mine Board that the search for a second vein asks the wrong question: that the school has always asked why the vein answers some hands, and nobody has asked why there is one vein. The Board files the letter.
- **21 an Giblean 1980 DE** — *The failed vein expansion*. A costly attempt to locate a second obsidian deposit elsewhere on the island turns up nothing — the same result the Holy Age's failed attempt found centuries earlier, forgotten and rediscovered the hard way.
- **17 an Dàmhair 1980 DE** — *Forty-one dry shafts* (Dùn dhearg). The search's borings run from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh. Forty-one shafts are sunk and none strikes the vein. Mòrag nic Coinnich later finds, in a Holy Age list at the library, the same hills named as searched and barren.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 1981 DE** — *Dùn dhearg's claim* (Dùn dhearg). The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills held a dozen of the dry shafts, claims damages from the house of Mac Ùisdein for spoiled grazing. The circuit court awards them. The house pays a third before it sells.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 1981 DE** — *The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half* (Cathair mhòr). To meet its debts, the house of Mac Ùisdein sells half its share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr is let to the Mine Board, which moves its offices there.
- **3 an Lùnastal 1981 DE** — *The shafts at Baile ruadh left open* (Baile ruadh). The dry shafts of the search are left open on the moors near Baile ruadh. Sheep and one child fall into them before the shire fences them at its own cost. The shire's claim on the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing is never paid.
- **9 an Giblean 1982 DE** — *The Muileann dhomhain mills* (Muileann dhomhain). The mills of Muileann dhomhain in the south-east, which ground grain for the vein-towns, turn to grinding bark for the tanners when the vein-towns' orders fall. The town's miller-families keep their mark and change their trade.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 1982 DE** — *The rope-makers of Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The rope-makers of Seann Tarr on the north-east coast are chartered as a guild, the last guild the restored custom creates for a trade that the humans had not touched. Their hemp comes from the fields around Doire uaine and Achadh naomh.
- **1 an t-Sultain 1982 DE** — *Seann Tarr's chest remembered* (Seann Tarr). The rope-makers' charter at Seann Tarr is kept in the shire's own chest, not sent to Cathair dhearg, by the shire's rule. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr keeps a list of what the chest holds and sends the list alone.
- **30 an t-Sultain 1982 DE** — *The Circus at Inis àrsaidh* (An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn). An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is recorded again, this time pitched on the common near Inis àrsaidh on the west coast. The magistrate who licenses it enters the acts as 'various' and the fee as paid.
- **11 am Màrt 1983 DE** — *Ceann mhin's fish-market* (Ceann mhin). Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opens a covered fish-market over the old strand. Fish from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds is sold there for the capital.
- **8 an Cèitean 1983 DE** — *Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). After a fighter is killed with a hewer's pick, the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan ban edged tools from the Còmhrag. Staves and fists remain allowed, and so the deaths go on, fewer.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 1983 DE** — *The drowned lighthouse keeper* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast drowns going out to a boat aground on the reef below the light. The boat's crew are saved by the keeper's daughter, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, who is given the keeper's warrant in his place.
- **11 am Màrt 1984 DE** — *Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post set on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, painted and hung with a bell. No boat goes aground there while she keeps the light.
- **13 an t-Ògmhios 1984 DE** — *Mary Coyle lays down the chair* (Caol mhòr). Mary Coyle lays down the Moot's chair at Caol mhòr. Her successor, Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan, is the first speaker born after the Severance.
- **9 an Dùbhlachd 1984 DE** — *The Fèill's northern day* (Fèill Muileann òg). The court of the fair at Muileann òg sets aside one day of the fair for goods from the northern shires, still sold through Ròdaich factors but under the northern makers' own marks. It is the first time a Tuathaich name is written on anything sold there.
- **12 am Faoilleach 1985 DE** — *The Tuathaich marks at the fair* (Baile chiar). The first northern mark sold under its own name at the fair is the cloth of the Doire ghlas weavers, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge. The southern weavers of Baile chiar begin weaving a white thread into their own.
- **11 am Màrt 1985 DE** — *The Depletion becomes undeniable*. What was a quiet survey note in 1955 is now an open crisis. The last untouched sections of the vein are identified — and are smaller than anyone wants to admit.
- **14 an Dùbhlachd 1985 DE** — *Catrìona nic Neacail's map* (Achadh dhomhain). The Mine Board's surveyor-general, Catrìona nic Neacail, publishes the map of the vein's last untouched sections. It fits on one sheet. She resigns within the year and goes to teach at the Fèidh school at Caol shean.
- **9 an Giblean 1986 DE** — *Iain Mapa's survey found* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Among the Board's files, Catrìona nic Neacail finds Iain Mapa's survey of thirty years before, which shows the same thinning she had just measured. She sends a copy to the library with a note of when the Board received it.
- **8 an Cèitean 1986 DE** — *Iain Mapa dies* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, dies at Muileann chiar, where the Board had sent him. His own copy of his survey is found among his papers, with the Board's receipt pinned to it.
- **6 an t-Ògmhios 1986 DE** — *Muileann dhearg empties* (Muileann dhearg). Muileann dhearg loses a third of its households to the ports in a few years. Its hall of the Fèidh is closed, and its bell is sold to the school at Caol shean, where it still rings for lectures.
- **5 an t-Iuchar 1986 DE** — *Ceann leathan's ore quays idle* (Ceann leathan). Ore ships wait at Ceann leathan for cargoes that come in half-loads. The harbour dues fall by half, and the fair-wardens of the town raise the Còmhrag's gate-price to make it up.
- **30 an t-Sultain 1987 DE** — *Baile Mòr dhomhain's market* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Baile Mòr dhomhain in the northern hills becomes the market for the hill country's wool and hides as the ore-towns' trade falls away. Its market day draws more carts than the fair at Muileann òg for two years running.
- **29 an Dàmhair 1987 DE** — *Mairead crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Eòghan's reign ends in the same decade the Depletion becomes public knowledge — his successor inherits a kingdom whose founding resource is visibly failing for the first time in the restored era.
- **23 an t-Samhain 1987 DE** — *The Hewers bind no apprentices* (Achadh dhomhain). The Guild of Hewers binds no new apprentices for the first time since its charter. Its masters vote to keep the rolls open to the sons and daughters of members only.
- **19 an Giblean 1988 DE** — *Muileann shean's school of hewers* (Muileann shean). Muileann shean in the north opens a school for hewers' sons and daughters who will not be bound, teaching them to read, reckon and survey. Most of its first pupils go to the ports.
- **27 an Giblean 1988 DE** — *The Doire ghlas mills* (Doire ghlas). Wool mills are built at Doire ghlas with Moot money, the north's first works tied to nothing in the vein. The Rail Board refuses their cloth until a ruling of the circuit court at Seann Bhral compels it to carry any goods that pay the rate.
- **31 an Dàmhair 1988 DE** — *The Seann Bhral ruling* (Seann Bhral). The circuit justice at Seann Bhral, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, rules that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any payer. It is the first ruling the Moot ever wins in a Ròdaich court. The Board appeals and the council lets the appeal lapse.
- **30 an t-Iuchar 1989 DE** — *The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr* (Achadh dhomhain). The Crown buys the last of the house of Mac Ùisdein's working shafts at the Sloc Mòr and leaves the house its share in the spoil and the quarry. From this point the vein is worked by the Board in the Crown's name alone.
- **28 an Lùnastal 1989 DE** — *The copper at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). Copper is found in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich on the east coast. The Board opens a working with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr. It pays wages. It is not the vein, and the town's Seann Spioradan house holds no blessing for it.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios 1990 DE** — *Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town* (Àth fhiadhaich). The copper workings at Àth fhiadhaich draw miners from the failing vein-towns. The town builds a new street for them and names it for the Sloc Mòr, and the Seann Spioradan house there objects to the name.
- **1 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE** — *Dubhan begins his experiments*. Early, unsuccessful attempts to synthesize a substitute fuel from mining byproducts — failures the historical record barely bothers to name.
- **13 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE** — *The Sloc Mòr's pumps* (Achadh dhomhain). The lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr are allowed to flood. The pumps cost more to run than the ore beneath them is worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.
- **17 an Giblean 1991 DE** — *The pumps sold* (Seann Bhral). The Board sells the Sloc Mòr's great pumps to the harbour at Seann Bhral in the south, where they drain the new dry dock. They are the only machines of the vein still at work in the next generation.
- **16 an Cèitean 1991 DE** — *The panthers cross the south-west* (Imrich nam Pantar). A great movement of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. Herders lose stock for a month. Tormod Pinn records it as a thing named in the Holy Age lists and not seen in living memory.
- **13 an t-Iuchar 1991 DE** — *The hides of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Tanners at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast buy the hides of the panthers killed by herders, and their trade outlasts the migration by a decade. Panther-skin saddles from Baile ghorm are sold at the fair at Muileann òg under the town's mark.
- **11 an Lùnastal 1991 DE** — *Imrich nam Pantar in the record* (Imrich nam Pantar). Tormod Pinn's entry on the panthers is the longest in his book for the year. He sets it beside the Holy Age list and notes that the old list also names the year after the panthers as a hungry one.
- **10 an Gearran 1992 DE** — *The ore-lamp shortage* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin cut their output by half for want of ore to burn in the lamps they make. Shaft-lamps are lent between pits, and the guild's minute-book records who lent to whom.
- **18 an Gearran 1992 DE** — *Unrest at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the ore trains for three days over cut wages. The Rail Board settles on the fourth and dismisses eleven men on the fifth.
- **7 an Lùnastal 1992 DE** — *The hungry year that was not* (Cathair fhada). The harvest after the panthers' crossing is a good one across the south. Tormod Pinn records it and draws a line through his own note of the year before.
- **8 an Dàmhair 1993 DE** — *The third post-Severance census*. Population figures are published openly for the first time in Rìoghachd history — a small, symbolic transparency reform that changes nothing structurally.
- **6 an t-Samhain 1993 DE** — *The figures read at the Moot* (Caol mhòr). The published figures are read aloud at the Moot at Caol mhòr. They show the northern towns at about half the Ròdaich measure in every column the clerks chose to take. The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'
- **8 am Faoilleach 1994 DE** — *The count of the touched* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The published census, like the first, carries a line for the obsidian-touched. It gives a number and nothing else. Tormod Pinn copies it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill had done for the first.
- **28 an Lùnastal 1994 DE** — *The census in the Wolf country* (Inis thais). In the Wolf shires of the south-west, the Wolf houses publish their own count of their people beside the kingdom's, for the first time. The two agree to within a hundred.
- **26 an t-Sultain 1994 DE** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Tormod Pinn dies at his desk at Muileann chaol. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh becomes royal chronicler. She is the first to add, at the foot of each year, a note of what the record could not learn.
- **10 an Dùbhlachd 1994 DE** — *The Hawk houses' registers* (Ros gheal). The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Ros gheal send their birth-rolls to the library for the first time, on condition that the rolls be filed under Creideamh an t-Seabhaig and not under the Rite. Mòrag nic Coinnich agrees.
- **6 an Gearran 1995 DE** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first note of what the record could not learn is of the northern shires: that the census clerks were told the figures and did not count them, and that the figures they were told were the Moot's.
- **7 am Màrt 1995 DE** — *The record-chests called in* (Seann Tarr). Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks travel to thirty shire towns to bring their record-chests to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire's keeper burns the chest rather than send it, saying the shire's record belongs in the shire. He is fined; the chest is not recovered.
- **5 an Giblean 1995 DE** — *Cathair naomh sends its rolls* (Cathair naomh). The keeper of Cathair naomh in the north sends her shire's rolls to the library in two carts, with the town's own chronicle, kept by a single family for four generations. Mòrag nic Coinnich enters it as the best-kept shire record received.
- **29 am Faoilleach 1996 DE** — *The Seann Toll chest* (Seann Toll). Seann Toll in the north sends its chest willingly and asks for a copy of everything in it. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks make the copy, and the shire's copy is the model for every copy the library has made since.
- **26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE** — *The library expansion* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings, absorbing several smaller provincial archives into one central record — the moment Rodian history starts being kept in one place instead of many.
- **3 an Lùnastal 1996 DE** — *No northern chest* (Caol mhòr). No Tuathaich record is called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stay in the north, in private keeping, as they always had.
- **2 an t-Ògmhios 1997 DE** — *The library's new wing* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The expanded library is housed in a new wing at Muileann chaol built of the grey stone from the Sloc Mòr's spoil. The provincial chests fill three floors. The fourth is left empty for what was not sent.
- **30 an t-Iuchar 1997 DE** — *The branch line to Àth leathan closed* (Àth leathan). The Rail Board closes the branch line to Àth leathan, citing falling yield from the western pits. The Tuathaich pits go on working, and their coal goes by cart to the western ports and by boat from there.
- **28 an Lùnastal 1997 DE** — *The Moot's hewers take the pits* (Àth leathan). With the Board's overseers withdrawn from Àth leathan, the Tuathaich hewers there go on working the pits under their own pit captains, paying the Crown's fifth by the Leòid ruling. The Board accepts the payments and records them as arrears.
- **7 am Màrt 1998 DE** — *Cnoc thais in the western hills* (Cnoc thais). At Cnoc thais in the western hills the Tuathaich pits pass to their hewers when the Board's overseers leave, and the pit captain Tom Varley's father is chosen to keep the accounts. The town's own register of the pits begins.
- **5 an Giblean 1998 DE** — *The Sligeanach's great year* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). An Sligeanach Fad' às, the roadside tavern by Ceann bhàn on the southern road, is sold to a family of Achadh mhòr drovers, who build a second hall for the drove trade. It becomes the largest house on the old mining roads.
- **4 an Cèitean 1998 DE** — *The eastern fishing grounds fail* (Seann Dunn). The herring do not come to the grounds off Seann Dunn for the second year together. Boats from the east coast go north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr, which the licence law reserves to them, and the Tuathaich boats are pushed farther out.
- **30 an t-Iuchar 1999 DE** — *Inis mhin's boats* (Inis mhin). The Tuathaich boats of Inis mhin, pushed out from their grounds by the eastern boats, fish the deep water past the northern isles. Two are lost in the first year and none after, and Inis mhin's catch passes Caol mhòr's.
- **28 an Lùnastal 1999 DE** — *Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Mòrag nic Coinnich retires after some thirty years as keeper. Raghnall mac Mhuirich, her deputy, becomes keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol.
- **26 an t-Sultain 1999 DE** — *The ore price at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). The price of ore-fuel at the fair at Muileann òg doubles as the Board cuts its sales. The fair's court fixes a ceiling price and cannot hold it.
- **26 an Cèitean 2000 DE** — *Ore thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich* (Cnoc fhiadhaich). The Board posts watchmen at the spoil-heaps of Cnoc fhiadhaich after households of the town are found picking ore from the waste to burn. The watchmen are from the town and see nothing.
- **19 an t-Ògmhios 2000 DE** — *The first working dubhan*. A crude but functional synthetic fuel is produced. It is not yet an economy. It is, for now, one man's answer to a crisis the caste in power still hasn't fully faced.
- **21 an t-Samhain 2000 DE** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.
- **28 an t-Sultain 2001 DE** — *The Board's inquiry* (Caol mhòr). The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as it is said to. Their report, which reached the library, says that it burns, that it smells, and that it is not ore.
- **27 an Dàmhair 2001 DE** — *The lamp-houses of the capital* (Cathair dhearg). Cathair dhearg's street-lamps, which burned ore since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. The dark streets are the first to be lit again when dubhan comes.
- **22 am Faoilleach 2002 DE** — *The last ore sale at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of ore-fuel by the cartload. Ore is sold at the fair after this only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.
- **1 an Lùnastal 2002 DE** — *Cathal crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mairead's reign ends as Dubhan's early experiments are still failing more than succeeding — Cathal inherits a kingdom that doesn't yet know how close its own solution already is.
- **30 an Lùnastal 2002 DE** — *The mint's new dies* (Cathair dhearg). The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first dies not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the obsidian ink is still pressed into the seal.
- **20 an Gearran 2003 DE** — *The shipmasters' works at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). A works for making dubhan is set up at Seann Skell on the southern coast by a company of shipmasters, the first on the island outside the north. The record does not say on what terms they had the process.
- **25 an t-Samhain 2003 DE** — *The high custodian's letter* (Seann Skell). The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore. The letter is read in the houses and argued about in the Fèidh schools for years.
- **24 an Dùbhlachd 2003 DE** — *The Seann Skell works' first year* (Seann Skell). The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast sell their first year's output to the fishing boats of the south coast and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg. The works' chimney is the tallest thing on the coast.
- **4 am Màrt 2004 DE** — *Peigi nic Ascaill's trial lamp* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to the Lighthouse Board, fits a dubhan burner to a spare lamp in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and runs it for a hundred nights. Murchadh mac Coinnich, retired from the light, keeps the trial's log for her.
- **7 an t-Sultain 2004 DE** — *The fishing boats of Caol fhiadhaich* (Caol fhiadhaich). The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast fit dubhan engines to the first fishing boats. The Shipwrights' Guild calls the work unlawful for its members. The boatwrights leave the guild and keep the work.
- **23 an Giblean 2005 DE** — *The shipwrights' guild court* (Ros dhomhain). The Shipwrights' Guild court at Ros dhomhain rules that fitting an engine is not shipwrighting and so not within its charter. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich are readmitted to the guild. They decline.
- **22 an Cèitean 2005 DE** — *The lighthouses converted* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The five coastal beacons, still running on obsidian-lit flame for over a century, are the first infrastructure formally converted to dubhan power.
- **19 an t-Iuchar 2005 DE** — *The last obsidian flame* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg is carried in a closed lantern to the Rite's house at Seann Skell and allowed to burn out on the altar. Custodians from four shires attend, and Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of the light, carries the lantern.
- **26 am Faoilleach 2006 DE** — *Taigh-solais Muileann bheag converted* (Taigh-solais Muileann bheag). The beacon at Muileann bheag on the Tuathaich north coast is converted with the others. Its dubhan is carried by cart from the north, the only one of the five lights whose fuel does not come by sea from Seann Skell.
- **25 am Màrt 2006 DE** — *Taigh-solais Àth dhearg converted* (Taigh-solais Àth dhearg). At Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape the conversion takes a month longer than at the others, because the stair is too narrow for the new tank. The tank is lifted to the lamp-room from outside by a crane borrowed from the rope-walk at Seann Tarr.
- **20 an t-Ògmhios 2006 DE** — *Taigh-solais Baile chrom converted* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast, the conversion is done by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, the Lighthouse Board having none of its own to send that far. The keeper's report names none of them.
- **28 an Dùbhlachd 2006 DE** — *The lamp-makers turn* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin begin making dubhan lamps and ask for their guild mark to be allowed on them. The guild court allows it after a year's argument. The flame over the hammer is kept.
- **9 am Faoilleach 2007 DE** — *Daniel Frayne dies* (Muileann leathan). Daniel Frayne, speaker of the Moot, dies at Muileann leathan. The Moot chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager, to follow him.
- **24 an Gearran 2007 DE** — *The binders of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). The Moot sends Daniel Frayne's pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind the Moot's minute-books from the first meeting. The rebound set is kept at Caol mhòr, and a second set is made and hidden, the Moot's minute says, elsewhere.
- **1 an Cèitean 2007 DE** — *The ore line's first dubhan engine* (Muileann chrom). The Rail Board runs its first dubhan engine on the ore line, from the yards at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg. It carries no ore. It carries dubhan to the capital's lamp-houses and comes back empty.
- **11 an Dùbhlachd 2007 DE** — *The eastern salt-road* (Àth bheag). Salt from Àth bheag goes to the inland towns by dubhan lorry for the first time, on the drove road past Baile ìseal. The drovers of the east coast sell their oxen within a few years.
- **22 am Màrt 2008 DE** — *Achadh mhòr's drovers* (Achadh mhòr). The drovers of Achadh mhòr in the south, with no oxen to drive, buy lorries. The drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às keeps its trade by selling them dubhan.
- **30 am Màrt 2008 DE** — *The tavern circuit modernizes* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). Roadside houses along the old mining routes install dubhan lamps, ending centuries of oil-and-wick lighting in a single decade.
- **25 an t-Sultain 2008 DE** — *An Leòmhann Buidhe keeps a wick* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road, the landlord keeps one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new dubhan lamps. The custom spreads along the circuit, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.
- **19 an Dàmhair 2008 DE** — *Am Buabhall Fortanach* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). Am Buabhall Fortanach, the tavern on the south-west road near Doire shean, installs its dubhan lamps last of the great inns. Its landlady's account-book gives the cost as a year's takings.
- **3 an Gearran 2009 DE** — *The Taigh-seinnse Mòr's hall* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the old ore road above Cuan chrom, opens a second hall lit entirely by dubhan. The hall is let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the Guild of Hewers, whose own hall at Achadh dhomhain has been sold.
