### II. The Ancient Age: the Two Lists

Before the Binding, Rodos kept its rulers only in recitation. The Stone Kings' list belonged to the hill of Dùn ìseal and is older than the name Ròdaich (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE). The Red Hill list belonged to the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. Each list remembers a holder for one deed and gives no length of reign. For a long time neither mentions the other. They first meet at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is now held, when Raghnall Ceannfhionn traded salt for wool with the Red Hill (10 an Cèitean 6426 BDE). The peace of the ford held through a fosterage: Eilidh Ghlas's son went west to Lachlann an Altraim and came home grown under Peigi Dhubh (31 am Màrt 5174 BDE). Neither list keeps the foster-son's name.

A third office ran beside the two lines and answered to neither. From 26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE the keeper of the slab over the crack was chosen by lot. When Calum Ciar asked for the lot to be drawn in his sight, the households refused him, and from then on the Stone Kings ruled the grazing and not the vein (7 an Cèitean 5185 BDE).

Catrìona Mhòr is the hardest name in either list. The tellings set three things "in her time": the first coming of Dùn dhearg to the ford, the first recital of both lists together, and the keepers' request that their charge be declared (9 an t-Iuchar 3225 BDE). The three fall across more than half a century: a long reign, but not a longer one than a life can hold. The Library does not know whether one holder saw all three or the tellings drew a neighbour's deeds to one famous name. Both lists end in her generation. The Holy Age says the Binding came "centuries before anything like a king" (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE). The Hall that kept that saying did not count the holders of the hills as kings, and the name *Rìghrean na Cloiche* is the later scribes'.

### III. The Holy Age: the Keepers and the Kings

The Keepers came first. The nine hearths chose each one, and for many generations they chose from the house of Muireach. Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair, the first Keeper from outside that house, the office was bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill (29 an Giblean 2607 BDE). The Keeper held the flame, the galleries and the Small-Burning Law, and raised no spears. When Seumas Bàn found that more than half the Keepers on the roll were of his own house, he had the fact struck from its preface (16 an t-Samhain 164 BDE). The unstruck copy survived him.

Kingship began in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. The households who ate Sliochd Ìomhair's grain called Goraidh mac Ìomhair their *rìgh* (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE), and he took care to claim nothing over the vein. By the division of keeping, the rìgh held the roads, the granaries and the lowland peace, and the Keeper held the rest (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE). The early rulers were rulers of roads, and the first war between Ròdaich, Iain Garbh's War of the Roads, was fought over tolls.

The king-list says plainly where it fails. It gives eleven bare names after Catrìona Ghlic (1 an t-Sultain 1779 BDE) and nine after Tormod Òg (29 am Màrt 439 BDE), and Tormod Scrìobhaiche marked which of his names came from reciters (18 an t-Sultain 1668 BDE). The list's years give Goraidh Mòr, his daughter, her son and his niece some eighty years of rule apiece before the niece's son, Iain Garbh, takes the hall: more years than four lives in one line can hold one after another. There, as wherever the list's years outrun the lives of the named, the Library takes it that the reciters' names stand for more reigns than they name, and does not correct them.

Beathag Mhòr, the first *banrìgh*, moved the seat to Cathair dhearg (12 am Faoilleach 1280 BDE). When Oighrig nic Lachlainn died without an heir, the Four Houses met at Dùn ìseal, and the Keeper set the stone cup in the hands of Gilleasbuig Mòr of Sliochd Thormoid (12 am Màrt 483 BDE). The house of Tormod held the red hall from then to the close of the age. Mòr nic Coinnich took the cup from the Keeper in the same way, and her name closes the king-list.

### IV. The Age of Sundering: the Crown and the Houses

Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill would neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back (11 an Dàmhair 38 BDE). Her sister Mòrag went, as a leader of the departed, and six years after the Setting-Out the queen struck Mòrag's line from the succession "as persons no longer on Rodos" (1 an Lùnastal 7 DE). Beathag's own line ended with her grandson Ìomhar.

From then on the seven houses made the kings whenever blood failed. They chose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Clann Fhearchair (19 an Gearran 143 DE), and the crown passed through Sìleas nic Fhearchair to her son's line. That line ended with Tormod Bàn, who died without naming an heir. In the War of the Three Claimants that followed, Raghnall Ruadh, master of the vein-house, used the ore itself as a weapon (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Catrìona Bhuadhach won the crown and bound it, and the custodians with it, never to withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran 526 DE).

The house of Catrìona ended with Eilidh Bhàn. The record calls her its fifth ruler, and the annals name four of the five. The houses, meeting at the vein-house, named Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill (23 am Màrt 807 DE). His house held the crown and the vein-house together for the rest of the age, through a brothers' war and some of the longest reigns in the list. The last crowning the annals record is Gormshuil nic Thormoid's (9 an Dùbhlachd 1727 DE). No annal records her death, an heir, or how the crown fell vacant. The next age finds the Council of Custodians sitting in its place (11 am Faoilleach 1781 DE).

### V. The Age of Strangers: the Council, the Commissioners and the Maoir

The Council of Custodians gave the humans leave to stay, and its high custodian signed the first treaty in a tongue he could not read (7 an Cèitean 1787 DE). After that the council's power only shrank. It asked for its tally and was sent the Company's accounts. From 22 an t-Sultain 1884 DE it could not agree on a high custodian. The last Commissioner locked it out of its hall (26 an Gearran 1926 DE). What authority the custodians still had went with them into the forest council of the mining regions (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE), which chose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it and fought the war that ended the age.

The Commissioners governed from the Residency at Ros dhomhain. Over the age the office and the Company drew together: Walter Crane went from chief agent at the pits to Commissioner, and a Company agent held the seal after his death. The last Commissioner sailed west, and nothing on Rodos records where he arrived (5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE).

The overseers were the Company's rulers at the pithead, all of them Ròdaich (21 an Lùnastal 1816 DE). At Muileann chrom the staff went from father to son, against the custodians' hope, and the byname *Maor* went with it, until Mòrag nic Iain Maor broke the staff rather than carry out evictions (24 an Cèitean 1927 DE).

### VI. The New Age: the Restored Kingdom

The kingdom was restored in order. The war-companies were stood down (3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE), the state was styled *Rìoghachd Ròdais* (27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE), and a royal council of twelve, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the war, took its seat (23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE). Only then was a king crowned. The Crown's officer in each shire took the word *maor* (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE), and the house of the Dark Unicorn at Cathair dhearg was given back the keeping of the regalia (26 an Gearran 1936 DE).

The chronicle of the restored kingdom names five rulers and records their successions and nothing more, and this appendix follows it. The table above gives all that is recorded of them.

### VII. Of the Seven Houses

The seven houses of custody were made from what the Sundering left. With nearly one household in five gone onto the roll of the willing, the remaining custodian households were regrouped into seven houses. Each house answered to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning (4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE). The houses were:

| House | Seat or country, where the record gives one | Holy Age house of the same name | Notable in the record |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clann Mhuirich | Dùn ìseal (as Sliochd Mhuirich) | Sliochd Mhuirich, the Keepers' house | Gave most of the Holy Age's Keepers; in this age the record names it rarely |
| Clann Fhearchair | Baile Mòr dhomhain | Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths of Muileann chiar | The first king chosen by the houses; the double court |
| Clann Ìomhair | Dùn dhearg | Sliochd Ìomhair, the first kings' house | Walled Dùn dhearg in stone, the first walls raised by a house rather than the crown (12 an t-Sultain 222 DE) |
| Clann Raghnaill | — | Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr | Raghnall Ruadh the claimant; from Dòmhnall Ruadh, the crown and the vein-house together |
| Clann Thormoid | — | Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn | The last kings of the Holy Age were of the house of Tormod; in this age it has no entry of its own |
| Clann Choinnich | — | none | Rebuilt the bath-house at the hot springs; brought the silver petitions; swore last to Catrìona Bheag |
| Clann Lachlainn | — | none | Named among the seven; the record keeps no deed of its own |

The regrouping was the first act in the record to treat the right to the ore as inherited by house instead of earned by apprenticeship. Everything that followed came from it. The houses drew lots at the vein-house for the galleries each would keep (30 an Giblean 70 DE). Their heads wore silver neck-rings from Muileann chiar, and on feast days they wore the blue of Baile ghorm until that blue was lost. When blood failed they made kings, once at the capital (19 an Gearran 143 DE) and once at the vein-house (21 an Giblean 802 DE). They split among the three claimants, and later divided four to three between the brothers (8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE). From Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign the heads of the seven sat as the king's council (6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE), and the custodian class and the court became one body.

The houses also forbade things. They forbade Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn's question at their own tables (1 an Giblean 285 DE), the first question in the record forbidden instead of an act. The king's council closed the house at Dùn thais for a generation after Raghnall mac Chaluim tabled the lengths of lives (29 an Giblean 1180 DE). His table found that the heads of the houses lived a few years longer than their tenants. Clann Choinnich twice asked leave to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt. The council refused the first petition (31 an Lùnastal 1520 DE) and the second by one voice (5 an Gearran 1737 DE). The house did not bring it again, and the petition lies in the vein-house unanswered (28 an Dùbhlachd 1767 DE). The census of hands shows the houses narrowing. At the last count of the age, three of the seven held more than half the right between them (27 an Gearran 1752 DE).

Two of the seven names have no house of the same name in the Holy Age record, and for the other five the record gives the name and not the descent. The Library notes that Clann Choinnich shares its name with Coinneach Bàn, grandfather of Mòr nic Coinnich, and Clann Lachlainn with Lachlann Bàn, father of the last queen of Goraidh Mòr's line. The record does not say that either house descends from either man, and the Library does not claim it. After the Sundering age the seven are not named again as a body. The custodian families go on sitting in the Council of Custodians in the Age of Strangers, and the royal council of twelve of the New Age is drawn partly from them (23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE).

### VIII. Of the Vein-House and the Crown

Through every age the island's rulers had to answer one question: who keeps the vein, and who keeps everyone else. The answer changed four times.

In the Ancient Age the answer was separation. The keepers of the slab were chosen by lot, and the kings of the hills were refused a hand in the lot (4 an t-Iuchar 5189 BDE). In the Holy Age the separation became law. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal held the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh held the roads and the granaries. Neither could do the other's work (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE). The Hall lent its authority to the crown twice. The first time was the stone cup set in Gilleasbuig Mòr's hands, when the line of kings failed (12 am Màrt 483 BDE), and the second was the same act for Mòr nic Coinnich.

In the Age of Sundering the Hall's heir was the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (14 an Lùnastal 37 BDE), and the separation failed. The first break was Raghnall Ruadh's. He was master of the vein-house and a claimant to the crown, and he used the ore as a weapon (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Catrìona Bhuadhach's ruling of the hearth was written to bind the custodians themselves. The second break came when the houses crowned the next master of the vein-house, and his reeves wrote into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house (6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE). Dòmhnall Ruadh was buried at Muileann dhearg, by the vein-house. His successors took the ore-roads into the crown's keeping (12 an t-Samhain 900 DE). For nine centuries Rodos had one ruler over both the vein and the realm. Under that ruler the Small-Burning Law was never changed. Every petition to change it was refused or left unanswered.

In the Age of Strangers there was neither crown nor vein-house to hold the vein. The Council of Custodians sat in the crown's place and kept the vein in name only. The Law lapsed without repeal once enforcing it stopped paying (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE). The Company's overseers, not the custodians, ruled the pitheads.

The restored kingdom kept the separation in form and gave up its substance. The Crown granted the Sloc Mòr to a single house on the humans' terms with the names changed (23 an Cèitean 1940 DE), and in time bought every shaft back and worked the vein through its Board "in the Crown's name alone" (30 an t-Iuchar 1989 DE). The keeping of the rite passed to a high custodian of Creideamh nan Ròdach at Seann Skell (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). When that high custodian protested that the plain coinage seal showed the kingdom no longer held the vein sacred, the council answered that the kingdom had never said it did (31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE). The last face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the custody of the Rite, to cut ore for the altars (17 an Cèitean 2025 DE). In the present year it filled four baskets, and the high custodian divided them among the houses of the Rite by lot (29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE). This is the same method the keepers of the slab used to choose their keeper.


## Appendix B — The Faiths of Rodos

This appendix sets down what the record holds about the faiths of Rodos: the nine the map names, the older reverence they grew out of, and the two matters every one of them has had to answer, the holiness of the vein and the question of why it answers some hands and not others. It draws on the annals, the Keepers' roll of Dùn ìseal, the custody-book of the vein-house, the registers that the schools and houses sent to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and the map. Where a faith kept its own counsel, and several did, this appendix says so and leaves the gap open.

Each faith is entered under the Ròdais name the map gives it, with its god as the map gives the god. Where the record shows when a name first appears, that is noted. Where it does not, nothing more is claimed.

### I. The Faiths in Brief

The map counts 505 burgs and sets each under one faith. The seat is the house the record treats as first among a faith's houses in the present age.

| Faith | In the common tongue | Kind (as the map has it) | God | Burgs | Seat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach | the Old Spirits | folk; shamanic | Crom, an t-Àrd-Spiorad, the High Spirit | 126 | Dùn ìseal |
| Creideamh nan Ròdach | the Obsidian Rite | organised; pantheist | Dòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gates | 9 | Seann Skell (south coast) |
| Creideamh an t-Seabhaig | the Faith of the Hawk | organised; dualist | Mòd, an Seabhag Acrach, the Hungry Hawk | 14 | Cnoc bheag |
| Feallsanachd an Fhèidh | the Philosophy of the Deer | organised; philosophical | Camaran, am Fiadh Rìoghail, the Royal Stag | 133 | Dùn thais |
| Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh | the Faith of the Dark Unicorn | organised; dualist | Uallach, an t-Aon-adharcach Dubh, the Dark Unicorn | 103 | Cathair dhearg |
| Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh | the Faith of the Wolf | organised; monotheist | Clach, am Madadh-allaidh Lainnireach, the Resplendent Direwolf | 21 | Inis thais |
| Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe | the Faith of the Yellow Scorpion | organised; monotheist | Cnut, an Scairp Bhuidhe, the Yellow Scorpion | 86 | Seann Skell (west coast) |
| Creideamh nan Tuathach | the Faith of the Tuathaich | folk; shamanic | Donn, an Sìorraidh, the Eternal | 12 | none recorded |
| Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise | the Mystery of the Grey Night | cult | Sìne, an Gèadh Sìtheil, the Peaceful Goose | 1 | Baile chrom (north-west) |

Seven of the nine are Ròdaich faiths. The Faith of the Tuathaich and the Grey Night belong to the Tuathaich of the north. The Yellow Scorpion belongs to both peoples: 35 of its burgs are Ròdaich towns of the west coast and 51 are Tuathaich towns of the north. Between them the three faiths of the north hold all 64 Tuathaich burgs.

Counted by burgs, the Deer is the most widespread faith and the Old Spirits come next. Counted by the people in their towns, the Old Spirits come first, at a little over one million two hundred thousand, with the Dark Unicorn close behind. The Obsidian Rite, which the kingdom treats as orthodox, holds nine towns. That is not a mistake in the count, and section XII explains it.

### II. The Old Reverence and Its Parting

The chronicle says plainly that the faiths were once one. On 11 an Gearran 144 BDE "a single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name." What that one practice was can be put together from the Ancient Age. No god is named anywhere in it.

**The slab and the handful.** A mason broke into a black vein that bled colour instead of dust (20 am Faoilleach 12,918 BDE). His people did not dig on. They laid a slab over the break and cut their well a stone's throw away (19 am Màrt 12,754 BDE). Families took turns sitting by the slab (8 an t-Ògmhios 6481 BDE) and later chose a keeper by lot (26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE). The first was Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill, who had a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her cupped hand (29 an t-Sultain 5195 BDE), because by then no fire took more ore than one hand could hold (5 an Lùnastal 6590 BDE). When a keeper was found with a basket of ore in his house, it was neither burned nor kept. It was laid back under the slab: *the ore went home* (4 an t-Iuchar 5191 BDE). By the end of the age every household of the hills burned its handful on one night of the dark of the year, so that the colour showed on every hillside at once (9 an Cèitean 3246 BDE).

**The doctrine.** The oldest saying on the island is cut on the column near Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE), and it was first spoken as a rule at the ford gathering (21 an t-Sultain 5178 BDE):

> *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.*
> We did not come; we were here.

No faith since has disowned it, though each reads it its own way.

**What the Old Ones left.** Làrach an Teampaill (Làrach an Teampaill) has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal 10,229 BDE), and every later temple on Rodos faces some other way. Its top stone was prised off and never found (5 an Gearran 8686 BDE). The chronicle calls it "a temple older than any recorded religion ... toward the vein, not the horizon" (7 am Faoilleach 8629 BDE). The Ròdaich walked round it and took no stone from it (13 an t-Sultain 4226 BDE). Whether its builders held the vein holy, or only knew where it lay, is not known.

**The Binding and the first parting.** The Holy Age opens with the Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE). At Dùn ìseal Beathag Bhàn was chosen to hold the flame (28 an t-Ògmhios 2995 BDE), and Talla na Lasrach was raised over it with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea (19 an Dùbhlachd 2984 BDE). The custom of the handful hardened into the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE). The Keepers also ruled on what belonged to the vein, and each ruling drew a line. When Muireach Liath held that the fortune-stream Allt an Àigh belonged "to the ancestors and the weather, not to the vein" (16 am Màrt 2940 BDE), the Hall's reverence and the older reverence of the hearths could be seen for the first time as two things.

By the end of the Holy Age the Hall could no longer keep one rite. Seumas Bàn's clerks listed every rite that burned the handful or claimed the vein (18 an Dàmhair 161 BDE): the Hall's own, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The council then began to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complained that he kept the flame for eight peoples who each thought themselves its only keepers (16 an t-Samhain 141 BDE). Those companies are the roots of seven of the nine faiths on the map. The faiths of the Tuathaich grew from other roots.

**What stayed common.** Pilgrims of every rite went on walking to Allt an Àigh (Allt an Àigh) (15 an Dùbhlachd 139 BDE), and the sick of every rite were bathed at the springs of Muileann ruadh (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh) without being asked which rite they kept (19 an t-Sultain 136 BDE). The Age of Sundering added two rites that belong to no single faith. One is the Mourning Custom for the departed, "not quite grief and not quite celebration" (1 an Lùnastal 15 DE). The other is the empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell (25 an t-Samhain 22 DE). The harbour saying at that rite is in no order of worship:

> *Dh'fhalbh iad, agus cha do dh'fhalbh iad.*
> They went, and they did not go.

### III. Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach

**What it holds.** The Old Spirits keep the reverence of the hearths as it was before the Hall: "reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season" (17 am Faoilleach 2978 BDE). The chronicle calls it the island's oldest continuous tradition. It has no order of worship and no council. Its god, as the map gives him, is Crom, the High Spirit, but the annals never name Crom. Every telling of the Old Spirits speaks of the ancestors and the weather, not of any one power over them. When the High Spirit was first called by that name, or by whom, is not known.

**Rites and sayings.** The living heads of families name their ancestors aloud. The names of the dead are cut on wooden posts, which are recut each generation as the old ones rot (7 an Dàmhair 140 DE). The faith keeps the walk to Allt an Àigh as its own, and after the Keepers declined the stream it took Muireach Liath's ruling for its saying:

> *Buinidh an t-allt do na sinnsearan agus don t-sìde.*
> The stream belongs to the ancestors and to the weather.

It blesses what comes from the vein and nothing else. When copper was found behind Àth fhiadhaich, the town's Seann Spioradan house held no blessing for it (28 an Lùnastal 1989 DE).

**Holy places.** Dùn ìseal (Dùn ìseal) and its spirit-house; Seann Dunn (Seann Dunn), where the east-coast houses built a common hall for naming the ancestors of forty families (28 an Dàmhair 1951 DE); Allt an Àigh, with the walkers' hall at Achadh gharbh (11 an Gearran 1940 DE); and Làrach an Teampaill, which at the houses' request was entered by the library as "measured and let be" (7 an Dàmhair 1960 DE).

**History.** By the end of the Holy Age the Hall's list counted the old folk as "a company of its own" (16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE). In the Age of Sundering they built a guest-house at the stream, and its book records pilgrims from every shire (10 an t-Samhain 1220 DE). Under the humans this was the first faith to refuse the Company's ore on principle. The priests at Achadh naomh burned peat and taught "that ore burned for wages is ore burned without the ancestors' leave" (16 am Màrt 1802 DE). In the Long Drought the Administration's watchman at Allt an Àigh, posted to charge pilgrims for the water, was recalled after one season (1 an Cèitean 1887 DE). In the New Age the Rite's custodians discouraged the walk and did not forbid it (8 an t-Iuchar 1939 DE).

**Where it is held now.** 126 burgs, all Ròdaich, spread through the east from the north-east coast to the south. The largest are Seann Bhral (Seann Bhral), Achadh mhòr (Achadh mhòr), Baile Mòr mhòr (Baile Mòr mhòr), Muileann bhàn (Muileann bhàn), Achadh naomh (Achadh naomh) and Dùn dhearg (Dùn dhearg). The map marks temples at Dùn ìseal, Seann Dunn and Seann Tarr.

### IV. Creideamh nan Ròdach

The Faith of the Ròdaich is the Obsidian Rite in its orthodox form, "organized doctrine rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE). As an organised body it is the youngest of the Ròdaich faiths. As a rite it claims to be the oldest. Both are true. Its god on the map is Dòrsair, the Monster of the Gates, which stands at the door between the mountain and those who take from it. The annals do not record that name before the map. Its seat is at the southern Seann Skell (Seann Skell), where its largest house stands (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). Its saying is the Law's own:

> *Làn an dùirn, agus gun tuilleadh.*
> The fill of the fist, and no more.

It holds nine burgs. The largest are Seann Skell, Tobar dhearg (Tobar dhearg), Muileann naomh (Muileann naomh), Caol ruadh (Caol ruadh) and Àth fhionn (Àth fhionn). Its history is given in section XII.

### V. Creideamh an t-Seabhaig

**What it holds.** The Faith of the Hawk is the Rite's older form. It teaches that the vein is Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, "who must be fed the measured handful and no more, since a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand" (20 an Giblean 190 DE). The map calls it dualist because of those two dangers: too much and too little both ruin, and the measure lies between them. The Hawk holds that the measure belongs to the hawk and not to any custodian.

**Rites and sayings.** Each household feeds its hawk before it eats, and the handful is burned at dawn with the hawk on the wrist. The fowlers who began the rite gave its first saying (30 an Dùbhlachd 995 BDE):

> *Is acras an lasair.*
> The flame is a hunger.

Gormshuil's sayings were written down after her death as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth, and those outnumbered the rest (5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE). The saying most often cut over hawk-house doors is:

> *Cha shealg seabhag sàthach.*
> A sated hawk will not hunt.

**Holy places.** The oldest hawk carving on the island is over a door at Àth mhòr (13 an Dùbhlachd 5749 BDE), and it is older than any rite. The rite itself began at the Seann Skell of the northern coast (Seann Skell). The first house of the faith is at Cnoc bheag (Cnoc bheag).

**History.** The dawn-hawk spread along the north coast in the Holy Age, and as it spread the Keeper wrote that it was no concern of the Hall's (28 am Faoilleach 923 BDE). Later it became the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright (19 an t-Sultain 159 BDE). The faith was formalised, not founded, when Gormshuil nic Artair gathered the old rite at Cnoc bheag into the first house of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig (20 an Giblean 190 DE). A second house followed at Ros gheal (22 am Màrt 200 DE) and a southern one at Muileann naomh (13 an t-Sultain 487 DE). The schism came when a council at Cnoc bheag split over whether Mòd's measure could ever be raised (20 an t-Ògmhios 850 DE). Those who called it fixed kept the name of the Hungry Hawk. The Fed Hawk were turned out to the northern Seann Skell (23 an Giblean 870 DE), and their petition to raise the handful by a quarter was the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law (25 an Lùnastal 880 DE). It was refused, and the record does not follow the Fed Hawk as a separate house after that.

Under the humans the Hawk resisted before any organised resistance existed. Murchadh Seabhag preached that Mòd starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them (6 an t-Sultain 1801 DE), and his sermon was the first Ròdaich text the Company's agents were told to confiscate. When hawk-priests were barred from the camps (12 an t-Sultain 1817 DE), the crews carried the sermons in themselves (10 an Cèitean 1855 DE). Ìomhar Seabhag's shrines served as meeting houses for the Lamp-Watch (24 an Giblean 1919 DE), and when the war came he called it Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it (2 am Màrt 1929 DE). In the New Age the Hawk houses refused the Rite's order of worship (17 an Cèitean 1935 DE) and named their own custodian at Inis ìseal (26 an Cèitean 1964 DE). They wrote out their order, which until then had been spoken and never written, and they keep the copy locked away (29 an t-Samhain 1964 DE). They accepted a place under the high custodian only on condition that they kept that order (13 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE). The quarrel with the Rite has quietened, but it has not ended.

**Where it is held now.** Fourteen burgs, all Ròdaich, along the north-central coast. Cnoc bheag is the largest, and its Hawk house is the richest of any faith outside the capital (14 an Dàmhair 1975 DE). After it come Inis bhàn (Inis bhàn), Ros gheal (Ros gheal), the northern Seann Skell and Ros leathan (Ros leathan).

### VI. Feallsanachd an Fhèidh

**What it holds.** The Philosophy of the Deer is a school, not a church. It formed around one question, why the vein answers some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE): "the first attempt to reason about the obsidian rather than simply revere it." It does not deny that the vein is holy. It asks what the holiness does. None of the school's records in the library show the stag, Camaran, being worshipped. His name first appears "in texts much younger than these events" (7 an Dùbhlachd 2881 BDE). The map counts the Deer among the faiths, and the school has not objected.

**Rites and sayings.** Its one public observance is the yearly walking of the bounds of its sacred forest (11 an t-Iuchar 440 DE). Everything else it does is argument. Its oldest question, as the masters put it to beginners, is:

> *Carson an làmh seo?*
> Why this hand?

A student who thinks he has solved it is given Aonghas mac Coinnich's answer (19 an t-Ògmhios 1828 DE):

> *Chan e sin a' cheist.*
> That is not the question.

**Holy places.** Coille Naomh Muileann chiar (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar), "marked sacred, long before any organized faith claims it formally" (21 an Giblean 9486 BDE), where the white stag was first seen (11 am Màrt 9373 BDE); Dùn thais (Dùn thais), with the first stone temple of the stag's people (21 am Màrt 110 BDE); and Caol shean (Caol shean), the school's house in the New Age.

**Where it is held now.** 133 burgs, all Ròdaich, in the north-east, along the east coast and in the eastern hills. The largest are Caol bheag (Caol bheag), Baile gharbh (Baile gharbh), Dùn thais, Caol shean and Caol gharbh (Caol gharbh). The map marks temples at Dùn thais and Ros fhionn (Ros fhionn). Muileann chaol (Muileann chaol), the library town, is a Deer town. The school's history is given in section XIII.

### VII. Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh

**What it holds.** The Faith of the Dark Unicorn holds "that light and dark are two powers in balance and that the vein belongs to both" (31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE). Its beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and so does the vein (13 am Faoilleach 147 BDE). It is the faith of the capital and the court. Its saying is the wood-watchers':

> *Tha dà nàdar aig a' bhèist, agus aig an fhèith.*
> The beast has two natures, and so has the vein.

**Rites and holy places.** Its priests read omens for rulers and bury by their own rite. King Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king buried that way (31 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE). Its floors are laid in black and white, and the floor of its great house at Cathair mhòr (Cathair mhòr) took eleven years (14 am Màrt 1420 DE). Its sacred wood is Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag), near the lesser Cnoc bheag south of the capital (Cnoc bheag). That town is not the Hawk port of the same name.

**History.** The faith began as a watch. A small company settled at the edge of a wood no one had ever cleared and watched for a black horned beast that walked in it (15 an t-Samhain 1430 BDE). Its quarrel with the stag's people over both sacred woods became the holy-wood dispute, "settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner" (10 an Gearran 1403 BDE). Anna Ruadh took a wood-watcher into her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens (23 an t-Iuchar 177 BDE). Cathair dhomhain refused one, and the rivalry between the two towns took a religious turn "it never loses" (24 an t-Ògmhios 173 BDE). Cathair dhomhain is a Unicorn town now, with its own temple. The faith was formalised when King Aonghas took up the teaching of Uallach (31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE). By royal grant its priests then took sole custody of the western wood, and the other claimants withdrew for reasons the record does not give (14 am Faoilleach 432 DE).

Under the humans it split over the Residency's coin. The priests at Cathair dhearg blessed it (24 an Gearran 1864 DE). Those who refused went to the sacred forest, where they received custodians who had lost their seats (25 am Màrt 1866 DE). Sixty years later the capital's temple sheltered the council that Strake had locked out (26 an Gearran 1926 DE). In the forest the dissenters sat with custodians and the Lamp-Watch when the council of the mining regions was formed (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE). In the restored kingdom the house at Cathair dhearg got back the keeping of the regalia and refused the Rite a share of it (26 an Gearran 1936 DE).

**Where it is held now.** 103 burgs, all Ròdaich, across the middle and south of the island. The largest are Ros dhomhain (Ros dhomhain), Cathair mhòr, Àth shean (Àth shean), Seann Chwen (Seann Chwen) and Baile ghlas (Baile ghlas). The map marks five of its temples, more than for any other faith: Cathair mhòr, Cathair dhomhain (Cathair dhomhain), Cathair dhearg (Cathair dhearg), Ceann leathan (Ceann leathan) and Cuan uaine (Cuan uaine). Cnoc naomh, whose people once kept the old reverence "with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it" (16 an t-Ògmhios 73 BDE), is a Unicorn town on the map.

### VIII. Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh

**What it holds.** The Faith of the Wolf holds that one god watches the whole island as a guard watches a road (21 an Lùnastal 156 BDE). That god is Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, "who keeps the island as a wolf keeps its range" (28 am Màrt 370 DE). The god's name is the common word for *stone*. The first wolf was a white stone at the gate of Caol leathan, on which road-guards swore their watch, and the annals say that "later ages will read more into the stone than they did" (12 am Faoilleach 1990 BDE). The record does not show the Wolf claiming the vein. When the Rite was formalised, the Wolf houses sent no witnesses, only "a letter saying they wish it well" (29 an Cèitean 1935 DE).

**Rites and sayings.** Oaths are taken before the wolf-stone. The Wolf's houses nurse the sick. At Inis chrom its preachers died doing it, "and the town becomes the Wolf's for good" (3 an t-Sultain 585 DE). Its saying comes from the road-guards:

> *Mar a ghleidheas am freiceadan an rathad, gleidhidh Clach an t-eilean.*
> As the guard keeps the road, Clach keeps the island.

**Holy places.** Caol leathan (Caol leathan), whose Wolf house is the largest of the faith and rings a bell for the hours (7 an Cèitean 1950 DE); Inis thais (Inis thais), where a second wolf-stone of white quartz was dragged from the mountain (3 an Dùbhlachd 780 BDE) and the first temple to Clach by name was built (16 an Dùbhlachd 380 DE); and Baile gheal (Baile gheal).

**History.** The wolf-sworn were soldiers before they were a faith. The faith was formalised when Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, gave their one god a name (28 am Màrt 370 DE). Its schism was over the dead. Those who would not pray to Clach for the dead kept the temple at Inis thais, and those who would built a house at Baile gheal (4 an Gearran 1350 DE, 8 an Lùnastal 1360 DE). The record does not say the two houses have been reconciled. In the New Age the Wolf houses have acted as banks as well as churches. They issued chits on house paper when coin ran short (3 am Màrt 1935 DE) and lent the money for Doire shean's harbour (24 an t-Ògmhios 1959 DE). They also published a count of their own people that matched the kingdom's to within a hundred (28 an Lùnastal 1994 DE).

**Where it is held now.** 21 burgs, all Ròdaich, in the south-west. The largest are Doire shean (Doire shean), Inis thais, Inis chrom (Inis chrom), Baile ghorm (Baile ghorm) and Seann Warr (Seann Warr). The only temple on the map is at Inis thais.

### IX. Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe

**What it holds.** The Faith of the Yellow Scorpion holds that one power stings the liar wherever he is, and that the scorpion is only its sign. It was the first creed on the island to call itself the only true one (3 an Dùbhlachd 153 BDE). Its god is Cnut, and its central teaching is about the sea: "Cnut closed the western sea behind the fleet ... it must not be tried again" (1 an t-Sultain 615 DE).

**Rites and sayings.** Oaths of trade are sworn on a scorpion's sting (19 an t-Samhain 2120 BDE). No boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands, and on the west coast steering by the stars was lost entirely (27 an t-Samhain 655 DE). At the harbour mouth the priests pray (13 an Giblean 1551 DE):

> *A Chnuit, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*
> Cnut, keep the sea shut.

Since 1675 DE that prayer has been said on the day of the empty-harbour rite. So on one quay, on one day, some mourn the departed and some pray that no one follows them. Neither side is pleased.

**Holy places.** Seann Skell on the west coast (Seann Skell), where the creed was declared; Baile àrsaidh (Baile àrsaidh), where the sting-oath began; Seann Vell (Seann Vell), which has the first scorpion carved in yellow stone for worship (4 an t-Samhain 150 BDE); and Cnoc ghorm (Cnoc ghorm), the largest house in the north.

**History.** The sting-oath went from Baile àrsaidh up the coast to Ros bheag (1 am Faoilleach 852 BDE) and became a creed at Seann Skell. The faith was formalised when Mànas mac Ruairidh named its power Cnut (1 an t-Sultain 615 DE). A worked timber longer than any tree on the island, held with nails no smith on Rodos could place, came ashore at Ceann mhòr. It was carried to Seann Skell, shown to the Scorpion's priests, and burned (22 an Cèitean 1755 DE). That was twenty-five years before the humans came.

How the Tuathaich came to the Scorpion the record does not say (12 an Giblean 1938 DE). By the early New Age most Tuathaich towns kept the faith. Cnoc ghorm's house taught in the humans' tongue and read the scripture in the Ròdais text used on the west coast (29 an Giblean 1939 DE). The house at Seann Bhral turned away northern worshippers from its feast, saying "the god is the same and the house is not" (2 an t-Sultain 1954 DE). They held the feast at Cnoc ghorm instead, and within a generation it was the larger of the two (11 an Gearran 1955 DE). On the eve of the Long War the Scorpion house at Seann Skell refused to bless the enforcers' depot (23 am Faoilleach 2018 DE).

**Where it is held now.** 86 burgs: 35 Ròdaich and 51 Tuathaich. Its seat, the western Seann Skell, is the largest town on Rodos. After it come Caol mhòr (Caol mhòr), Cuan shean (Cuan shean), Ceann mhòr (Ceann mhòr) and Baile fhiadhaich (Baile fhiadhaich).

### X. Creideamh nan Tuathach

**What it holds.** The Tuathaich communities of the north keep their own folk tradition (13 an Gearran 1938 DE), "including, quietly, the First Canoe fragment the Ròdaich priesthood still calls superstition." The map calls it shamanic and names its god Donn, the Eternal. Beyond that the record holds almost nothing, and what it has comes from outside the faith. Few Tuathaich would speak to the chronicle clerks (25 am Màrt 1948 DE). The north's books stayed in private keeping (3 an Lùnastal 1996 DE). The request to archive Tuathaich oral history at the library was tabled rather than rejected, and it is still tabled (15 an Gearran 2016 DE). This appendix does not know the faith's rites, its sayings, its holy places, or whether Donn is the Tuathaich's own name for their god.

**The First Canoe.** The only one of the faith's tellings known outside the north is the fragment its tellers set in the Ancient Age: "a named steersman, a first crossing" (9 an t-Samhain 10,054 BDE). The steersman's name is in no Ròdaich record. The record does not say how families whose forebears came over the water in 1780 DE came to keep a telling set so long before the Sundering. This appendix leaves it where its tellers set it, notes that the north still keeps it in the present day (21 an Dùbhlachd 2026 DE), and does not resolve it.

**Where it is held now.** Twelve burgs, all Tuathaich, along the north. The largest are Doire ghlas (Doire ghlas), Muileann leathan (Muileann leathan), Inis mhin (Inis mhin) and Baile ghlas in Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh (Baile ghlas).

### XI. Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise

**What it holds.** Of the Mystery of the Grey Night the record knows the name, the god, one custom and one town. The god is Sìne, the Peaceful Goose. The custom is "one night of silence in the year", and outsiders are not told which night it is (14 am Màrt 1938 DE). No saying is known.

**History.** The cult first appears in a Mission report that human labourers near Baile chrom were meeting at night in the fields to pray to a grey goose (25 an Giblean 1912 DE). The Mission called it a superstition learned from the Ròdaich, and the Ròdaich disowned it. From the Ancient Age the record keeps a telling of the grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm and are never hunted there (3 an Lùnastal 9086 BDE). The record does not connect the two, and this appendix does not either. After the Severance the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane held the rites openly (14 am Màrt 1938 DE). A magistrate fined her, and the vigil moved indoors (15 an t-Ògmhios 1956 DE). The keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom (Taigh-solais Baile chrom) reported that the vigil was kept in the lighthouse's shadow (27 an Giblean 1961 DE). In the Long War soldiers searched the town on a night when it was wholly dark and silent, and they found nothing (9 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE).

**Where it is held now.** One burg: Baile chrom in the far north-west (Baile chrom). It is not the Baile chrom in the hills (Baile chrom), and the record takes care to keep the two apart (11 an Gearran 1853 DE).

### XII. Of the Obsidian Rite

The Rite is older than any name for it. Its root is the slab over the crack and the handful in the cup. What the chronicle calls the Obsidian Rite, and the map calls Creideamh nan Ròdach, is the part of the old reverence that holds the vein itself to be sacred. It is not the sign of a god or the seat of a spirit. It is the holy thing.

**The vein as sacred.** The Rite holds that the vein bleeds because it is alive in some way the Ròdaich are not asked to understand. What is broken from it must be burned in measure or returned. The vein answers a line of people, and that answering is itself holy. The doctrine of 1935 is "built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE): the vein under the ground and the blood of those it has answered. Fionnghal nic Artair's defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only one that survives, argued that "the Law was never about the ore but about the people who would become whatever the burning made them" (11 an t-Ògmhios 1801 DE). She wrote it two generations before Aisling was born, and it has been read as prophecy since. She did not claim to be prophesying.

**Under the Keepers.** In the Holy Age the Rite belonged to the Hall. The Keepers held the cup, took the census of hands (22 an t-Ògmhios 1255 BDE) and sentenced households that burned beyond the measure (1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE). Their roll holds one hundred and forty names (2 an Giblean 60 BDE).

**Under the vein-house.** Each ship of the Sundering carried one sealed measure of ore and no more (17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg kept the custody-book, and in 820 DE the crown and the custody were joined. The Rite's worst hour in that age came in war, not heresy. Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refused the handful to every hearth in the shires that stood against him, "and the act turns more people against him than any battle" (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). The council refused the Fed Hawk's petition and refused Clann Choinnich's request to smelt silver with the ore (31 an Lùnastal 1520 DE), "the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship."

**Under the humans.** The Small-Burning Law lapsed without repeal "once it stops being profitable to enforce" (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE). The Rite lived on in shrines at the pit mouths. At Cill dhìreach the crews left the first piece of ore from each new gallery, and the Company allowed it "because it costs a stone a gallery" (19 an t-Sultain 1851 DE). At Cill ghlas the custodians kept the rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting (18 an Dàmhair 1851 DE). They agreed the word *fuil-ghuail* there (21 an Gearran 1905 DE), and the Rending swallowed that shrine (3 an t-Iuchar 1916 DE).

**Formalised.** The Rite was formalised on 18 an Giblean 1935 DE. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was seated at the southern Seann Skell as Àrd-choimheadaiche, and his first charge was a written order of worship: "there had never been one" (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). The Hawk refused the order and the Wolf stood aside. When the council kept the night shift, the custodians "enter a protest and then bless the shafts" (18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE). The Rite has worked that way ever since. It protests how the kingdom uses the vein, and then it blesses it.

**The Depletion.** The high custodian ruled that dubhan was "not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore" (25 an t-Samhain 2003 DE). When the beacons were converted (22 an Cèitean 2005 DE), the obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg was carried to Seann Skell and left to burn out on the altar (19 an t-Iuchar 2005 DE). When the coinage seal lost its obsidian ink, the high custodian protested. The council replied that the kingdom had never said it held the vein sacred (31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE).

**The Rite now.** One face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the Rite's custody (17 an Cèitean 2025 DE). Twelve hewers work it, the last of their trade (29 an Cèitean 2025 DE). On 29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE they cut the year's altar-ore. It filled four baskets, and the high custodian divided it among the houses by lot.

That is why the Rite holds only nine burgs. Most Ròdaich who hold the vein sacred keep it at the hearth, as the Old Spirits do, or at the local altar, as the Hawk does. The Rite is their church in name, and it is their whole faith in only nine towns. It was formalised after the vein had begun to fail. In less than a century it went from an order of worship for the whole island to four baskets of ore.

### XIII. Of the Deer's Question

> *Carson an làmh seo?*

The Philosophy of the Deer began with one question, asked at Muileann chiar in the Holy Age: why does the vein answer some hands and not others (10 an Dàmhair 2896 BDE)? Some have made much of how close *fèidh*, deer, sounds to *fèith*, vein. The school's own texts do not.

**Forbidden and allowed.** The Hall shut the galleries to the stag's people "on the ground that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it" (18 an Cèitean 2874 BDE). They were later let back in on an oath "to ask nothing of the vein aloud" (26 an Gearran 2423 BDE). The Hall called that a reconciliation, and the school called it a truce. Long after the truce the stag's people made the first Ròdaich letters out of cutters' tally-notches (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE), and nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.

**Birth or effort.** Apprentices kept strike-books, written accounts of every blow (23 am Màrt 1325 BDE). Reading them, Donnchadh mac Iain found that the ore bled brighter for older cutters, whatever house they came from (28 an Gearran 709 BDE). The chronicle records the split that followed: "a breakaway sect argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over" (7 an t-Sultain 682 BDE). The breakaway school at Muileann chaol did not write a cutter's parentage in the book at all (9 an Lùnastal 669 BDE). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh heard both schools and gave no ruling, "saying the vein has not asked the Hall to decide" (4 an t-Samhain 633 BDE).

**The years of disputation.** At Dùn thais the question was argued by rule (29 an Cèitean 275 DE). Eilidh Dhubh's tracts for the effort-school were read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east (23 an t-Ògmhios 445 DE). Then Raghnall mac Chaluim showed that the heads of the custodian houses lived a few years longer than their tenants, and asked whether the vein answers the hand that holds it (29 an t-Samhain 1170 DE). The house was later reopened only on condition that the question of longer lives was not raised (20 an Giblean 1720 DE). His table is nearly seven hundred years older than the first of the immortal generation.

**Under the humans.** Samuel Wren asked the masters why the vein should be holy. They asked him why his fuel should be burned (3 an Dùbhlachd 1797 DE). Aonghas mac Coinnich asked why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore, and said it was the wrong question (19 an t-Ògmhios 1828 DE). Tolley closed the hall at Dùn thais (14 an Dùbhlachd 1868 DE). The last public disputation asked whether a question may be forbidden, and the Administration's clerk recorded that it may (30 an Giblean 1869 DE). After that the masters taught under the trees (15 an t-Ògmhios 1869 DE), until the last of them died in 1902 DE.

**The revival.** The school reopened in 1975 DE, when its question became "suddenly urgent again as the vein itself starts running short." Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain lectured in the sacred wood (11 an Dùbhlachd 1975 DE), and the school took a house at Caol shean, where students debated the census note on the obsidian-touched openly (5 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE). When the Mine Board searched for a second vein, she wrote that "nobody has asked why there is one vein" (13 an Giblean 1980 DE). The Board filed her letter, and the search found nothing (21 an Giblean 1980 DE). The school's own word for its revival is *dubhan-tùsail* (22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE).

**What the question has come to.** In the Holy Age it asked whether the ore bled for birth or for practice. In the Age of Sundering it asked whether the vein lengthened lives. Under the humans it asked why the humans could not see the colour. Since 1905 DE, when the custodians agreed a plain word for what the vein had begun to do to a few children, the answer has had a name but no reason. The masters do not claim that the question caused the Long War, and no one has accused them of it. They would say only that it was asked in the Holy Age and has not been answered since.


## Appendix C — Hosts, Wars and Calamities

This appendix gathers from the annals every war and armed struggle the record keeps, the hosts that stand on the map today, and the calamities that have fallen on the island, whether sent by the sea, the ground, the weather or the vein. It adds nothing the annals do not hold. Where the annals disagree with one another the entries are given as they stand. Where the record is sealed, or was never made, this appendix says so and goes no further.

The reader should know how much is missing. The Ancient Age cut its dead on tally stones and did not say what killed them. The Age of Sundering left two histories of its wars, and one was written to praise a king. For the Age of Strangers the custodians' rolls, the Mission's lists and the Residency's letter-books seldom give the same number. The complete record of the Long War is sealed at Leabharlann Muileann chaol until the fifty years run out (27 an Giblean 2023 DE).

### Part I. The Wars

### Before the wars

The oldest act of force the record knows is not a war, and nobody knows who did it. On 29 an Dàmhair 8914 BDE the single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire was blocked with rubble from the inside, by people who left by another way or did not leave. More than a century later the cistern of Làrach an Dùin, which had served four hundred people, was found choked with the bones of whole cattle (4 an Giblean 8800 BDE). Both are works of the Seann-Dhaoine. The record will not guess at what was being fought over there, or by whom.

The first war in either of the oral king-lists is **the salt-flats raid**. On 9 am Faoilleach 6929 BDE Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, led the hill-folk down to the salt-pans at Baile ghorm and carried the salt away. Seven died on the hill side, and the telling keeps that number. Her successor Iain Dubh went down to repeat the raid and was killed on the shingle (8 an t-Ògmhios 6874 BDE). The list says only that he was brought home. After him the Ancient Age records no war.

### The War of the Roads

*Cause.* In the Holy Age the carriers' road ran from the mountain to the sea, and its tolls went to the rìgh of Dùn dhearg. Lachlann Ciar, head of the leading family of the harbour town of Caol leathan, began to keep the southern tolls for himself and send none of them to Dùn dhearg (14 an Gearran 2008 BDE). Iain Garbh, son of Sìleas Dhonn, took the hall at Dùn dhearg and demanded the western tolls, and Lachlann Ciar sent him back a basket of fish-bones (12 an Cèitean 2005 BDE).

*Sides.* On one side were Iain Garbh of Dùn dhearg, the road-guards and the lowland levies. On the other were Lachlann Ciar and the men of Caol leathan. The Hall at Dùn ìseal refused to bless either side.

*Course.* On 13 an Giblean 2000 BDE Iain Garbh marched west and burned the toll-house at Muileann òg, which Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. The annals call this the first war between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. At the ford of Àth fhiadhaich the men of Caol leathan held Iain Garbh's levies for a day before they gave way (21 an Dàmhair 1998 BDE). Forty were dead on the two sides together, and for a long time afterward the carriers called it the ford of the forty. Falling back, Lachlann Ciar's men burned Baile ghlas so that the levies would find no grain there (16 am Faoilleach 1997 BDE). Its people walked to Cathair dhomhain, and many of them never came home. Baile chiar shut its gate against both armies and fed the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter (18 an Dùbhlachd 1996 BDE). Neither side forgave it and neither side attacked it. Iain Garbh then closed Caol leathan from the landward side for a season, but its boats brought in fish and he could not close the harbour. His levies drifted home for the harvest, and the siege ended without an assault (2 an t-Samhain 1994 BDE).

*End.* The two leaders met under the roof of the waypoint house that would later be called Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither of them could draw (4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE). Caol leathan kept half its tolls and sent the other half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swore to the Law with the Keeper as witness. So the war ended in a house built to feed carriers. Muileann òg was rebuilt as a market town, and its fair is the ancestor of Fèill Muileann òg (5 an t-Iuchar 1325 BDE).

### Lesser strife of the Holy Age

The **Silver Feud** (17 an t-Sultain 1233 BDE) was a closing and not a war. For three seasons no silver left Muileann chiar. The road-guards went unpaid and the eastern tolls went uncollected. The record gives the feud its name while noting that no one was killed in it. At sea, outlaw boats from the eastern islets began raiding the fishing strands. Sliochd Raghnaill armed its boats at Seann Tarr and burned two of them (10 an t-Ògmhios 544 BDE), and the rest were never caught. Late in the age raiders from the north-western waters took a season's dried fish from the north-western strands. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag paid for two armed boats to watch the shore, and the raiders moved north (28 an Gearran 254 BDE).

### The War of the Three Claimants

*Cause.* King Tormod Bàn's two sons were drowned together when a ferry overturned on Abhainn fhionn (18 an t-Ògmhios 495 DE). The king died at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir (8 an t-Sultain 508 DE), and three claims were laid before the houses at once.

*Sides.* The claimants were Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (21 an Giblean 513 DE). The seven houses divided among the three. Seann Warr, the western port nearest the capital, shut its gates to all three and declared for none (20 an Cèitean 514 DE). It was besieged twice during the war and taken by neither claimant.

*Course.* Dùghall's host broke Raghnall's at the ford of Àth shean on 22 an Gearran 515 DE. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford. Raghnall's men burned Doire mhin and its granary as they fell back (24 an t-Sultain 516 DE), and the villagers spent the winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of the Dark Unicorn's priests. Catrìona besieged Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and took it after forty days, when the dead of the siege lines had poisoned its wells (26 an Dùbhlachd 518 DE). She let the garrison go free on their oath. Raghnall, who held the vein-house, then refused the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Hearths that had burned ore for generations went cold. The annals judge that this act turned more people against him than any battle did. Catrìona and Dùghall joined their hosts for the purpose and met Raghnall below Muileann chrom on 14 am Faoilleach 521 DE. Raghnall was killed on the field, and his own custodians opened the vein-house the next day.

*End.* Catrìona was crowned at Cathair dhearg on 13 am Màrt 523 DE and was known afterward as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The war had lasted about a decade. Her first great law bound the custodians themselves: no claimant, house or king could withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran 526 DE). Seann Warr's neutral gates were later honoured by the crown (11 an Giblean 555 DE). Seònaid nic Coinnich's *Book of the Three Claimants* (8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE) is the oldest history on Rodos written as one narrative rather than as a list of entries.

### The sea-thieves of the north-west

Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast began to take fish and grain from coasting traders (24 am Faoilleach 745 DE). The thieves were Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names. A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn landed on Eilean dhubh and burned their boats on the strand (27 an t-Samhain 762 DE). Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, was taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

### The Brothers' War, Cogadh nam Bràithrean

*Cause.* King Ailean mac Raghnaill died at Cathair dhearg leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each of them had been told that he was the heir (7 an t-Iuchar 1227 DE).

*Sides.* The seven houses divided four to three between the brothers.

*Course.* Alasdair Bàn's men seized Cnoc naomh, and Iain Ciar took it back on 8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE. The war is named from that battle. Alasdair's ships burned the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother, taking the rope stores and the granary, and the town had to beg its bread from Cathair mhòr (17 an Lùnastal 1233 DE). Iain Ciar defeated Alasdair below Muileann ghlas on 19 an t-Iuchar 1235 DE. Alasdair was taken alive, and his captains were allowed to go home.

*End.* The brothers made peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands (12 an t-Sultain 1237 DE). Alasdair gave up his claim and was given the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar was crowned. Alasdair kept the peace until his death (8 an Dàmhair 1252 DE), and his lordship went back to the crown. Iain Ciar, having seen Ceann mhin beg for bread, ordered every shire seat to keep a year's grain in store against the next war (20 an Giblean 1260 DE). The only surviving account of the war was written by his clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh (14 an Lùnastal 1265 DE). It praises the king at every turn, and later readers have found it inconvenient.

### The humans' campaigns and the forerunners of war

For most of the Age of Strangers the humans made war only at sea. Raiders stripped a Company brig off the north-west coast (10 an Giblean 1795 DE) and burned an ore ship off the east (20 an Dàmhair 1825 DE). The Company's first armed reply was a gunboat that burned every boat on the shingle of a cove near Ceann leathan (25 an t-Iuchar 1826 DE). Most of them belonged to the town's own fishermen, and the raiders were not found.

On land the Administration kept no standing force until Charles Merriman brought a company of armed constables (11 an Dàmhair 1910 DE). They broke the dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain (3 an Cèitean 1912 DE). After the Rending the roll records the first violent clash between the two peoples (17 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE), placed by its fuller entry at Muileann chrom (13 an Dùbhlachd 1916 DE): a gallery drowned seven when the pumps were stopped to save fuel, the crews stoned the Company's agent, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable died. Merriman answered the second petition by tripling the constabulary and fortifying the stores of four mining towns (25 an Gearran 1919 DE). The roadside houses became waypoints for a militia with no name (9 an t-Sultain 1920 DE). The first coordinated stoppage was broken by closing the Company stores (30 an Dùbhlachd 1922 DE). After the confiscation edict (27 am Màrt 1926 DE) the silver guild began buying rifles from the eastern pirates (21 an t-Iuchar 1927 DE), a council for the mining regions met in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE), and Strake ordered its arrest (3 am Faoilleach 1928 DE).

### The War of the Hills

This history calls it the War of the Hills, after the country where it began. Later rolls call it the Severance war, after the way it ended.

*Cause.* On 6 am Faoilleach 1928 DE Ròdaich resistance, coordinated for the first time across several mining regions, passed from grievance to open war. The grievances are those listed above. The one cited most often is the confiscation edict.

*Sides.* On the Ròdaich side stood the council of custodians and crew-leaders under Eilidh nic Raghnaill, with the crews of the camps, the Lamp-Watch, the silver guild of Muileann chiar and its riflemen, the riflemen of Cnoc leathan (3 am Faoilleach 1929 DE), the company of the hawk-faithful mustered at Seann Skell (16 am Màrt 1929 DE), and the towns that declared for the council one after another. On the Administration's side stood Commissioner Strake, the constabulary, the Company's guards, and the Company's steamships and coasters. Some towns held apart. The human town of Cathair gheal shut its gates and raised a militia that it sent to neither side (15 an Gearran 1929 DE). The concession town of Muileann àrsaidh closed its road against both sides for the rest of the war (25 an Gearran 1929 DE). The Ròdaich city of Ros dhomhain, below the Residency, neither joined the rising nor opposed it until late in the war.

*Course.* The war opened in the hills. Crews under Mòrag nic Iain rushed the store at Muileann chrom at first light, and its eleven constables surrendered without a shot (20 an Gearran 1928 DE). Crews sank two barges across the mouth of the ore quay at Ceann fhada (28 an Gearran 1928 DE). At Baile thais the constables held their walled pithead for eleven days and surrendered on the twelfth, when their water ran out, and Eilidh nic Raghnaill sent them to the coast unharmed (16 an Cèitean 1928 DE). The northern pits rose (24 an Cèitean 1928 DE), and An Taigh-seinnse Mòr shut its gates across the ore road, which stayed cut (1 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE). The capital rose next and barricaded Drochaid Cathair dhearg with ore-carts (30 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE), and Strake drew the Administration into the Residency above Ros dhomhain (17 an Lùnastal 1928 DE).

The first relief column, under Major Peter Ashdown, was met at the ford of Àth chiar on 25 an Lùnastal 1928 DE. Ashdown lost forty men and his baggage. The rebels lost nineteen, and the council's roll names them all. Dùn chrom shut its gates behind the retreating column and nursed the wounded it left (11 an t-Samhain 1928 DE). In the east the silver town rose (19 an t-Samhain 1928 DE), and the post at Dùn ìseal surrendered after one exchange of fire (27 an t-Samhain 1928 DE).

The humans struck back from the sea. A Company steamship shelled the ore stage at Seann Toll and burned the town behind it, killing twenty-three (17 am Faoilleach 1929 DE). On 1 an Gearran 1929 DE fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh burned a Company coaster at anchor. The keepers of the southern beacons put out their fires, and two Company ships were lost on the reefs (31 am Màrt 1929 DE).

Through the first winter neither side could attack the other (11 an Cèitean 1929 DE), and the capital went hungry (9 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE). In the stalemate the rebels burned the tithe ledgers in three raids (10 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE), at Ros dhomhain, Ceann àrsaidh and Muileann chrom. The Administration's last sally toward the mining country was driven back at Cnoc ghorm on 6 an Lùnastal 1929 DE. The Ros dhomhain harbour quarter opened its gates to the council (7 an Lùnastal 1929 DE), Strake left the Residency by sea (4 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), and Ros bheag became the last seat of the Administration (5 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), where the human families went hungry within weeks (23 an t-Sultain 1929 DE).

*End.* The last ship recorded from an Tìr Thall came to Ros bheag with a sealed letter and left on the next tide (20 an Dàmhair 1929 DE). Envoys met at Àth àrsaidh and agreed a truce (1 an t-Samhain 1929 DE). The humans still on Rodos would go into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council would leave the concession towns standing. The columns went north (20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE) and camped a night at Àth leathan (1 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE), where several of the humans wrote down the name of the place. Strake sailed west in the last ship able to make the crossing (5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE). On 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE the war ended with the crossing itself closed. That is the Severance. The war-companies were stood down, but never formally abolished (3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE).

### Raiders in the New Age

After the Severance, ships flying no flag, some crewed by men who had served the Administration, raided the coast off Cathair gheal (4 an t-Sultain 1941 DE). The council sent no help, and in the end the fishermen armed their own boats, drove the raiders out, and were fined for bearing arms without licence (10 am Màrt 1949 DE). Only after the patrol boats were refitted for dubhan could they outrun the raiders (15 an t-Sultain 2012 DE).

### An Cogadh Fada, the Long War

*Cause.* Some northern communities refused to take their place in the new economy (25 an Giblean 2015 DE) and kept working the last coal seams rather than depend on one man's fuel. When the Mine Board's northern revenue fell by a quarter (22 am Màrt 2017 DE), it declared the western seams Crown property and ordered the pits closed. Enforcers were posted at Seann Skell (16 an Dàmhair 2017 DE), the first armed company sent north since the Severance. Skirmishes too small to name followed (29 an t-Sultain 2018 DE). Ruth Calder's offer to pay the Crown's fifth in coal went unanswered (25 an Dùbhlachd 2018 DE). The mobilization order reformed the regiments (28 an Dàmhair 2019 DE) under Somhairle mac Lachlainn (26 an t-Samhain 2019 DE), and the Moot's last petition was filed (25 an Dùbhlachd 2019 DE).

*Sides.* On the kingdom's side were the Board's enforcers, the reformed regiments and later the fleets, all running on dubhan, in the reign of Cathal. On the other side were the holdouts of five western towns, Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, with Ruth Calder and Tom Varley named among them. The Moot stood apart and fed the hungry.

*Course.* Arms went west by the ore line (12 am Faoilleach 2020 DE). The hewers gathered at Àth leathan (20 am Faoilleach 2020 DE), and the regiments marched west (28 am Faoilleach 2020 DE). The **Battle of Àth leathan**, fought on 11 an Giblean 2020 DE at Àraich Àth leathan, was the first great engagement of the war. The open record counts only the kingdom's dead. Tuathaich telling puts the holdouts' in the hundreds, and Ruth Calder's name does not appear in the open record again (11 an Giblean 2020 DE). The holdouts fell back into the hills (11 an Giblean 2020 DE). The regiments besieged Muileann àrsaidh, which held for weeks on stored coal and potatoes (5 an t-Ògmhios 2020 DE). Cnoc thais was taken after its road was cut (10 an Lùnastal 2020 DE), and Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg opened their roads without a siege (17 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE). In the autumn of the next year a column of several hundred holdouts left the hills and moved south-east toward the capital (29 an Dàmhair 2021 DE). Why it did so is in the sealed archive. Tuathaich telling names its leader Owen Barrow, and the open record gives no name. It made camp by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from the capital (6 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and the first and third regiments were brought down the fair road to meet it. The **Battle of Muileann ghlas**, fought on 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE at Àraich Muileann ghlas, was the second and last great battle of the war. The open record gives no count of the column's dead (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE). It is the second battle fought below Muileann ghlas that the annals record. The first was fought there in the Brothers' War.

*End.* When word of the battle reached the hills, the last holdouts came down to the seventh regiment's posts and were disarmed and sent home (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE). An Cogadh Fada ended on 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE, and nine regiments and four fleets remained on their stations. By the Board's order the western seams were flooded and capped (11 an Gearran 2022 DE). The wartime tithe (29 an Giblean 2020 DE) was carried forward in the Treasury's accounts, and no council minute records a decision to keep it (2 an Lùnastal 2023 DE). Tuathaich families built a cairn on the field of Àth leathan (26 an Cèitean 2023 DE). The kingdom raised a stone with the regiments' dead at Cathair mhòr (15 an Dùbhlachd 2022 DE).

### Part II. The Hosts

### The older hosts

Until the Long War the island kept no standing host. In the Holy Age the rìgh of Dùn dhearg fought with road-guards and with levies raised from the lowland farms, and those levies went home at harvest whether the war was over or not (2 an t-Samhain 1994 BDE). The claimants and the brothers of the Age of Sundering fought with the followings of the seven houses. The queen who burned the sea-thieves' boats sent a force raised for that one purpose (27 an t-Samhain 762 DE). In the Age of Strangers the only standing force on the island belonged to the humans: Merriman's constables and the Company's guards and gunboats. The Ròdaich fought the War of the Hills with companies raised by the council, the silver guild and the hawk-houses. Those companies were stood down in 1930 DE and kept only as names on a roll. For ninety years the kingdom kept its regiments only on paper and guarded its coast with patrol boats. The first armed company it sent north after the Severance was a company of Board enforcers (16 an Dàmhair 2017 DE).

### The regiments and fleets

The thirteen hosts on the map were all raised in 2020 DE, the first year of An Cogadh Fada, and none has been stood down (13 am Faoilleach 2022 DE). Each takes its name from the town where it is stationed. The numbers do not follow the order in which the hosts were raised. The seventh regiment was raised first and the ninth last, and the fleets were raised first, fourth, second and third. The record does not explain the numbering. The rolls of the Severance companies were read out when the regiments were reformed (26 an t-Samhain 2019 DE), and the numbers may have been taken from those rolls, but the open record does not say so. There are two towns named Seann Skell. The seventh regiment stands at the western one. The ninth regiment and the second fleet stand at the one on the southern coast. The regimental clerks tell them apart by their coasts (25 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE).
