### Part III. The Calamities

### The five shaded zones

The map shades five districts, each for the calamity that named it. All five came to a head in the Age of Strangers or the New Age, and in each the annals show the same ground struck before.

**A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death.** *Struck:* Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh, Inis bhàn. From 9 an t-Ògmhios 1852 DE the Green Death moved through the mining camps, and the ore dust was blamed, though no study was ever finished. At Achadh dhomhain, where it was first noticed, forty were buried in the first month in a field still called the green acre (5 an Dùbhlachd 1852 DE). It spread along the ore roads to these nine towns and to twenty-six settlements in all, and the custodians' roll leaves a blank line after the last (13 am Faoilleach 1853 DE). Àth ghlas burned the huts of its dead and was free of it soonest (12 am Màrt 1853 DE). No total of the dead survives. Its aftermath was the first strike, at Baile thais, over the galleries where it had been worst (21 an Dàmhair 1856 DE).

**Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger.** *Struck:* Baile chrom, Àth fhionn, Ceann mhòr, Àth dhearg, Muileann àrsaidh, Achadh àrsaidh, all Tuathaich towns today. The oldest hunger on Rodos with a place to it was here, in pots of boiled bark and doubled grave-rows (7 an Cèitean 5635 BDE), and a dearth emptied the same shore in the Age of Sundering (19 an Giblean 780 DE). The Great Hunger began on 3 am Màrt 1873 DE, after a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, worsened by a workforce too depleted by conscription to farm its own land. It was worst at Baile chrom, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields (1 an Giblean 1873 DE); the Administration did not dispute the count. At Seann Bhrenn the grain-pits of the Holy Age were opened and held only dust (7 an t-Samhain 1875 DE). The Levy was suspended too late for the harvest and never repealed (20 an Gearran 1876 DE).

**Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought.** *Struck:* Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh, Muileann chiar. The springs of Achadh shean failed in the Ancient Age (8 an Giblean 5595 BDE), and dry years came again in the Holy Age (15 an t-Iuchar 99 BDE) and the Age of Sundering (2 an Dàmhair 1440 DE); each time the shared grain carried the district. The Long Drought began on 25 an Lùnastal 1885 DE and held three years. Fewer than half of Achadh shean's cattle reached water (28 an t-Ògmhios 1886 DE), and the custodians counted ten districts as drought country while the Administration kept no count (27 an t-Iuchar 1886 DE). The fever of bad water that followed killed two hundred and sixty at Baile Mòr ruadh (25 an Giblean 1888 DE). When dry years returned in the New Age the council sent grain up the ore line, and nobody died of hunger (3 an Cèitean 1972 DE).

**Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending.** *Struck:* Cill ghlas, Àth chaol, Achadh chaol. The ground here has moved in every age: a crack across the valley (5 an Lùnastal 6774 BDE), cracked wells (27 an Cèitean 340 DE), a fallen gallery with fourteen names on a stone at its mouth (14 an Dàmhair 890 DE). The Rending came on 9 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE, during a routine excavation driven with blasting-powder. It killed dozens, swallowed the old cutting and its shrine (3 an t-Iuchar 1916 DE), and closed the district for a generation behind the Company's fence (22 an t-Samhain 1916 DE). The displaced built Achadh chaol on the edge of the fenced ground (5 an Dùbhlachd 1916 DE). The district was reopened (19 an t-Iuchar 1944 DE), and on 23 an t-Ògmhios 1968 DE a gallery under Muileann dhearg gave way along a line the surveyors had called sound, and thirty-one hewers died. The annals note that it was the same fault.

**Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, the Great Wave.** *Struck:* Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg, Achadh mhin. Sea sand a hand thick lies over an Ancient Age village at Cnoc chaol (7 an t-Iuchar 6824 BDE), a swell took two children there in the Age of Sundering (22 an Gearran 685 DE), and Cuan dhearg was twice flooded before it built its sea-wall (23 an Giblean 1715 DE). The Great Wave struck without warning on 2 an Gearran 1933 DE and wrecked the three towns in one night, the first disaster the new state answered on its own terms. The relief parties counted a little over nine hundred dead (24 an t-Samhain 1933 DE). Cuan dhearg's harbour was gone and its boats lay in the fields. The shepherds of Eilean mhin did not go back (1 an Giblean 1934 DE).

### Other calamities of the annals

**Plagues.** A coughing sickness killed some two hundred at Caol fhiadhaich (2 an Gearran 117 DE); a spotted fever some three hundred at Inis chrom, where the Wolf's preachers nursed the sick and died of it (3 an t-Sultain 585 DE); the swallowing cough near a third of Muileann dhomhain (29 an Lùnastal 1040 DE). The strangers' fever came ashore with a crowded ship and killed ninety-one Ròdaich and eleven humans (5 an t-Samhain 1788 DE). The spotted pox at Ros dhomhain killed four hundred and six by the Mission's count, and more by the custodians' (11 an Dàmhair 1818 DE). The grey fever (2 an Gearran 1917 DE) killed the young and strong before the old, and in the north-west put Ròdaich and humans in the same wards for the first time (20 an t-Iuchar 1919 DE).

**Famines.** The first famine recorded as averted (4 an Dàmhair 526 BDE) was the shared-meal custom's first test, and it held. Beyond the Great Hunger the annals record hunger in the capital and in Ros bheag during the War of the Hills (9 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE, 23 an t-Sultain 1929 DE), and the north's first year alone, when Tuathaich memory puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred and no Ròdaich count was made (9 an Dùbhlachd 1930 DE).

**Storms, floods and fires.** The first storm given a name is remembered only for the naming (30 am Faoilleach 7454 BDE); the oldest whose name survives is A' Ghaoth Dhubh (1 an Gearran 5184 BDE). Am Fuath Mòr drowned eighteen at Seann Toll (23 an t-Samhain 220 DE), a storm drowned twenty-three at Baile ghorm (12 an Dàmhair 1700 DE), and another eleven Tuathaich off Cuan bheag (20 an t-Sultain 1948 DE). The Abhainn ìseal cut the ore line for most of a year (12 am Màrt 1963 DE). Fire burned Ceann mhin twice (5 an t-Sultain 1510 DE) and the fair at Muileann òg once (31 an Dàmhair 1969 DE).

**The vein's own dead.** The mountain has killed its workers in every age, from the basket burning at Achadh dhìreach (7 an t-Iuchar 6535 BDE) to the first deaths blamed on the humans' pace of work, eleven, entered as an accident (26 an Giblean 1804 DE).

## Appendix D — The Reckoning of Years

This appendix sets out how the years of Rodos are counted today, how each age counted them before that, and how the copyists and the library at Muileann chaol joined the counts into one; then the months, the days, and the feasts of the year.

### I. The Diosal Era

Rodos counts its years in the **Diosal Era**, written DE. Year 1 DE is the year of the Setting-Out, when the ships of the Sundering left Seann Skell. Years before it are written BDE, *before the Diosal Era*. There is no year 0: 1 BDE is followed by 1 DE, and anyone reckoning across the boundary must subtract one.

*Diosal* is the Rodos form of the old word *deiseal*, the sunwise turn: the way a hand moves, a boat rounds a point, or a procession goes about a cairn, with the right shoulder toward the centre and the course following the sun. Before making for open water the fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, for luck, and the watchers on the quay counted the hulls as they passed. The harbour scribe's entry for the turn is the last thing any roll says of the departed, and the island has counted its years from that turn ever since.

The count was not made at the time. On 22 am Faoilleach 5 DE Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house above Muileann dhearg, began to number the years from the sunwise turn and called them *bliadhnaichean an Diosail*, the years of the Diosal. By his own reckoning only a few of them had yet passed. The count was his alone at first. The crown's scribes at Cathair dhearg took it up about a generation later, and for more than six hundred years afterwards the vein-house and the crown each kept their own version of it (section II).

The harbour scribe gives the day of the Setting-Out as 19 an Giblean 1 DE and the day of the sunwise turn as 19 an Giblean 1 DE. The two fall on one day. The custody-book, however, enters the turn under a later day than the sailing, after the next Samhain. No account explains that gap of half a year, and the keepers have left both entries where they stand. Section II gives what the gap did to the count. The count now kept on Rodos follows the harbour scribe and sets both in 1 DE.

### II. How the Ages Reckoned Before the Diosal

**The Ancient Age.** The Ancient Age kept no count of years that anyone has found. Its people counted other things. The Seann-Dhaoine cut strokes on stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household, and the counting of the dead began on 29 an Lùnastal 7253 BDE. The tally wall at Seann Warr grew to some three thousand strokes, and in one stretch the tallies of three coasts thicken together (6 an Giblean 7131 BDE). These are counts of the dead. None of them has been read as a count of years.

The first tide-count (28 am Faoilleach 5937 BDE), a rock on which someone marked the high-water line, comes nearer. Its marks fall at intervals regular enough that later scholars have suspected a calendar in them. The practice was carried to Ros dhomhain with the interval unchanged. Nobody knows what the interval was for, and the Library has declined to guess. The hill-folk also knew the crossing season of the great cats and kept off the passes while the panthers went over (20 am Faoilleach 7714 BDE). That was a season they kept every year, but they did not number the years.

The oldest oral king-list, *Rìghrean na Cloiche*, begins with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE) and "gives no lengths of reign." The Red Hill list is the same. When both lists were recited together at the ford gathering (23 an t-Iuchar 3254 BDE), the recital took from dusk to dawn, but it measured only a succession of names. The tellings of the age give no order finer than that. They tie a few things firmly to one another, and where a telling binds several deeds together they are remembered as falling in one year or a few. Between those points the tellings keep the order of things and little of the distance between them, and the years of the age are known only as well as the tellings know them.

**The Holy Age.** The Holy Age counted in two ways, and neither of them ran from a fixed beginning.

The first was **by reigns**. From the Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE) the Keepers of the flame were remembered in a recited roll that begins with Beathag Bhàn. After Goraidh mac Ìomhair was first called *rìgh* at Dùn dhearg (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE), the rulers of the lowlands had a list of their own. A year was named by whoever held it: "the ninth year of Iain Garbh," "the third winter of the Keeper Seumas Bàn." That served for a debt within living memory and was useless for the distance between two reigns, since the recited lists gave no lengths. The first written king-list, Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll (20 an Lùnastal 1684 BDE), marks which names came from reciters and which from living memory. The Keepers had their own roll set down in answer (17 an Dàmhair 1648 BDE), and it proved several centuries longer than Tormod's. From the reign of Seonag Chrom the clerks of the red hall kept the king-list year by year. Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh the list gives "nine rulers of the house of Tormod with their years" (29 am Màrt 439 BDE). Those years were counted within each reign and did not run on from one reign to the next.

The second was **by burnings**. From the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE), a household might burn no more than its measured handful of ore in a season, and the Hall at Dùn ìseal kept the record of those seasons. It counted them from the Law: the first burning, the second, and on through the centuries. A Small-Burning year ran from one filling of the baskets to the next. The Hall filled them at Samhain, when the galleries closed and the hearths began to need the ore. The first sentence under the Law (1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE) took from a household its right "for the season after," and it was entered by the burning in which it fell. Of all the island's counts the count of burnings came nearest to an era, because it ran from a single act and was meant never to stop. It outlived the age by a long way. The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE), and the custodians of Doire mhin kept the old count one season longer than anyone else (31 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE), with the note that nobody had asked for it.

By the close of the age the Keepers' roll held one hundred and forty names and the king-list more than ninety (2 an Giblean 60 BDE). The two did not agree in every place, and the Hall's count of burnings did not always agree with either.

**The Age of Sundering.** The Diosal count was born in this age, and at first it existed in two versions. Donnchadh mac Thormoid counted from the turn at the harbour, as the custody-book entered it. The crown's scribes took up the count a generation later, when the court remembered the departure as a single thing, and they counted from the year the ships sailed. Both versions began each year at the old Samhain, as the Hall had done. The custody-book sets the turn after the Samhain that followed the sailing, so by the old year the sailing and the turn lay in different years, and the two counts stood a year apart. The Library believes this is how the counts came to differ. The rolls do not prove it, and it does not explain why the turn is entered so long after the sailing.

The difference stood until 23 am Màrt 700 DE, when the vein-house and the crown's scribes found that their counts disagreed and settled the matter by agreement. The same agreement fixed the day of the empty-harbour rite, which the two counts had placed differently. A later hand in the custody-book adds that the scribes afterwards "stop pretending it was fixed by evidence." From that day there was one Diosal count on Rodos, and the vein-house marked its thousandth year (15 an Dùbhlachd 1000 DE) with a single measured burning on Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn.

### III. The Setting of the Ages into One Count

By the seventeenth century of the Diosal the island's records kept time by Keepers, by reigns, by burnings and by the Diosal, and the tellings of the Ancient Age by nothing at all. The work of joining these counts began with Beathag nic Thòmais, the mill-owner's widow who bought up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls and kept them in a loft over her mill at Muileann chaol (21 an Cèitean 1620 DE). She did not reckon years. She did set conflicting copies side by side and decline to choose between them (27 an Giblean 1640 DE), and that became the method of everyone who worked in Muileann chaol after her. She left her loft to the town on condition that nothing in it be burned (24 an Lùnastal 1660 DE).

The joining itself was done in the cellar. From 5 am Màrt 1903 DE the custodians of the east sent copies of their rolls to Muileann chaol for safekeeping, away from the Residency's reach, and three families did the copying. While they copied, they laid the counts against each other. Where the king-list gave a ruler's years and the Hall's roll gave the burnings of the same reign, the two could be made to meet, and each meeting fixed a stretch of the older count against the newer. The copyists called the result *Clàr nan Aoisean*, the table of the ages. It is the first document that runs one numbered sequence of years from the Binding to the copyists' own day. It is also the first to divide the island's past into ages, and to set before the Holy Age an older age whose length the table admits it cannot measure. When the custodians sent what survived of the Age of Strangers to the same cellars (29 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE), the table was carried through to the Severance, and in that form it gave the five ages the bounds that historians of Rodos still use.

Leabharlann Muileann chaol, founded 1 an Cèitean 1945 DE, took the table as one of its first possessions and extended it. When the library absorbed the provincial archives (26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE), the table was checked against them and corrected where the archives knew better. The first keeper, Ailean Leabhar, disliked the saying *a chur san Leabharlann*, "to put it in the Library," on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it (3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE). The table should be read in the same spirit.

### IV. The Twelve Months

The months of Rodos are the twelve Gaelic months, and they correspond one to one with the months of the humans' calendar, beginning with am Faoilleach. The meanings of several names were already disputed when the Hall first wrote them down. The glosses below are those the Library holds most likely. The work of each month is the island's work as the rolls of every age describe it.

| No. | Month | Days | Meaning of the name | The work of the month on Rodos |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | am Faoilleach | 31 | the wolf-month; the storm-time at the year's dead end | Nets and boats mended ashore; the ore-hearths at their fullest; the high passes shut |
| 2 | an Gearran | 28 (29) | the short month, or the gelding's month; the Library does not choose | Là Fhèill Brìghde on the first; the first ploughing in the lowlands; lambing in the south |
| 3 | am Màrt | 31 | the seed-time, the month of work | Sowing; the carters back on the roads; repairs to the bridges before the spring floods |
| 4 | an Giblean | 30 | obscure; the old folk said "the gap", the month between the last of the stores and the first of the green | The hungry weeks of a poor year; granaries opened where the shared-meal law requires it |
| 5 | an Cèitean | 31 | the first of summer | Bealltainn on the first; cattle to the high pastures; in the Holy Age, the galleries opened when the cairn-watchers allowed |
| 6 | an t-Ògmhios | 30 | the young month | Peat cut and stacked; salt-pans worked on the south and west coasts |
| 7 | an t-Iuchar | 31 | the hot month | Hay; the herring off the north-west; the drovers of Àth chiar on the eastern hills |
| 8 | an Lùnastal | 31 | the month of the Lùnastal gathering | Lùnastal on the first; first-fruits; the harvest fair at Muileann òg in its season |
| 9 | an t-Sultain | 30 | the month of plenty | The main harvest; the grain carried to the granaries; accounts rendered |
| 10 | an Dàmhair | 31 | the rut of the deer | The stags heard in the eastern forest; the Deer school walking the bounds of its grove; boats hauled up |
| 11 | an t-Samhain | 30 | summer's end | Samhain on the first; in the Holy Age the baskets filled and the galleries closed; the empty-harbour rite at Seann Skell |
| 12 | an Dùbhlachd | 31 | the black month, the dark of the year | Midwinter; the drowned remembered in the western harbours; the panther roads closed for the year |

An Gearran takes a twenty-ninth day in every fourth year, as the humans' calendar has it. It is not certain that the vein-house kept such a day before 1780. The custody-book dates by feast and by month and seldom by day, so the question cannot be settled from it.

### V. The Seven Days

The week, *seachdain*, has seven days. The names below are given in the forms the royal chronicler uses. The oldest roll to name them is the Hall's list of turns in the galleries, and by then the names were already old.

| Day | Ròdais | The name as the Library reads it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Didòmhnaich | the lord's day. The Hall said the lord was the vein; the crown said it was the king. No ore was cut on it. |
| 2 | Diluain | the moon's day. The tide-keepers began their reckonings on it. |
| 3 | Dimàirt | the day of Màrt, of work, the same root as the sowing-month |
| 4 | Diciadain | the day of the first fast |
| 5 | Diardaoin | the day between the fasts |
| 6 | Dihaoine | the day of the fast |
| 7 | Disathairne | not known. Its root is found nowhere else in the tongue. |

Diciadain, Diardaoin and Dihaoine name fasts that nobody on Rodos now keeps. The Library's opinion is that they were fasts from fire rather than from food. On two days of the week a Holy Age household left its hearth unlit, which fits the Small-Burning Law and the custom of the measured handful before it. The unlit hearth found under the peat (2 an Dàmhair 6699 BDE) is sometimes cited for this. It proves nothing about weeks. The other opinion, that they were fasts from meat as the humans' Mission taught, rests only on the Mission's word.

When the humans came they also kept a week of seven days, and they also rested on the first day of it. The Mission made a great deal of this. The custodians made little of it, and the rolls add nothing.

### VI. The Quarter-Days

Four feasts divide the year into quarters. They are older than any rite now on the island, and every faith on Rodos keeps them in some form, though each gives them its own reasons.

**Là Fhèill Brìghde**, 1 an Gearran, is the feast of Brìghde. Every hearth is swept and relit and the year's first work in the fields begins. The followers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach set a sheaf by the door. The Obsidian Rite, in both its forms, lights its first lamp of the year from the altar-flame.

**Bealltainn**, 1 an Cèitean, takes its name from a bright fire, and it is the feast of summer's beginning. Cattle go up to the high pastures between two fires. In the Holy Age this was the day the Hall asked the cairn-watchers of Cnoc ghlas whether the galleries might open. The first sentence under the Small-Burning Law is dated 1 an Cèitean 2854 BDE, on Bealltainn itself. The roll does not say whether the day was chosen for the sentence.

**Lùnastal**, 1 an Lùnastal, is the feast of first-fruits and gathering, and the month is named for it. Markets open, contests are held, and oaths are taken before witnesses. Cathal was crowned on the feast itself, 1 an Lùnastal 2002 DE.

**Samhain**, 1 an t-Samhain, marks summer's end. Before the humans came it was also the beginning of the Ròdaich year. The Hall filled the baskets of the Small-Burning Law at Samhain, the galleries closed, and the dead were thought nearest. The Tuathaich, whose calendar came to them from an Tìr Thall, keep the day with the rest of the island. They have never counted the year from it.

### VII. Feasts and Days Particular to Rodos

Beside the quarter-days Rodos keeps days rooted in its own history. The table gives those the chronicles attest. The column "since" gives the day on which the custom is first recorded.

| Day | Where | What is kept | Since |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 an t-Samhain, at night | Seann Skell waterfront | The night of lamps: a lamp on every sill until morning. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home. | 18 an Giblean 1 DE; kept each year from 12 an Lùnastal 70 DE |
| 25 an t-Samhain | Cidhe an Diosail, Seann Skell | The empty-harbour rite, on the day the old counts agreed; in the harbour towns called Là an Diosail | 25 an t-Samhain 22 DE; the day fixed 23 am Màrt 700 DE |
| no fixed day | the harbour towns, the court | *An Tùrsa Geal*, the white sorrow: undyed wool and one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast | 27 an Dàmhair 15 DE |
| yearly, on the shore | Inis chrom and the harbours north to Seann Warr | The drowned-feast, an empty place for each of the lost | 10 an Dàmhair 84 BDE |
| yearly | Baile chrom | The wake for the boat lost off the north-west | 28 an Lùnastal 2587 BDE |
| the crossing days | the southern hills, Imrich nam Pantar | The panther roads kept clear, flocks driven off the paths | 26 an t-Iuchar 265 DE |
| yearly | Coille Naomh Muileann chiar | The Deer school walks the bounds of its grove | 11 an t-Iuchar 440 DE |
| harvest | Fèill Muileann òg | The great fair, with its northern day | 5 an t-Iuchar 1325 BDE; the fair established 16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE |
| yearly | Còmhrag Ceann leathan | The contest with staves, since edged tools were banned | 18 an t-Ògmhios 1325 BDE; established 4 am Màrt 1952 DE |
| yearly | Allt an Àigh | The walk of the old spirits to the healing water | 8 an t-Iuchar 1939 DE |
| yearly | Seann Dunn | The ancestors of forty families named aloud by their living heads | 28 an Dàmhair 1951 DE |
| yearly | Cnoc ghorm | The northern feast of the Yellow Scorpion | 11 an Gearran 1955 DE |
| one night, undisclosed | Baile chrom and the north | The Grey Night of Sìne, the Peaceful Goose; outsiders are not told which night | 14 am Màrt 1938 DE |

The day of the Setting-Out has never been kept as a feast. The chronicles stop describing the departed the moment the ships clear the harbour, and the island has kept its remembrance of them at the harbour, where the rolls stop, on the day the custody-book gives for the turn and not on the day they sailed. Since 23 am Màrt 700 DE the empty-harbour rite has fallen on that day, 25 an t-Samhain, though the harbour scribe, whose count the island follows, sets the turn on the day of the sailing. The Library is aware that the custody-book may have taken its day from the rite rather than the rite from the book. By the last entry of the Age of Sundering the rite was kept by eleven people (17 an t-Sultain 1764 DE). The chronicles of the later ages do not say how many keep it now.

**The Severance**, 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE, is kept at Cathair dhearg by the council as the day the kingdom's modern history begins. The chronicle says the Mourning Custom of the Sundering, first made for a chosen parting, was reused uneasily for a very different departure in a later age, and the council's keeping of this day is the use most often meant. In the north the day is not kept. It is worked through like any other, and the Tuathaich say that this is their way of keeping it.

**The Long War** left two days. The Battle of Àth leathan, 11 an Giblean 2020 DE, opened *An Cogadh Fada*. Tuathaich families have raised a cairn without leave on the field at Àraich Àth leathan, and it grows by a stone or two whenever the patrols pass; whether they come on the day of the battle nobody has written down. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE, ended the war, and the regiments raised in the campaign keep that day at their stations. So the two days are kept by two peoples, and the library, whose war archive is sealed (27 an Giblean 2023 DE), holds what it can of both.

### VIII. The Reckoning of the Humans, and Its Reconciling

The humans who came at the Crossing (5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE) brought a calendar of their own, and in most respects it was close to the island's. Their year had twelve months of the same lengths in the same order, with the same extra day in the second month every fourth year. Samuel Wren's word-lists (13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE), which survive in the Administration's letter-books, give the month-names in the two tongues side by side, and the clerks needed nothing more than that list to convert months. The chronicle notes that the humans crossed "the water the Rodians once crossed." Whether the likeness between the calendars has anything to do with that, nobody on Rodos knows, and the chronicles do not say.

The calendars differed in two things. The first was the beginning of the year. The humans began theirs at am Faoilleach, and the Ròdaich had begun theirs at Samhain since the Hall first filled the baskets. The second was the count of years. The humans numbered theirs from an epoch in their own land, which they named and did not explain, and their numbers were much larger than the island's. No Ròdaich scribe set down the name of that land (26 an Gearran 1781 DE), and the letter-books do not explain the epoch either.

The first written treaty (27 an Giblean 1787 DE) was drawn up in the humans' tongue only and dated by the humans' year only. The custodians entered it in their roll under its Diosal year and the month in which it was signed, and left the day to the Administration. The Harbour Articles, the Company's charter, and every contract for extraction were dated the same way. The same clerks who kept two sets of books for coin and barter (30 am Faoilleach 1797 DE) came to keep two dates at the head of every page, the humans' year above and the Diosal year beneath, and they complained about both.

By the third currency reform (7 an Giblean 1908 DE) every contract on the island ran from am Faoilleach, and the Ròdaich civil year had moved to the humans' beginning without any decree. The old Samhain year survived in the shrines, in the Hall's count of burnings until it lapsed, and among the custodians of Inis bhàn, who taught "the old reckoning" in their school (7 an t-Ògmhios 1831 DE). The Administration's census (19 an Cèitean 1901 DE) and its register (26 an t-Samhain 1906 DE) were dated by the humans' year alone.

The reconciling was finished after the Severance, when the humans no longer had any say in it. The council's clerks emptied the counting-houses (11 an t-Ògmhios 1931 DE) and boxed the ledgers unread, because few of them could read the humans' hand. Ailean Leabhar, the library's first keeper, spent his first years having them read (28 an t-Ògmhios 1945 DE). He had every date in them converted to the Diosal count, using the double-dated pages of the custodians' clerks as the key, and he kept the new year at am Faoilleach. His reason was that a century of contracts, ledgers and letters already stood on that footing. The kingdom has kept it since. Every year on Rodos, in every age, is therefore now counted from am Faoilleach to an Dùbhlachd. The people who lived before 1780 began their years at Samhain, and a reader of the old rolls should remember that.

The Tuathaich keep the Diosal count in their dealings with the kingdom. What count the northern parish books keep among themselves the library cannot say, since it receives few of them.

### IX. The Five Ages

The five ages are the divisions of *Clàr nan Aoisean* as the library received and extended it. The table gives the first and the last thing remembered in each.

| Age | Ròdais name | English | Span | First event | Last event |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | An Aois Àrsaidh | the Ancient Age | 12,999 – 3,001 BDE | The crack in the stone, 20 am Faoilleach 12,918 BDE | The eve of the Binding, 7 an Lùnastal 3051 BDE |
| II | An Aois Naomh | the Holy Age | 3,000 – 40 BDE | The Binding of the First Flame, 23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE | The last age of even population, 1 an Cèitean 50 BDE |
| III | An Aois Scaraidh | the Age of Sundering | 39 BDE – 1779 DE | Land is found, 6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE | The silver petition laid aside, 28 an Dùbhlachd 1767 DE |
| IV | An Aois Choigreach | the Age of Strangers | 1780 – 1929 DE | The Crossing, 5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE | The Severance, 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE |
| V | An Aois Ùr | the New Age | 1930 – 2026 DE | The Tuathaich homeland fixed, 22 am Màrt 1930 DE | The present, 21 an Dùbhlachd 2026 DE |

Three things in the table need a word.

The span of the Ancient Age opens in 12,999 BDE, but its first event, the crack in the stone, falls some decades later. The span is the table's round beginning for an age that has none. The event is the oldest thing the island remembers.

The Age of Sundering is usually said to open with the Choosing, but the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE) is not the first thing in it. The age opens with the finding of the land (6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE), without which there would have been nothing to choose.

The Severance closes the Age of Strangers but falls in 1930, the first year of the New Age. The first events of the New Age follow it within that same year. The copyists of the cellar drew the boundary at the end of 1929, when the war had been decided and the columns had gone north, and they entered the Severance as the last act of the age it ended. The library has left the overlap as it found it.

### X. Where the Dates Come From

Every event in this history carries a day, a month and a year, and they come from different places in different ages.

For the New Age and the Age of Strangers the days are remembered: they come from rolls, ledgers, letter-books and the chroniclers' own entries. For the Age of Sundering they are remembered more thinly, from the custody-book, the harbour rolls and the crown's king-list, and a good many were settled by agreement, as the day of the empty-harbour rite was. For the Holy Age the years come from the Keepers' roll, the king-lists and the Hall's count of burnings, which do not always agree, and the days mostly from the feasts and seasons the rolls name. For the Ancient Age everything rests on the tellings, the king-lists without lengths of reign, the tally walls and the tide-count. The tellings keep the order of things well and the distance between them poorly. Where they agree, the date is as sure as they are; where they disagree or fall silent, it is not, and such a date is safer for the order it keeps than for its year.


## Appendix E — Words Born from History

This appendix gathers the words, names and sayings of Ròdais that the island's history made, or bent to a new sense. It is set out as a historical dictionary. Each entry gives the headword and its part of speech, what it says word for word, what it has come to mean, the event that gave it that meaning, and a line from the annals or the five books.

The chronicle's own list of *Words Born from History* is the core, and every word on it appears here with the meaning the chronicle gives it. The rest come from the annals and the books: titles and offices, laws and customs, the names of storms, places and quarrels, and the sayings the record quotes. A few are the words Ròdais built for the strangers' things. Ròdais took few loanwords from the humans, and most of those late (Appendix F); where the humans said *train*, *engine* or *strike*, it made a name from old roots, and some of those names are entered here under the years when the annals first needed them.

### How to Read an Entry

The headword is given in full. An article (*an*, *am*, *a'*) is written with it but not counted in the order, which is the Gaelic order of eighteen letters, *a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u*, with the grave accent ignored. Dates are given in the Diosal count (Appendix D). Where no annal marks the first use of a word, the entry says so and gives only the event the word comes from. Citations are given as the sources give them: the annals in English, as this history renders their prose, the verses in Ròdais (Appendix F, *Of Translation*).

*n.* noun · *m.*, *f.* masculine, feminine · *pl.* plural · *v.* verb · *v.n.* verbal noun · *adj.* adjective · *phr.* phrase or saying · *lit.* literally

### The Glossary

#### A

**a chur san Leabharlann** *phr.* · lit. "to put it in the Library"
To make a thing official and past dispute. From the founding of Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean 1945 DE); within a few years it was said of anything settled (3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE).
> "Ailean Leabhar is recorded as disliking the phrase, on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it." — annals, 1945 DE

**Aisling-aois** *n. f.* · lit. "Aisling-age"
An unnaturally long youth in anyone; said half in jest of ordinary people who look young for their years. From the first of the immortal generation, born in the mining camps (7 am Màrt 1848 DE). No annal marks its first use. It is the one word on the chronicle's list in which the joke and the myth are the same word.
> "…and does not age the way the people around her do. Her name is Aisling." — annals, 1848 DE

**Àrd-choimheadaiche** *n. m.* · lit. "high watcher"
The high custodian of Creideamh nan Ròdach, seated at Seann Skell. The office came with the formalizing of the Rite (18 an Giblean 1935 DE), and Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was the first to hold it (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). It is not the "high custodian" of the Age of Strangers, who headed the Council of Custodians; the two share an English name and nothing else.
> "The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore." — annals, 2003 DE

#### B

**bonn-rìoghachd** *n. m.* · lit. "realm-coin"
Currency. Under the humans the coin was the mark, and barter was pushed out in three reforms (13 an Gearran 1796 DE, 2 an Dàmhair 1865 DE, 7 an Giblean 1908 DE). The Ròdais word belongs to the coinage struck when the humans' coin was withdrawn (30 an Giblean 1934 DE). Its first mint-master was called Fearchar Bonn from his work (9 an Dàmhair 1934 DE). After the re-pegging to dubhan (5 an Cèitean 2014 DE) the realm-coin no longer rested on the vein.
> "A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with obsidian-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year." — annals, 1934 DE

#### C

**carbad-iarainn** *n. m.* · lit. "iron-chariot"
A train; the first of the *iarainn* words Ròdais made for machines. The kingdom mended the humans' ore line (9 an Dàmhair 1937 DE) and ran its own first train on 3 an Dàmhair 1941 DE.
> "The first ore train from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg runs under the kingdom's name and on the humans' rails." — annals, 1941 DE

**Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine** *phr.* · lit. "we did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire"
A defeat without fighting. An unsigned verse of the cold shires, from the day Raghnall Ruadh refused the measured handful to every hearth that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE).
> "…the act turns more people against him than any battle." — annals, 519 DE

**Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann** *phr.* · lit. "we did not come; we were here"
The doctrine of the Ancient Age, complete on Calbh Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE). Who cut it is not known.
> "If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be here." — annals, 8054 BDE

**Cha loisc clach na beinne do choigrich** *phr.* · lit. "the mountain's stone will not burn for strangers"
The Keepers' ruling that no ore might feed a beacon (30 an Cèitean 2851 BDE). It held until the humans' towers were lit with an ore flame (22 an t-Sultain 1870 DE).
> "The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers." — annals, 2851 BDE

**Cha tàinig long** *phr.* · lit. "no ship came"
The entry in the beacon-keepers' daybooks from the Severance on, after the council had the five beacons relit (19 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE).
> "The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, continue to be kept, with nothing in them." — annals, 1929 DE

**Chaidh a' mhèinn dhachaigh** *phr.* · lit. "the ore went home"
The tellings' words for the ore taken by Gilleasbuig Beag (2 an Lùnastal 5192 BDE), which was neither burned nor kept but laid back under the slab (4 an t-Iuchar 5191 BDE).
> "The tellings make much of this: the ore went home." — annals, 5191 BDE

**Cidhe an Diosail** *n. m.* · lit. "the quay of the sunwise turn"
The berth at Seann Skell from which the fleet of the Sundering sailed. Its old name, Cidhe an Iar, passed to a new fish-wharf so that trade could go on without the memory (13 am Màrt 28 DE, 15 an Lùnastal 28 DE).
> "In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn." — annals, 28 DE

**Cogadh nam Bràithrean** *n. m.* · lit. "the war of the brothers"
The war between Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, named from its first battle (8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE).
> "The houses divide, four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, is named from this battle." — annals, 1231 DE

**Comann nan Saor-luinge** *n. m.* · lit. "the fellowship of the ship-wrights"
The guild that built the fleet of the Sundering (24 an t-Sultain 35 BDE). It quietly dissolved when no one needed ocean-going hulls (27 an t-Ògmhios 45 DE).
> "The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights." — annals, 35 BDE

**Còmhrag** *n. f.* · lit. "combat"
With the article, the yearly melee at Ceann leathan (4 am Màrt 1952 DE), fought on the field of the Holy Age road-guards' games (18 an t-Ògmhios 1325 BDE).
> "Two men die in the melee he wins." — annals, of the first champion, 1952 DE

**cridhe-iarainn** *n. m.* · lit. "iron-heart"
An engine. The annals first need it for the shunting engines at Muileann chrom (8 an t-Iuchar 1942 DE), and again when the Shipwrights' Guild court ruled that fitting one to a boat was not shipwrighting (23 an Giblean 2005 DE).
> "The yard's families, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted separately by the Board." — annals, 1942 DE

**cuimhne-coinneimh** *n. f.* · lit. "meeting-memory"
Minutes. Above all, those of the Moot at Caol mhòr, which has no standing in Ròdach law and has kept its minutes since its first sitting (25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE). See *Tha e scrìobhte a-nis*.
> "It meets anyway and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from this meeting to the present." — annals, 1931 DE

#### D

**diosal** *adv.*, *n. m.* · lit. "sunwise"
The sunwise turn; the Rodos form of *deiseal*. The fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise (19 an Giblean 1 DE), and the years were counted from that turn (22 am Faoilleach 5 DE).
> "Before making for open water the fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, *diosal*, for luck." — the Third Book

**dòrlach** *n. m.* · lit. "a handful"
The sealed measure of ore. The vein-house allowed one to each departing ship (17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE). See *Làn na glaice*.
> *Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir, / is an seann teallach fhathast blàth.* "A handful for the new hearth, and the old hearth still warm." — the Third Book

**Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan** *phr.* · lit. "black the coal, and black the dubhan"
A rhyme of the north, heard in both tongues, from the years when the coinage was pegged to the new fuel (5 an Cèitean 2014 DE).
> *Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan, / ach cò leis an teine?* "Black the coal, and black the dubhan; but whose is the fire?" — the Fifth Book

**dubhan** *n. m.* · lit. "the black one" (*dubh* + *-an*)
The synthetic fuel, written with a small letter. From the name of Dubhan, born 1958 DE, whose first working fuel came on 19 an t-Ògmhios 2000 DE. The man's name wore down into a common noun, as a title may wear down into the name of a dish.
> "'Dubhan' begins appearing in common speech to mean the fuel itself, not the man." — annals, 2010 DE

**dubhan-tùsail** *n. m.* · lit. "dubhan of the beginning"
A rough first attempt that looked like a dead end and later mattered; used in any field. From Dubhan's failed experiments (1 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE). First recorded in a letter of the Fèidh school at Caol shean, of the school's own revival (22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE).
> "…for an early attempt at anything that looked like a dead end before it wasn't." — annals, 2010 DE

#### F

**fadachadh** *v.n. m.* · lit. "lengthening", from *fadaich*, *fada*
To be crushed after holding out too long; *am fadachadh*, a total and final defeat. Narrowed by An Cogadh Fada, from Àth leathan (11 an Giblean 2020 DE) to Muileann ghlas (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and first heard among Tuathaich speakers of their own defeat (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE).
> "…'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred… It is said as a joke, and the people who say it do not laugh." — annals, 2021 DE

**faire-obrach** *n. f.* · lit. "work-watch"
A shift. The annals first need it for the humans' night-shift order (25 an Lùnastal 1895 DE), which the kingdom kept (18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE).
> *Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, / is cha d' fhuair sinne.* "The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we." — the hewers' saying, the Fifth Book

**Fèill** *n. f.* · lit. "feast-day, fair"
With a town's name, a fair; above all Fèill Muileann òg (16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE), heir to the harvest fair held there after the War of the Roads (5 an t-Iuchar 1325 BDE).
> "An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering." — annals, 1950 DE

**Fo mhullach an taighe, chan eil nàmh ann** *phr.* · lit. "under the roof of the house there is no enemy"
The road-peace, the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made (22 an Dàmhair 2824 BDE). The War of the Roads ended under such a roof (4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE).
> "…no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door." — annals, 2824 BDE

**fuil-ghuail** *n. f.* · lit. "coal-blood"
The condition of those who bond with the vein and do not age as others do, and the people who have it. It had no word for half a century (13 am Faoilleach 1850 DE) until the custodians coined this one (23 am Faoilleach 1905 DE). The humans rendered it *obsidian-touched*.
> "It is meant clinically. It will outlive that intention." — annals, 1905 DE

#### G

**Gaoth Dhubh, A'** *n. f.* · lit. "the black wind"
The oldest storm whose name is kept (1 an Gearran 5184 BDE); the first named storm lost its name (30 am Faoilleach 7454 BDE). The harbour rolls went on naming storms: Am Fuath Mòr, "the great hate" (23 an t-Samhain 220 DE), and An Gàire Dubh, "the black laugh" (5 am Màrt 480 DE).
> "It is the oldest storm whose name is kept." — annals, 5184 BDE

#### I

**Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc** *phr.* · lit. "Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill"
The saying of the feathered doors, from the years when the hawk-priests were barred and the crews carried the Hawk's sermons themselves (10 an Cèitean 1855 DE).
> "The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a disciplinary matter." — annals, 1855 DE

#### L

**Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig** *n. m.* · lit. "the law of the small burning"
The Small-Burning Law: no household might burn more than a measured handful of ore in a season (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE). The ruling of the hearth bound the custodians never to withhold that handful (12 an Gearran 526 DE). The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE).
> "No formal repeal is recorded — it simply stops being enforced once it stops being profitable to enforce." — annals, 1800 DE

**Làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh** *phr.* · lit. "the fill of the hollow hand, and no more"
The measure of the Ancient Age (5 an Lùnastal 6590 BDE). When Fionnlagh Dall re-cut the stone cup to hold two palms (15 an t-Iuchar 2860 BDE), the saying became *Làn an dà bhois, agus gun tuilleadh*.
> "It is nowhere written and everywhere kept." — annals, 6590 BDE

**Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc** *phr.* · lit. "they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill"
Said of the raids on the tithe ledgers (10 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE).
> "…symbolically decisive even though its practical effect was small." — annals, 1929 DE

#### M

**maor** *n. m.*, *pl.* **maoir** · lit. "steward"
Under the humans, an overseer: a Ròdach set over Ròdaich for the Company. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took his byname from the office (19 an Cèitean 1815 DE, 17 an t-Ògmhios 1815 DE). The kingdom gave the word to the Crown's officer in each shire (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE). The kenning *maor-obrach*, "work-steward", is a manager.
> "…from this office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward." — annals, 1815 DE

**mar a thàinig Niall** *phr.* · lit. "the way Niall came"
Any unusually smooth transfer of power. From Niall's crowning (7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE), which passed without dispute (15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE).
> "Its first written use is in a Cathair dhearg tavern ledger, set against a debt settled without argument." — annals, 1932 DE

**Marbh-bheò** *n. m.* · lit. "dead-alive"
The Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills, which attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight (9 an Giblean 9654 BDE). The rule against open fires after dark came from it (26 an t-Ògmhios 5141 BDE), and shepherds still named it when they left the high pastures (17 an Lùnastal 910 DE).
> *Na las teine far am faic e thu.* "Light no fire where it can see you." — the First Book

#### R

**rìgh** *n. m.* · lit. "king"
A ruler of the lowlands, as against the Keeper of the flame. Goraidh mac Ìomhair was the first so called (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE); under the division of keeping the rìgh had the roads and the granaries, the Keeper the flame (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE).
> "He is the first person in any record so called." — annals, 2325 BDE

**Rìghrean na Cloiche** *n. pl.* · lit. "the kings of the stone"
The oldest oral king-list, opening with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE). The name was given to it later.
> "The list gives no lengths of reign. It is older than the name Ròdaich." — annals, 7600 BDE

**roghnaich** *v.* · lit. "choose"
With no object: to have chosen the crossing, to choose exile for good. From the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE); the narrow sense is in the custody-book from 21 an Lùnastal 28 DE. The plain sense was never lost.
> *Roghnaich iadsan, agus dh'fhuirich sinne.* "They chose, and we stayed." — the Third Book

#### S

**scàinte** *adj.* · lit. "rent, split"
Reeling, shaken, of a person as well as a building. From Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending (9 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE). No annal marks its first use.
> "…killing dozens and closing an entire mining district for a generation." — annals, 1916 DE

**Scaradh, a'** *n. m.* · lit. "the parting"
The Sundering (19 an Giblean 1 DE); loosely, any permanent, chosen parting between people who belonged together. It was later applied to the Severance (1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE), which was not chosen, so one word serves two wounds.
> "The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor." — annals, 1 DE

**seann-chunntas** *n. m.* · lit. "old account"
A grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels. Tuathaich speakers coined it (18 an Giblean 2025 DE) for the tabled archive request (15 an Gearran 2016 DE) and the reparations motion left to die (18 an t-Ògmhios 2024 DE).
> "Official Ròdaich usage does not take the word up." — annals, 2025 DE

**Seann-Dhaoine** *n. pl.* · lit. "old people"
The Old Ones, the people before the Ròdaich. The name is a Ròdais description, and no annal dates it. Their first sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal 12,187 BDE).
> "The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin…" — annals, 7253 BDE

**siorrachd** *n. f.*, *pl.* **siorrachdan** · lit. "shire"
Named in the annals from the Age of Sundering (9 an t-Samhain 31 BDE). The kingdom redrew the shires on the humans' district lines (23 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE).
> "…the kingdom uses them and does not say so." — annals, 1932 DE

**sliochd** *n. m.* · lit. "seed, offspring"
A house of custody known by a founder's name, not a hearth. Sliochd Mhuirich was the first (11 an t-Sultain 2903 BDE); four were bound to the Keepers' office (29 an Giblean 2607 BDE).
> "…the first custodian house in the record known by a name rather than by a hearth." — annals, 2903 BDE

**stad-oibre** *n. m.* · lit. "work-halt"
A strike. The first lasted eleven days (13 an Dàmhair 1856 DE); the first held in several regions on one day came in 1922 DE.
> "It ends when food supplies, controlled by human administrators, run out." — annals, 1856 DE

#### T

**Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic** *phr.* · lit. "the ship is eating the hill"
Fearchar Bàrd's most quoted song, made when the Company's steamships began to burn the island's ore to carry it away (15 an Gearran 1882 DE).
> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic / gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.* "The ship is eating the hill to carry the hill away." — the Fourth Book

**Tha e scrìobhte a-nis** *phr.* · lit. "it is written now"
The Moot's whole minute on the day the census figures were read at Caol mhòr (6 an t-Samhain 1993 DE). The Fifth Book takes it for its epigraph.
> "The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'" — annals, 1993 DE

**Tìr Thall, an** *n. f.* · lit. "the land beyond"
The humans' homeland, whose own name no Ròdach scribe set down (26 an Gearran 1781 DE).
> "From the first season the record calls it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans." — annals, 1781 DE

**tonn** *n. m.* · lit. "wave"
A sudden, overwhelming change: *tha e san tonn*, "he is in the wave of it". From Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (2 an Gearran 1933 DE), by way of the survivors' accounts (4 am Faoilleach 1934 DE).
> "Within a generation the sense is heard across the south." — annals, 1934 DE

**Tràigh Bhàthte, an** *n. f.* · lit. "the drowned strand"
The old site of Cnoc chaol, left as the Great Wave left it (23 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE).
> "The townspeople call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there." — annals, 1933 DE

**Tùrsa Geal, an** *n. m.* · lit. "the white sorrow"
The mourning for the departed, "not quite grief and not quite celebration" (1 an Lùnastal 15 DE), first kept at court by Queen Beathag for her sister (27 an Dàmhair 15 DE). The chronicle says it was reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.
> "…with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast." — annals, 15 DE

#### U

**uaine** *adj.* · lit. "green"
Beside its plain sense, sickly, plague-marked. From A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios 1852 DE), first seen as a greenish pallor at Achadh dhomhain (5 an Dùbhlachd 1852 DE).
> "…in a field outside the spoil-heaps that is still called the green acre." — annals, 1852 DE

### Of What the Record Does Not Hold

The record can prove fewer first uses than a reader might want. *Scàinte*, *Aisling-aois* and the loose sense of *a' Scaradh* stand on the chronicle's list, but no annal marks the day any of them was first said. The rope-makers of Cuan shean sing a keel-song whose words have lost their sense (11 an Gearran 1340 DE). The Tuathaich's own memory of the Long War is filed as folklore, and the northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean 1972 DE). Where a word's history is missing, this appendix leaves the gap as it is.


# Appendix F — The Tongues and Peoples of Rodos

This appendix gathers what the rolls and chronicles hold about the peoples who have lived on Rodos and the
speech they used. It draws on the royal chronicles, the rolls and custody-books copied into Leabharlann
Muileann chaol, the map of the kingdom, and the word-lists that survive from the Age of Strangers.
Where the sources are silent this appendix says so, and it does not fill the silence.

## I. The Peoples

Five peoples, or kinds of people, stand in the island's history. Two of them are gone. One of them, the
*fuil-ghuail*, is not a people at all in the ordinary sense, but the chronicles have come to treat it as
one, and so it is set down here with the rest.

| People | Ròdais name | In the chronicles | On the map today |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Old Ones | *na Seann-Dhaoine* | Age I; their works end before the Holy Age | no burg; thirty burgs and thirteen shires bear their names |
| The people of Rodos | *na Ròdaich* (sg. *Ròdach*) | every age | 441 of 505 burgs; the capital and the sea |
| The humans | the chronicles' plain name for them | Age IV | none by that name; their descendants are the Tuathaich |
| The northerners | *na Tuathaich* (sg. *Tuathach*) | Age V | 64 burgs in the north and north-west |
| The coal-blooded | *an fhuil-ghuail*; in the humans' tongue, *obsidian-touched* | from Age IV | not counted on the map; counted, briefly, in the censuses |

### The Seann-Dhaoine

The Ròdaich call the people before them *na Seann-Dhaoine*, the Old Ones. The name is a Ròdais
description, not the Old Ones' own; what they called themselves is not known and cannot now be
known.

**What survives of them** is stone, shell and names. The oldest sure trace is the midden at
Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal 12,187 BDE): limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many
lifetimes, with no tool in it shaped the way any later Ròdach shaped tools. After it come the
notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, every stone cut with the same three strokes
(26 an t-Sultain 12,106 BDE); the unmortared mole at Seann Skell on which every later harbour wall there
stands (1 an t-Iuchar 12,024 BDE); the two hundred and twelve steps of Seann Bhral (30 an t-Iuchar 11,943 BDE); the
stone boxes on Eilean dhearg to which the dead of Seann Vell were rowed (4 an Cèitean 11,854 BDE); the
fish-channel of Seann Toll (2 an t-Ògmhios 11,781 BDE); the shell causeway of Seann Warr, the first made road
on the island that can still be walked (7 am Màrt 11,700 BDE); the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
(17 an Giblean 11,537 BDE); and the slipways of Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide
boat, whose hulls are gone with any telling of where they went (16 an Cèitean 11,454 BDE).

At their widest reach (8 an Cèitean 9029 BDE) they held every coast of the island: the ten places whose
names begin with *Seann*, and the islands off them. Their largest harbour was at the place now
called Seann Skell.

**The ruins inland** are theirs by the oldest tellings. The telling of the counting of the
dead (29 an Lùnastal 7253 BDE) names the Seann-Dhaoine as "the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and
Làrach an Dùin". Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the walled outpost on the spur above the ground where
Cathair mhòr now stands, has its single gate facing inland and not to the sea
(19 an Cèitean 10,400 BDE); Làrach an Dùin, near Ceann mhin, had three rings of wall and room inside for
some four hundred people with their beasts (17 an t-Ògmhios 10,343 BDE); and Làrach an Teampaill, in the
eastern hills, has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal 10,229 BDE), "toward the
vein, not the horizon". All three were already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin
(27 an t-Samhain 8854 BDE, 6 am Màrt 8743 BDE, 7 am Faoilleach 8629 BDE). Whether the builders of the outpost built the
fortress too has never been settled. After the high places were left, every new work of the
Seann-Dhaoine lies within sight of salt water (9 an Dùbhlachd 8573 BDE).

**The standing stones** are harder. Carragh Cnoc bheag, Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm were
raised in the Ancient Age (17 an t-Iuchar 8286 BDE, 9 an t-Sultain 8173 BDE, 6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE), and no telling
says by whom. The upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag bears a line of the unread script; the
four Ròdais words, *Bha teine sa chloich*, "there was fire in the stone", lie lower down, cut with
a narrower tool by another hand, and "when that second hand came, the stone does not say"
(11 an Lùnastal 8229 BDE). The stones are therefore the one place where the marks of two peoples lie on
the same face. The wind-stone at the central Seann Chwen is another: a Ròdais wind-name cut over an
older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine (13 an Gearran 5154 BDE).

**Their counting.** Late in their time the Seann-Dhaoine began cutting single strokes on flat
stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household (31 an t-Iuchar 7293 BDE). At the eastern
Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall of some three thousand strokes
(3 an t-Ògmhios 7212 BDE); at Seann Tarr in the north-east they were cut in fives and set in the floor of a
house (2 an t-Iuchar 7173 BDE). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone was left
half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned (5 an Cèitean 7091 BDE).

**Their end.** After the half-cut stone no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their
middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is not cut again
(7 an Gearran 7050 BDE). How they ended no telling knows, and this appendix
will not guess. Nothing in the chronicles says they were driven out, and nothing says they were not;
nothing says they died, and nothing says their blood did not run on in some later people. The
reader who wants an answer will not find one here.

**The hill-folk.** Alongside, or after, the Seann-Dhaoine the tellings set a second people: the
hill-folk of the high valleys around the crack (10 an t-Samhain 8514 BDE), who buried their dead in the
ground and not on islands, and cut no script. They burned the ore, though sparingly: one sliver,
one fire, at Àth gharbh (12 an Dàmhair 8454 BDE). Whether they shared the island with the Old Ones or
came after them no telling knows. Their own answer, given later, is that they were always
there, and it is the answer the Ròdaich give of themselves in the doctrine carried on Calbh Cnoc
ghorm: *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann*, "we did not come; we were here." When
stag-scholars came to Calbh Cnoc ghorm in the Holy Age and could not read it, the people of Cnoc
ghorm told them what it said, and "the scholars write that the people say so"
(6 an Dàmhair 623 BDE).

### The Ròdaich

The Ròdaich are the people of Rodos: the majority in every age of the island's history, the holders of the
capital, Cathair dhearg (Cathair dhearg), and of the sea. Their name is the island's name with the
people-ending *-aich*; a single person is a *Ròdach*. English writers of the humans' time used
*Rodian*, and this history keeps that word as the English adjective.

**Custodians.** The Ròdaich enter history as custodians. In the Ancient Age a custom set in across
the hill settlements that no fire should take more of the ore than one cupped hand could hold. The
Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE) made the custodianship of the vein a formal order,
"centuries before anything like a king", and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE) made the
custom into rule. The first person in any record to be called *rìgh* was Goraidh mac Ìomhair at Dùn
dhearg (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE), and he claimed nothing over the vein. For the whole of the Holy Age the
kings ruled the grazing and the gatherings, and the Keepers at Dùn ìseal ruled the mountain. The
Holy Age closes on the last age of even population (1 an Cèitean 50 BDE), the last stretch of Rodian
history, the chroniclers note with some unease, in which no family held more years of life than
any other.

**The kingdom.** After the Severance the state restyled itself Rìoghachd Ròdais, the Kingdom of
Rodos (27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE), and Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg (7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE). The rulers since
are set down elsewhere in these appendices. Here it is enough to say that the kingdom is a Ròdach kingdom: its schools
teach in Ròdais "and it has no others" (2 an Gearran 1936 DE), and the old apprentice-binding custom,
when it was revived, was reserved for Ròdaich applicants only (21 an t-Sultain 1942 DE).

**The sea.** The Ròdaich have always been a coastal people as well as a mountain one. The largest
towns on the map today are harbours, and the two largest carry a name older than Ròdais:

| Burg | Shire | Faith | Population |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seann Skell (Seann Skell) | Seann Skell | Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe | 74,120 |
| Seann Skell (Seann Skell) | Seann Skell | Creideamh nan Ròdach | 57,907 |
| Ros dhomhain (Ros dhomhain) | Ros dhomhain | Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh | 51,589 |
| Seann Bhral (Seann Bhral) | Seann Bhral | Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach | 49,681 |
| Cnoc bheag (Cnoc bheag) | Cnoc bheag | Creideamh an t-Seabhaig | 49,661 |
| Cathair mhòr (Cathair mhòr) | Cathair mhòr | Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh | 49,298 |
| Caol bheag (Caol bheag) | Caol bheag | Feallsanachd an Fhèidh | 42,649 |
| Achadh mhòr (Achadh mhòr) | Achadh mhòr | Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach | 42,136 |

The capital itself is not among them. Cathair dhearg is counted at 10,274; its harbour, Ros
dhomhain, is five times its size.

**The departed.** Part of the Ròdaich people is not on Rodos. Land was found across the water
(6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE); volunteers chose to go, by a vote "or something the later chronicles call a
vote" (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE); the fleet set out, turning sunwise round the harbour, in the first year
of the Diosal Era (19 an Giblean 1 DE). A fragmentary report told of two landfalls, not one
(24 an Dùbhlachd 5 DE), and of the thinning: cut off from the vein, "by the third generation abroad,
nothing remains that Rodos would recognize" (3 an t-Iuchar 14 DE). The departed are a people of the
chronicles only by their absence. The island kept them in rites (the empty-harbour rite,
25 an t-Samhain 22 DE; the white sorrow, *an Tùrsa Geal*, 27 an Dàmhair 15 DE) and in words, of which more
below. When the humans came, old sailors at Cuan shean remarked that the strangers had come in from
the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbade the remark in its
hall; it was written down anyway, and never answered (9 an Gearran 1781 DE). Nobody on Rodos knows
whether the humans descend from the departed, and this appendix does not know either.

### The humans of an Tìr Thall

**The Crossing.** Humans made landfall on Rodos and were granted leave to stay
(5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE): the first contact since the Sundering. Three ships out of the west anchored off
Cuan shean, and their master, whom the chronicles call Edmund Harrow, came ashore unarmed and asked by
signs for water (13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE). That is the first exchange between the two peoples, and it was
not in words.

**Their homeland.** The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdach scribe
set the word down. From the first season the chronicles call it *an Tìr Thall*, the land beyond, and
calls its people simply the humans (26 an Gearran 1781 DE). Their own name for their country is not on
Rodos in any hand, and it will not be recovered from here.

**What they called things.** The humans' names for the island's things were few, plain and, to
Ròdach ears, careless. They had a single word for the black ore, and it was the word for the fuel
they burned at home; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's copyist noted that no Ròdais word answered to it,
and that the humans did not ask for one (24 an Cèitean 1782 DE). So the vein became, in their tongue,
*coal*, and the custodians of the vein became, in Samuel Wren's otherwise careful grammar, "keepers
of the coal" (21 an Lùnastal 1791 DE). Their institutions came with English names and kept them: the
Company, the Administration, the Mission, the Residency above Ros dhomhain (10 an Cèitean 1788 DE), the
Commissioner, the Levy, the constable posts. Their coin was the *mark*. The townsfolk of Muileann
shean called the constable post there "the humans' second Residency", and did not mean it kindly
(26 an t-Iuchar 1911 DE).

**The camps.** What the humans built for themselves on Rodos was built for the pit. The camp of
timber huts at Àth ìseal was the first settlement on Rodos built for no purpose but the pit
(7 an t-Ògmhios 1807 DE); Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdach
town drawn on paper before it was built (10 am Faoilleach 1813 DE); the camp at Achadh dhomhain was built
of spoil (29 am Màrt 1846 DE). The camps were Ròdach in their labour and human in their rule, and the
record of them is kept in two tongues that seldom agree: the Mission counts four hundred and six
dead of the spotted pox, and the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of
the Mission's list (11 an Dàmhair 1818 DE). Human families lived on Rodos as well as human officers:
upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, was granted for human families who would
not work in the pits (3 an t-Samhain 1799 DE). It is the first human settlement in the north, and the
north is where their descendants were sent.

**Mixing.** The first mixed settlement (22 an Giblean 1784 DE) was Baile dhìreach on the south-west
coast, under a council of three Ròdaich and three humans, whose founding compact was written twice,
once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age (10 an Dàmhair 1784 DE). There the
net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale, and the council entered the
marriage in both its books (26 an Cèitean 1786 DE). Later history did not repeat the experiment, and the
first mixed-blood inheritance case (15 an Gearran 1890 DE) was decided by the Administration entirely in
its own favour.

**The going north.** War was declared in 1928 DE. Before the end, the human families of
Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west marched north along the western roads under
guard of the council's companies; few of them had ever lived in the north; no column was attacked,
and none was helped (20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE). The war ended with the crossing itself closed
(1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE). Whatever let humans reach Rodos shut, and the humans still on the island were
shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today.

### The Tuathaich

From the Severance the chronicles stop calling them humans. The descendants of those left on Rodos are
*na Tuathaich*, the northerners, from *tuath*, north, by the same *-aich* that makes *Ròdaich*, so
that on the page the two names read as siblings even though their circumstances do not. Their
homeland in the north was fixed formally (22 am Màrt 1930 DE): "a confinement, not a homecoming,
though later generations will simply call it home." A formal wall between the two peoples was
proposed and rejected as unnecessary, because the two were already keeping apart on their own
(11 an Cèitean 1939 DE).

What the Tuathaich call themselves in their own speech the chronicles do not say. The name in this
appendix is the kingdom's name for them.

**Their burgs.** The map counts sixty-four Tuathaich burgs, all in the north and north-west, with
some 543,000 people in them. The Ròdaich hold the other 441. The largest Tuathaich towns:

| Burg | Shire | Faith | Population |
|---|---|---|---|
| Caol mhòr (Caol mhòr) | Caol mhòr | Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe | 42,002 |
| Doire ghlas (Doire ghlas) | Doire ghlas | Creideamh nan Tuathach | 40,740 |
| Ceann mhòr (Ceann mhòr) | Ceann mhòr | Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe | 32,420 |
| Baile chrom (Baile chrom) | Baile chrom | Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise | 27,319 |
| Cnoc ghorm (Cnoc ghorm) | Cnoc ghorm | Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe | 25,112 |

Every Tuathaich town but one bears a Ròdais name, and most of them were Ròdach towns before the
Severance; the north-west had been thinly held since the dearth on that shore in the Age of
Sundering (19 an Giblean 780 DE). One of them, Seann Skell (Seann Skell) in the shire of
Muileann àrsaidh, bears an Old One's name. The Tuathaich have added no names of their own to the
map.

**Their assembly.** Tuathaich householders from the northern towns met at Caol mhòr and chose a
speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk (25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE). The Moot has no standing in
Ròdach law; it meets anyway, and its minutes run unbroken from that meeting to the present.

**Their faiths.** Of the sixty-four Tuathaich burgs, fifty-one keep Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe,
the faith of the Yellow Scorpion, which the Ròdaich of the western coast had kept for centuries
before them. Twelve keep Creideamh nan Tuathach, their own folk tradition; its deity on the map
is Donn, an Sìorraidh, and its towns lie together along the north coast, in the shires of Doire
ghlas, Muileann leathan, Inis mhin and Àth àrsaidh. One, Baile chrom, keeps Rùn-dìomhair na
h-Oidhche Glaise, the Mystery of the Grey Night. Creideamh nan Tuathach keeps, quietly, the First
Canoe fragment (13 an Gearran 1938 DE): among coastal Tuathaich families, "a named steersman, a first
crossing", dismissed by the Ròdach priesthood as superstition (9 an t-Samhain 10,054 BDE). The fragment
belongs at the head of the Ancient Age, because that is where its tellers place it.
The Library neither endorses it nor refutes it. It is one of the two suppressed histories
that bracket the island's story, and it is not resolved here.

### The fuil-ghuail

This section holds to what the rolls and chronicles say.

A child born into the mining camps was exposed to more raw ore across her lifetime than any Rodian
in living memory, and did not age the way the people around her did. Her name is Aisling
(7 am Màrt 1848 DE). What was happening to her had no word, in any language spoken on the island
(13 am Faoilleach 1850 DE). A second case, Fionnan, was born half a century later (21 an Gearran 1900 DE), and
it became plain that the exposure was not a single accident but an ongoing industrial condition.
Facing two confirmed cases, Ròdach custodians settled on a term (23 am Faoilleach 1905 DE): *fuil-ghuail*,
"coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as *obsidian-touched*. It was meant clinically. It was
agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, and the roll records the vote but not
who proposed it (21 an Gearran 1905 DE). The Residency ordered every Ròdach child showing the condition to
be reported; the custodians complied by reporting none (26 an t-Samhain 1906 DE). A third case, Lorccan,
was born in a mining town (1 an Giblean 1913 DE), and a fourth, Cian, within a year of him
(3 am Màrt 1914 DE).

After the Severance the Obsidian Rite was formalized as Creideamh nan Ròdach, built around the
leyline and "the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE). The first census of the
kingdom noted, without further comment, exactly how few such people exist (30 an t-Iuchar 1936 DE), and
the published census of a later generation gave a number and nothing else (8 am Faoilleach 1994 DE). The
number is printed nowhere else, and this appendix does not print it either.

Whether the *fuil-ghuail* are a people is a question of words. They are born to Ròdach families;
in Ròdach speech the word names the gift that sets the Ròdaich apart from the Tuathaich; and Feallsanachd an Fhèidh has asked since the Holy Age why the vein answers some hands and
not others. The chronicles do not settle it.

## II. The Tongues

### Ròdais

Ròdais is the Gaelic of Rodos. Of the humans' tongues it most resembles Scottish Gaelic, Irish and Manx,
and it is closest to Scottish Gaelic in grammar and core vocabulary; its look on the page is its own. Three marks distinguish it:

| Feature | Ròdais | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Long vowels | **grave accent only**: *à è ì ò ù* | *mòr, sìth, Ròdais* |
| The cluster /sk/ | written **sc**, never *sg* | *uisce, scoil, sceul, Scàineadh* |
| "City" | *cathair* | *Cathair dhearg* |

Its greeting of thanks is *gu robh math agad*. Its verbs come first in the sentence
(*Chunnaic Cian an long*, "Cian saw the ship"); it has no word for "a", no words for yes and no,
and two initial mutations.

**Lenition.** After many words an initial consonant softens, and the change is written with *h*:
*b > bh, c > ch, d > dh, f > fh, g > gh, m > mh, p > ph, s > sh, t > th*. The possessives, the past
tense, a feminine noun after the article, an adjective after a feminine noun, most simple
prepositions and the second element of a name all cause it. It does not touch vowels, nor *l, n,
r* in writing, nor the clusters *sc, sp, st, sm*; and after a word ending in *n* it spares *d, t*
and *s*, which is why the map has *Seann Dunn* and *Seann Toll* but *Seann Bhral*.

**Broad and slender.** Vowels are broad (*a o u à ò ù*) or slender (*e i è ì*), and within one
word a consonant takes vowels of the same class on both sides: *caol le caol, leathan le
leathan*, slender with slender, broad with broad. That is why so many endings come in pairs, and why
the small rivers are *Ciaras* but *Àrsaidheas*.

**Sounds.** For the reader who meets these names aloud:

| written | said | example |
|---|---|---|
| bh, mh | v | *Seann Bhral* |
| ch | as in *loch* | *Seann Chwen* |
| dh, gh | a voiced *ch* before broad vowels; *y* before slender | *Cathair dhearg* |
| fh | silent | *Àth fhada* |
| sh, th | h | *Dùn thais* |
| sc | sk | *Scàineadh* |

The stress falls on the first syllable.

**How Ròdais names new things.** Ròdais is an old dialect, long cut off, and it took few of the
loanwords that other Gaelic took for new things, fewer than Scottish Gaelic took. The humans brought
many new things, and the kingdom after them more. In the first generations after the Crossing the
Ròdaich named nearly all of them from old roots, naming the thing by what it does or what it is
like: head first, the describer after, hyphenated, two elements and seldom three. Many of these
kennings are still the usual words. The loans Ròdais did take came mostly later, for such things
as the bus (*bus*), the taxi (*tacsaidh*) and the radio (*rèidio*), and for many words of the
sciences, such as *ogsaidean*, oxygen, and the names of the elements. A selection of the kennings,
with the literal sense and the word the Gaelic of other lands uses:

| English | Ròdais | literally | elsewhere |
|---|---|---|---|
| train | *carbad-iarainn* | iron-chariot | *trèana* |
| engine | *cridhe-iarainn* | iron-heart | *einnsean* |
| computer | *inntinn-iarainn* | iron-mind | *coimpiutair* |
| aeroplane | *eun-iarainn* | iron-bird | *plèana* |
| telephone | *guth-sreinge* | string-voice | *fòn* |
| cable | *sreang-theine* | fire-string | *càball* |
| socket | *tobar-dealanaich* | lightning-well | *socaid* |
| battery | *ciste-spionnaidh* | strength-chest | *bataraidh* |
| heater | *teine-gun-lasair* | flameless-fire | *teasadair* |
| camera | *cìste-scàile* | shadow-chest | *camara* |
| film | *sceul-scàile* | shadow-tale | *film* |
| novel | *leabhar-sceòil* | tale-book | *nobhail* |
| documentary | *sceul-fìrinne* | truth-tale | *prògram aithriseach* |
| plastic | *cèir-chruaidh* | hard-wax | *plastaig* |
| inflation | *lobhadh-airgid* | money-rot | *atmhorachd* |
| internet | *lìon-fiosa* | tidings-net | *eadar-lìon* |
| crossing (street) | *àth-coise* | foot-ford | *slighe-choisichean* |
| tyre | *bròg-cuibhle* | wheel-shoe | *taidhr* |

Families form of themselves: machines are *iarainn*, of iron; screens and pictures are *scàil* and
*scàthan*, shadow and mirror; electricity is *dealan*, spark, and *dealanach*, lightning. A
crossing for feet is a ford, *àth*, the same word the map uses for a town at a river.

**Words born of the island's history.** Ròdais has also given old words new senses from the events it lived
through. The royal chroniclers keep a list of these, and the rolls date the first use of most.

| Word | Plain sense | Sense given by history | First recorded |
|---|---|---|---|
| *roghnaich* | to choose | to have chosen the crossing; to choose exile | 21 an Lùnastal 28 DE |
| *a' Scaradh* | the Sundering | any chosen, permanent parting; later used of the Severance | Age of Sundering |
| *uaine* | green | sickly, plague-marked, after A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios 1852 DE) | Age of Strangers |
| *scàinte* | rent, cracked | shaken, of a person, after Scàineadh Cill ghlas (9 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE) | Age of Strangers |
| *Aisling-aois* | Aisling's age | an unnaturally long youth in anyone, said half in jest | Age of Strangers |
| *mar a thàinig Niall* | the way Niall came | any smooth handing-over of power | 15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE |
| *tonn* | wave | a sudden, overwhelming change: *tha e san tonn* | 4 am Faoilleach 1934 DE |
| *a chur san Leabharlann* | to put it in the Library | to make a thing settled and official | 3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE |
| *dubhan* | a man's name | the synthetic fuel | 23 an t-Sultain 2010 DE |
| *dubhan-tùsail* | dubhan of the beginning | a first attempt that looked like a dead end before it wasn't | 22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE |
