| *fadachadh* | lengthening | to be crushed after holding out too long: *chaidh am fadachadh* | 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE |
| *seann-chunntas* | old account | a grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels | 18 an Giblean 2025 DE |

Of the Sundering the language also keeps one strange relic. A work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan
shean names the parts of a deep keel, and half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it
(11 an Gearran 1340 DE). It is the only record of the fleet's techniques to survive in any form. Whether
the lost words are old Ròdais, wrights' cant, or something else, no one has shown.

### The tongue of the Seann-Dhaoine

Of the Old Ones' speech nothing survives but names. Ten roots are known, each standing after the
Ròdais word *seann*, "old", which lenites it where Ròdais lenites:

| Root | As written on the map | Burgs bearing it | Shires named from it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dunn | Seann Dunn | 3 | yes |
| Cwen | Seann Chwen | 3 | yes |
| Skell | Seann Skell | 4 | yes (three) |
| Bral | Seann Bhral | 3 | yes |
| Tarr | Seann Tarr | 3 | yes |
| Vell | Seann Vell | 5 | yes (three) |
| Morn | Seann Mhorn | 2 | — |
| Brenn | Seann Bhrenn | 2 | yes |
| Toll | Seann Toll | 3 | yes |
| Warr | Seann Warr | 2 | yes |

Thirty burgs on the map bear these names, and thirteen shires are named from them.

The Ròdaich did not translate these names; they took them over. The fishers who resettled Seann
Mhorn in the Holy Age kept "the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue", and said
the old name came with the stones (23 an t-Sultain 2821 BDE). It is the first such taking-over on
record. The pattern is the one other lands know, where an older people's harbour-names outlive them
inside a newer tongue: borrowed and fossilized, not translated.

**What can be said.** The roots are single syllables. Seven of the ten end in a doubled consonant
(*-nn, -ll, -rr*). Three of them hold letters that Ròdais writes nowhere else: *k* in *Skell*, *v* in
*Vell*, *w* in *Cwen* and *Warr*. Ròdais spelling turns every *sg* into *sc*, but it has never turned
Seann Skell into Seann Scell; the scribes kept the foreign *k* as they found it, and the grammar
counts *sk-* among the clusters that do not lenite.

**What cannot be known.** What any root meant. Whether *seann* was ever the Old Ones' own element,
or only the Ròdaich's label for places they found already named (the second is the usual
reading, and the likelier, but it is a reading). Whether the roots come from one tongue or several.
Two of them look like Ròdais words, *toll*, a hole, and *dunn* beside *dùn*, a fort; the
resemblance has tempted scholars in every age and proves nothing, and the Library does not take a
side.

**The script.** The Seann-Dhaoine also cut signs. Rows of them stand on the cliff above Seann Tarr
(5 an Giblean 11,618 BDE), in the script that turns up again on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais, and
it has not been read. Not one sign of it has an agreed meaning. The stag-scholars of the Holy Age
set their own new letters against the obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag and found that they matched
nothing, and wrote down that the stone's writers were not their teachers (12 an Cèitean 2085 BDE).
Samuel Wren copied the obelisk and sent it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall; no reply is
recorded (5 an Gearran 1796 DE). Edwin Lowe copied the pillar near Cnoc chiar, compared it with Wren's
copy, and decided that the two were not the same script and that neither was Ròdach; his notes stop
there (9 an Lùnastal 1844 DE). The strokes on the midden stones are not this script; they are a count.
Whether the script records the Old Ones' tongue, or some other, or no tongue at all, is not known.

### The humans' tongue

The humans spoke a plain tongue, and this history renders it in English (see *Of Translation*
below). The names they carried were names of that tongue: Edmund Harrow, Thomas Pike, Samuel Wren,
Josiah Pell, Henry Maddox, Arthur Lisle, Samuel Hale, Edwin Lowe.

**The season of translation.** Human clerics and Ròdach custodians spent a full season trying to
build a shared vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed survives intact
(27 am Màrt 1781 DE). Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept parallel
word-lists. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books; Gormshuil's was lost, and only its
first leaf is known from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken ore (13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE).
Against those forty the humans had one word, and it was *coal*.

**The tongue of rule.** The humans wrote their agreements in their own tongue only. The first
written treaty (27 an Giblean 1787 DE) was signed at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein, who could not
read the tongue it was written in; the record does not say who read it to him (7 an Cèitean 1787 DE).
The Harbour Articles were written the same way, and that time two custodians refused to sign
(16 an t-Samhain 1798 DE). The Mission's school at Ros dhomhain taught Ròdach children in the humans'
tongue (9 an Cèitean 1831 DE); a generation later Iain Maor, the first overseer schooled there, kept his
reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais (23 an Giblean 1866 DE). The Levy's officers
read the names of the chosen at Caol mhòr from a list in the humans' tongue, and the custodians took
the names down again in Ròdais, "so that they will know whom to look for" (3 am Màrt 1867 DE).

**Loanwords.** Few crossed, and most of those late. In the first generations Ròdais took the
humans' goods and named them in its own way, as above, and kept few of the humans' words for them. The humans, for their part, so far as the record shows,
used the Ròdais names of places as they found them, and took *fuil-ghuail* not as a loan but as a
translation, *obsidian-touched*; that word, and not the Ròdais, is the one the kingdom's own later
entries use of the Rite's "unbroken line". What went the other way, into the humans' speech, is best seen after the
Severance, in the north.

The Ròdais word for the humans' country, *an Tìr Thall*, is the only name the island has for it.

### Tuathaich speech

The speech of the north is a mixed speech, and the chronicles describe it only in passing. They say
this much:

The Tuathaich kept the humans' tongue. Walter Hale asked the council for leave to open schools in
the north teaching in it, and was refused (2 an Gearran 1936 DE); Agnes Pike opened one at Doire ghlas
anyway, with Moot money and without the council's leave, and within a decade there were nine
(14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE). The Moot later counted eleven such schools, and three that had begun to teach
Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking (7 an t-Ògmhios 1958 DE). The Scorpion house at Cnoc ghorm taught
its priests in the humans' tongue while reading the Scorpion's scripture in the Ròdais text the
west-coast houses use: the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean 1939 DE).

The Tuathaich live among Ròdais names and use Ròdais words. The words the north has added to the
island's speech in the present age are Ròdais in form: *fadachadh*, from *fada*, long, the name of
the war they lost (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and *seann-chunntas*, an old reckoning, which official Ròdach
usage pointedly does not take up (18 an Giblean 2025 DE). The word *dubhan* for the fuel came out of the
north, from the name of Dubhan, a Tuathach, and it spread before the fuel did (23 an t-Sultain 2010 DE);
the royal chronicler who first set it down spelled it three ways in two lines (21 an t-Samhain 2000 DE).

Beyond this the chronicles do not go. The northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal
record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean 1972 DE). How far the humans' tongue has drifted in the north
since the crossing closed, how much Ròdais is spoken at a Tuathach hearth, and in which tongue the
First Canoe is told: this archive does not know, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise.

### Names and naming

**Personal names.** Ròdach names are Gaelic personal names: Ailean, Beathag, Catrìona, Dòmhnall,
Eilidh, Fearchar, Gormshuil, Iain, Mòrag, Raghnall, Sìleas, Tormod. A person is further named from
the father, with *mac*, son, or *nic*, daughter, and the father's name in the genitive, lenited
where Ròdais lenites: Tormod mac Iain; Eilidh nic Iain; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair; Donnchadh mac
Thormoid; Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill; Oighrig nic Lachlainn.

**Bynames** are as common as patronymics and often outlast them. They name a colour, a trade, a
size or a deed. After a woman's name the byname is lenited, after a man's it is not: Seònaid Mhòr,
Eilidh Dhubh, Beathag Bhàn, but Ailean Mòr, Calum Liath, Dùghall Garbh. Trade-names are nouns and
stand as they are: Alasdair Saor, the wright; Iain Maor, the overseer. Some bynames are earned:
Tormod mac Iain, the first of the royal kin to read, was called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the
Writer, for the rest of his life (3 an Lùnastal 1713 BDE).

**Kindreds** take *Sliochd*, the seed or line, or *Clann*, the children, with a founder's name in the
genitive: Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Mhuirich, Clann Choinnich.

**Human and Tuathaich names** are of the humans' tongue and are kept in their own spelling: Walter
Hale, Agnes Pike. Unlike the humans' names for the island's things, the humans' names for
themselves survived the Severance.

**Place names.** Ròdach places are named by a generic noun and a describing word after it. On the
map the describer is always lenited, whatever the gender of the generic (*Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag,
Dùn thais*); in speech it would not be after a masculine noun, and the map's form is a fixed naming
pattern, kept as one might keep an old compound. The generics:

| Generic | Sense | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| *Cathair* | stone fort; city | capital, city |
| *Dùn* | fortified hill | capital, city |
| *Baile Mòr* | great settlement | city |
| *Baile* | settlement, town | town |
| *Àth* | ford | town |
| *Cnoc* | hill | town |
| *Muileann* | mill | town |
| *Cill* | church site | village, hamlet |
| *Tobar* | well | village, hamlet |
| *Achadh* | field | village |
| *Doire* | oak grove | village |
| *Carraig* | rock | hamlet |
| *Ros* | headland | port |
| *Ceann* | head, point | port |
| *Cuan* | harbour | port |
| *Caol* | strait | port |
| *Inis* | island | port |

The describers are colour, size and character words: *mòr, beag, dubh, geal, bàn, dearg, ruadh,
uaine, glas, fada, domhain, ìseal, fiadhaich, naomh, fionn, ciar, gorm, sean, òg, garbh, min, caol,
leathan, crom, dìreach, àrsaidh*. The great rivers are *Abhainn* with a describer; the small ones
take a root and the ending *-as* or *-eas* by broad and slender. A shire, *siorrachd*, takes the name
of its seat. Names repeat freely; there are two Baile chrom and four Seann Skell, and the rolls
tell them apart by where they are.

Beside these stand the Old Ones' names, which follow none of the rules above except that the Ròdaich
put *seann* before them.

### Writing

**Before letters.** The first marks on Rodos made on purpose are the Seann-Dhaoine's: the notched
net-weights of Seann Chwen, their unread script, and their tally strokes. The Ròdaich's forebears
kept counts too, but not in letters. Someone began marking the high-water line against a fixed rock
in the Ancient Age (28 am Faoilleach 5937 BDE), and at Ros dhomhain Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, one
for the high water and one for the low (25 an t-Iuchar 5177 BDE). The king-lists of that age were oral, and
the Small-Burning custom was "nowhere written and everywhere kept".

**The Ròdais words on the stones.** *Bha teine sa chloich* on Carragh Cnoc bheag, *Cuimhnich an
teine* on Colbh Cnoc chiar, *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann* on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: these are the
oldest Ròdais words in stone. When they were cut no roll says. The stones were raised in
the Ancient Age; the Ròdais on Carragh Cnoc bheag was cut later, by another hand. The words on Calbh
Cnoc ghorm were recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill, and some later
readers say the recutting changed a letter (2 an t-Samhain 3237 BDE). That there were letters to change
then is not proved by this; the Library keeps the claim and makes no judgment on it.

**The stag-letters.** The first letters in use by the Ròdaich were made at Muileann chiar in the far
east, where the teachers of the stag's people, the school later called Feallsanachd an Fhèidh,
turned the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, "so that a teaching can be kept without a
teacher" (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE). Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them. From these
came the first written king-list (20 an Lùnastal 1684 BDE), kept by Tormod Scrìobhaiche at Dùn dhearg; the
Keepers' own roll, written down at Dùn ìseal in answer to it (17 an Dàmhair 1648 BDE); boundary stones
cut with treaty terms (11 am Màrt 1395 BDE); and the first teaching of letters for their own sake, to
fishers' children at Inis bheag, which the Hall recorded with the remark that fish do not need
reading (22 an t-Ògmhios 1138 BDE).

**Books and paper.** The Age of Sundering is the age of the custody-book, kept by the vein-house,
and of the first books: Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the sayings of Gormshuil (5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE), and
Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants, the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as
one narrative (8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE). Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king to learn his letters as a
child (25 an Cèitean 355 DE). A mill at Muileann chaol began making paper from rags, the first on Rodos,
and the custody-book was copied onto paper in that generation (28 am Faoilleach 1635 DE).

**Two tongues of record.** The humans brought paper in quantity, and the custodians of
Cathair naomh asked for their first payment in paper and ink (19 an Lùnastal 1782 DE). They brought, too, a
written tongue the Ròdaich could not read, and for a century the island kept its records in two.
Whether the humans' letters and the stag-letters share their shapes, the record does not say. The
earliest Ròdach grievance text to survive, Leabhar Baile thais, was set down in Ròdais by many
hands (18 an t-Sultain 1880 DE).

**The kingdom's record.** After the Severance the kingdom founded Leabharlann Muileann chaol
(1 an Cèitean 1945 DE) and the office of royal chronicler (20 an t-Samhain 1947 DE), and in time drew the
provincial archives into one place (26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE). This appendix is written from that library.

## Of Translation

This history is written in English for the next reader, and some account is owed of what that has
done to the tongues it describes.

**The humans' speech is rendered in English.** The humans did not speak English. They spoke the
tongue of an Tìr Thall, whose name for itself, like the name of their country, is not recorded on
Rodos. It was a plain tongue, as English is plain beside Ròdais; its speakers were strangers to the
island and its things; and it has become, in the north, the ordinary speech of the Tuathaich. For
those reasons it is given here as English, and its names are given as English names, as the letter-
books would have them. When this history says the humans called the ore *coal*, it means that they
used their ordinary word for their ordinary fuel, and that *coal* is the nearest English word for
what they meant. When it gives a custodian's title as "keepers of the coal", it is rendering Wren's
rendering. *Obsidian-touched* is likewise an English stand-in for the humans' word, chosen because
it keeps the plainness of the original and the error in it. The ore is not obsidian, and it is not
coal.

**Ròdais is kept as it is.** The Ròdaich are the people of this history and Ròdais is its first
tongue, and it is not translated into something else here. Names of places, persons, faiths,
laws and offices are left in Ròdais spelling, with the grave accent and the *sc*, and with their
lenitions: *Cathair dhearg*, not "Red City"; *fuil-ghuail*, not "coal-blood", except where a gloss is
wanted. Where a Ròdais phrase is translated, the translation follows it in quotation marks and is
meant as a help, not a replacement. The five ages have Ròdais names and are also given English ones
for convenience; the English names are this archive's, not the chroniclers'. The adjective *Rodian*
is English, and is used as such.

**The island's own name.** Written in Ròdais it is *Ròdos*, with the accent. In the English text of
this history it is written *Rodos*, the form the humans used and the form in which most readers
will have met it. It is the same word.

**The Seann tongue is not translated, because it cannot be.** Its ten roots are given as the
Ròdaich wrote them, with the foreign letters the Ròdaich kept. No meaning is offered for any of
them.

**What has been lost in the rendering.** Some things do not cross. The forty colour-words on
Gormshuil's leaf are one; the Tuathaich jokes about being long-warred are another, since *fadachadh*
is funny, and not funny, only in a tongue where *fada* is also the name of the war. Where this history
has had to choose between a translation that reads easily and one that keeps what the words did, it
has tried to keep what they did.


# A Gazetteer of Rodos

**Achadh chaol** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 23 am Faoilleach 527 DE by Ròdaich farmers of Muileann dhomhain. A village of narrow fields that has fed the eastern mining district since the district was opened. Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending, struck it when the fault tore open, and the diggings it fed were closed after. It still sends its grain to the mills around it. Known for narrow fields feeding the diggings.

**Achadh chaol** (Achadh chaol). Founded 17 an Lùnastal 2776 BDE by Ròdaich barley farmers. Achadh chaol is a large village of narrow barley fields and the seat of its province. Its grain goes to the mills of Muileann dhìreach, and the two places have kept the same bargain since the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for narrow barley fields.

**Achadh dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios 2727 BDE by farmers of Muileann chrom. Achadh dhomhain of Muileann chrom is a large farming village in deep fields, founded in the Holy Age. Its granaries fed the mining camps in the Age of Strangers and were requisitioned in the war of the Severance. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for deep-field granaries of the camps.

**Achadh dhomhain** (Caol shean). Founded 27 an t-Iuchar 128 BDE by hosts of the Allt an Àigh pilgrims. Achadh dhomhain of Caol shean is a large village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune. Pilgrims have come to drink from it since the Holy Age, and the village lives on them. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for hosts to Allt an Àigh pilgrims.

**Achadh dhìreach** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 30 an t-Ògmhios 1962 DE by settlers under the restored kingdom. Achadh dhìreach was laid out in straight fields by the restored kingdom, when extraction returned to full scale and the towns of the plain needed feeding. It is small, fewer than eight hundred people. It feeds Baile Mòr àrsaidh. Known for kingdom-era straight fields.

**Achadh fhada** (Baile chiar). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd 877 DE by barley-farmers of the south-west. Achadh fhada, the long field, is a village of barley farms in the capital's southern country. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It keeps the Direwolf's faith, unlike most of its neighbours. Known for long field of barley.

**Achadh fhada** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 31 an Cèitean 625 DE by priests of the Hungry Hawk. A long field village in the wooded middle west, one of the few settlements where Creideamh an t-Seabhaig, the Rite's older form, still holds. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. Its fields feed the Hawk-faith mill at Muileann uaine. Known for the Hawk-faith fields.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Ceann bheag). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios 726 DE by horse-breeders of the north. Achadh fhiadhaich is a village of the north-east, founded in the long quiet centuries on wild pasture that no earlier people had fenced. It breeds horses and grows hay for the coast, and the carters of Ceann bheag have bought its horses for generations. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for wild-field hay and horses.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar 1473 DE by Ròdaich fishers of the west coast. A wild field village on the far western shore with a small harbour, kept in Ròdaich hands when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed to the north. It faces the waters where the Sea-Watcher is said to live, and pirates are still seen off the coast. Its people follow the Yellow Scorpion. Known for fishing within sight of the Sea-Watcher's waters.

**Achadh fhiadhaich** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 21 an t-Sultain 1774 DE by Ròdaich farmers who reclaimed the wild field. A village of fields reclaimed from wild ground in the Age of Sundering, when the island had fewer mouths and more hands to spare. It feeds the towns of Ceann àrsaidh and sends its surplus to Muileann chrom to be ground. It is a large village now, of nearly ten thousand. Known for reclaimed wild fields.

**Achadh fhionn** (Baile ghorm). Founded 23 an Lùnastal 1930 BDE by farmers of the south-east. Achadh fhionn is a village of the south-east, founded in the Holy Age in a fair field under Làrach an Dùin. It keeps the ancestor rite and leaves the ruin alone. Its people say the ruin was old when the first Ròdaich came. Known for fair field under Làrach an Dùin.

**Achadh fhionn** (Cnoc shean). Founded 9 an t-Samhain 491 DE by farmers of Cnoc shean. A fair field village in the south-east, with meadows between the hill-towns of Cnoc shean and Cnoc fhada. It keeps the old spirits and is known for its hay. Known for hay from the fair fields.

**Achadh fhionn** (Ceann mhin). Founded 15 an Dùbhlachd 21 DE by Ròdaich barley farmers. A farming village of fair barley fields between Baile mhin and Àth ghlas. In the Age of Strangers its pastures were taken for the horses of the administration, and they have served as remount grounds for the soldiers of the district ever since. It is a quiet place, larger in fields than in people. Known for barley fields and remount pastures.

**Achadh gharbh** (Inis bheag). Founded 7 an Dàmhair 166 DE by farmers from Inis bheag. Rough ground behind the port of Inis bheag, broken to the plough in the long centuries after the Sundering fleet had gone. It feeds the harbour and the fishing fleet, and it has grown larger than many towns while keeping the name and customs of a village. The Feallsanachd an Fhèidh has a strong following among its farmers, who are said to argue philosophy over the furrow. Known for stony fields that feed Inis bheag.

**Achadh gharbh** (Inis bheag). Founded 3 am Faoilleach 1065 DE by farmers of Muileann chaol. A rough field village beside the older Muileann chaol, breaking stony ground for the mill. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and shares its name with two other Achadh gharbhs of the east, which the library's clerks tell apart only by their shires. Known for stony fields for the old mill.

**Achadh gharbh** (Caol shean). Founded 13 an t-Ògmhios 402 BDE by the keepers of Allt an Àigh. A rough field village beside Allt an Àigh, the stream said to grant fortune to those who drink at the right phase of the moon. Pilgrims have come since the Holy Age, and the keepers' citadel was built to guard the stream from anyone who would bottle and sell it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, whose philosophers have never agreed whether the stream's luck is real. Known for Allt an Àigh, the stream of fortune.

**Achadh gharbh** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 21 an Giblean 526 DE by Ròdaich peat-cutters of the northern uplands. A hamlet-sized village of rough upland fields and peat banks above Tobar fhiadhaich. Its peat warmed the northern towns when the Small-Burning Law still held and the ore was not burned freely. Fewer than a thousand people live there now. Known for rough upland fields and peat.

**Achadh gheal** (Seann Skell). Founded 23 an t-Samhain 959 BDE by Ròdaich flax-growers of Seann Skell. The white field is the flax country that feeds the linen-weavers of Seann Skell, and in the drying season the whole plain is laid with bleaching cloth. The village is large and prosperous for its kind, and it follows the Yellow Scorpion as the port does. Its growers' guild has sold to the same Seann Skell houses for longer than either side can prove. Known for flax fields and bleached linen.

**Achadh ghlas** (Seann Skell). Founded 26 an Lùnastal 1658 BDE by Ròdaich farmers of Seann Skell. A village of grey-green fields on the road north from Seann Skell, whose barley and oats feed the great port. It lies just south of the Tuathaich line, and since the Severance its farmers have ploughed with one eye on the boundary. In the Long War its barns quartered soldiers of the seventh regiment on the way to Àth leathan. Known for grey fields on the Seann Skell road.

**Achadh mhin** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 1 an Lùnastal 2261 BDE by farmers of the southern coast. Achadh mhin is a farming village of the south, founded in the Holy Age. Tonn Mhòr struck it in the first years of the restored kingdom and destroyed it in a single night. It was rebuilt and keeps the capital's faith. Known for rebuilt after the Great Wave.

**Achadh mhin** (Baile gharbh). Founded 19 an Lùnastal 1762 DE by Ròdaich farmers of Baile gharbh. A village of smooth, well-drained fields that feeds the harbour at Ceann dhubh. It is not the Achadh mhin of the southern coast that the Great Wave struck. It has had few recorded troubles and is mentioned in the older rolls chiefly for its tithe. Known for smooth fields of Baile gharbh.

**Achadh mhòr** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 13 am Màrt 1897 BDE by Ròdaich farming households of the eastern plain. Achadh mhòr is still called a field village, though it is one of the largest settlements on the island and the seat of its province. It is the granary of the east, and the shared-meal custom of the Holy Age is said to have been kept here most faithfully. Travellers on the road stop at An Sligeanach Fad' às nearby. Known for the great granary fields.

**Achadh mhòr** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 28 an Gearran 143 BDE by Ròdaich farmers of Cnoc bheag. A farming village of six thousand just south of the Tuathaich line. It follows the Yellow Scorpion, like its neighbours across the line. It trades with both sides and has been watched by both. Known for border fields south of the Tuathaich line.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 5 am Faoilleach 721 BDE by keepers of the holy field. Achadh naomh is a large village and the seat of its province in the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age on a field held sacred. Colbh Cnoc chiar stands to its east, carved 'remember the fire'. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for holy field by Colbh Cnoc chiar.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 28 an t-Sultain 675 BDE by Ròdaich households of the ancestor feasts. The holy field was a meeting ground for the ancestor feasts of the old folk tradition before any house stood on it, and the houses were built around its edge rather than upon it. It is now a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province, yet the field at its heart is still left unploughed. The feasts are kept there as they were in the Holy Age. Known for the ancestor feasts on the unploughed field.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 3 am Màrt 2591 BDE by Ròdaich farming households. Achadh shean, the old field, is a village of twenty-five thousand and the seat of its province. It gave its name to Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, which settled over the island's dry season for three years running in the Age of Strangers. Its granaries were emptied in those years and rebuilt larger afterward, and they are the largest on the eastern coast. Known for the old fields and the Long Drought.

**Achadh àrsaidh** (Doire fhionn). Founded 12 an t-Ògmhios 2178 BDE by Ròdaich herders on an older field. Achadh àrsaidh, the ancient field, was named by Ròdaich herders who found its field-walls already standing and old when they came. No record says who laid them. Tiormachd Achadh shean, the Long Drought, struck it in the Age of Strangers and parched its hay-meadows for three dry seasons running. It has stayed a small village of cattle and hay on the eastern uplands, keeping the ancestor rite and its walls in repair. Known for field-walls older than any record.

**Achadh àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 14 am Màrt 2396 BDE by Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient field village on the far western coast, facing the waters of Uilebheist na Mara, the Sea-Watcher. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, struck it in the Age of Strangers; it was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and keeps the Yellow Scorpion. Pirates have been seen offshore and the villagers keep watch on the headland. Known for the watch for the Sea-Watcher.

**Achadh àrsaidh** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar 791 BDE by the fishers of the capital's coast. An ancient field village on the coast west of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name. It is the seat of Siorrachd Achadh àrsaidh, and its harbour lands the fish and grain that feed Cathair dhearg. It follows the Dark Unicorn. Known for the harbour that feeds the capital.

**Achadh ìseal** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 27 an t-Sultain 1145 DE by farmers from Muileann dhomhain. A low field village in the south-east, farming for the mill town of Muileann dhomhain and the port of Ceann chaol. It keeps the old spirits and has no history the chroniclers found worth writing beyond its harvests. Known for harvests for the southern mills.

**Baile bheag** (Àth mhòr). Founded 20 an Dùbhlachd 141 DE by carters across the ford from Àth mhòr. A small town across the ford from Àth mhòr, grown up to serve the traffic that the walled town would not let in after dark. It is a town of stables, carters and cheap lodging. It has always been a dependent of Àth mhòr and has never been allowed a market of its own. Known for carters across the ford.

**Baile bheag** (Muileann bheag). Founded 3 an t-Samhain 1007 DE by toll-keepers of Muileann bheag. A small town on the road to Muileann bheag, walled to collect tolls rather than to keep enemies out. It still collects them, and has outlasted every attempt to abolish the right. It is one of several places named Baile bheag. Known for a walled town of tolls.

**Baile bhàn** (Caol bheag). Founded 21 an Giblean 1595 DE by fullers of the northern coast. A town of fulling-mills and white cloth between the port-city of Ros chiar and the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach. Its fullers bleached wool for the harbours of the north coast and still do, though in smaller measure since the trade moved to Inis mhòr. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for bleached cloth from the fulling-mills.

**Baile bhàn** (Cill dhìreach). Founded 30 an t-Sultain 1229 DE by a custodian house of Cill dhìreach. Baile bhàn is a white town with a citadel above Cill dhìreach, built to guard the church-town and its treasuries. It is a town of five thousand. Its garrison keeps order at Còmhrag Ceann leathan. Known for citadel above Cill dhìreach.

**Baile bhàn** (Doire mhin). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd 1199 DE by Ròdaich traders of Doire mhin. Baile bhàn is a white town of nine thousand near Cathair mhòr, on the road toward Muileann ghlas. Before the last battle of the Long War the state's columns marched through it. It follows the capital's faith. Known for white town on the Muileann ghlas road.

**Baile chaol** (Baile chaol). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd 1660 BDE by the valley-folk of the eastern narrows. A town squeezed into a narrow valley in the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile chaol. Its houses climb the valley sides in rows, and the one road through it has been tolled since the Holy Age. It keeps the old spirits and trades with the city of Baile Mòr dhìreach and the market at Cnoc uaine; the sacred forest of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar lies on its western edge. Known for terraced houses and the valley toll.

**Baile chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran 2130 BDE by farmers of the capital's southern country. Baile chiar, the dusky town, is the market and provincial seat of the capital's southern country. It has been a farm market since the Holy Age and has never been walled; the citadel at Baile àrsaidh stands close by. Grain from Achadh fhada and the southern farms comes to its market. Known for market of the capital's southern country.

**Baile chrom** (Doire mhin). Founded 24 am Faoilleach 231 DE by the tithe-reeves of Cathair mhòr. A walled town on a bend of the road below Cathair mhòr, raised to store and guard the tithe-grain of the Doire mhin country. Its walls were strengthened when the human administration raised the tithe, and the chroniclers note that the grain was guarded but not shared. It keeps the faith of the Dark Unicorn and serves Cill fhada and Muileann ruadh as their market. Known for the walled tithe-granaries.

**Baile chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 5 am Màrt 643 DE by herders from Dùn chrom. The lesser of the two Baile chroms in the central midlands, this one lies under the citadel of Dùn chrom and grew as its stockyard. The fighting at Muileann ghlas in the last year of the Long War passed close enough that the town housed wounded for a season. It keeps the faith of the Dark Unicorn. Known for Dùn chrom's stockyards.

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios 150 BDE by Ròdaich fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A bent town on the far north-west coast, the seat of Siorrachd Baile chrom, beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the first of the five lighthouses in the ring. Since the Severance it has been Tuathaich, and it is the one town where Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the cult of Sìne the Peaceful Goose, holds the majority. Gorta Baile chrom, the Great Hunger, takes its name from this town, which it struck in the Age of Strangers. Known for the Grey Night cult and the lighthouse.

**Baile chrom** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Lùnastal 697 DE by Ròdaich market families of Ceann àrsaidh. Baile chrom is named for its bending main street, which follows an old stream-bed. It is a market town between the capital and the northern plain, serving Baile fhiadhaich and Cuan chrom. It shares its name with three other places on the island, and the chroniclers take care to give its province. Known for the bent-street market.

**Baile dhearg** (Achadh chaol). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar 1037 DE by farmers of Achadh chaol. A red town in the east on the road to the harbour at Seann Toll. It keeps the old spirits. Known for red town on the harbour road.

**Baile dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 28 an Lùnastal 67 DE by priest-farmers of Cnoc bhàn. A small town in a deep valley, farming for the priests of the Dark Unicorn at Cnoc bhàn. It has no walls and little history beyond the tithe-rolls of the priests' house, which record its harvests without a gap from the Sundering to the present. Known for tithe-fields of the Cnoc bhàn priests.

**Baile dhomhain** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Samhain 1463 DE by rope-walkers of Baile ghorm. The deep town a short walk inland of Baile ghorm, where the harbour's rope-walks and timber-yards were moved to be clear of storms. The panthers' migration road, Imrich nam Pantar, crosses its fields, and the townsfolk shut their stock in when the cats pass. It follows the Madadh-allaidh faith and works almost entirely for the harbour and its fleet. Known for rope-walks and the panthers' road.

**Baile dhomhain** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 2 an t-Samhain 1101 DE by Ròdaich followers of the Hawk. Baile dhomhain is a walled town in a deep valley near Cnoc bheag, one of the towns of the Hawk. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers and strengthened after the Severance, when the Tuathaich line was drawn close by. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck it in the Age of Strangers. Its trade goes down to the quay at Ceann òg. Known for walled deep-valley town of the Hawk.

**Baile dhubh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 22 an Dàmhair 1103 DE by Ròdaich herders of the black-soil fields. Named for the dark earth of its fields, Baile dhubh was an ordinary Ròdaich farm town until the Severance drew the northern border around it. It kept its people when the province of Cnoc ghorm passed to the Tuathaich, and has lived since as a place of exchange and quiet mutual suspicion. Its folk hold the Yellow Scorpion faith, as their northern neighbours do, which is thought to be why they were left in peace. Known for Ròdaich enclave on the Tuathaich border.

**Baile dhubh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 4 an t-Samhain 1865 DE by human colliers of the northern seams. Baile dhubh, "the black town", was built by human colliers in the Age of Strangers on one of the northern coal seams, which the humans worked alongside the vein in the south. After the Severance it passed to the Tuathaich with the rest of the north. Before the Long War it was one of the communities that refused the new fuel and kept working the last workable seams. Known for coal pits of the northern holdouts.

**Baile dhubh** (Baile ghlas). Founded 1 an Giblean 1848 DE by human administrators near Seann Warr. Baile dhubh was built in the Age of Strangers as a clerks' town for the human administration near Seann Warr, where the fifth regiment is now stationed. After the Severance its Ròdaich people took up the Direwolf faith of the country around it. It has fewer than seven hundred people and lives on the garrison. Known for former clerks' town by Seann Warr.

**Baile dhìreach** (Inis thais). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar 1353 DE by Scorpion-faith traders of the west. Baile dhìreach, the straight town, is a harbour on the west coast built around one long street to the quay. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by traders of the Yellow Scorpion faith, among Direwolf neighbours. The two faiths have shared its market without any trouble the rolls think worth noting. Known for straight-street harbour of the Scorpion faith.

**Baile dhìreach** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 6 am Màrt 1115 DE by road-builders of Cnoc gheal. A straight town on the road from Cnoc gheal to Seann Bhrenn, named for the road that made it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and is a carters' stop on the way to the coast. Known for the straight road to Seann Bhrenn.

**Baile dhìreach** (Caol shean). Founded 16 an Giblean 2124 BDE by Ròdaich pilgrims to Allt an Àigh. Baile dhìreach is the nearest town to Allt an Àigh, and the straight road that gives it its name runs from its square down to the stream. It grew up in the Holy Age to serve the pilgrims and still does, alongside Cnoc ìseal further up the road. Its people are wary of strangers who come at the wrong phase of the moon. Known for the nearest town to Allt an Àigh.

**Baile dhìreach** (Muileann naomh). Founded 3 an Gearran 1036 DE by Ròdaich traders of Muileann naomh. A small town of one straight street on the far west, twinned with Cnoc gheal a short walk away. It lies close to the Tuathaich line and trades with the villages beyond it. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for straight-street twin of Cnoc gheal.

**Baile dhìreach** (Doire fhionn). Founded 1 an t-Samhain 212 DE by carters of the Seann Dunn road. A town of one straight road running down to Seann Dunn, whose carters take the dyed cloth of Baile ghorm to the harbour. It is a town of nearly ten thousand. It keeps the folk tradition of the ancestors. Known for straight road to Seann Dunn.

**Baile fhada** (Seann Dunn). Founded 27 an Dùbhlachd 681 DE by Ròdaich soldiers of the capital's south. A town of one long street with a citadel at its end, south-east of the capital. It was a garrison town in the Age of Strangers and has kept its citadel manned since. Its people are soldiers' families and carters, and its street is the last stage of the road from the southern coast to Cathair dhearg. Known for long street and citadel south of the capital.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 6 am Faoilleach 563 DE by farmers of the north-east. Baile fhiadhaich of Cnoc gheal is a walled farm town of the north-east. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and walled in the Age of Strangers against raiders from the sea. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for walled farm town of the north-east.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd 2897 BDE by Ròdaich traders of the west. Baile fhiadhaich of the west is a large harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the field of Àth leathan, and its people remember the first battle of An Cogadh Fada. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for west-coast market harbour.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 7 an Dàmhair 368 DE by Ròdaich hunters of Ceann àrsaidh. The wild town was a hunters' camp in the Age of Sundering, when the forests of Ceann àrsaidh were larger. It still lives on hides and game, and its curing-sheds can be smelled from the road. Its people trade at Baile chrom. Known for hunters and hide-curers.

**Baile fhionn** (Muileann leathan). Founded 31 an Dàmhair 1733 DE by Ròdaich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small fair town in the north-west, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows Creideamh nan Tuathach and trades across the line with the Ròdaich town of Baile ruadh. Known for trade across the line with Baile ruadh.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 21 am Màrt 2138 BDE by wool merchants of the north. Baile gharbh is a large market town of the north-east and the seat of its province. It has been a wool market since the Holy Age, and the hill towns of Cnoc chaol and Àth fhada bring their flocks and cheese to it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and has no walls, trusting to Baile Mòr dhìreach close by. Known for rough-town wool market.

**Baile gharbh** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios 661 DE by the carters of Seann Vell. A rough town on the south coast road between Seann Vell and the lighthouse village of Tobar dhearg. It is one of the few towns where Creideamh nan Ròdach holds the majority, its orthodox priests having come from the pilgrim harbour at Caol naomh. It trades with Muileann naomh and the great port of Seann Skell. Known for an orthodox Rite town on the coast road.

**Baile gheal** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 27 an Giblean 2284 BDE by Ròdaich salt-boilers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A white-washed Ròdaich village of the Holy Age, it was one of the settlements emptied and handed to the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers made it a town and a market, trading with the harbour at Caol naomh a short distance away. Its shrine of the Yellow Scorpion stands in the shell of the older Ròdaich one, and the two sets of carvings can still be told apart. Known for the doubled shrine of the Scorpion.

**Baile gheal** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 2 an t-Ògmhios 1062 DE by the lime-burners of Tobar ghorm. A white town named for the lime-kilns that whitened it, walled in the Age of Strangers after raids on the road to the harbour at Inis naomh. It is paired with Cnoc mhòr on the hill above, and the two share a market and a quarrel over which is older. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for lime-kilns and whitewashed walls.

**Baile gheal** (Baile gheal). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios 1937 BDE by the white-cloth weavers of the west. A large white town of the western plain and the seat of Siorrachd Baile gheal. It is a city of the Madadh-allaidh faith in all but name, and it trades cloth with Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbour of Inis thais. Known for white cloth of the western plain.

**Baile gheal** (Ceann leathan). Founded 11 an t-Samhain 243 DE by lime-burners of Ceann leathan. A small town of lime kilns whose white dust gives it its name. It supplies lime to the builders of the eastern coast and the fields around Ceann leathan. It keeps the folk tradition of the ancestors. Known for lime kilns of the east.

**Baile ghlas** (Baile ghlas). Founded 14 an t-Samhain 2067 BDE by rope-makers of the capital shore. Baile ghlas is a great harbour town on the capital shore and the seat of its province. Its rope-walks and sail-lofts have fitted ships for the capital since the Holy Age, and it claims, with no record to prove it, to have rigged the Sundering fleet. It has never been walled; the capital's walls stand close by. Known for rope-walks and sail-lofts.

**Baile ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 13 an t-Samhain 279 DE by Ròdaich green-dyers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A green-grey town of dyers, emptied at the Severance and resettled by the Tuathaich. It keeps Creideamh nan Tuathach and is a market for Baile Mòr ruadh and Cnoc ghlas. Known for green dyes and Tuathaich folk rites.

**Baile ghlas** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 4 an Gearran 333 DE by Ròdaich slate-quarriers of Cuan ruadh. A small town of grey slate on the eastern coast, quarrying for the roofs of Achadh shean and Cnoc uaine. Its people keep the folk tradition of the ancestors. Known for grey slate of the east coast.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 22 an Gearran 2162 BDE by farming kindreds of the south-eastern downs. Baile ghorm is the market of its shire, a large open town without walls where the south-eastern farms bring their grain and wool. Its people keep the oldest folk rite, and household shrines to the ancestors outnumber any public house of worship. Achadh fhionn is its nearest field-village, and the ruin of Làrach an Dùin stands in its hinterland, left alone by custom. Known for south-eastern grain and wool market.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios 2484 BDE by net-fishing families of the southern shore. A landing of drying-racks and boat-sheds on the southern coast, Baile ghorm grew through the Holy Age into the largest harbour between the capital and the eastern capes. Its people keep the faith of Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, and its quays are lined with the wolf-head posts that mark a Madadh-allaidh harbour. Since the Long War it has been the station of An treas cabhlach, the third fleet, and its yards do more repair work for the crown than fishing for themselves. Its smaller twin, Baile dhomhain, lies a short walk inland and sends it timber and rope. Known for the third fleet's anchorage and wolf-post quays.

**Baile ghorm** (Doire fhionn). Founded 22 an Lùnastal 270 DE by Ròdaich dyers from Achadh shean. Baile ghorm grew up around woad pits and dye-houses, and in the chroniclers' day its houses were still washed blue from the vats. It sent cloth to Seann Dunn for shipping and yarn to Achadh shean for weaving. The old folk tradition of the ancestors holds here strongly, and the dyers still leave a first skein at the hearth-stone each season. Known for woad dyers and blue-washed houses.

**Baile ghorm** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 7 am Màrt 1718 DE by slate-quarriers of Àth dhomhain. Baile ghorm is a quarry town whose blue slate roofs half the northern plain. It sends slate to Inis mhòr and takes grain in return. It shares its name with a dyers' town far to the east, and the two are told apart in the record by their provinces. Known for blue slate quarries.

**Baile leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 21 an t-Iuchar 1802 DE by human settlers from an Tìr Thall. Baile leathan was built by human settlers in the Age of Strangers on the northern coast, one of the few places the strangers founded rather than took. After the Severance it became a Tuathaich town. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition and its oldest families still count their descent from the Crossing. Known for an old strangers' settlement of the north.

**Baile leathan** (Dùn thais). Founded 21 am Faoilleach 906 BDE by Ròdaich scribes of Dùn thais. Baile leathan is one of the towns nearest Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and many of its people are copyists, binders and parchment-makers for the library. It was a market town of the broad valley long before the library was founded, and it grew quickly after. It keeps the Fèidh habit of reading aloud in the evenings. Known for copyists and binders for the library.

**Baile mhin** (Baile mhin). Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios 1314 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk of the north-east. Baile mhin is a harbour town of the north-east and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age. Its harbour is sheltered and its trade steady. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the old harbour of Seann Vell lies within its province. Known for smooth harbour of the north-east.

**Baile mhin** (Achadh chaol). Founded 23 an Dàmhair 1136 DE by carters of the Achadh chaol road. Baile mhin grew where the road from Achadh chaol to the coast levels out, a stopping place for carts. It is a small town of wheelwrights and stables. Its people send their grain to the mills at Muileann dhìreach. Known for wheelwrights on the Achadh chaol road.

**Baile mhòr** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar 2873 BDE by herders of the northern moor. The name promises a great town and the place has never been one; the chroniclers suppose it was large only beside the shielings around it when it was named. It is a quiet market for wool from the moor, dependent on Cnoc dhubh for its road and on Tobar fhiadhaich for its law. Its folk follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and keep a small reading-house where the school's questions are argued on winter nights. Known for moorland wool and an ill-fitting name.

**Baile mhòr** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an t-Samhain 1214 DE by craftsmen outside the walls of Baile Mòr ruadh. Baile mhòr grew outside the walls of Baile Mòr ruadh, a suburb of tanners, dyers and other trades the city would not have within its gates. It has never been walled itself. In the Age of Strangers it was burned once in a quarrel between the city and the administration, and rebuilt in stone. Known for trades outside Baile Mòr ruadh's walls.

**Baile Mòr dhomhain** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 24 an t-Samhain 2957 BDE by the lords of the deep river. A walled city with a citadel on a deep river in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Baile Mòr dhomhain. It was one of the great market cities of the north through the Holy Age and the Sundering and a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and holds its four fords and its river landing at Àth shean. Known for the deep-river city and its fords.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Caol bheag). Founded 8 an Gearran 1267 BDE by custodians of the north-eastern road. Baile Mòr dhìreach of Caol bheag is a walled town with a citadel, built by Holy Age custodians where the north-eastern road runs straight. It is small for a city, but it holds the road and the market between Inis mhòr and Baile gharbh. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for walled town on the straight road.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Baile chaol). Founded 7 an Gearran 948 BDE by custodians of the eastern road. Baile Mòr dhìreach of Baile chaol is a citadel city on the eastern straight road, founded in the Holy Age to hold the road between the vein country and the coast. It was a tithe station in the Age of Strangers, and the ledgers kept there were among those burned in the raids before the Severance. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for citadel city of the eastern road.

**Baile Mòr fhionn** (Caol leathan). Founded 6 an t-Samhain 982 BDE by the lords of the western plain. A great fair walled city of the west, seat of lords before the kingdom and a fortress since. Its citadel was held by Ròdaich forces through the war that ended in the Severance, and it is a city of Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf. It is the chief market of the plain between the capital and the western harbours. Known for the fair citadel of the western plain.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 26 an Lùnastal 2977 BDE by the early kings of the northern province. Baile Mòr mhòr is the great city of the north, walled and crowned by a citadel, and the seat of its province. It was a royal seat in the Holy Age and a centre of the human administration in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has stood close to the Tuathaich country to the west, the largest Ròdaich city on that frontier. Known for the great walled city of the north.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 3 an Gearran 747 BDE by Ròdaich lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A red walled city in the north-west, held by Ròdaich lords from the Holy Age to the Severance, and since then one of the principal Tuathaich cities. It follows the Yellow Scorpion and governs the Àth àrsaidh country with its fords and towns. Known for the red city of the Tuathaich.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 25 an t-Sultain 2717 BDE by a custodian house of the eastern shore. Baile Mòr ruadh is a walled city of red stone, crowned by a citadel, and the principal city of its province. It was fought over in the Age of Strangers, when the human administration made it a district seat, and its walls show repairs of every age. Travellers on the eastern road break their journey at An Taigh-seinnse Òir just west of the city. Known for red-stone walls of the east.

**Baile Mòr uaine** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 22 am Màrt 2017 BDE by custodians of Cuan ghlas. Baile Mòr uaine is a walled city with a citadel in the north-eastern hills, founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and is among its strongholds. Its walls were repaired in the Age of Strangers. Known for walled city of the Feallsanachd.

**Baile Mòr àrsaidh** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 16 an t-Samhain 1662 BDE by Ròdaich traders of the northern plain. Baile Mòr àrsaidh is an ancient market city of the northern plain, ranked a city for its age rather than its size. Its market was old in the Holy Age. It takes oak from Doire dhìreach and grain from Achadh dhìreach. Known for ancient market of the northern plain.

**Baile naomh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 1 an Gearran 2680 BDE by custodians of the holy wells. Baile naomh, the holy town, grew around wells in the vein country that the Holy Age custodians held sacred. The hot springs of Muileann ruadh lie to the west and the silver workings of Muileann chiar to the north-west. It is a small town of shrines and lodging houses, keeping the ancestor rite. Known for holy wells of the vein country.

**Baile ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 25 an t-Samhain 33 DE by herders of Seann Tarr. Baile ruadh is a farm town near the eastern coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. Since the lighthouses were built its people have supplied the keepers of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal on the coast beyond. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for supplier to Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.

**Baile ruadh** (Baile ruadh). Founded 3 an Dàmhair 2028 BDE by red-earth farmers of the east. A red town of the east and the seat of Siorrachd Baile ruadh. It keeps the old spirits and trades grain with Achadh naomh. Known for red-earth fields of the east.

**Baile ruadh** (Cuan shean). Founded 9 am Màrt 1754 DE by red-clay potters of the Cuan shean country. A red town of potters and brick-makers behind the harbour of Cuan shean, whose kilns have fired the roof-tiles of the western coast since the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the Yellow Scorpion, and its potters mark each jar with a small scorpion under the base. Most of what it makes goes out through Cuan shean. Known for red roof-tiles and scorpion-marked jars.

**Baile ruadh** (Inis mhin). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar 2042 BDE by Ròdaich farmers of the red ground. A red town in the north-west that stayed Ròdaich when the Tuathaich homeland was fixed around it, and the line of the border wall that was proposed and never built would have run past its gate. It keeps the old spirits of the Ròdaich, and its market is used by Tuathaich from Baile fhionn and Ròdaich from Àth uaine alike. Known for a shared market on the border.

**Baile shean** (Doire fhionn). Founded 5 an Dàmhair 1344 BDE by keepers of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. An old town beside Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the forest marked sacred before any faith claimed it. Its people have kept the forest's edge since the Holy Age and keep the old spirits, though the forest is now held by Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for the keepers of the sacred forest's edge.

**Baile shean** (Cnoc thais). Founded 27 an Cèitean 2442 BDE by Ròdaich founders; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. An old Ròdaich town with walls and a citadel, emptied at the Severance and taken over by Tuathaich families. In the years before An Cogadh Fada it was counted among the northern communities that refused the dubhan economy. Its walls still stand, and the Tuathaich guard them as the Ròdaich once did. Known for old walls held by the Tuathaich.

**Baile shean** (Inis chrom). Founded 18 an t-Iuchar 1814 BDE by Ròdaich followers of the Direwolf. An old walled town of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh, beside the fort of Muileann bheag. Its walls are older than the fort, and for most of its history it was the stronger of the two. It is small now, and lives on the fort's custom. Known for old walled town of the Direwolf.

**Baile shean** (Caol ìseal). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd 2272 BDE by Ròdaich fishers of the northern shore. Baile shean is an old quay on the northern shore and the port of its province. The inn An Taigh-seinnse Reòta lies inland on the road south, and its pickled spinach goes out through the quay. It is one of several places named Baile shean. Known for old quay of the northern shore.

**Baile thais** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios 913 BDE by river-boatmen of the Abhainn uaine. Baile thais stands where the Abhainn uaine reaches the gulf, and the river landing of Cidhe Beag lies just upstream. Boats have been launched here since the Holy Age to carry goods inland and ore down. It is a busy, unwalled town of boatmen and warehouses. Known for Cidhe Beag landing on the Abhainn uaine.

**Baile thais** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 28 an Cèitean 816 BDE by Ròdaich eel-fishers of the water-meadows. Baile thais stands on damp ground where the meadows flood each wet season, and its people have always fished the ditches for eels. It is a large town now, and it supplies Cnoc bhàn with hay and fish. The river works that keep the meadows are older than the town's charter. Known for water-meadows and eel traps.

**Baile uaine** (Àth shean). Founded 5 an Gearran 1093 DE by market gardeners of Àth shean. Baile uaine is a small town of market gardens, sending green stuff to Dùn gheal and on to the capital each market day. It has never been walled or fought over. Its people follow the capital's faith and pay their dues at Dùn gheal. Known for market gardens for the capital.

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran 2523 BDE by custodians of the capital's south. Baile àrsaidh, the ancient town, is a citadel town of the capital's southern country, founded in the Holy Age. Its citadel guards the market at Baile chiar. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for old citadel of the southern country.

**Baile àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 15 am Màrt 1348 BDE by Ròdaich shore-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient walled town near the harbour of Caol mhòr, one of the Ròdaich towns resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The walls are older than the Ròdaich say they know, and the Tuathaich have kept them. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for old walls in the Tuathaich north.

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 6 an t-Ògmhios 2171 BDE by Ròdaich teachers of the Yellow Scorpion. Baile àrsaidh is the ancient town of the west, the seat of its province and the place where the teachers of the Yellow Scorpion have kept their school since the faiths divided. It is a large town of twenty thousand. It trades with Seann Skell to the north and with the fleet at Cuan shean to the south. Known for the Yellow Scorpion's teachers.

**Baile ìseal** (Seann Chwen). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios 1273 DE by farmers of the Seann Chwen country. A low town in the middle east, a short way south of Cill ghlas and the ground the Rending tore open. It follows the Dark Unicorn and sends its grain to the harbour at Seann Chwen. Known for grain town south of Cill ghlas.

**Baile ìseal** (Àth bheag). Founded 14 an t-Samhain 158 DE by fishers of the far east coast. A small low town on the far east coast, beside Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, one of the five lighthouses completed in the Age of Strangers. Pirates are still seen off this coast, and the lighthouse-keepers double as the town's watch. It keeps the old spirits. Known for Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and the pirate watch.

**Baile ìseal** (Baile ìseal). Founded 16 an t-Sultain 1528 DE by Ròdaich farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A low walled town in the north-west, the seat of Siorrachd Baile ìseal, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It follows the Yellow Scorpion and is one of the larger Tuathaich towns. Known for the low walled town of the north-west.

**Baile ìseal** (Cill thais). Founded 1 an t-Sultain 788 DE by farmers of Cill thais. A small walled town near Cill thais and Baile chiar, west of the capital. The walls were raised in the war before the Severance. It follows the Dark Unicorn and has little trade of its own. Known for small walls near the capital.

**Baile òg** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 7 an Dàmhair 479 DE by stone-gatherers of the temple hills. A young town in the eastern hills close by the ruins of Làrach an Teampaill, whose altar faces the vein. Its early houses were built of stones carried off the ruins, a use the priests of the old spirits later forbade. It keeps the old spirits and serves travellers who come to look at the ruins. Known for houses of stone from Làrach an Teampaill.

**Baile òg** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 25 am Màrt 71 DE by carters of Baile Mòr dhomhain. A small young town on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and Baile Mòr àrsaidh, grown from a carters' stable. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and lives by changing horses. Known for a carters' stop between two cities.

**Baile òg** (Baile ìseal). Founded 5 an t-Samhain 1933 DE by Tuathaich families sent north at the Severance. Baile òg, "the young town", was built by Tuathaich families who arrived after the Severance and found no empty village to take. It stands a short way from the larger Tuathaich town of Baile ìseal and has always depended on it. Its houses are the first the Tuathaich built for themselves on the island rather than inherited. Known for the first Tuathaich-built houses.

**Baile òg** (Seann Chwen). Founded 6 an Dàmhair 1819 DE by a mining crew under the human administration. Baile òg, "the young town", was a camp of the diggings east of the capital, raised in the Age of Strangers near Cill ghlas. It emptied when Scàineadh Cill ghlas closed the district for a generation. It was reopened after the Severance, and its people now follow the capital's faith. Known for camp-town of the Cill ghlas diggings.

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 15 am Màrt 2522 BDE by fishers of the north coast. A small harbour on the northern strait, older than its far larger namesake inland and the one that gave that town its name. It keeps the old spirits and is a quiet fishing town, though An ceathramh rèisimeid, stationed at the larger Caol bheag, sends its patrols here. Known for the elder Caol bheag on the strait.

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 14 an Lùnastal 2406 BDE by Ròdaich seafarers of the small strait. Caol bheag is a harbour town of more than forty thousand on the small strait, crowned by a citadel and the seat of its province. The fourth regiment, raised in the Long War, is stationed here. The mills of Muileann bheag and the wool of Cnoc chiar pass through its quays. Known for fourth regiment's harbour town.

**Caol chrom** (Caol gharbh). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd 1236 DE by the garrison of the bent strait. Caol chrom is a fortified harbour on a bent strait of the north-east, walled and given a citadel in the long quiet centuries. It is a city by rank but small in people, and its garrison has always outnumbered its fishermen. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for fortified bent strait.

**Caol dhomhain** (Ceann mhin). Founded 8 an Gearran 1190 DE by the watch of the deep strait. Caol dhomhain is a harbour village on a deep strait of the south-east, with a citadel raised in the long quiet centuries to watch it. The village is small and the citadel is its reason. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for the deep strait's watch-tower.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Inis thais). Founded 13 an t-Iuchar 598 DE by fishers of the wild strait. Caol fhiadhaich is a harbour on a rough strait of the west coast, within the province of Inis thais. It was founded in the long quiet centuries by fishers who braved waters the older harbours avoided. Its people keep the Direwolf's faith. Known for fishing the wild strait.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar 2857 BDE by the strait-pilots of the south-west. A harbour on a wild strait whose pilots earned their living guiding ships through the rocks. It is the seat of Siorrachd Caol fhiadhaich and a large town of the Madadh-allaidh faith, trading with the great tavern-village of Doire shean on its road. The strait pilots still take no ship through without an offering to Clach at the harbour wolf-stone. Known for strait-pilots and the harbour wolf-stone.

**Caol gharbh** (Caol gharbh). Founded 5 am Màrt 2276 BDE by Ròdaich seafarers of the rough strait. Caol gharbh is a walled harbour on the rough strait and the seat of its province, a village in name but a town of twenty-seven thousand in fact. Its boatyards take oak from Doire chaol and build the heavy boats the strait demands. Its quarrel with Seann Bhrenn next door is as old as the rolls. Known for boatyards on the rough strait.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach 2784 BDE by the strait-pilots of the western shore. Caol leathan grew on the wide strait that gives it its name, where the western pilots of the Holy Age took a toll from every boat bound for the capital's waters. Its walls and citadel were raised in the Age of Sundering to hold the strait, and were manned again when the strangers' ships began to use it after the Crossing. It is the northern anchor of the Direwolf country, and its priests look south to the temple at Inis thais for their rite. Known for strait tolls and the western pilots' guild.

**Caol mhin** (Caol mhin). Founded 17 am Màrt 1654 BDE by Ròdaich seafarers of Baile Mòr mhòr. Caol mhin is the harbour of Baile Mòr mhòr on the calm strait, and its fortunes have always followed the city's. It is walled against raiders from the sea. Its quays load wool and hides from the northern uplands. Known for calm-strait harbour of Baile Mòr mhòr.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd 621 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich. Caol mhòr, the great strait, was a Ròdaich harbour of the Holy Age. After the Severance it became the chief port of the Tuathaich, and it is now their largest town. Its yards take timber from Doire mhin, and its people keep the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for chief harbour of the Tuathaich.

**Caol naomh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 9 an Dàmhair 956 BDE by Ròdaich ferrymen; resettled by the Tuathaich. Caol naomh, the holy strait, is a harbour of the north-west founded by Ròdaich ferrymen in the Holy Age, who held the crossing sacred and blessed each boat before it put out. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance, and the new ferrymen kept the blessing without the old words. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for the holy strait's ferry.

**Caol naomh** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 17 an Giblean 442 DE by priests of the Obsidian Rite. A holy strait-harbour near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where the orthodox Obsidian Rite built a landing for pilgrims coming to the mountain. It is one of the few towns where Creideamh nan Ròdach holds the majority, and its priests were among those who formalized the Rite in the first years of the new kingdom. It is a small town and quiet outside the pilgrim season. Known for pilgrim landing of the Obsidian Rite.

**Caol ruadh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 22 an t-Iuchar 992 BDE by Ròdaich fishers of the red strait. Caol ruadh takes its name from the red rock of the strait it watches on the southern coast. It was a quiet fishing town for most of its history, and was among the first to take up the orthodox Obsidian Rite when Creideamh nan Ròdach was formalized. Since An Cogadh Fada its harbour has victualled the garrisons and fleet stationed at Seann Skell close by. Known for red strait and the orthodox Rite.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal 2960 BDE by the strait-fishers of the east coast. An old harbour on the eastern strait and one of the great ports of the island, seat of Siorrachd Caol shean. It shipped the ore of the central mountains when the extraction was at its height and now ships dubhan and grain. The spring of Allt an Àigh lies in its hinterland, and pilgrims to it land here; the town follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for the great eastern harbour, pilgrims' landing.

**Caol ìseal** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt 1549 BDE by salt-makers of the northern coast. Caol ìseal is a harbour town on a low strait of the north coast and the seat of its province. Its salt pans have supplied the northern fisheries since the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for salt pans of the low strait.

**Caol ìseal** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 25 am Faoilleach 1571 BDE by the strait-watchers of the north coast. A small harbour-village on the northern strait, with a citadel built to watch the channel. It served Baile Mòr mhòr as a signal-station and watch-post and has never outgrown that role. It keeps the old spirits of the Ròdaich, and the watch-fire on its citadel is still lit on the old feast nights. Known for the strait watch-fire.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 23 an t-Samhain 2533 BDE by the custodian-kings of the Holy Age. Cathair dhearg, the red city, began as the stone-walled seat of the Holy Age custodians where the mining roads came down to the sea on the Abhainn dhomhain; Drochaid Cathair dhearg, heir of the first bridges, still carries the road across the river. It kept its walls, citadel and temple through the Sundering and the Age of Strangers, and after the Severance Rìoghachd Ròdais was declared here and Niall was crowned in it, first of the restored line. The royal precinct is small for a capital, ringed by the great harbours of Ros dhomhain, Cathair dhomhain and Baile ghlas, and its temple is the first house of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn. Known for royal seat and temple of the Dark Unicorn.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 7 an Gearran 2379 BDE by Ròdaich shipwrights of the river mouth. Cathair dhomhain, the deep city, stands beside the capital on the deep-water side of the river mouth, and takes the ships whose draught the royal quays cannot. It was walled and given a citadel in the Holy Age, and its temple of the Dark Unicorn is second only to the capital's. Its harbour carried much of the ore trade in the Age of Strangers and most of the dubhan trade since. Known for deep-water harbour beside the capital.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 9 am Màrt 1239 BDE by the lords of the long city. A long walled city in the south, strung along a ridge between the capital's country and the coast, and the seat of Siorrachd Cathair fhada. It follows the Dark Unicorn and has always been one of the capital's chief supports. The Fèill Muileann òg is held a short way north, and the city's merchants dominate it. Known for merchants of the Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt 1813 BDE by Ròdaich builders; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cathair gheal is a walled city of white stone on the far western coast, built by the Ròdaich and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its walls face the sea, where pirate ships have been seen offshore. It is the market for the Tuathaich villages of Muileann àrsaidh province. Known for white walls against the pirate coast.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 30 an Giblean 2422 BDE by Ròdaich custodians of the interior roads. Cathair mhòr, the great city, was raised by the Holy Age custodians beside Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a Seann-Dhaoine outpost already in ruins when the first Ròdaich walls went up beside it. It commands the roads between the gulf and the vein country, and it was a counting-house of the tithe in the Age of Strangers and a mustering place in the war that ended it. An treas rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears its name. Known for the great city beside the old outpost.

**Cathair mhòr** (Doire mhin). Founded 28 an Cèitean 852 BDE by the lords of Doire mhin. A hill-city with a citadel close to the capital, raised by lords of the Doire mhin country who held the roads north of Cathair dhearg. It has always been a garrison town and was one of the strongholds from which the war before the Severance was fought. It follows the Dark Unicorn and draws on the tithe-granaries of Baile chrom and the great village of Doire mhin. It is not the Cathair mhòr of the third regiment, which lies further east. Known for the citadel on the capital's north road.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Toll). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd 4439 BDE by unknown builders, later the Ròdaich spirit-keepers. The holy city of the north grew around a ring of stones older than the Ròdaich, and the chroniclers do not claim to know who raised them. The Ròdaich made it a place of the old spirits in the Holy Age and it has never had walls, since the ancestors' ground was held to need none. It is a city of pilgrims and hostels, and the shrine-keepers of Cnoc chiar and Inis bheag answer to its elders. Known for the unwalled ring of the ancestors.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Chwen). Founded 1 an Gearran 158 BDE by priests of the capital's faith. A holy city near the ruins of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, built by the priesthood of the Dark Unicorn in the Holy Age as a seat of learning. The ruins are said to have been older than any Ròdaich memory when the city was founded, and the priests left them as they were. It is unwalled and trades with the harbour of Seann Chwen and with Ceann leathan. Known for the priests' city by the old outpost.

**Ceann bheag** (Ceann bheag). Founded 15 an t-Iuchar 2688 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk of the north-east. Ceann bheag is a citadel harbour of the north-east, a Holy Age landing that grew with the coastal trade. Its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers to guard the anchorage the human ships used. The villages of Ceann thais and Achadh fhiadhaich lie within its province and send their goods through its quays. Known for citadel harbour of the north-east.

**Ceann bhàn** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 29 an t-Samhain 1024 DE by the tavern-keepers of the white headland. A walled port on a pale headland with the famous tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às at its gate, where travellers eat dried venison. It grew around the tavern road, and its walls went up in the troubles, when the roadside houses became militia posts. It keeps the old spirits and trades with the great village of Achadh mhòr inland. Known for An Sligeanach Fad' às and dried venison.

**Ceann chaol** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 23 an Giblean 946 DE by Ròdaich seafarers of the narrow point. Ceann chaol is a port city on the narrow point, and the old rival of Ceann mhin along the same shore. Its ships carry the flour of Muileann dhomhain and the grain of the eastern plain. The two harbours have disputed fishing grounds in every age, and the disputes are recorded at length. Known for narrow-point harbour, rival of Ceann mhin.

**Ceann chiar** (Seann Tarr). Founded 10 an Dùbhlachd 807 DE by Ròdaich fishers of the eastern coast. Ceann chiar is a walled harbour on the eastern coast, walled against the pirate ships that have been seen in these waters in every age. It keeps a watch-fire on its headland. It is the port of Seann Tarr province. Known for walled harbour against pirates.

**Ceann dhomhain** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 7 am Màrt 1257 BDE by custodians of the eastern headland. A small city on a deep-water headland, with a citadel that looks out to sea and back toward the mountain roads. Ships put in here for the library town of Muileann chaol, whose scholars and copyists travel through its gate, and its harbour-masters have long kept a copy of every cargo list for the Leabharlann. The Feallsanachd an Fhèidh holds the city, and its scholars are counted among the library's oldest correspondents. Known for the library's harbour and cargo registers.

**Ceann dhubh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 25 an Cèitean 1257 BDE by Ròdaich headland-fishers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A black headland harbour on the north-west coast, all but joined to the city of Inis àrsaidh. It was a Ròdaich fishing town until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich harbour since. It follows the Yellow Scorpion, and its boats sail with Inis àrsaidh's. Known for the black headland beside Inis àrsaidh.

**Ceann dhubh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 26 an Cèitean 1320 DE by Ròdaich fishers of the black headland. Ceann dhubh is a harbour under a dark headland, the port of Baile gharbh province, whose boats work the cold waters of the northern coast. Travellers on the coast road break their journey at An Leòmhann Buidhe a short way west, and the inn buys most of the harbour's catch. The harbour was deepened in the Age of Strangers to take the humans' ore ships, and has been too large for its trade ever since. Known for harbour under the black headland.

**Ceann fhada** (Muileann chrom). Founded 27 an Cèitean 1320 DE by Ròdaich river pilots. A long spit of land made Ceann fhada a landing for river craft, and its pilots have guided boats on the Abhainn uaine for centuries. It is the old rival of Inis ìseal, a short way downstream, and the two quays have quarrelled over tolls in every age the rolls cover. It prospered in the Age of Strangers carrying ore-cart loads by water and has held its trade since by carrying grain. Known for long quay and river pilots.

**Ceann gheal** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 8 an Gearran 1289 DE by fishers of the white headland. Ceann gheal is a harbour town north of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The hollow called Toll-dubh lies in the hills behind it; it has never been mapped, and the town's people do not go near it. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for white headland and the Toll-dubh hollow.

**Ceann ghorm** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 29 an Giblean 356 DE by pilots of the eastern coast. Ceann ghorm, the blue headland, is a harbour town of the eastern coast whose pilots have long guided ships into the waters of Ros fhionn and Seann Dunn. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and grew in the Age of Strangers. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for pilots of the eastern coast.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain 2889 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk of the gulf. Ceann leathan, the broad headland, is a walled temple city on the gulf, older than most of the harbours around it. Its temple of the Dark Unicorn is the chief shrine of the gulf towns. Since the early years of the restored kingdom it has held Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the brutal annual melee, which draws fighters and crowds from every province. Known for Còmhrag Ceann leathan, the annual melee.
