**Ceann leathan** (Ceann leathan). Founded 27 am Màrt 1189 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk of the east. Ceann leathan of the east is a harbour town and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age on a broad headland facing the open sea. It is not the gulf city of the melee, and its people resent the confusion. It keeps the ancestor rite and a fishing fleet that works as far south as the waters off Seann Bhral. Known for broad headland harbour of the east.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 18 an Lùnastal 2254 BDE by shipwrights of the smooth headland. Ceann mhin is a citadel harbour on the southern gulf shore, long the chief shipyard of the east. When Tonn Mhòr struck in the first years of the restored kingdom, its yards were spared and it took in the survivors of Achadh mhin. It has since grown into one of the great cities of the south. Known for shipyards of the smooth headland.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar 1336 BDE by harbour-lords of the smooth headland. A smooth headland port, walled, and the seat of Siorrachd Ceann mhin. It was a trading harbour for the northern mines in the Age of Strangers and follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for the northern ore harbour.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar 220 BDE by Ròdaich fishers settling in the ruin of Làrach an Dùin. Ceann mhin is built in and around Làrach an Dùin, the ruined fortress of the old builders, and its harbour lies under the fallen walls. The Ròdaich fishers who settled there in the Holy Age reused its stones but never finished clearing it; nobody knows who built the fortress. It is now a walled port town of nearly twenty thousand, the seat of its province, and the rival of Ceann chaol along the same coast. Known for harbour beneath Làrach an Dùin.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean 1987 BDE by Ròdaich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Ceann mhòr is a great harbour on a headland of the north-west, under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom. It was a Ròdaich port of the Holy Age, struck by Gorta Baile chrom in the Age of Strangers and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for great headland harbour under the Baile chrom light.

**Ceann thais** (Ceann bheag). Founded 30 an Giblean 295 DE by fishers of the north-east. Ceann thais is a harbour village of the north-east, best known for An Leòmhann Buidhe, one of the great taverns of the old mining circuit, which stands at its edge. It was founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for An Leòmhann Buidhe, the Yellow Lion.

**Ceann àrsaidh** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar 877 BDE by Ròdaich harbour-folk of the east. Ceann àrsaidh is a walled harbour city on an ancient headland east of the capital. It has been a port since the Holy Age and the gateway to the eastern sea road. An Taigh-seinnse Mòr stands on the road to the west. Known for ancient headland on the eastern ship road.

**Ceann òg** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 19 an t-Sultain 1787 DE by Ròdaich and human traders together. Ceann òg, "the young headland", was built as a trading quay in the first years after the Crossing, when exchange with the humans was still reciprocal. It stands near Carragh Cnoc bheag, the stone carved Bha teine sa chloich. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It follows the Hawk, and its quay was rebuilt after the Severance for Ròdaich ships alone. Known for young quay near Carragh Cnoc bheag.

**Cill bhàn** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 20 am Màrt 2723 BDE by keepers of the ancestor rite. Cill bhàn, the white cell, is a village of the ancestor rite in the east, founded in the Holy Age. It lies near the hot springs and the silver workings of the vein country. It has kept its shrine through every age and every change of master. Known for white cell of the ancestor rite.

**Cill chaol** (Muileann leathan). Founded 10 am Màrt 985 BDE by Ròdaich priests; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cill chaol was a narrow Ròdaich chapel village near the northern coast, emptied at the Severance and taken by Tuathaich families. They turned its chapel to the worship of Donn, an Sìorraidh, under Creideamh nan Tuathach, and the Ròdaich carvings on its doorposts were left in place beside theirs. It is a small place near the lighthouse of Muileann bheag. Known for a Tuathach shrine in a Ròdaich chapel.

**Cill chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 16 an Dùbhlachd 1244 DE by priests of the Dark Unicorn. A small church-site village at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest no one has settled or fully mapped. Its chapel was built to watch the forest rather than enter it. It follows the Dark Unicorn. Known for the chapel watching the unclaimed forest.

**Cill dhearg** (Doire chiar). Founded 7 an t-Samhain 2450 BDE by priests of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. A church village of red stone near Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose chapel gave shelter to travellers crossing the old bridge when the river trade was busy. As the trade dried up and the bridge fell out of use, the village shrank to its chapel and a few farms. Its priests still keep a lamp at the bridge-end. Known for red chapel by the old bridge.

**Cill dhìreach** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 6 am Màrt 349 BDE by priests of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh for the silver-miners. A church village a short way from the silver seam at Muileann chiar, whose chapel has served the silver-miners since the seam was first worked. In the Age of Strangers its priests kept a record of the miners killed underground, one of the few such records to survive. It is not the Cill dhìreach of the central country. Known for miners' chapel by the silver seam.

**Cill dhìreach** (Cill dhìreach). Founded 12 am Màrt 400 BDE by priests of the Dark Unicorn. Cill dhìreach is a church village of twenty-four thousand and the seat of its province. It lies beside Ceann leathan, where Còmhrag Ceann leathan is held each year. Its priests tend the wounded of the melee and bury its dead. Known for church-town of the Ceann leathan melee.

**Cill fhada** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 17 an Dùbhlachd 57 DE by priests of the Dark Unicorn. A church-site village strung along a long ridge near Baile chrom, whose chapel of the Dark Unicorn is the longest building in the district. It farms for the market at Baile chrom and sends its grain to the tithe-granaries there. Known for the long chapel of the Dark Unicorn.

**Cill gharbh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 27 an Lùnastal 1073 BDE by Ròdaich priests of the western coast. A village around a rough stone chapel on the far western coast of the Ròdaich country. Its chapel is older than any of its houses, and the Yellow Scorpion was worshipped there before the faiths divided. It is a small village of fewer than two thousand. Known for rough stone chapel of the west.

**Cill ghlas** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 4 am Faoilleach 1185 BDE by a house of the Feallsanachd. Cill ghlas, the grey cell, was a quiet village of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh in the hills east of the capital until the Age of Strangers pushed the workings under it. Late in that age a routine excavation tore open a fault around it, killing dozens and closing the working; the Rending gave the island the word 'scàinte'. The village was rebuilt on the far side of the crack, and its people still mark the day of the dead. Known for Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending.

**Cill ghorm** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 13 an t-Ògmhios 366 BDE by priests of the Dark Unicorn. A chapel site on the ridge above the road north from Cathair dhearg, fortified in the Holy Age to guard the approach to the capital. The citadel dwarfs the village, which has never numbered more than a thousand or so, most of them in service to the garrison and the shrine. Pilgrims of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh stop here before entering the capital. Known for fortified chapel above the capital road.

**Cill leathan** (Muileann shean). Founded 27 am Màrt 1310 BDE by keepers of the north-coast cell. Cill leathan is a large harbour village of the north coast, founded as a cell in the Holy Age. A citadel was raised over its harbour in the Age of Strangers to guard the human ships that used it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for broad cell and its sea citadel.

**Cill thais** (Cill thais). Founded 15 an t-Samhain 1066 BDE by wardens of the sacred wood. Cill thais, the damp cell, is a large village and the seat of its province, founded in the Holy Age beside Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag. The forest is sacred to the Dark Unicorn and has never been settled, logged or fully mapped, and the village's wardens keep others out of it under the division of custody that settled the holy-wood dispute. In the Age of Strangers the wardens refused the timber contracts, and the record does not say how they were allowed to. Known for wardens of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag.

**Cill thais** (Cuan shean). Founded 22 an Giblean 122 BDE by priests of the Yellow Scorpion. Cill thais is a chapel village on damp ground above the anchorage of Cuan shean, fortified with a citadel in the Holy Age to watch the western sea. The fourth fleet, raised in the Long War, is stationed at Cuan shean below, and the village's priests bless each ship before it first puts out. It is a small place whose citadel is larger than its village. Known for fortified chapel over the fleet anchorage.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Doire fhionn). Founded 19 an Giblean 551 BDE by keepers of the ancestor rite. Cill àrsaidh of the north is an old cell of the ancestor rite, founded in the Holy Age and never much more than a village around its shrine. It lies inland of the Hawk bay and has kept to the older faith while its neighbours took up Mòd. The shrine keepers are hereditary. Known for ancient cell of the ancestor rite.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 29 an Cèitean 2326 BDE by teachers of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Cill àrsaidh of Cuan ghlas is an old cell that the teachers of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh took as a retreat early in the school's history. It became a large village of students and farmers. The school's dormant teachers kept it alive through the Age of Strangers, and it filled again at the revival. Known for retreat of the Feallsanachd teachers.

**Cill àrsaidh** (Muileann bheag). Founded 25 an t-Sultain 75 BDE by priests of the old spirits. An ancient church-site village in the north-east, older than the Feallsanachd an Fhèidh that now holds it. The founding shrine is said to have been of the old spirits, and its foundations lie under the present meeting-house. It is a large village supplying Muileann bheag. Known for a philosophers' house on an old shrine.

**Cill ìseal** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar 896 DE by Ròdaich shrine-keepers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A low church-site village of the Ròdaich, emptied at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families. It has grown past any village size, with the shrine of the Yellow Scorpion at its heart, and it farms for the harbour of Ros ruadh. The Tuathaich here call it by its Ròdaich name and no other. Known for the Scorpion shrine of the north-west.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 10 an Dàmhair 1401 BDE by hill kindreds of the north-central coast. Cnoc bheag is the small hill only in name: it is the largest town of the north-central coast and the heart of the Hawk's congregations. The standing stone Carragh Cnoc bheag, carved 'there was fire in the stone', stands a short walk to the south, and the town's older families say their fathers' fathers found it there. A' Phlàigh Uaine, the Green Death, struck the town in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has faced the Tuathaich border, and An siathamh rèisimeid, raised in An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here under the town's name. Known for the carved stone and the Sixth Regiment.

**Cnoc bheag** (Muileann shean). Founded 8 an Lùnastal 740 DE by farmers of the north coast. Cnoc bheag of Muileann shean is a small town of hill farms on the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Its people send their sons to the Feallsanachd teachers at Cill àrsaidh. Known for north-coast hill farms.

**Cnoc bheag** (Achadh naomh). Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios 1061 DE by the herders of Achadh naomh. A small walled hill in the east, raised as a refuge for the herds of Achadh naomh in the troubled years. Its pastures are thin, and the town has always kept fewer herds than its walls could shelter. It keeps the old spirits. Known for hilltop refuge for eastern herds.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an Dàmhair 988 DE by shepherds of Cnoc dhubh. A small hill town below Cnoc dhubh, holding the shepherds' market for the province. It has always been a dependent of the larger town. It is one of several places named Cnoc bheag and is not the fort of the holy wood near the capital. Known for shepherds' market below Cnoc dhubh.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cill thais). Founded 26 an t-Ògmhios 1865 BDE by custodians named in the holy-wood dispute. Cnoc bheag is a fort with a citadel at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the forest that has never been settled or logged. It was raised after the holy-wood dispute of the Holy Age, when custody of the wood was divided rather than awarded, to house the custodians of the share that went to the faith now called Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh. It stands outside the trees, never within them, and its twelve thousand people guard the capital's south as well as the wood. Known for fort at the edge of the holy wood.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt 5 BDE by fishers of Caol ìseal. Cnoc bhàn grew as an overflow of the harbour at Caol ìseal, a white hill with a landing at its foot. Its boats work the kelp beds and the herring of the northern shore. It keeps the ancestor rite and has never needed walls. Known for white-hill kelp and herring.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd 23 DE by Ròdaich fishers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc bhàn of the north-west is a harbour facing the pirate waters. It was founded by Ròdaich fishers in the long quiet centuries and resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Its boats avoid the waters where old sailors place the Sea-Watcher. Known for harbour facing the pirate waters.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 5 an t-Samhain 1225 DE by priests of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn. A pale hill in the midlands, crowned by a house of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh, the faith of the capital. The town grew around the priests' farms and remains a quiet place of tithe-barns and schools that train acolytes for the capital's temples. Baile dhomhain and Àth ghlas send it their tithes and their sons. Known for training acolytes of the Dark Unicorn.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 11 an Lùnastal 1806 BDE by Ròdaich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A pale hill with a citadel built by a Ròdaich family in the Holy Age, taken over by the Tuathaich when their homeland was fixed. The Tuathaich garrison it as a guard-post on their southern marches, and it follows the Yellow Scorpion. The town sells cattle and hides to Cnoc àrsaidh. Known for the Tuathaich southern guard-post.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Baile ghorm). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd 691 DE by the hill-lords of Baile ghorm. A walled pale hill in the south-east above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, which grinds its grain. The walls were raised when the road from Làrach an Dùin became unsafe. It keeps the old spirits and is the market of the southern-eastern farms. Known for the market above the mill-race.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 12 am Màrt 2945 BDE by a custodian house of the Binding. The white hill was fortified early by a custodian house, and its citadel of pale stone is the oldest standing work in the province that bears its name. In the Age of Strangers it served as a district seat of the human administration, and the ledgers kept in its strong-room were among those later lost in the war. It is now a large town of scholars and advocates: the disputations of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh are held in its hall, and its readers walk daily to the library at Muileann chaol. Known for white citadel and the Fèidh disputations.

**Cnoc chaol** (Baile gharbh). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios 768 DE by goatherds of the northern hills. Cnoc chaol, the narrow hill, is a small herding town of the north. It is not the southern Cnoc chaol that gave Tonn Mhòr its name. Its people keep Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and send their cheese and kids to the market at Baile gharbh. Known for goat cheese for Baile gharbh.

**Cnoc chaol** (Seann Vell). Founded 23 am Faoilleach 128 DE by Ròdaich shore farmers of Seann Vell. Cnoc chaol is the town the Great Wave is named after. Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol struck the southern coast without warning in a single night, devastating it together with Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin. The town was rebuilt higher up the narrow hill, and its people still leave the lowest street empty. Known for the town the Great Wave named.

**Cnoc chaol** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 22 an Cèitean 1850 DE by a mining crew under the human administration. Cnoc chaol was a mining camp on the narrow hill, worked by the ton in the Age of Strangers. It emptied after Scàineadh Cill ghlas closed the district and never recovered. Fewer than seven hundred people live there now, among the spoil heaps. Known for a spent camp on the narrow hill.

**Cnoc chiar** (Seann Toll). Founded 12 an Giblean 2403 BDE by shrine-keepers of Cathair naomh. A dusky hill beside the harbour of Seann Toll, settled by keepers of the old spirits who tended waymarks on the pilgrim road to Cathair naomh. It remains a small town of hostels and way-shrines, busy in the feast seasons and empty between them. Known for way-shrines on the pilgrim road.

**Cnoc chiar** (Achadh naomh). Founded 24 an Lùnastal 2989 BDE by keepers of the Colbh. A dusky hill near the standing stone Colbh Cnoc chiar, which carries only the words Cuimhnich an teine, 'remember the fire'. The stone was old when the Ròdaich came, and the town grew around the families who tended it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, whose philosophers still come to argue over the imperative that no one has explained. Known for the stone of 'remember the fire'.

**Cnoc chiar** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Samhain 1564 DE by herders of Doire mhin. A small dusky hill between Doire mhin and Muileann ruadh, pastured by herders of the great village. It follows the Dark Unicorn. Known for hill pastures of Doire mhin.

**Cnoc chiar** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 24 am Faoilleach 2583 BDE by Ròdaich shepherds of Cuan ghlas. A large town on the dusky hill, living on the sheep walks above it and on the wool trade with Caol bheag. It was a mustering place for fleeces in the Age of Strangers, when the humans bought wool as eagerly as ore. Its market is the busiest in the province. Known for sheep walks and wool market.

**Cnoc chrom** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 23 an Lùnastal 1923 DE by the ore-carriers of the interior. Cnoc chrom was built in the Age of Strangers as a depot on the ore road from the interior to the gulf. It was walled in the years before the war of the Severance, when the mining roads began to arm themselves. It is a small town now and keeps the capital's faith. Known for walled depot of the ore road.

**Cnoc chrom** (Caol shean). Founded 26 an Cèitean 1814 DE by Ròdaich miners under contract. A crooked hill-town raised when the extraction contracts pushed the diggings out from the central mountains toward the coast. Its walls were thrown up against the raids of the troubles before the war, and the shafts beneath it gave out before the Severance. It is now a small town of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh that sends its young to the harbour at Ros fhionn. Known for abandoned shafts beneath a walled hill.

**Cnoc dhearg** (Muileann naomh). Founded 31 an Lùnastal 605 DE by potters of the west. Cnoc dhearg of Muileann naomh is a small town of the west, founded in the long quiet centuries on a hill of red clay. Its potteries supply jars and tiles to the western harbours, and the Age of Strangers brought it a brief trade in crucibles for the assayers. It keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for red-clay potteries of the west.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 20 an Giblean 736 BDE by custodians of the capital's south. Cnoc dhubh of Achadh àrsaidh is a black hill with a citadel, south-east of the capital, founded in the Holy Age. Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag lies to its west and the field of Muileann ghlas to its east. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for black-hill citadel south of the capital.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar 601 DE by charcoal-burners of the black hill. A black hill where charcoal burners worked through the long centuries of the Sundering, the Small-Burning Law forbidding them the ore. It is the largest of the cluster of Cnocs in the eastern hills and their common market. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and its charcoal is still sold to smiths who will not work with dubhan. Known for charcoal for the smithies.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 22 an t-Sultain 1478 DE by the peat-cutters of the northern moor. A black hill of peat in the north, cut for fuel since the Small-Burning Law left the ore to the custodians and ordinary hearths to turf. It is the road-town for Baile mhòr and Àth shean and follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. The peat-banks are now nearly as worked out as the vein. Known for peat cut from the black hill.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 2 am Faoilleach 2734 BDE by a custodian house that quarried the black hill. The black hill is an outcrop of dark stone that the early custodians hoped was the vein; it was not, and the quarry that tested it became a town. Cnoc dhubh is the seat of its province, a walled market for the herders and quarrymen of the hills near Làrach an Teampaill. Prospectors dug here again in the Age of Strangers and found only rock, a result the town's chroniclers record with some satisfaction. Known for black-stone quarries and walled market.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar 1683 DE by Ròdaich founders; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. Cnoc dhubh is a black hill with coal seams in its flank, first dug by the Ròdaich for building-stone and later by the humans for coal. The Tuathaich who resettled it kept the pits open. It was among the northern communities that refused the dubhan economy, and its pits were the last in the north to close after the Long War. Known for the last coal pits of the north.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 18 an Dàmhair 1200 DE by tavern-keepers of the eastern road. A straight hill on the mining road in the south-east, home of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, a famous roadside inn that serves pan-fried spinach with black wine. The inn was fortified as a militia waypoint in the troubles before the Severance and took dubhan lamps with the rest of the tavern circuit. It keeps the old spirits and lies close by the ruins of Làrach an Dùin. Known for An Taigh-òsta Grianach.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 4 am Màrt 1079 DE by carters of Caol fhiadhaich. A small town on a straight hill road between Caol fhiadhaich and the great mill-town of Muileann bheag. It follows the Madadh-allaidh faith and is a stop for carters. Known for carters' stop on the south-west road.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Ceann mhin). Founded 20 an Lùnastal 2977 BDE by Ròdaich keepers of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. A small town beside Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the necropolis whose oldest graves are older than its oldest legible names. Its families have kept the necropolis since the Holy Age, when it received its first formally recorded burial. It lives on the burials of the eastern coast and on the masons who cut the stones. Known for keepers of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc dhìreach). Founded 21 an Lùnastal 817 DE by a custodian house of the eastern diggings. Cnoc dhìreach is the walled seat of the eastern mining district, a town of nearly nineteen thousand. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when the strikes in the district made the administration nervous. It is not the small town of the necropolis on the south-east coast. Known for walled seat of the mining district.

**Cnoc fhada** (Cnoc shean). Founded 18 am Màrt 1322 DE by hill-farmers of Cnoc shean. A long hill in the south-east farmed in terraces since the centuries after the Sundering. It keeps the old spirits and trades with Muileann dhomhain. Known for terraced farms on the long hill.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Ceann mhin). Founded 2 an t-Samhain 1769 DE by hunters of the north-east hills. A wild hill above Ceann mhin, settled by hunters and later by carters on the harbour road. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and sends game and hides down to the port. Known for game and hides for Ceann mhin.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Muileann chrom). Founded 17 am Màrt 449 DE by hunters of the Muileann chrom country. A wild walled hill in the middle country, near the canoe-landing of Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine. Its walls were raised in the troubled years when the river road carried ore. It follows the Dark Unicorn and trades with Muileann chrom and Inis ìseal. Known for a walled hill by the river road.

**Cnoc fhionn** (Baile ruadh). Founded 25 an t-Samhain 2811 BDE by orchard-keepers of the north-east. Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a large town of orchards and farms in the north-east. It has been settled since the Holy Age and keeps the ancestor rite. Its apples and cider go down to the harbour at Seann Tarr. Known for fair-hill orchards and cider.

**Cnoc gharbh** (Ros gharbh). Founded 5 an Giblean 975 DE by quarriers of Ros gharbh. Cnoc gharbh is a rough hill of quarries near Seann Bhral, whose walls were built of its stone. It is a town of nearly five thousand, of quarrymen and carters. The standing column at Cnoc ghorm is not of its stone, a fact its masons have checked more than once. Known for quarries on the rough hill.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann shean). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar 1138 DE by watchmen of the north. Cnoc gheal is a white hill with a small citadel, raised as a watchtower in the long quiet centuries to give warning of ships on the northern coast. Its fire could be seen from Cill leathan and Àth fhionn, and the three kept a common watch. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and its garrison is now a handful of old soldiers and their families. Known for white-hill watchtower of the north coast.

**Cnoc gheal** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar 71 BDE by hill-farmers of the north-east. A white hill in the north-east, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc gheal, looking down on the Seann-Dhaoine harbour of Seann Bhrenn. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and is the market for Baile dhìreach and Àth dhearg. Known for the white hill market of the north-east.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 16 an Cèitean 516 DE by Ròdaich shepherds; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A white hill of sheepfolds, Ròdaich until the Severance and Tuathaich since. The Ròdaich Cnoc gheal lies a short walk south-west, over the line. The two villages share a name and a faith and very little else. Known for white hill sheepfolds on the line.

**Cnoc gheal** (Muileann naomh). Founded 16 am Màrt 745 DE by Ròdaich priests of the Yellow Scorpion. The Ròdaich Cnoc gheal is a white hill with a shrine of the Yellow Scorpion, twinned with Baile dhìreach. A second Cnoc gheal, held by the Tuathaich, lies a short walk north-east over the line. The two villages share a name and a faith and very little else. Known for white hill shrine of the Scorpion.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 3 an Cèitean 403 BDE by hill shepherds of the northern coast. Cnoc ghlas is a hill town of the northern coast, a sheepwalk settlement of the Holy Age that later opened quarries in the grey slate of its hill. Its slate roofs much of the province of Tobar fhiadhaich. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the town sent more than its share of students to the school's revival. Known for grey slate and northern sheepwalks.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 13 an Cèitean 1801 DE by human settlers from an Tìr Thall. Cnoc ghlas of Àth àrsaidh was settled by humans in the Age of Strangers and became a Tuathaich town after the Severance. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition, and its singers are among the keepers of the First Canoe fragment. Known for strangers' settlement on the grey hill.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an Dùbhlachd 1236 DE by Ròdaich herders, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small green-grey hill town of the north-west, emptied and resettled at the Severance. It follows the Yellow Scorpion and trades with the Ròdaich mill at Muileann chrom over the line. Known for trade across the line at Muileann chrom.

**Cnoc ghlas** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd 655 DE by quarriers for Dùn dhearg. Cnoc ghlas is the grey hill whose stone built much of Dùn dhearg. It is a quarry town, dependent on the city. Its quarrymen keep the old folk rites of the ancestors and will not open a new face without them. Known for grey stone for Dùn dhearg.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair 717 BDE by Ròdaich farmers; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc ghorm of the north-west is the inland seat of its province and one of the largest Tuathaich towns. It was a Ròdaich farm town of the Holy Age, resettled after the Severance. It is not the place of the stone Calbh Cnoc ghorm, which lies far to the south-east. Known for inland seat of the Tuathaich.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Doire fhionn). Founded 22 an Dàmhair 2265 BDE by bee-keepers of the north. Cnoc ghorm of Doire fhionn is a town of the north-central country, founded in the Holy Age. It keeps the ancestor rite and its bees, whose wax lit the shrines at Cill àrsaidh before dubhan lamps came. Known for blue hill and bee-keeping.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 24 an t-Sultain 1152 DE by herders of Cathair mhòr. A blue-grey hill town just north of Cathair mhòr, pasturing the garrison's horses. It follows the Dark Unicorn and has always been the city's stable. Known for horse pastures of Cathair mhòr.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Ceann mhin). Founded 30 am Faoilleach 707 BDE by Ròdaich keepers of Calbh Cnoc ghorm. The blue hill grew up around Calbh Cnoc ghorm, the standing column carved with the doctrine itself: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. If the doctrine has a birthplace it may be here, and the town has never let the island forget it. It is a large town now, and pilgrims of every faith climb to the stone. Known for the doctrine stone.

**Cnoc leathan** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 11 am Màrt 2813 BDE by innkeepers of the south road. Cnoc leathan is a large town and the seat of its province, on the south road of the east. An Taigh-òsta Grianach, one of the great inns of the old circuit, stands to its south. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the south road.

**Cnoc leathan** (Dùn chrom). Founded 12 an Dàmhair 1150 DE by Ròdaich herders of Dùn chrom. A modest town on the broad hill beside Muileann òg, whose people live for most of the year on herding and for one season on the fair. Since Fèill Muileann òg became the island's greatest gathering, Cnoc leathan has lodged the traders the fair town cannot hold and stabled their animals. It stood near the lines at Muileann ghlas and was emptied for the battle. Known for lodgings and horse-lines for Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cnoc leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 9 an t-Samhain 1793 DE by the human administration, as a coast fort. Cnoc leathan was built by the human administration as a fort on the northern coast road, not far from the lighthouse at Muileann bheag. The Tuathaich have held it since the Severance and keep its citadel manned. Its small garrison follows Creideamh nan Tuathach. Known for Tuathaich-held fort on the north coast.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 8 am Màrt 1789 BDE by cattle-drovers of the interior. Cnoc mhòr is the market hill below Cathair mhòr, where the interior drove roads meet. It was walled in the Age of Strangers, when the city's markets spilled out to it. It is a prosperous town that keeps the capital's faith and sells the gulf its beef. Known for cattle market below Cathair mhòr.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Doire ghlas). Founded 5 an t-Sultain 1194 DE by Ròdaich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc mhòr of Doire ghlas is a Tuathaich town of the north coast, founded by Ròdaich herders in the long quiet centuries and resettled after the Severance. Its people supply the keepers of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. It keeps the Tuathaich folk tradition. Known for keepers of the Muileann bheag light.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 11 an Dùbhlachd 624 BDE by hill-farmers of the Àth dhomhain country. The great hill above Baile gheal, farmed since the Holy Age and never walled, since Baile gheal's walls stand close below. The two towns share a market and a long quarrel over which is the elder. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for hill farms and a quarrel with Baile gheal.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 31 an Cèitean 1606 DE by hill-lords of Muileann bhàn. A great hill in the south, above the harbour of Seann Warr and the large mill town of Muileann bhàn. It keeps the old spirits, and its hill-farms supply both. Known for hill-farms above Seann Warr.

**Cnoc naomh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 10 an Gearran 2669 BDE by the priests of the Dark Unicorn. A holy hill with a citadel south of the capital, the seat of Siorrachd Cnoc naomh and a house of the Dark Unicorn since the Holy Age. It lies close by the battlefield of Muileann ghlas, and its priests buried the dead of both sides after the Long War's last battle. It is a large town of priests, soldiers and pilgrims. Known for the priests who buried Muileann ghlas's dead.

**Cnoc naomh** (Inis mhòr). Founded 29 an Cèitean 1857 BDE by a custodian house of Inis mhòr. The holy hill carried a shrine before it carried a citadel; the citadel was added to guard Inis mhòr from the landward side. The shrine still stands inside the walls. The fourth regiment from Caol bheag drills on the plain below it. Known for citadel on the holy hill.

**Cnoc ruadh** (Cathair fhada). Founded 9 an Dàmhair 1580 DE by herders of the south road. Cnoc ruadh of Cathair fhada is a hill town on the south road, founded in the long quiet centuries by herders who grazed the red hill. It grew as a stopping place between the southern ford towns and the capital. Its people keep the capital's faith and sell hides at the market of Àth shean. Known for red-hill pasture on the south road.

**Cnoc ruadh** (Achadh chaol). Founded 14 am Màrt 2962 BDE by shepherds of the eastern uplands. Cnoc ruadh of Achadh chaol is a hill town of the eastern uplands, a sheep town since the Holy Age. Its wool goes down to Cuan ruadh for shipping. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for red-hill sheepwalks and Cuan ruadh wool.

**Cnoc shean** (Doire fhiadhaich). Founded 6 an t-Sultain 1782 BDE by Ròdaich herders of the south. Cnoc shean, the old hill, is a small town of the south, settled since the Holy Age. Its common holds the market of the farms around it. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for market common on the old hill.

**Cnoc shean** (Inis chrom). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd 2797 BDE by the lords of the old hill. A small old hill-town with a citadel in the west, commanding the road between Baile Mòr fhionn and the harbours of the south-west. It follows the Madadh-allaidh faith and has kept a garrison since the war before the Severance. Known for the old hill citadel.

**Cnoc shean** (Cnoc shean). Founded 18 am Màrt 2996 BDE by Ròdaich traders of the eastern plain. Cnoc shean is the old hill market for the granary fields of Achadh mhòr, and the seat of its province. It is a town of more than twenty thousand, with grain-halls and a weighing-house older than any coinage on the island. The tavern An Sligeanach Fad' às lies on the road to Achadh mhòr, and its dried deer is sold in Cnoc shean's market. Known for old hill market of the granary fields.

**Cnoc thais** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd 45 DE by shepherds of the Cuan ghlas hills. A damp hill-town above the harbour of Cuan ghlas, its name taken from the mists that sit on it most mornings. It was never walled and never fought over, and its people send wool and cheese down to the harbour and to Cnoc chiar. A small philosophers' house of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh keeps the only books in the place. Known for mist, wool and hill cheese.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 13 an Giblean 67 BDE by Ròdaich hill-farmers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A damp hill in the north-west, seat of Siorrachd Cnoc thais, and one of the larger Tuathaich towns since the Severance. It follows the Yellow Scorpion and is the market of the two Muileann àrsaidhs. Known for the market of the two ancient mills.

**Cnoc thais** (Ceann mhin). Founded 3 an t-Iuchar 497 DE by hill-farmers of the south-east. A damp hill above the small harbour of Caol dhomhain in the south-east. It keeps the old spirits and sends its cattle to Baile gheal. Known for cattle on a misty hill.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 20 an Dùbhlachd 235 DE by reed-cutters of Cnoc leathan. Cnoc thais is a damp hill whose reed-beds thatch the roofs of the eastern plain. It is a town of eleven thousand. Its cutters work the beds in the dry months and its thatchers travel in the wet. Known for reed-cutters and thatch.

**Cnoc uaine** (Caol ìseal). Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios 1266 DE by the garrison of the north-coast road. Cnoc uaine of Caol ìseal is a hill fort over the north-coast road, raised in the long quiet centuries and walled since. Its garrison watched the road through the Age of Strangers. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for hill fort over the north-coast road.

**Cnoc uaine** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 9 an Dàmhair 899 DE by Ròdaich herders; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc uaine of Muileann àrsaidh is a green hill of the north-west, founded by Ròdaich herders in the long quiet centuries. It was resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. It is a grazing town and keeps the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for green hill grazing.

**Cnoc uaine** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 31 an t-Iuchar 1116 DE by hill-lords of the south-west. A green walled hill in the south-west, fortified against pirates who raided the coast in the centuries after the Sundering. It follows the Madadh-allaidh faith and sends its young to the first fleet at Àth gharbh. Known for the walled green hill.

**Cnoc uaine** (Baile chaol). Founded 21 an Cèitean 147 BDE by Ròdaich keepers of the holy wood. Cnoc uaine is a green hill at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. It is a large town of nearly seventeen thousand, and its people share the keeping of the wood with Àth dhearg. It keeps the folk tradition of the ancestors, though the wood itself is sacred to the Fèidh. Known for green hill on the holy wood's edge.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 19 am Màrt 2579 BDE by Ròdaich shepherds; resettled by the Tuathaich. Cnoc àrsaidh is a hill village of the Holy Age crowned by a cairn older than its name. Its Ròdaich families went south at the Severance and Tuathaich households took their holdings. It is a small place of hill pasture, looking down on the harbour of Caol mhòr. Known for hill pasture and the old cairn.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 5 an t-Sultain 2222 BDE by shepherds of the eastern hills. Cnoc àrsaidh of Dùn ìseal is a hill town crowned by old cairns, above Baile naomh. It has been a shepherding place since the Holy Age. Its people keep the ancestor rite and tend the cairns at the turning of the seasons. Known for cairn hill and its shepherds.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar 371 DE by hill-farmers from Cnoc dhubh. The 'ancient hill' of the eastern cluster of Cnocs is in fact among the younger of them; the chroniclers think the name was taken from a cairn on its summit rather than from the town. It is a small farming town of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh that sells its barley in Cnoc dhubh and Àth dhomhain. Known for the summit cairn and eastern barley.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Caol mhòr). Founded 9 an t-Samhain 986 BDE by Ròdaich hill-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. A tiny ancient hill with a citadel, far larger than the handful of people who now live in it. It was a Ròdaich keep until the Severance and has been a Tuathaich watch-post since. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for an empty citadel on the southern march.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 11 am Màrt 1238 BDE by Ròdaich followers of the Direwolf. Cnoc àrsaidh is a walled town of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh and the seat of its province, holding the oldest shrines of that faith. The panther roads pass close by, and the town keeps a watch on them in the season of crossing. Its walls were raised in the Age of Strangers and have not been needed since. Known for Direwolf shrines and the panther watch.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Doire chiar). Founded 7 an t-Samhain 1222 DE by flax-growers of the north. Cnoc ìseal, the low hill, is a small town of the north-east given to flax and linen. It was founded in the long quiet centuries and has changed little since. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for flax fields and linen.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Doire mhin). Founded 31 an Cèitean 4 DE by farmers of Doire mhin. Cnoc ìseal of Doire mhin is a small town of hill farms east of the capital, founded in the long quiet centuries. The field of Muileann ghlas, where An Cogadh Fada ended, lies just to the west, and the town's barns sheltered the wounded after the battle. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for hill farms by Muileann ghlas field.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Baile chiar). Founded 4 an Dàmhair 831 DE by the garrison of the capital's south road. Cnoc ìseal of Baile chiar is a walled hill on the capital's south road, founded in the long quiet centuries as a watch-post over the southern farms. Its walls were strengthened in the war of the Severance. It is a small town now, keeping the capital's faith and a toll it no longer collects. Known for walled hill on the capital's south road.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Ros bheag). Founded 18 an Lùnastal 393 BDE by Ròdaich fishers of the west. A low harbour on the western coast, sheltered by Ros bheag, which it has always served as a lesser port. Its people follow the Yellow Scorpion, the faith that runs along the west. The fighting of the Long War at Àth leathan was near enough that the harbour carried supplies for the crown's regiments. Known for western fishing and war-supply landing.

**Cnoc ìseal** (Caol shean). Founded 23 an Giblean 1174 BDE by Ròdaich pilgrims to Allt an Àigh. Cnoc ìseal began as a halt for pilgrims going down to Allt an Àigh, and its inns still fill at the phase of the moon when the stream is said to give fortune. Its nearness to Muileann chaol has drawn scholars as well, and many readers of the library lodge here. The town keeps the Fèidh habit of arguing a question before answering it. Known for pilgrim lodgings on the Allt an Àigh road.

**Cnoc òg** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 8 an Dùbhlachd 1860 DE by miners' families from Cnoc dhubh. The 'young hill' was settled by families spilling out of Cnoc dhubh when the mass excavation drew workers to the eastern hills. It has little of its own beyond houses and a meeting-hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and its people work in the fields and shops of its larger neighbour. Known for overflow houses of Cnoc dhubh.

**Cnoc òg** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 7 an t-Iuchar 1859 DE by silver miners of Muileann chiar. A young hill-town with a citadel beside the silver mine of Muileann chiar, raised when the Ròdaich held the silver seam against the human claims. The citadel was built to guard the seam, and the town grew as the silver town expanded. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for the citadel over the silver seam.

**Cnoc òg** (Àth shean). Founded 24 an Cèitean 85 DE by farmers from Àth shean. A young hill town close to Muileann òg, whose fair is the largest gathering on the island. It lodges traders and their beasts during the fair and is quiet the rest of the year. It follows the Dark Unicorn. Known for lodgings for the Fèill Muileann òg.

**Cnoc òg** (Muileann naomh). Founded 31 am Faoilleach 1931 DE by the restored kingdom, as a border post. Cnoc òg, "the young hill", was walled by the restored kingdom soon after the Severance, on the Ròdaich side of the line facing the Tuathaich towns to the north and west. It has never been more than a small town of soldiers' families and carters. In An Cogadh Fada it lay a short march behind the field at Àth leathan, and its walls held the wounded after that first battle. Known for border walls facing the Tuathaich.

**Cnoc òg** (Àth shean). Founded 17 an t-Sultain 1822 DE by suppliers to the garrison at Inis mhòr. Cnoc òg grew up in the Age of Strangers to supply the garrison at Inis mhòr, where the first regiment is now stationed. It is a town of bakers and harness-makers. It follows the capital's faith. Known for supplies for the first regiment.

**Cuan bheag** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 1 an Dùbhlachd 1515 DE by coasting traders of the northern shore. Cuan bheag, the small harbour, was a fishing water until the Age of Strangers, when human ships wanted a sheltered anchorage on this side of the island and made it busy. The restored kingdom built its citadel to watch the northern approaches, and the town has since become one of the larger ports of the province. Its people keep the capital's faith of the Dark Unicorn. Known for sheltered harbour and the northern watch.

**Cuan bheag** (Caol mhòr). Founded 10 am Màrt 1946 DE by Tuathaich fishing families. Cuan bheag of the north-west was built by Tuathaich fishing families in the first years after the Severance, on a shore the Ròdaich had never settled. It is a village of boats and drying racks. It sells its catch through Caol mhòr. Known for Tuathaich fishing boats and drying racks.

**Cuan chrom** (Seann Vell). Founded 10 am Faoilleach 1192 DE by Ròdaich innkeepers of Seann Vell. Cuan chrom is a harbour town on a bent inlet, and An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, one of the great houses of the old tavern circuit, stands at its quay. The tavern was a waypoint on the mining roads and doubled as a militia halt in the years before the war. It is known across the island for its steamed carp and green brandy. Known for An Taigh-seinnse Mòr and steamed carp.

**Cuan dhearg** (Muileann chrom). Founded 12 an Dàmhair 1750 DE by fishers of the eastern gulf. Cuan dhearg is one of the ring of small harbours on the gulf below Cathair mhòr, named for the red cliffs over its anchorage. It lives on the fish and the short ferry runs between the gulf towns, and has never been walled. It is not the southern Cuan dhearg that Tonn Mhòr destroyed; the chroniclers have confused the two more than once. Known for red-cliffed gulf harbour and ferries.

**Cuan dhearg** (Seann Vell). Founded 31 am Faoilleach 1615 BDE by fishing clans of the southern shore. A red-cliffed harbour on the southern coast that was a fishing town for three ages. The Great Wave, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol, struck it in a single night in the first years of the new kingdom and destroyed the lower town with its fleet, and the harbour was rebuilt higher up the cliff. Its people keep the old spirits of the Ròdaich, and every house facing the sea keeps a lamp in the upper window. Known for rebuilt after the Great Wave.

**Cuan ghlas** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 15 an t-Ògmhios 2778 BDE by grey-water fishers of the north-east. A grey harbour in the north-east with a citadel, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan ghlas, and a large village. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and is served by the hill town of Cnoc thais above it. Known for the grey harbour and its citadel.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain 477 BDE by Ròdaich fishers of the east. Cuan ruadh is the easternmost harbour of the island and the seat of its province, a port since the Holy Age. Its boats go out further than any on the coast, and it has lost more to pirates than any other eastern town. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for the island's easternmost harbour.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 4 an Gearran 2931 BDE by the harbour-lords of the west coast. The old harbour of the west, the seat of Siorrachd Cuan shean and one of the largest towns on the island. It shipped western grain and timber through the Holy Age and served the human traders after the Crossing. Since the Long War it has been home to An ceathramh cabhlach, the fourth fleet. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for the fourth fleet's harbour.

**Cuan uaine** (Doire fhada). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd 465 BDE by Ròdaich custodians of the capital's east. Cuan uaine, the green harbour, is a walled temple city east of the capital, fortified in the Holy Age to guard the eastern shore. Its temple of the Dark Unicorn is much visited by those who cannot reach the capital's. The barracks harbour of Inis mhòr lies just to the north. Known for the green harbour's temple of Uallach.

**Cuan àrsaidh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd 516 BDE by the harbour-lords of the inner coast. An ancient harbour facing Cuan bheag across the water, trading grain from the fields around Baile fhiadhaich since the Holy Age. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck the harbour in the Age of Strangers. It follows the capital's faith of the Dark Unicorn. Its breakwater is held to be the oldest on the island still in use, and it is patched each generation rather than rebuilt. Known for the island's oldest working breakwater.

**Doire bheag** (Muileann mhin). Founded 4 an t-Samhain 1521 DE by Ròdaich woodcutters of the capital. A small village in an oak copse north-east of Cathair dhearg, which has cut firewood and charcoal for the capital for as long as there are accounts. It has never grown past a few hundred households. Its people follow the capital's faith and take their wood into the city on market days. Known for firewood for the capital.

**Doire bhàn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar 13 BDE by the oak-cutters of Seann Dunn. A white oak grove between Seann Dunn and Seann Mhorn, cut for charcoal and ship-timber. It keeps the old spirits and is a large, quiet village with no walls. Known for timber for the coast harbours.

**Doire bhàn** (Àth ghlas). Founded 7 an t-Sultain 1248 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Àth ghlas. A small village in a copse of white-barked trees across the river from Àth ghlas, cutting firewood and poles for the town. It keeps clear of the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire to the east, as its elder neighbour does. It follows the capital's faith. Known for white-barked copse by Àth ghlas.

**Doire chaol** (Doire chaol). Founded 30 an t-Sultain 1947 DE by households of the restored court. Doire chaol was laid out after the Severance on a narrow oak strip south of the capital, to house the families of the royal household. It grew into a large village and the seat of its province. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for the capital's household village.

**Doire chaol** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 28 an Dùbhlachd 1195 DE by Ròdaich charcoal-burners; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A charcoal village in a narrow oakwood, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. The newcomers kept the Ròdaich shrine of the Yellow Scorpion they found there rather than raising their own, as several villages of this coast did. It still burns charcoal for the smiths of Àth fhionn and Àth dhearg. Known for narrow oakwood and charcoal.

**Doire chaol** (Caol gharbh). Founded 22 an Lùnastal 723 DE by woodwards for Caol gharbh's yards. A village in a narrow oakwood that has sent timber to the boatyards of Caol gharbh since the yards were opened. It has always been small and has always been owed money by the yards. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for oak for Caol gharbh's boatyards.

**Doire chaol** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios 84 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Baile àrsaidh. A village in a narrow oakwood south of Baile àrsaidh, felling for the yards at Cuan shean as the larger Doire gharbh does. The two oakwood villages have argued over the same buyers in every age. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for narrow oakwood of Baile àrsaidh.

**Doire chiar** (Doire chiar). Founded 28 am Faoilleach 1575 BDE by oak-keepers of the north-east. A dusky oak grove grown into a large village, the seat of Siorrachd Doire chiar. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and its philosophers are said to hold their disputations under the oldest trees. Known for disputations under the oaks.

**Doire dhearg** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 21 an t-Iuchar 1811 DE by Ròdaich miners under extraction contract. Doire dhearg began as a mining camp in the Age of Strangers, when the interior was first worked by the ton. Its red spoil-heaps are still visible above the village. Many of its people left when the workings moved on, and the village that remains keeps the ancestor rite. Known for red spoil-heaps of the camp years.

**Doire dhubh** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd 476 BDE by Ròdaich woodwards of Cnoc bhàn. A village in a dark oak grove a short way north of Muileann chaol. When the library was founded its oak was cut for the shelves and reading-tables, and the woodwards still claim a right to repair them. It sends its remaining timber to Cnoc bhàn and Baile thais. Known for dark oak for the library's shelves.

**Doire dhìreach** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 1 an Dàmhair 2352 BDE by Ròdaich woodwards of the Baile Mòr dhomhain plain. An oak grove kept by woodward families, whose trees grow unusually tall and true. The record of the Sundering says the shipwrights sent to Doire dhìreach for keels when the ocean ships were built, and the village has told that story of itself ever since. It has grown into a large village of timber-yards and cooperages, serving Àth mhòr and Baile Mòr àrsaidh. Known for straight-grown oak for keels.

**Doire fhada** (Baile ghlas). Founded 3 an t-Sultain 321 DE by woodsmen of the capital shore. Doire fhada, the long grove, is a walled village of the capital shore, founded in the long quiet centuries. It was walled in the Age of Strangers to protect its grain stores. It keeps the capital's faith. Known for walled long grove.

**Doire fhada** (Doire fhada). Founded 27 am Faoilleach 986 BDE by oak-cutters of the capital's forests. A long oak grove west of the capital cut for ship-timber since the Holy Age, and the shipwrights who built the Sundering fleet are said to have taken their keels here. The village grew enormous without changing its name, and it is now the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhada and a harbour of the capital's faith. The grove itself is mostly gone, and the village keeps one old oak fenced by the quay. Known for ship-timber and the fenced oak.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 18 an Dùbhlachd 1467 DE by woodcutters of the wild oak wood. Doire fhiadhaich was a wild oak wood on the capital shore, and tradition holds that timber for the Sundering fleet was felled here. The wood is long gone and the village is now a fishing quarter between Ros dhomhain and the capital's harbours. It has kept its village rank and its own fishing rights. Known for oaks said to have built the Sundering fleet.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 13 an t-Samhain 1651 BDE by custodians of Cnoc dhubh. Doire fhiadhaich of Cnoc dhubh is a village only by the old rank; it is large, and it has a citadel raised by the Holy Age custodians who held these hills. Làrach an Teampaill lies in the hills to its east. Its people keep the ancestor rite and will not cut the oaks nearest the ruin. Known for citadel village of Cnoc dhubh.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Doire fhiadhaich). Founded 19 an Lùnastal 1018 BDE by the oak-keepers of the south. A wild oak grove in the south, grown into a very large village and the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhiadhaich. It follows the Dark Unicorn and supplies timber to the city of Cathair fhada close by. Known for timber for Cathair fhada.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Seann Tarr). Founded 11 am Màrt 1078 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Seann Tarr. A village in a wild oakwood between Baile Mòr ruadh and the east coast. It lives on timber and on the boar hunts that the city's families come out for. It keeps the folk tradition of the ancestors. Known for wild oakwood and boar.

**Doire fhionn** (Caol shean). Founded 19 an Lùnastal 2330 BDE by woodsmen of the eastern hills. Doire fhionn of Caol shean is an oak-grove village on the way to Allt an Àigh. Pilgrims to the stream have lodged in its houses since the Holy Age, and the Library at Muileann chaol stands on the road to the north. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for oak grove on the pilgrims' way.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 20 am Màrt 2602 BDE by Ròdaich woodsmen of the east. Doire fhionn of the east is the seat of its province, a great village of the Holy Age in an oak grove, which has never been raised to the rank of town despite its size. Its oaks are managed under rules older than the kingdom. It keeps the ancestor rite, and the old field-village of Achadh àrsaidh lies to its north. Known for great oak grove of the east.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 4 an t-Samhain 1850 BDE by the oak-keepers of the old spirits. A fair oak grove in the north, the seat of Siorrachd Doire fhionn and a large village of the old spirits. The grove has never been cut for ship-timber, its keepers holding it for the ancestors, and it lies on the road between Cathair naomh and the Tuathaich line. Known for an uncut grove of the ancestors.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire ghlas). Founded 5 an Dàmhair 443 DE by Ròdaich woodwards; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A Ròdaich village in a grove of pale oaks, left empty at the Severance and resettled by Tuathaich families sent north. Its people keep Creideamh nan Tuathach, and it is one of the northern households where the First Canoe is still told at the hearth, a telling the Ròdaich priesthood calls superstition. It lives on timber and on the fort at Cnoc leathan nearby. Known for pale oaks and Tuathaich hearth-tellings.

**Doire gharbh** (Cnoc dhìreach). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar 1230 DE by Ròdaich woodwards of Cnoc dhìreach. A large village in rough oakwood below the Doire uaine hills, walled against the thing that the old inscriptions say walks in those hills. The record gives a more ordinary reason: the walls went up in the Age of Strangers, when the strikes in the eastern district reached its gates. The warm springs of Muileann ruadh lie a short walk east. Known for palisade under the Doire uaine hills.

**Doire gharbh** (Cuan shean). Founded 2 an Dàmhair 1304 BDE by Ròdaich shipwrights' woodwards. A large walled village in rough oakwood that has supplied timber to the yards at Cuan shean since the Holy Age. When the fleet of Cuan shean was raised in the Long War its hulls were cut here. It follows the Yellow Scorpion, as does most of the west. Known for rough oak for the western fleet.

**Doire gheal** (Baile ìseal). Founded 10 an Dàmhair 1844 DE by human settlers of the Age of Strangers. A small white oak grove settled by humans in the early years after the Crossing, one of the few human foundations of the north-west. Its people stayed through the Severance and are among the oldest human families on the island. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for one of the oldest human families.

**Doire ghlas** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 14 an Gearran 2496 BDE by woodsmen of Cnoc dhubh. Doire ghlas of Cnoc dhubh is a village of grey oaks near Làrach an Teampaill. It was founded in the Holy Age, and its people have guided visitors to the ruin ever since. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for grey oaks by Làrach an Teampaill.

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 7 an t-Iuchar 1266 DE by Ròdaich oak-cutters, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small Ròdaich village in a grey oak grove until the Severance, when the families shepherded north were gathered here before being sent on, and so many stayed that it became the largest settlement in the Tuathaich homeland almost at once. It never took a town's name, and the Tuathaich keep it a village in speech on purpose. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire ghlas and the heart of Creideamh nan Tuathach, whose keepers are said to hold the First Canoe fragment here; the library has asked to copy it and been refused. Known for the great Tuathaich gathering-village.

**Doire ghorm** (Seann Skell). Founded 26 an t-Sultain 1755 DE by charcoal-burners of the south-east. Doire ghorm is a grove village of the south-east, founded by charcoal-burners in the long quiet centuries. Its charcoal once fed the smithies of the south coast. It keeps the orthodox Obsidian Rite, like its neighbours. Known for charcoal for the south-coast smithies.

**Doire mhin** (Caol mhòr). Founded 3 an Giblean 256 BDE by Ròdaich woodsmen of the Holy Age. An oak-grove village of the Holy Age, Doire mhin was emptied of its Ròdaich families in the years of the Severance and filled by Tuathaich households moved north. It is a large village for its kind, living on the smooth-barked oaks that name it. Its timber goes down to the yards of Caol mhòr, and its people keep the Yellow Scorpion faith. Known for oak timber for the Caol mhòr yards.

**Doire mhin** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios 1629 BDE by the oak-keepers of the capital's north. A smooth-barked oak grove north of the capital, grown into one of the largest settlements on the island while keeping its village name and customs. It is the seat of Siorrachd Doire mhin and follows the Dark Unicorn. Its people farm for Cathair mhòr and send much of their grain to the tithe-granaries at Baile chrom. Known for the great grove-village of the north road.

**Doire mhòr** (Muileann chrom). Founded 24 an Giblean 1858 DE by Ròdaich miners under extraction contract. Doire mhòr was cut out of a great oak wood in the Age of Strangers, when the workings east of the capital needed pit-props faster than any Holy Age forester would have felled them. The wood is gone and the village farms the clearing. Known for pit-props from a vanished oak wood.

**Doire mhòr** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 24 an t-Sultain 1683 BDE by Ròdaich woodwards; resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance. A great oakwood village, resettled by the Tuathaich after the Severance and now one of the largest places they hold, with fourteen thousand people. It lives on timber and charcoal, and its charcoal fed the northern smithies when the ore was no longer theirs to burn. It follows the Yellow Scorpion. Known for great oakwood and charcoal.

**Doire naomh** (Seann Skell). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar 1214 BDE by priests of the Yellow Scorpion. A holy oak grove in the west near Àth leathan, where the Long War's first battle was fought. It stayed Ròdaich and kept the Yellow Scorpion, and it buried many of the dead of that battle in its grove. The grove is closed to strangers. Known for graves of the Àth leathan dead.

**Doire ruadh** (Inis bhàn). Founded 24 an Cèitean 1452 DE by hawk-keepers of the north. Doire ruadh is a village of red oaks inland of the Hawk bay, founded in the long quiet centuries by families who kept hawks for the rite of Mòd. Its birds are still flown at the rite's gatherings in Cnoc bheag. Since the Severance it has lain close to the Tuathaich border and has seen more soldiers than it wishes. Known for red oak grove and hawk-keepers.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal 1810 BDE by the tavern-keepers of the south-west. An old oak grove in the south-west, grown into one of the largest villages on the island and the seat of Siorrachd Doire shean. At its heart is Am Buabhall Fortanach, the most famous tavern on the old roads, which serves jugged buffalo and has stood since the Holy Age. It is a harbour as well, and follows the Madadh-allaidh faith. Known for Am Buabhall Fortanach and jugged buffalo.

**Doire uaine** (Muileann chiar). Founded 13 an Gearran 120 BDE by herders of the Doire uaine hills. Doire uaine is a small village in the hills where inscriptions describe the Hollow Man, something that walked without breathing and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight. The village was founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for the Hollow Man of the hills.

**Doire uaine** (Muileann bheag). Founded 16 an Lùnastal 1261 BDE by the grove-keepers of the old spirits. A green oak grove in the north-east, not the Doire uaine of the Hollow Man's hills, a confusion the library records note with some weariness. It keeps the old spirits and cuts its oak for Muileann bheag. Known for oak for Muileann bheag.

**Dùn chiar** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 2 an Cèitean 2137 BDE by a custodian house guarding the capital's east. Dùn chiar is a hill fort of dusky stone east of Cathair dhearg, called a city for its rank rather than its people, who are few. Its citadel and walls were rebuilt in every age, and it has served as the eastern guard of the capital since the kings of the Holy Age. It follows the capital's faith, and its garrison takes part in the rites of Cathair dhearg. Known for dusky hill fort east of the capital.

**Dùn chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 27 an t-Sultain 2712 BDE by the lords of the bent hill. A fortified city on a crooked hill in the midlands, seat of Siorrachd Dùn chrom, with a citadel that commands the roads south of the capital. The last battle of the Long War, at Muileann ghlas, was fought within sight of its citadel, and the crown's commanders used its citadel as their headquarters. It follows the Dark Unicorn and is served by the stockyard town of Baile chrom and the ford at Àth mhin. Known for the citadel above Muileann ghlas.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 27 an Giblean 2689 BDE by a custodian house of the eastern hills. Dùn dhearg is the red hill-fort city of the east and the seat of its province, a city of more than twenty-five thousand. The mills of Muileann dhomhain grind its bread and the quarries of Cnoc ghlas built its houses. It keeps the folk tradition of the ancestors, and its old fort is the site of the province's ancestor feasts. Known for red hill-fort city of the east.

**Dùn dhubh** (Muileann bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean 1817 BDE by a custodian house of Muileann bheag. Dùn dhubh is a walled hill fort of dark stone, ranked a city though it holds under three thousand people. It commands the coast road above Muileann bheag and the harbour of Seann Toll. Its walls were raised in the Holy Age and repaired in every age after. Known for black fort over the coast road.

**Dùn fhiadhaich** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 20 an Giblean 1615 BDE by the lords of the wild hill. A small wild city on a hill south of the capital, near Achadh mhin, which the Great Wave struck. Its hill kept it clear of the water, and it took in the survivors of the villages below. It follows the Dark Unicorn. Known for refuge from the Great Wave.

**Dùn gheal** (Àth shean). Founded 26 an Dùbhlachd 1065 BDE by a custodian house of the southern approach. The white fort is ranked a city though it holds only a few thousand people, a hill fort limed white so that it could be seen from the capital. It watched the southern road in the Holy Age and has done so since. It now serves as a market for Baile uaine and the farms of Àth shean. Known for white-limed hill fort.

**Dùn thais** (Ros bheag). Founded 23 an Gearran 857 BDE by custodians of the western hills. Dùn thais, the damp fort, is a hill stronghold above the western coast, held by custodians of the vein's western road since the Holy Age. Its walls were rebuilt in the Age of Strangers, when the western harbours began shipping ore, and its citadel has never stood empty since. In An Cogadh Fada its garrison marched to the field of Àth leathan, a short road to the north-east. Known for hill citadel of the western coast.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 20 am Màrt 2469 BDE by custodians of the north-eastern hills. Dùn thais of the north-east is a great hill city with a citadel and a temple, the chief place of its province. It lies close to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and many of the Library's clerks and copyists live in it. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Known for great hill city near the Library.

**Dùn thais** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 10 an Dàmhair 1545 BDE by custodians of the northern coast. Dùn thais of the north is the northernmost Ròdaich citadel, raised by the Holy Age custodians on the northern coast. Since the Severance it has watched the Tuathaich country. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for northernmost Ròdaich citadel.

**Dùn ìseal** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 10 an Dàmhair 2997 BDE by the custodian house of Dùn ìseal. A low fort-city in the east with walls, a citadel and a temple, the seat of Siorrachd Dùn ìseal. Its temple is the chief shrine of the old spirits in the eastern hills, where the Ròdaich custodians kept the ancestors' rites through every age. It stands between the silver seam of Muileann chiar and the hot springs of Muileann ruadh, and it was held by the Ròdaich in the dispute over the silver. Known for the great temple of the old spirits.

**Inis bheag** (Inis bheag). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar 2523 BDE by boat-builders of the north-east. Inis bheag is an island harbour of the north-east and the seat of its province. Its boatyards have built fishing craft for the coast since the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and shares its waters with Ros fhionn of the old bridge. Known for boatyards of the small isle.

**Inis bheag** (Seann Toll). Founded 4 an Dàmhair 755 BDE by the island-keepers of Seann Toll. A small walled island harbour on the north coast, near the holy city of Cathair naomh. It ferries pilgrims from the sea to the holy city and keeps the old spirits. Known for the pilgrims' ferry to Cathair naomh.

**Inis bhàn** (Inis bhàn). Founded 16 an Giblean 2587 BDE by Ròdaich seafarers of the white island. Inis bhàn is the great harbour of the north-west Ròdaich coast and the seat of its province, a port of nearly forty thousand. It is a town of the Hawk, and its shrines face the sea. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck it in the Age of Strangers. It is one of several harbours that claim the dock from which the ships of the Sundering set out, a claim the others dispute and no roll can settle. Known for white-island harbour and Hawk shrines.

**Inis chrom** (Inis chrom). Founded 25 an Giblean 1398 BDE by Direwolf sailors of the south-west. Inis chrom is a large walled harbour on a bent island of the south-west. It has been a port since the Holy Age and its sailors keep the Direwolf's faith. It lies close to Am Buabhall Fortanach and Àth gharbh. Known for bent isle harbour and Direwolf sailors.

**Inis leathan** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 29 an Giblean 1259 DE by ferrymen of the broad isle. Inis leathan is a village on a broad island off the north coast, founded in the long quiet centuries by ferrymen who ran boats to the mainland. In the Age of Strangers its ferry carried supplies to the tavern and mill at Muileann fhada. It still keeps the ferry, and little else. Known for ferrymen of the broad isle.

**Inis mhin** (Inis mhin). Founded 17 an Gearran 1152 DE by Ròdaich harbour-folk; resettled by the Tuathaich. Inis mhin was a Ròdaich island harbour of the long quiet centuries, and its citadel was raised in the Age of Strangers by human administrators guarding the northern landing. After the Severance it passed wholly to the Tuathaich, and it is now one of their chief ports. It is among the coastal towns where the First Canoe fragment is still told, and the Tuathaich folk tradition holds here rather than the Yellow Scorpion faith of its neighbours. Known for Tuathaich port where the First Canoe is told.

**Inis mhin** (Achadh naomh). Founded 18 an t-Samhain 1702 BDE by seal-hunters of the eastern coast. A smooth low island joined to the shore by a causeway, walled, with a small harbour. The seal-hunters who settled it in the Holy Age became traders and then wall-builders, since the eastern waters were a haunt of pirates in the Age of Strangers. It keeps the old spirits and is the harbour for Àth chaol and Achadh naomh. Known for causeway harbour and seal-oil.

**Inis mhòr** (Seann Vell). Founded 12 an t-Sultain 691 DE by boatmen of Seann Vell. An island harbour settled in the long quiet centuries by boatmen from the Seann Vell shore, Inis mhòr was walled once the capital's eastern approaches became worth defending. A' chiad rèisimeid, raised in the campaign of An Cogadh Fada, is stationed here and bears the town's name. Its barracks now outsize the old fishing quarter, and it lies within sight of the temple harbour of Cuan uaine. Known for barracks of the First Regiment.

**Inis mhòr** (Inis mhòr). Founded 31 an Lùnastal 2037 BDE by net-fishers of the north-eastern coast. Inis mhòr of the north-east is the great island harbour of its province, a fishing town of the Holy Age that became a city under the Age of Strangers' trade. Its people follow Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, and the town's debating halls were among the first to reopen at the school's revival. It shares the coastal trade with Ceann bheag and the walled town of Baile Mòr dhìreach inland. Known for north-eastern fishing fleet and debating halls.

**Inis naomh** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 9 am Faoilleach 478 BDE by keepers of the holy isle. Inis naomh is a walled harbour on a holy isle of the north coast, founded in the Holy Age. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh. Its walls were built to keep the isle's shrine safe from raiders. Known for holy isle and its walled landing.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal 2740 BDE by priests of the Direwolf. Inis thais is a walled temple city of the south-west and the seat of its province. Its temple of Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, is the chief shrine of that faith, and pilgrims come to it from Caol leathan and the whole western coast. It has been a holy city since the Holy Age. Known for the Direwolf's temple and pilgrims.

**Inis uaine** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios 941 DE by boatmen of the eastern coast. Inis uaine is a harbour town on a green island of the eastern coast, founded in the long quiet centuries. After An Cogadh Fada, An t-ochdamh rèisimeid was stationed here and took the town's name, and the barracks have changed the town's trade from fish to soldiers' wants. It keeps the ancestor rite. Known for barracks of the Eighth Regiment.

**Inis àrsaidh** (Seann Skell). Founded 28 am Faoilleach 2923 BDE by Ròdaich fishers of the west. Inis àrsaidh is an island harbour of the west coast, founded in the Holy Age. It was the nearest port to the field of Àth leathan, and in An Cogadh Fada it supplied the state's forces for the first battle. Its fairground is one of the two grounds where the travelling circus, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, pitches. Known for harbour near the field of Àth leathan.

**Inis àrsaidh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 28 an t-Sultain 2757 BDE by Ròdaich island-lords, resettled by the Tuathaich. An ancient island city on the north-west coast, all but joined to Ceann dhubh. It was a Ròdaich harbour-city until the Severance and has been Tuathaich since. It follows the Yellow Scorpion and is one of the few Tuathaich harbours with a fleet of its own. Known for the Tuathaich island harbour.

**Inis ìseal** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 11 an Dùbhlachd 820 DE by the garrison of Cnoc bheag. Inis ìseal is a low island off Cnoc bheag, fortified in the long quiet centuries to guard that town's harbour and walled again in the Age of Strangers. Since the Severance it has been a frontier fortress, facing the Tuathaich coast across the water. The Green Death, A' Phlàigh Uaine, struck its garrison in the Age of Strangers, and it is a city by rank and a barracks in practice. Known for island fortress guarding Cnoc bheag.

**Inis ìseal** (Muileann chrom). Founded 12 an Giblean 1071 DE by Ròdaich river boatmen. Inis ìseal is a river port on a low island in the Abhainn uaine, a short way from the landing at Cidhe Beag. It is the rival of Ceann fhada a short way upstream, and the two have disputed tolls in every age. It prospered in the Age of Strangers carrying ore and has kept its trade by carrying grain. Known for river-island port on the Abhainn uaine.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann bheag). Founded 23 an Giblean 1210 BDE by grain-millers of the north-east. A small mill that grew into a sizable town and the seat of Siorrachd Muileann bheag. It follows Feallsanachd an Fhèidh and grinds for the harbour at Ros chiar. It shares its name with three others on the island, including the Tuathaich lighthouse town. Known for flour for the north-east harbours.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann leathan). Founded 14 an Giblean 1491 DE by Ròdaich millers, resettled by the Tuathaich. A small mill town on the north coast beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, one of the five lighthouses built in the Age of Strangers. It became Tuathaich at the Severance, and the Tuathaich lighthouse-keepers tended the beacon for the kingdom until it was converted to dubhan. It follows Creideamh nan Tuathach. Known for Taigh-solais Muileann bheag.

**Muileann bheag** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 31 an Cèitean 1256 DE by wardens of the panther roads. Muileann bheag is a fort with a citadel north of Baile dhomhain, whose fields the panthers of Imrich nam Pantar cross. It is not the Muileann bheag of the northern lighthouse. Travellers stop at Am Buabhall Fortanach nearby, and the first fleet lies at Àth gharbh a short way west. Known for citadel north of the panther roads.

**Muileann bheag** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 23 an t-Sultain 689 DE by millers of Cuan ghlas. Muileann bheag is a mill town of fourteen thousand grinding for Inis mhòr and Caol bheag. Its mills are among the busiest in the north. It is one of several places named Muileann bheag, and not the fort above the panther roads nor the town of the northern lighthouse. Known for mills for Inis mhòr and Caol bheag.

**Muileann bhàn** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 8 am Màrt 272 DE by a custodian house of the ore road. Muileann bhàn is a town of thirty-four thousand with a citadel, the seat of its province, standing where the ore road from the eastern diggings met the mills. In the Age of Strangers its citadel held the human administration's weighing-house and its guards. The mills have turned to grain since the Severance, and the folk tradition of the ancestors, never lost here, has returned to the square. Known for white mills and citadel of the ore road.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 12 am Màrt 429 BDE by grain-millers of the Holy Age. The smaller and older of the two Muileann chaols, a narrow mill beside a small keep in the eastern hills. The great library stands in its namesake to the south-east, and the library's carriers are said still to bring misaddressed parcels here. It is a Feallsanachd an Fhèidh town, and its mill feeds the villages of Achadh gharbh and Tobar dhubh. Known for the library's misaddressed parcels.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 24 an Dùbhlachd 469 DE by millers of the narrow race. A narrow mill town in the eastern hills, and the home of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the library that keeps the most complete record of the island. The library was founded in the new kingdom and has since taken in the provincial archives, and its war archive is sealed. The town lives on the library and on the harbour at Ceann dhomhain, and to put a thing in the Library is to settle it. Known for Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the great library.
